context: Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration or revocation of plant variety protection may appeal to the appellate authority. Failure to comply with a summons issued by the civil court registry, acting on behalf of the Authority, shall render the defaulter liable for penalties as determined by the Authority and recoverable through civil courts. The Authority may direct the civil court registry to seize any infringing material or records pertaining to unauthorized propagation or sale of protected plant varieties. Further, any individual found guilty of wilful misrepresentation regarding the origin or characteristics of a registered variety shall be subject to fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, as deemed appropriate by the civil court.

Where a patent holder institutes any proceeding relating to infringement of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, and obtains a decree in favour of the patent holder, the costs of such proceedings shall be borne by the defendant; provided that where the defendant establishes, subject to appeal, that the claim asserted against him was made in good faith and without malice, the Court may award reasonable compensation to the defendant. Further, a patent shall cease to have effect if it is determined under this Act to be invalid due to lack of novelty or inventive step, and any party aggrieved by such determination may pursue remedies as provided herein for recovery of damages sustained prior to the cessation of the patent’s force.

An aggrieved party seeking redressal against any decision made by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent, or concerning objections raised during examination, may file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be submitted within ninety days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented and provide reasoned findings. Provided that, in cases where the decision relates to a compulsory license or revocation based on non-working, the *appeal period* shall extend to one hundred twenty days. Further, any society registered under this Act as a registration copyright society may, with the permission of the Tribunal, intervene in such appeals presenting arguments relevant to the broader public interest concerning patentability and innovation. The appellant is responsible for ensuring timely filing and adherence to procedural requirements as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark contains a reference trade mark, the Registrar shall consider whether the applicant has demonstrated reasonable grounds for believing that the use of the proposed trade mark is unlikely to cause confusion amongst consumers. Such demonstration must include evidence establishing consumer familiarity with both marks and their respective goods or services. The Registrar may require further information from the applicant concerning the nature and extent of such familiarity, including market surveys conducted in accordance with prescribed guidelines. Provided that the reference trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall not refuse registration solely on the basis of similarity between the two marks unless it is satisfied that there exists a likelihood of dilution or unfair appropriation.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed trade mark, when used in relation to the goods or services for which it is sought to be registered, conflicts with any existing prior right. Such conflict may arise from similarity to an earlier trade mark, whether registered or not, and where such earlier trade mark is used in connection with identical or similar goods or services. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by the applicant demonstrating that there exists no likelihood of confusion on account of a phonetic or visual resemblance between the applied-for trade mark and any prior right. Provided that, an application may proceed notwithstanding such conflict if the Registrar deems the earlier right to be weak or inactive under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step as defined under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during the opposition proceedings may render the notice inadmissible and result in penalties for frivolous filings. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to present evidence and arguments; any attempt at obstruction or misleading testimony will be subject to fines and potential criminal prosecution. Decisions of the Controller regarding opposition are final, but appeal lies to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Where any application for registration of a trademark is filed with the Registrar, and such application requires verification under this Act by a designated individual, that verification may be undertaken instead by a *required registrar person* duly authorised on behalf of the applicant. This authorisation shall be in writing and submitted alongside the application or at the time of subsequent amendment. The required registrar person must possess demonstrable experience in trade mark matters and provide confirmation of their appointment as per prescribed guidelines. Further, where any communication relating to an opposed trademark is addressed to the applicant, such communication may be forwarded by a *required registrar person* acting on behalf of the applicant, subject to providing proof of authority.

Where a trade mark proprietor licenses the use of their registered trade mark within a Contracting State, such license shall constitute a contractual arrangement governed by Indian law, and any breach thereof may render the licensor entitled to injunctive relief under this Act. The terms governing the royalty payable for such licensed usage must be clearly stipulated in writing; failure to do so shall be deemed evidence of an intent to circumvent provisions relating to fair trade practices. Any person found to have wilfully infringed a registered trade mark, acting on behalf of or in conjunction with a Contracting State’s entity without proper authorization, shall be subject to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and damages proportionate to the extent of commercial detriment caused.

The proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief from acts of adaptation, application, or importation contrary to the provisions of this Act. Any person seeking to oppose the registration of a proposed certification trade mark may submit evidence demonstrating that the mark falsely suggests an association with a person not authorized by the applicant, or that its use would be detrimental to consumers. The Opposition Board shall consider such evidence and may direct rejection of the application if it finds merit in the objection. Further, where infringement is established, remedies available include injunctions restraining further infringing acts, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and the delivery up for destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, subject to any orders made under this Act concerning disposal.

Where any person has made use of a registered trade mark in contravention of the rights conferred by registration, and such use has resulted in damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark, the owner shall be entitled to seek damages from the offending party. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to, the extent of the infringing use, the loss of profits suffered by the owner as a direct result of the infringement, and any other financial detriment incurred. Further, where the infringing activity constitutes an act of unfair competition under this Act, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the Court. The remedies available to the registered proprietor shall include an injunction restraining further use of the mark, and an order requiring the defendant to account for profits derived from the sale of goods or services bearing the effect registered trade mark.

Where a patent has become *patent expired*, any person may apply to the Controller for an order revoking the grant of the patent on grounds specified herein. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the patent expires, or where the expiry was due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fees, within six months from the date on which the default occurred. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such information and documentation as deemed necessary to substantiate the claim for revocation. Notice of the application shall be served upon the patentee, who shall have an opportunity to file a written response under this Act. Subject to compliance with procedural requirements regarding service and timelines, the Controller shall consider all submissions before passing any order concerning the validity or continuation of rights derived from the expired patent.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is opposed, the Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, issue a temporary register effect order pending determination of the opposition. Such order shall remain in force for a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of its issuance, or until the disposal of the opposition, whichever occurs earlier. The Controller shall provide notice to all interested parties before issuing any such order, and may require them to submit written arguments within thirty days. Any party aggrieved by the temporary register effect order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The tribunal’s decision on an appeal under this Act shall be binding on the Controller. Further, the Controller may, at any time, revoke a temporary register effect order if satisfied that it was issued without due consideration of relevant facts.

Any person who, having benefited from the use of plant genetic resources for the development of a new variety, fails to make a contribution to the Gene Fund as determined by the Authority shall be liable to pay such amount as may be prescribed. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint or suo moto, initiate inquiries into instances of non-compliance and issue notices requiring the person concerned to demonstrate due remittance. Failure to comply with such notice within the stipulated period shall render the person subject to penalties including fines not exceeding five times the assessed contribution amount. Further, any entity found repeatedly defaulting in contributions may have its registration as a Plant Breeder Rights holder suspended for a period determined by the Authority. Appeals against orders of the Authority under this Act regarding Gene Fund contributions lie before the Appellate Board.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical product is filed, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates the working of the invention in India within the time specified under this Act. Such evidence shall include details regarding manufacturing processes, quality control measures employed, and clinical trial data, if applicable, pertaining to the efficacy and safety of the pharmaceutical substance. Failure to comply with a requirement issued by the Controller may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to make representations against any adverse findings arising from the examination of submitted documentation. Any objection raised concerning the patentability of the invention on grounds of prior publication or lack of novelty must be addressed comprehensively within the response filed before the Controller.

An applicant seeking to amend a patent specification after the date of publication under this Act shall file a request with the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. Such request must clearly identify the specific portions of the specification intended for alteration and provide justification demonstrating the necessity for the amendment. The Controller may allow an amendment only if it is shown to be merely clarificatory or supplementary to the original disclosure, and does not substantially alter the scope of protection sought. Any proposed amendment affecting the claim language constitutes a modification of the patent’s claims and requires careful scrutiny. A request for amendment involving a specification shall not be granted if it introduces new matter that was not adequately described in the originally filed document. The Controller may direct an applicant to submit further information or arguments concerning any proposed specification amendment claim before rendering a decision.

Where an application for registration of a patent is opposed, the Controller may require the applicant and the opponent both to submit written arguments and such evidence as they deem relevant to the merits of the opposition. Should either party present a certificate purporting to be a record of proceedings before a lower authority concerning prior use or publication relating to the invention, that certificate shall be admissible as evidence subject to challenge regarding its authenticity and proper execution. The Controller may, at his discretion, order an inspection of the original records upon which such certificate is based. Any party aggrieved by a decision made following opposition registration may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This right of appeal shall not prejudice any other rights or remedies available to that party as provided herein.

Where a copy translation work is undertaken by an individual acting as an employee, the copyright therein shall vest initially in the employer. The employer shall be deemed the author of such copy translation work for the purposes of this Act, subject to any agreement entered into between the employer and the employee specifying otherwise. Any dispute arising concerning the ownership of a copy translation work under this provision may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted as provided herein. Such tribunal’s decision shall be final and binding on all parties involved. The application for arbitration must be made within three years from the date of completion of the copy translation work. Further, where permission is sought to reproduce or distribute a copy translation work, such permission may only be granted by the copyright owner after due consideration of any contractual obligations existing between the employee and employer.

Any person who without leave of the Controller makes, uses, exercises, sells or offers to sell any patented invention, or attempts to do so, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent. Where such infringement involves the reproduction of literary, artistic or musical works incorporated within the patented process or product, the infringing party shall also be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than five per cent and not exceeding ten per cent of the aggregate sales of the infringing goods. Further, upon conviction for infringement, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both, subject to review by the High Court. The Controller may issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising from orders relating to infringement of layout-design rights and penalties imposed for contravention of provisions herein. Subject to any rules made by the Central Government, the Member Appellate Board may, while hearing an appeal, require the attendance of witnesses, examine them under oath, and order the discovery of documents relevant to the matter before it. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the appellant liable to a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. An appeal section shall be maintained by the board for public access, excluding sensitive personal data.

Where a patent holder elects to grant a non-exclusive license conferring rights to use or exploit an invention protected by a granted patent, and such license is subsequently assigned to another party, the assignor shall retain the right to initiate proceedings for cessation patent against the assignee if the terms of the original license agreement are materially breached. Material breach includes, but is not limited to, unauthorized sub-licensing without prior written consent from the original patent holder or use of the patented invention in a manner inconsistent with the scope defined within the licensed territory as provided herein. The right to seek cessation patent shall be subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the assignee’s actions. Further, any assignment of such license agreement must explicitly acknowledge the assignor's retained rights concerning potential cessation patent proceedings under this Act.

An applicant seeking protection of an invention through an application patent cooperation procedure shall furnish with the request a statement indicating whether the claim is for priority right or not; failure to do so may render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Controller, upon receipt of an international application designating India, shall notify the International Bureau and undertake such actions as are prescribed by the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an applicant elects to enter regional phase in India, the request for further examination shall be processed according to established guidelines. Any fees payable relating to the processing of the application shall be remitted within the stipulated timeframe; otherwise, the application may be deemed abandoned. The Controller is empowered to require additional information or clarification from the applicant at any stage of the proceedings, provided that such requests are reasonable and relevant to assessing patentability.

Where a compulsory license is granted under this Act for the purpose of enabling the manufacture and export concerned pharmaceutical product, the patentee shall be entitled to receive royalties calculated at a rate not exceeding six per cent of the aggregate sales in India of such exported product. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the manner of calculation of such royalties, provided that the prescribed rate shall reflect fair compensation for the exploitation of the patented invention. Any person manufacturing and exporting under a compulsory license shall be liable to pay to the patentee the royalty amount as determined, subject to appeal before an appellate authority constituted under this Act. Failure to remit the royalty amount within the time specified may result in penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention territory India” shall mean the territory comprising the Union of India and its territorial waters. An application for patent shall be deemed to be made within the invention territory India if the applicant is domiciled or has a place of business within that territory. Where any person falsifies trade by representing as genuine an article produced otherwise than under authority, such action shall not preclude them from being held accountable under this Act regarding matters pertaining to patent validity or infringement. The Registrar may require proof of domicile or establishment of a place of business as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the assessment or recovery of registry fees may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which shall be binding on the Registrar. Failure to pay any prescribed registry fee within the time specified in a notice issued by the Registrar shall render the trade mark liable for removal from the register. In cases where an alleged offence has been committed involving fraudulent representation concerning the ownership of a registered trade mark and the subsequent evasion of applicable fees, the offender shall be subject to penalties as determined by the Board, without prejudice to any other action that may be taken under this Act.

Where any registered trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, and such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods, the proprietor of an earlier registered trade mark relating to identical or similar goods shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. Such injunction may extend to prohibiting the display, offering for sale, or importation of the infringing goods. The Court may, in determining whether infringement has occurred, consider the inherent similarity between the marks and the nature of the goods involved; a finding of deceptive mark relation goods is conclusive evidence of such contravention. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall be deemed a contempt of court and subject to penalties as provided herein.

The National Gene Fund shall comprise funds contributed by breeders registering plant varieties under this Act, and any sums received from grants, donations, or investments made in accordance with regulations framed by the Central Government. Contributions towards the Fund shall be determined based on a percentage of the sale proceeds derived from propagating material of registered varieties, as notified periodically. The accrued interest and other income generated by the National Gene Fund may be utilized to support research relating to plant genetic resources, provide financial assistance to farmers for conservation of traditional crop varieties, and fund programs promoting sustainable agricultural practices, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government.

Applications for patents shall be examined by a Controller appointed under this Act, who may, after giving notice to the applicant and opportunity to be heard, reject any application if he finds that the invention is not novel or does not involve an inventive step. Where a patent has been granted, it shall entered in the Register of Patents maintained at the Patent Office, detailing the title of the invention, the name and address of the patentee, and the date of grant. The Controller may require amendments to be made to the specifications prior to entry if they are necessary for clarity or precision. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period specified herein. Patents shall entered with such particulars as prescribed, subject to any modifications directed by the Controller and provided that the Register remains open to public inspection during normal business hours.

Where any goods manufactured or produced in India bear a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark for goods of the same class, and those goods were originally imported into India prior to the date of registration of the said earlier trade mark, then such importation shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the importer demonstrates good faith reliance on a valid license agreement executed before the relevant date, permitting use of the mark for *imported India produced* goods, no penalty shall apply; however, continued importation without such license constitutes actionable misrepresentation. Any person infringing as provided herein shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods and may also face imprisonment extending to three years.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and the accused pleads registration, the Court shall consider the validity of the said registration. For the purposes of this sub-section, “pleads registration” means that the accused expressly raises as a defence the assertion that the registered trade mark was improperly registered or is otherwise invalid. The court may require the proprietor of the trade mark to provide evidence supporting the registration’s validity. Subject to any order made by the Court, such evidence shall be considered only for the purpose of determining whether the charge should proceed; provided that a separate action regarding the validity of the registration remains unaffected as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "means transmission operation" includes any instance where data representing a layout design is electronically transferred from one storage medium to another, or between processing units, whether such transfer occurs during manufacturing processes, simulation testing, or routine archival procedures. Such transmissions shall be deemed to occur irrespective of the physical location of the transmitting and receiving devices, provided that the transmission adheres to established protocols as defined by the relevant industry standards body. The Trade Marks Registrar may, upon application from a registered proprietor demonstrating reasonable grounds for concern regarding unauthorized data transfer, issue directives pertaining to secure transmission practices within designated manufacturing facilities. This provision is subject to compliance with prevailing cybersecurity regulations and shall not impede legitimate research activities approved under guidelines issued periodically.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark desires to grant a license permitting the use of their trade description applied to particular goods or services, such license shall be documented and entered into the Register of Trade Marks. The entry register document relating to such licenses must specify the precise scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and duration. Any subsequent assignment of rights pertaining to this licensed application may only occur with the prior written consent of the proprietor, recorded as a separate entry in the aforementioned register. Provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere strictly to the terms initially stipulated within the original license agreement. Further, any alteration or modification of the goods or services covered by the trade description applied requires notification to and approval from the Registrar before such changes become effective under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall remit filing application fees as prescribed in Schedule A, subject to adjustments notified periodically by the Controller. The amount payable shall be determined based on the denomination variety of the layout-design being applied for, with distinct fee structures applying to designs classified as simple, moderate, or complex, according to guidelines issued by the Office. Provided that applicants registered as Small Scale Industrial Undertakings, as defined under this Act, may claim a reduction in filing application fees not exceeding fifty percent, upon submission of relevant certification. Any deficiency in payment shall render the application deemed withdrawn until such time as the outstanding amount is remitted, and further processing will only resume after compliance.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person owning a specification patent shall be entitled to grant a license to use or exercise the patented invention to another party, either wholly or partially, for a specified period and on such terms as may be agreed upon between the parties. Such license agreement shall be in writing and duly executed by both licensor and licensee. Assignment of rights under a specification patent, including the right to grant licenses, may be made by instrument in writing and registered with the Controller. Provided that any assignment or license granted prior to registration under this Act shall be deemed invalid unless subsequently registered as provided herein. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party, inquire into the reasonableness of royalty rates stipulated in such assignments or licenses and make recommendations accordingly.

An application for a patent that is presented in the prescribed form and contains information required under this Act, but which does not fully comply with all formal requirements as provided herein, shall constitute a form filed patent. Where deficiencies are identified following examination, the Controller may issue an error amendment notice to the applicant specifying the particulars of such deficiencies. The applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rectify these errors and file amended documents. Failure to address the concerns raised in the error amendment notice within the stipulated time period may result in rejection of the application under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under subsection (1) of section 48. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal and shall comply with the requirements as provided herein regarding form and content. The Appellate Board may, after affording an opportunity for a hearing to both the applicant and the Controller General, allow or dismiss the appeal, subject to such modifications as it deems fit. Further, any decision made by the International Bureau concerning the examination of an application for registration shall be taken into consideration by the Appellate Board in its deliberations regarding the merits of the appeal filed by a registered proprietor layout.

An application for entry into the design register shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or other representations of the integrated circuit layout-design sought to be registered, conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or clarification regarding the layout-design and its representation as deemed necessary for proper examination. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. Any alteration made to the drawings or representations after the assignment of the serial number shall be inadmissible unless sanctioned in writing by the Registrar. The design register shall be maintained electronically and shall be accessible for public inspection subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Information pertaining to pending applications shall not be disclosed, provided that this does not impede due process.

An application for registration of a biotechnological invention relating to a genetically modified microorganism shall include particulars specifying the source organism and the nature of the genetic modification effected, along with details of any vector utilized. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning such aspects as are deemed necessary for proper evaluation under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall assign it to an adjudicating officer period, who will conduct a preliminary examination regarding compliance with formal requirements and novelty assessment. Any objection raised by any person during the publication process may be addressed by the applicant within two months from the date of such objection; failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection by the adjudicating officer.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to submit evidence and arguments justifying the registrability of the mark. Such justification must demonstrate that the proposed mark does not conflict with any prior registered marks or pending applications, taking into consideration phonetic and visual similarities as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider such submissions diligently; however, a registration shall only be granted if the applicant satisfactorily demonstrates distinctiveness acquired through use, where applicable, and provides conclusive evidence supporting the claim of *disclosed justified registration*. Failure to adequately address objections raised during examination may result in continued refusal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any producer holding a patent shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the patented invention. Such licenses may be granted for consideration or otherwise, as determined by the producer, and such determination shall be binding on all parties deriving benefit from the use of the patented process or product. Assignment of rights under a license shall require prior written consent from the patent holder, and any unauthorized assignment shall render the licensee liable to damages. Further, where a license is granted for the manufacture and sale of a pharmaceutical product, the producer may stipulate conditions regarding quality control and bioequivalence testing as provided herein. The terms of any such license agreement are subject to review by the Controller if it appears that they unduly restrain competition amongst producers or impede access to essential medicines.

An appeal shall be instituted in the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The Board may, if satisfied that there were sufficient grounds for such delay, entertain an appeal lodged after the expiry of the said period, provided that the applicant satisfies the Board regarding the reasons for the delay and that the delay has not prejudiced the other party. Subject to this provision, any person aggrieved by any decision or order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the High Court as provided herein. The High Court shall dispose of such appeals expeditiously.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be a mark registered proprietor may apply for registration of a service mark used in relation to goods, provided that such application is made within six months from the date of initial trade mark registration. The Registrar shall consider applications relating to colour marks only if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. Where an opposition is filed against an application by a mark registered proprietor, the evidence presented must clearly establish likelihood of confusion with existing registrations or prior use. Further, any alteration to the representation of a registered mark requires consent from all registered proprietors sharing identical rights under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a person claiming rights in a plant variety shall be entitled to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the multiplication, sale, distribution, or export of propagating material of that regard plant varieties. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding five years, renewable by mutual agreement between the licensor and licensee. Any assignment of rights under this Act concerning a registered variety shall require prior notification to the Authority, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the assigned rights. Further, any judicial proceeding relating to infringement of plant variety protection shall be subject to mediation as an initial step, with failure to reach amicable resolution leading to adjudication by the designated court. The terms of such licenses and assignments are governed by principles of fairness and transparency as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar in relation to the registration or refusal of registration of a plant variety shall have recourse to appeal under this Act. The Registrar case shall be deemed to include decisions pertaining to infringement notices and revocation proceedings, and any failure to comply with a direction issued by the Registrar regarding reporting of unauthorized multiplication or sale of protected varieties will attract penalties as prescribed herein. Further, where an infringer fails to remit the assessed damages within thirty days of notification, the Registrar may initiate recovery proceedings through designated enforcement officers. Such officers shall be empowered to seize infringing material and impose fines not exceeding five times the value of the illegally obtained benefit, subject to judicial review.

Subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licenses as provided herein, any person holding a patent outside India may, with the written consent of the Controller, grant an exclusive license to manufacture, use, or sell the patented invention within the territory of India. Such license shall specify the duration thereof and the royalty payable by the licensee to the patent holder, which royalty shall be determined in accordance with principles of fairness and equity, taking into account the nature of the invention and the extent of exploitation permitted under the license. The Controller may require the patent holder to furnish security for the due performance of the obligations undertaken by the licensee. Further, any assignment or transmission of such a license shall also be subject to prior approval from the Controller, ensuring continued compliance with the terms initially agreed upon.

Any broadcasting organisation that reproduces any work protected under this Act for transmission via radio or television signals shall be liable for damages proportionate to the extent of commercial detriment suffered by the copyright owner. An applicant patent person who, acting on behalf of a broadcasting organisation, knowingly facilitates such reproduction without obtaining the requisite license as provided herein, shall be deemed an agent of that organisation and subject to the same penalties. Failure to provide accurate records of copyrighted material used in broadcasts, upon demand from the Controller, will incur fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Repeated or wilful violations may result in revocation of broadcasting licenses and criminal prosecution under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a patent shall be dated as of the date on which the application for the grant of the patent was first filed, whether in India or outside India. Where such application has been filed in respect of a package comprising multiple inventions, the date patent shall pertain to the earliest priority date claimed for any element within that package. Any assignment or license granted prior to the date patent shall be deemed valid only if it explicitly acknowledges and is consistent with the invention’s scope as defined by the subsequently granted patent. Further, where a compulsory license is sought under this Act, the terms of such license, including royalty rates, may be adjusted to reflect the relative contribution of each element within the original package towards the patented technology. The Controller shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses pertaining to patents relating to packages.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application made outside India, and such foreign application has been published under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the publication as provided herein. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable to be deemed abandoned, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. The appellate determination concerning abandonment shall be final, unless it is shown that the failure arose from circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the applicant and prejudiced their ability to secure the certified copy; in such cases, the Controller may, at his discretion, allow a further period for compliance.

Where a person misrepresents goods or services as being those of another, or allows others so to do, and thereby causes or is likely to cause damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the trademark or brand of that other person, such action constitutes passing off. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark or any person possessing goodwill in an unregistered trade mark may apply to the Commercial Court for relief against such misrepresentation. The court shall grant such injunctions, account for damages suffered and award costs as it deems just, subject to considerations of public interest and fair competition. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act shall be deemed a contempt of court and punishable accordingly.

For the purposes of this Act, a mark shall be deemed to lack distinctive character if, by its very nature, it directly signifies the common name or characteristics of goods or services with which it associates. This determination shall consider whether the sign functions solely to describe those qualities and does not indicate origin. However, a mark that initially lacks distinctiveness may acquire such character through consistent use over time, provided that such use has resulted in the relevant consuming public perceiving the mark as an indication of origin rather than merely descriptive information. The limitations on registrability under this Act apply equally irrespective of whether the mark is inherently distinctive or subsequently acquires distinctiveness.

Any registered trade mark owner aggrieved by an application for registration filed by another person may institute proceedings under this Act in the form of an opposition registration. Such opposition shall be based on grounds that the proposed trade mark is likely to be confused with a prior trade mark or is descriptive of the goods or services, and prejudices the distinctiveness or reputation of the earlier mark. The opponent must provide evidence substantiating these claims; failure to do so may result in dismissal of the opposition.

The applicant for registration shall have the right to file a counterstatement responding to the grounds raised by the opponent within a prescribed period. Further opportunities for submitting written arguments and documentary proof shall be afforded to both parties as provided herein. The Registrar, after considering all submissions, may allow or dismiss the opposition, subject to appeal to an appropriate forum.

Following an expiry term patent, any person desiring to exploit the invention commercially shall apply to the Controller for a license of compulsory use, provided that such application is made within six months of the patent’s expiration. The Controller may grant such license if it is satisfied that refusal of the license would result in reasonable public need not being met. Failure to comply with the terms stipulated in any license granted under this Act shall render the licensee liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees for each offence, and a further daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. The Controller may also order seizure of goods manufactured or imported without authorization, subject to due process as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against a patent grant alleging non-compliance with the provisions relating to inventiveness, the Controller shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. Any certificate purporting to be signed by the Controller affirming the validity of such inventive step, following due consideration of these submissions, shall be admissible as evidence in any subsequent proceedings under this Act concerning the patent’s revocation or infringement. Provided that, if either party disputes the authenticity of the certificate purporting to be the Controller's signature, the burden of proving its genuineness shall lie upon the party producing it. The Controller may, at his discretion, require further expert testimony regarding the technical aspects of the invention in question.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a registered trade mark for a drug shall be permitted to grant licences conferring the right to use such trade mark relating to that drug. Such licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover all or part of the territory of India. The owner of the trade mark shall retain ownership of the trade mark and may specify conditions within the licence regarding quality control measures for the manufactured drug. Assignment of a registered trade mark relating to a drug is permissible with the prior written consent of the Controller General, provided that such assignment includes all rights and obligations pertaining to any existing licences associated with the trade mark. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the terms of those licences as if they were an original party thereto.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout design shall submit detailed technical documentation pertaining to the integrated circuit, including schematics, mask data, and manufacturing processes employed. The application must clearly identify the features constituting the original layout design for which protection is sought, distinguishing them from standard or commonly used elements. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may require further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with the requirements under this Act. If the applicant demonstrates that the layout design is novel and possesses aesthetic merit as defined herein, the Registrar shall proceed to enter it into the register of layout designs. The entry in the layout design register shall include particulars of the applicant, the date of registration, and a concise description of the layout design.

For the purposes of this Act, "film sound" means sounds exclusively fixed in relation to a cinematographic work and which are capable of reproduction, including musical scores, dialogue, ambient noise, and effects recorded during or after the filming process. Film sound shall be deemed an integral part of the cinematograph film for copyright subsistence; however, it may also exist independently as a separate copyrighted work if such separation is demonstrably intended by the producer. The rights in film sound are subject to any contractual agreements between the producers and those involved in its creation, provided that such agreements do not contravene the principles of fairness under this Act.

Where an infringement action is brought before a competent court, and the defendant alleges that the patent in question lacks novelty or involves an obvious invention, the patentee shall be entitled to present evidence demonstrating the inventive step. Should the court find, upon review of such evidence, that the alleged lack of novelty or obviousness substantially impacts the scope of the claims as initially granted, it may order a rectification of the patent. This rectification shall clarify the legitimate subject matter protected by the patent. Further, if the defendant demonstrates through credible testimony and documentary proof that attempts to secure a voluntary license from the patentee were made on reasonable terms and conditions, yet remained unsuccessful within a reasonable period, the court may consider this factor in determining damages for infringement. The assessment of what constitutes a reasonable period shall be guided by principles of fairness and equity.

For the purposes of this Act, an “independent scientific adviser” means a person possessing qualifications and experience in a relevant field of science or technology, appointed by the Controller to provide expert guidance on matters relating to patentability, novelty, inventive step, and undue preference. Such an individual shall not be employed by any applicant for patents or possess a significant financial interest in such application. The Controller may determine the terms and conditions of engagement of an independent scientific adviser, provided that their remuneration is commensurate with their expertise and time commitment. An opinion rendered by an independent scientific adviser under this Act shall be advisory to the Controller and not binding.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the use by any person of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the registered trade mark is registered, provided that such use constitutes infringement under this Act. Further, where damage has been caused to the proprietor by reason of the infringing use, he shall be entitled to claim damages from the infringer, subject to limitations as may be prescribed by rules made under this Act. The Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing sign, and any materials used in making such goods. Any false representation concerning respect registered trade marks shall be deemed a civil wrong actionable at the suit of the aggrieved party.

For the purposes clause invention, an act constituting an alleged offence under this Act shall be deemed to include the unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale of any article embodying a patented invention if it is established that the accused had knowledge, or reasonably ought to have had knowledge, of the existence of such patent. Provided that, where the infringement involves a process, the accused’s actions shall be considered in relation to the products derived from that process. Any person found guilty of an offence as provided herein shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees and may extend to fifty thousand rupees; or both. The Court may, subject to appeal, order seizure and forfeiture of the infringing goods.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a proposed collective mark if he considers that the conditions for eligibility are not met, and such refusal shall be accompanied by an order specifying the reasons therefor. Any applicant aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, where a collective mark is registered, any member of the association entitled to use the mark may challenge a decision of the Registrar regarding the scope of permissible usage or the conditions for maintaining registration, through a similar process of appeal before the Appellate Board. The Association shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with these conditions and may face revocation proceedings under this Act if it fails to do so.

Where a patent has been granted under this Act, the patentee shall have the right to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the invention disclosed in the specification filed and proceeded with. Such license may be granted subject to any terms and conditions agreed upon between the patentee and the licensee, provided that the license agreement explicitly states the scope of the licensed rights and duration thereof. Further, a patentee may assign their entire interest in a patent or specific rights relating to it, including but not limited to licensing agreements already entered into, to another party by way of an instrument in writing. Any assignment shall be recorded with the Controller as provided herein. The assignee shall become vested with all rights and privileges which the patentee previously held under this Act concerning the specification filed proceeded with.

A registered proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act against any person who, without the leave of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to the *described trade mark* in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the registration is made. Such proceedings may be commenced in the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurs, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The Board shall consider applications for leave based upon factors including the bona fide nature of the use and any demonstrable consumer confusion arising therefrom. Evidence presented to the Appellate Board is admissible under this Act as evidence before the High Court in subsequent proceedings relating to the same matter. The Registrar may, following a complaint received from an aggrieved party, issue directions concerning cease and desist orders pending judicial determination.

An application for registration of a proprietor certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include particulars relating to the standards established by the applicant for ensuring that the goods certified there under conform to those standards. The applicant must demonstrate, as part of the application, their capacity to consistently monitor and enforce adherence to these standards amongst producers utilizing the proposed certification trade mark. Further, the registrar may require submission of detailed operational manuals outlining quality control procedures. Registration shall be granted only if the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant possesses adequate resources for maintaining the integrity of the certification process and ensuring consumer confidence in goods bearing the proprietor certification trade mark.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods claiming origin from a registered geographical indication shall be liable for damages if it is established that such enterprise has knowingly used a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said geographical indication. Such use constitutes a *geographical indication falsifies* and prejudices the interests of the registered proprietor and consumers alike. The authorised user may, subject to due process, seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further misrepresentation and demand compensation for losses incurred as a direct consequence of the deceptive practice. Further, goods bearing the false or misleading geographical indication shall be liable for seizure and destruction at the expense of the offending enterprise, provided that such action is proportionate to the infringement.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include an assertion that the mark is capable of distinguishing the applicant’s goods or services from those of others. Where the Registrar has reason to believe that a proposed trade mark qualifies as a well-known trade mark in relation to particular goods or services, he may direct the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary to substantiate this claim. Such direction shall specify the geographical area and the relevant consumer perception within India which supports the assertion of ‘well-known’ status. The Registrar is empowered to request evidence demonstrating extensive prior use and recognition of the mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates a genuine and reasonable basis for believing it enjoys such reputation.

The Controller shall maintain an entry register pertaining to all applications for patents relating to inventions involving processes for the manufacture of use certification trade marks, and such entry register shall record particulars including but not limited to the date of filing, applicant details, claims submitted, and examination reports issued. Any party aggrieved by any entry or omission in the entry register may within sixty days from the date on which such entry is made, file an appeal before the Appellate Board, subject to payment of the prescribed fee; provided that the appellate authority shall consider only those grounds specifically alleging errors of fact or law appearing in the record. The Controller’s decision regarding entries shall be final, unless overturned by the Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been duly produced before the Registrar when it is presented at his office and accompanied by the prescribed fee. For the purposes of this Act, "produced registrar application" signifies an application that has undergone initial verification regarding its formal requirements under this Act and which remains pending for substantive examination. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or modifications to the layout-design as provided herein, subject to the applicant’s right to submit a written representation against such requirement. Any alteration made pursuant to such direction shall be recorded in the register.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon his copyright in respect of any work, such person may institute proceedings seeking remedy and damages. The Court shall, prior to adjudicating on the merits of the claim, undertake a preliminary *cc inquiry* into the validity of the asserted copyright. This inquiry shall encompass examination of evidence pertaining to originality, ownership, and compliance with all requirements for registration as provided herein. Failure to adequately demonstrate these elements will result in dismissal of the infringement action without further hearing. The Court may impose costs upon any party found to have initiated frivolous or vexatious proceedings designed solely to harass or delay resolution of a copyright dispute; such costs shall be recoverable under this Act.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark relating to goods desires to grant a license for its use, he may do so by entering into an agreement with another party, specifying the scope and duration of such usage. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to the terms stipulated within the licensing agreement itself, provided that any assignment requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days of execution. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments relating to trade mark licenses concerning goods. Further, where a registered proprietor assigns his entire undertaking including the ownership of a trade mark relation goods, the assignee shall be deemed to have acquired all rights and obligations pertaining to any existing license granted under that trade mark. Any subsequent modification or termination of such a license will require written consent from both licensor and licensee.

An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a trade mark in India through the Madrid Protocol shall file a request for extension of protection with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a certified copy of the international registration and the prescribed fee. Such request must specify the goods or services in respect of which protection is sought, ensuring these correspond to those listed in the international registration unless an amendment is included within the request itself. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence as deemed necessary to verify compliance with the provisions under this Act relating to registrability and distinctiveness. Any opposition to the extension shall be treated as an opposition under this Act, subject to such modifications as are required by the Madrid Protocol.

An application for a patent relating to an invention made in an application convention country shall be deemed to be laid before the Controller, subject to the provisions regarding priority under this Act. Where the applicant claims a right of priority based on such convention application, it shall be incumbent upon them to furnish, within six months from the date of filing the Indian application, a certified copy of the earlier application as proof of said claim; failure to do so may result in the rejection of the patent application. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating compliance with international treaty obligations concerning such convention applications, and any dispute regarding the authenticity or interpretation of these documents shall be subject to appeal before an appellate authority constituted under this Act.

An application for registration as a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation establishing distinctiveness and stability across successive generations. The Registrar may require submission of data pertaining to morphological characteristics, genetic uniformity, and disease resistance relevant to assessing the traits of the applied-for new variety. Such data must demonstrate that the variety maintains its essential features under specified environmental conditions as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Further, an applicant shall provide a comprehensive pedigree chart tracing lineage and demonstrating derivation from known parentage where applicable. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the claimed new variety does not meet the criteria for novelty, or if the documentation submitted fails to adequately substantiate its stability.

Where an invention disclosed in a patent application relates to technology incorporated within a licensed field under a prior agreement, the Controller may permit a specification amendment if such amendment is deemed necessary to accurately reflect the scope of the licensee's rights. Provided that the proposed amendment does not broaden the claims beyond the originally filed disclosure and does not adversely affect any third party’s existing patent or application, the Controller shall consider the request. Any assignment of a patent, or an interest in a pending patent application, including rights arising from a specification amendment, must be executed in the prescribed form and duly registered under this Act. The assignor shall remain liable for ensuring compliance with all conditions precedent to grant, even where such conditions pertain to matters addressed by a subsequent specification amendment.

An indication certification trade mark application shall specify the characteristics or qualities, production method, or origin of goods or services which it purports to certify. Such specification must be precise and verifiable under this Act. The applicant seeking registration as a proprietor of an indication certification trade mark must demonstrate control over the conformity assessment process for certified goods or services, ensuring adherence to the prescribed standards. The Trade Marks Registry may require submission of detailed operational manuals outlining these procedures prior to acceptance of the application. Provided that the applicant demonstrates adequate resources and expertise, the Registrar shall consider the suitability of the proposed certification scheme. Any alteration to the specified characteristics requires notification to the Trade Marks Registry for approval.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for the recovery of damages for the infringement of a trade mark under this Act, the court shall cognizance of such suit subject to the provisions regarding limitation as provided herein. The measure of damages recoverable shall be proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor and may include compensation for injury to reputation or goodwill arising from the use of the infringing mark. Further, where the infringement is established, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and may order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark, as it deems fit. Provided that any counterclaim alleging validity challenges to the registered trade mark shall be adjudicated concurrently with the main suit.

Where a registered trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, and such use causes confusion amongst the public as to the origin of goods or services, any person aggrieved may apply to the Commercial Court for an injunction. The application shall specify the nature of the infringement and the remedies sought. Upon receiving such an application, the Court shall issue notice to the defendant, affording them a reasonable opportunity to respond. Failure by the defendant to appear or adequately defend against the allegations will result in ex parte proceedings. Any person whose name appears on the register shall be deemed to have standing to bring such action under this Act. The register shall brought before the court as prima facie evidence of ownership and validity, subject to challenge based on fraud or misrepresentation.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the applicant and any opposing party. Failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein regarding the filing of appeals will render the appeal inadmissible.

The Trade Marks Registry shall, in determining whether a trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, take into account not only the visual appearance of the marks but also their phonetic similarities and conceptual meanings. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further petition the Supreme Court on a point of law.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to rectification of entries in the Register of Patents may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of service of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals expeditiously and may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing a section 94 appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible, subject to any relaxation granted by the Appellate Board where default was unintentional and did not cause prejudice to another party. Costs of the appeal may be awarded at the discretion of the Appellate Board.

Any person found to have knowingly made a false statement or representation in a patent application before the Controller shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, and further subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Controller may, at any time during the examination of a patent application, require the applicant to furnish such additional information or particulars as he deems necessary for determining whether the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. Failure to comply with such a requirement within the prescribed period shall render the patent application liable for rejection. Any appeal against an order refusing a patent application may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person employing a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered application registration mark without leave from the Registrar shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender is liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the said mark, and may also face prosecution for passing off, subject to judicial determination of wilful intent. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the infringer. The Registrar shall have power to issue injunctions restraining the use of a mark that creates likelihood of confusion with a pending application registration mark, even prior to its formal registration. Repeated or systematic infringement will attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority.

Applications for the registration of registry trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Such applications must clearly indicate the goods or services with which the mark is associated, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The applicant shall provide proof of use of the trademark in relation to those goods or services if required by the registrar. Where an application contains more than one representation of the mark, each representation shall date filing separately for the purposes of determining priority under this Act. Any alteration made to an application after it is filed shall be noted and shall not affect the original filing date, provided that such alterations do not substantially change the nature of the mark as described herein.

Any person who represents, directly or indirectly, that goods or services are offered under a *mark registered manner* without authorization from the proprietor shall be deemed to have contravened this Act. Such representation includes the display of the mark in a way calculated to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Where an infringement is established, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions preventing further infringing activity and orders for the delivery up or destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark. Furthermore, damages shall be awarded to the proprietor of the *trade mark recognised*, reflecting the loss suffered due to the unauthorized use, provided that willful infringement is proven.

Where an application patent shall relate to an invention already claimed in a previously filed application, the controller may grant such patent subject to the condition that the applicant provides written consent from the holder of the earlier application allowing for the subsequent claim. Such consent must explicitly detail the scope of permitted use and commercialization relating to the licensed technology. Further, any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be recorded in the prescribed manner with the Controller, and such recording shall create a public record accessible to all interested parties. The applicant may also offer a cross-license agreement as part of fulfilling requirements for novelty assessment. Failure to provide accurate details regarding licensing arrangements during examination will render the patent liable for revocation proceedings under this Act.

Any person utilizing data derived from plant varieties protected under this Act for commercial research purposes shall be obligated to contribute a portion of their profits, as determined by the Central Government, to the national gene fund. This contribution is intended to ensure equitable benefit sharing and support further agricultural innovation. Provided that, where such utilization involves transient incidental storage of genetic information during data processing, solely for facilitating analysis and not for reproduction or distribution, this obligation shall be waived subject to audit verification by a designated authority. Failure to remit the prescribed amount within the stipulated timeframe will constitute an offense, rendering the offender liable to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and potential revocation of research permits. The Central Government may issue guidelines detailing acceptable methods for profit calculation and auditing procedures.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a design, including decisions concerning the validity of a registered design or the rectification of the register, shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, subject to any directions issued by the Board, impose a penalty for making false statements or suppressing material facts in connection with an application for registration or regarding a permitted register trade mark. Any infringement of design sub section rights is actionable under this Act and will be dealt with summarily.

A registered user shall, upon application made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, be entitled to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services for which it is registered, subject to compliance with the terms and conditions stipulated in its registration. Such a registered user’s right to use the trade mark as provided herein shall not extend beyond the scope of the geographical area specified during the application process, unless expressly authorized by the proprietor of the trade mark. The rights respect registration conferred upon a registered user are further subject to any limitations or qualifications imposed under this Act concerning fair competition and consumer protection.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses for the use of their trade mark within India, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify geographical limitations, restrictions on goods or services covered, duration, and royalty payments. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether partial or complete, must be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein; failure to do so renders the assignee not vested with the rights of the assignor until registration is completed. The Registrar may require proof of consideration paid for any such assignment. A licensee may further sub-license their rights under this Act, but only with the prior written consent of the trade mark owner and notification to the Trade Marks Registry. Any alteration to a registered trademark requires approval from the registry before it can be implemented.

The proprietor of an entitled produce variety shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights pertaining to its propagation, subject to any conditions stipulated within the grant certificate. Such rights extend to the production and sale of seeds or planting material derived from the entitled produce variety, provided that a written license agreement is executed with any entity seeking to undertake such activities. Any assignment of these rights must be registered with the Plant Varieties Registry, detailing the scope of transfer and associated royalties payable to the original proprietor. Further, under this Act, the Registrar may grant compulsory licenses for the production and sale of seeds of an entitled produce variety in circumstances where the proprietor has failed to adequately serve the needs of farmers within a designated geographical area, as determined by the relevant Agricultural Committee.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a device comprising one or more letters which are commonly used in ordinary language, the Registrar shall not refuse the registration solely on the ground that those letters do not possess distinctive character when applied to the goods or services specified in the application. Provided that such refusal may be made if it is established that, prior to the date of application, use of the device by another person in relation to identical or similar goods or services has resulted in a reputation among the relevant section of the public. The Registrar shall give due regard to any provisions act reference relating to acquired distinctiveness and consider whether such use would create confusion amongst consumers. Further, an appeal against this decision lies under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall furnish proof of business india situate within the territory of India, demonstrating continuous use of the proposed mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Such proof may include, but is not limited to, invoices, advertisements, sales records, and statutory declarations affirming commercial activity. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain authenticity and establish genuine usage. Provided that an applicant who has previously abandoned a similar trade mark shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny regarding the distinctiveness of the current application. Any representation made in support of the application is subject to verification under this Act, and false statements render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party demonstrating substantial and ongoing disuse of a registered trade mark for a period exceeding three years immediately preceding the date of such application, grant leave to another person to utilize a confusingly similar sign in relation to goods or services not identical with those for which the trade mark is registered. Such permission shall be conditional upon the applicant proving that the continued registration of the original trade mark impedes their own legitimate commercial activities and that any resulting consumer confusion will be demonstrably minimal. The Registrar may impose such limitations on the permitted use as are deemed necessary to protect the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark, provided that these limitations do not render the authorized use commercially unviable.

Any person seeking to file a document with the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark shall do so in the registrar prescribed manner, utilizing forms specified on the Trade Marks Registry website and accompanied by all requisite fees as detailed in Schedule I. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the application void ab initio, precluding any subsequent consideration thereof. Where an applicant knowingly or wilfully submits a false statement within such a document, they shall be liable for penalties not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and may face prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar is empowered to reject applications demonstrably lacking in clarity or completeness, without providing opportunity for amendment.
