No person shall knowingly make, offer for sale, sell, import or distribute a layout-design which infringes an existing layout-design, subject to the proviso that fair dealing with a layout-design for research without a commercial purpose does not constitute infringement. Where any act of infringement has occurred, the owner of the layout-design may apply to the Commercial Court seeking relief including damages and an injunction restraining further infringing acts. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the owner as well as the profit made by the infringer, provided that such determination takes into account any measures taken by the owner to protect their layout-design. Any party found to have wilfully infringed a registered layout-design may also be ordered to deliver up for destruction infringing copies and materials used in their manufacture, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry, or omission from entry, in the included register geographical indications shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the publication of the Register. Such appeal may be based on grounds that the indication is not distinctive of the goods for which it seeks registration, or that use of the indication would constitute unfair competition under this Act. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during application and subsequent proceedings shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Appellate Board may, after affording opportunity for hearing, direct rectification of the Register; non-compliance with such direction shall attract daily penalties until compliance is achieved.

The Register of Designs shall maintain a record of all registered designs, including particulars relating to the proprietor, inventor, and the date of registration. An application for the registration of a design may be filed by any person claiming to be the owner of the design, provided that such claim is substantiated with appropriate documentation as prescribed herein. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the novelty or originality of the design under this Act. Any interested party may challenge the validity of a registered design before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, demonstrating grounds for revocation relating to lack of distinctiveness or prior use. To respect patent rights, any alteration made to a registered design post-registration shall be reported to the Register within three months.

A case proceeding relating to rectification of a registered trademark shall be instituted only by way of an application made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such applications must specify the grounds for seeking rectification and comply with all requirements as provided herein regarding form and content. The Board may, upon receiving an application, issue a fee payable notice to the applicant requiring payment of the prescribed fees within a specified period. Failure to pay such fees within that period shall result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Further, any party to a case proceeding may appeal to the High Court under this Act.

Any person who reproduces a registered layout-design without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant court, taking into account the loss of profits suffered by the registered proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized reproduction and any other incidental harm. Further, where an infringement is proven to have been committed with the intent to deceive or cause confusion regarding the source or ownership of the layout-design, enhanced penalties may be imposed under this Act. The court shall also order the infringer to cease all infringing activities and account for profits made through such actions. This provision applies irrespective of whether the reproduction was for commercial gain or private use, provided that it constitutes an infringement as defined herein.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may apply to the Geographical Indications Registry, and such application shall specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that the register contains errors or omissions. The Registry shall give notice of the application to the applicant for registration and any other party appearing to have an interest, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit objections or counter-claims. Upon consideration of all materials presented, the Registrar may order rectification as applied for, wholly or in part, or dismiss the application. Any order made under this Act is subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals and determine the matter according to principles of natural justice, reporting its findings to both Houses of Parliament each parliament year.

For the purpose of this Act, “new chemical entity” with reference to pharmaceutical products means a compound not previously known in India or elsewhere, subject to the proviso that salts, esters, ethers, and other derivatives of a new chemical entity shall be considered as such only if they possess substantially enhanced therapeutic efficacy compared to the parent compound. A pharmaceutical product incorporating a new chemical entity shall be deemed non-obvious where it demonstrates unexpected technical effect relative to existing knowledge in the field of medicinal chemistry, provided that such effect is clearly and consistently demonstrated through clinical trials conducted under established protocols.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, examine whether the layout-design incorporates inventive features beyond those dictated by commercially available technology. An applicant seeking registration must demonstrate that the design represents a unique configuration and arrangement of elements, distinguishing it from existing designs within the relevant field. The right to use registered layout shall be granted subject to the condition that the layout-design does not unduly restrict further innovation or constitute an invention far claimed beyond its functional purpose. Any challenge to the validity of registration may be brought before the Controller under this Act, asserting a lack of novelty or inventive step in the design’s features.

Where an advertising campaign prominently features a registered trade mark, and that campaign has demonstrably generated goodwill for the proprietor, unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of substantial elements of said advertising shall constitute infringement of the advertising trade. This right extends to instances where the infringing advertisement creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or sponsorship of goods or services. The remedies available under this Act in cases of infringed advertising trade include an injunction restraining further use of the infringing material and damages, calculated to compensate for lost sales and harm to reputation. Genera species specified within a registered mark shall not limit the scope of protection afforded to its advertising trade; any depiction that exploits the distinctive character of the mark is actionable.

An applicant for registration of a plant variety who has obtained a granted certificate under this Act may, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent as provided herein, elect to surrender said certificate at any point during its term of protection. Such election shall be made by submitting a formal declaration in the prescribed form to the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee specified in Schedule B. The Registrar shall acknowledge receipt of the declaration and publish notice thereof in the Plant Varieties Journal within thirty days. Upon verification that all procedural requirements have been satisfied, including confirmation of any outstanding obligations relating to benefit-sharing agreements entered into under this Act, the certificate shall be deemed surrendered and removed from the Register of Registered Plant Varieties.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance is rejected under this Act on the grounds of novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence demonstrating the contrary. Such submissions may include expert testimony regarding prior art disclosures and comparative data establishing non-obviousness. The Controller, while considering such arguments, shall give due weight to any evidence presented by third parties claiming a conflicting right arising from a deceptively similar substance already in public use. Any order of rejection or grant shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, where the Board may direct further inquiry into the matter and consider additional expert opinions as it deems necessary for just determination.

Any infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall render the infringing party liable to damages, calculated at the option of the owner either on the basis of lost profits resulting from the infringement or reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. The owner may also seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement and requiring delivery up of all infringing layouts. Where a legal practitioner person acting as an agent for the layout-design owner has knowingly participated in the infringement, such practitioner shall be jointly and severally liable with the principal for any damages awarded under this Act. Further, where an infringement is committed by a body corporate, the liability shall extend to its officers in default, provided that they were directly involved in the infringing activity. The court may order seizure of materials used in or resulting from the infringement, as deemed necessary in the prescribed manner.

Any person found to have reproduced a registered integrated circuit layout design without authorization from the owner shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five per cent of the plaintiff’s net profits attributable to the infringing acts. The Layout Design Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by an affidavit alleging infringement and accompanied by a detailed application patent specification outlining the claimed novelty and inventive step of the layout design, issue summons to the alleged infringer requiring them to appear before the Registrar for a hearing. Failure to comply with such summons shall be deemed conclusive evidence of admission of guilt, rendering the offender liable to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar’s decision in matters concerning infringement is final and binding, subject to appeal to the relevant High Court.

Where an applicant seeks to introduce alterations to a patent application beyond those permissible under this Act relating to clerical errors or typographical omissions, such proposed changes constitute an amendment specification. The Controller may allow such amendment only if he is satisfied that the amended matter does not substantially alter the nature of the invention claimed and maintains consistency with the originally disclosed subject matter. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Controller regarding the acceptance or rejection of an amendment specification may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate board shall consider whether the controller acted reasonably in interpreting the scope of permissible amendments, taking into account prevailing standards of patentability as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a variety is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the applicant relies in challenging the decision. The Appellate Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Appellate Board relating to a varieties registered act may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days of such order, subject to just cause shown. A record of rectification applications and their disposition shall be maintained in a court rectification register for public inspection.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish with the application such particulars as are prescribed, including detailed representations demonstrating the novelty and industrial applicability of the proposed design. The Controller may require the applicant to submit additional documentation or specimens to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and freedom from prior publication. Where the design incorporates elements indicative of national security, particularly those pertaining to infrastructure protection or critical systems, the application shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act. Such designs may necessitate a security india clearance certificate issued by the designated authority before proceeding towards registration. The grant of registration mark certification will only follow verification that the design does not compromise national interests as determined by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Geographical Indication” means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin; and includes signs that signify such geographical origin and are used to define the same. The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act defines "place" to mean any defined geographic area. An application for registration shall be examined by the Geographical Indication Registrar, who may request further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. The Registrar’s decision on such requests is final subject to appeal as provided herein.

A person shall not engage in the business of representing applicants before the Controller for the purposes of applying for, obtaining, revoking, or defending patents, nor perform any act relating to such representation, unless that person is a registered practitioner. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe qualifications and conditions for registration as a practitioner, including requirements concerning educational background and experience within the field of patent law. An application for registration as a practise patent agent shall be made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receiving an application, the Controller may require such further information or documentation as deemed necessary to assess eligibility. Registration shall remain valid subject to compliance with continuing professional development requirements as specified under this Act. Any person found to violate these provisions is liable for penalties as provided herein.

An applicant seeking patent protection for an invention relating to a novel pharmaceutical composition shall file a request for examination within twelve months from the date on which the application was first filed in any convention country, provided that such period may be extended under this Act if the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds for delay. Where an application claims priority from a previous filing, the time limit for requesting examination is calculated from the initial india filed months of the earlier application. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the application liable for rejection unless the Controller deems it appropriate to grant a condonation of delay supported by satisfactory evidence of unavoidable circumstances preventing timely compliance as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, applies for registration of a geographical indication which falsely suggests an association with any goods originating from a place different than the one claimed, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication discovers that another person is using the said indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act, they may apply to the relevant authority for an order restraining such use and recovering damages sustained. A geographical indication shall be deemed infringed if it is used in a manner which misrepresents the origin of the goods or services.

Where a Plant Variety is found to infringe upon the rights of another person under this Act, any aggrieved party may file a complaint with the Agriculture Commissioner. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Agriculture Commissioner shall serve notice on both the complainant and the alleged infringer, affording each an opportunity for hearing and presentation of evidence. The Agriculture Commissioner may order the cessation of infringing activities, including but not limited to the unauthorized sale, cultivation, or distribution of the infringing Plant Variety. Further, where damages are proven, the Agriculture Commissioner may award compensation to the affected party, taking into account the extent of the infringement and the profits derived therefrom. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to lack novelty if it was disclosed to the public prior to the date of filing of the patent application, whether by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way. This disclosure must have enabled a person skilled in the art to produce and operate the claimed invention without undue experimentation. However, information obtained during an exhibition expressly for the purpose of applying for a patent shall not be considered prior art under this Act, provided that adequate records of the exhibition were maintained as evidence. The burden of proving lack of novelty rests upon the party alleging it.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to assignment and licensing agreements concerning said mark, provided that any licensee granted permission under such an agreement may further sub-license those rights with the prior written consent of the proprietor. Where a third party alleges an offence relating to the use of a licensed trade mark without authorization, the alleged offence reason will be assessed considering the terms stipulated within the original licensing contract and any subsequent sub-licensing agreements. The proprietor shall provide documentation detailing the chain of licenses where such an allegation arises. Failure to obtain consent for sub-licensing as provided herein constitutes a breach of contract and does not diminish the registered proprietor’s underlying rights under this Act. Any transfer or assignment of a trade mark license must be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to prescribed fees.

Where an applicant aggrieved by any decision of the patent office relating to the grant, refusal, or revocation of a patent, or concerning the rectification of the register, may appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the applicant. The Controller may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller under this Act may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be open for the patent office to require production of evidence relating to a new invention claimed in the application and to demand rectification of errors appearing on the register.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the source germplasm utilized in the development of the variety, including its geographical origin and any relevant access agreements. Where a plant variety incorporates genetic material originating from sources within India that are not readily available or accessible to the public, the applicant shall contribute a percentage of the benefit sharing amount towards the National Gene Fund. This contribution is calculated as specified by the Registering Authority, taking into account the extent of reliance on such germplasm and the potential for future research and development. The funds received into the National Gene Fund may be utilized for supporting conservation efforts, promoting access to genetic resources, and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in traditional plant breeding practices, subject to guidelines framed by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license under this Act shall be required to submit a detailed memorandum to the Controller outlining the scope and terms thereof. Such memorandum must specify the territory covered by the license, the royalty rate payable, and the duration for which the license is granted. Where the patentee has assigned the patent rights to another party, that assignee shall possess all powers of licensing as if they were the original patentee, provided that such assignment was registered under this Act. The Controller may, after due consideration and public notice, approve or reject any proposed license agreement, taking into account whether the terms are manifestly unfair or restrictive concerning the exploitation of the clause invention within India. Any modification to a licensed clause invention requires prior consent from the Controller.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent shall furnish a detailed specification outlining the scope and boundaries of the claimed invention. The description must clearly articulate all elements encompassed within the claims, ensuring that any matter not explicitly described is understood to be excluded. Where an invention far claimed extends beyond the originally disclosed subject matter, the Controller may require further clarification demonstrating the inventive step relating to each additional element. Such requirements shall be considered met only upon submission of a revised specification and accompanying drawings, if applicable, accurately reflecting the broadened scope. The applicant’s compliance with these stipulations is essential for determining patentability under this Act and preventing subsequent challenges regarding claim interpretation.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall include any representation, indication, or suggestion relating to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, quantity, or intended purpose of goods or services. Such a description is deemed misleading if it deceives or is likely to deceive the public regarding the identity of the source of the goods or services. A depiction employing fanciful imagery, provided that such imagery directly and unambiguously conveys information about the aforementioned attributes, shall also be considered within this definition. This understanding applies irrespective of whether the representation is expressed in words, symbols, marks, figures, shapes, colours, sounds, or any combination thereof, as provided herein.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (zb) “trade mark” means any sign, symbol, device, letter, numeral, shape, colour, or container, or any combination thereof, adopted to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. A trade mark shall be capable of being represented graphically and may include a three-dimensional element used in relation to goods. The Registrar shall maintain an entry register wherein particulars relating to applications for registration of marks are recorded as provided herein. This entry register shall be open to public inspection, subject to any conditions prescribed under this Act concerning confidentiality or sensitive information.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief under this Act relating to passing off, an applicant shall demonstrate possession of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India. The existence of such an establishment shall be evidenced by verifiable documentation including, but not limited to, registered agreements for leasehold property, utility bills demonstrating consistent consumption at a specific location, and records of employee payroll and taxation compliance pertaining to operations conducted within the territory of India. Where an applicant’s activities are primarily directed towards export markets, evidence establishing a dedicated warehousing or distribution facility operated under their direct control within India shall be considered sufficient for satisfying this requirement. Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates substantial engagement in marketing and promotional activities targeted at Indian consumers, the Trade Marks Registry may consider such activity as indicative of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment even absent physical infrastructure.

The Registering Authority shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a patent licence agreement, verify compliance with the prescribed format and requisite fees. Such agreements must clearly delineate the scope of rights granted, including territorial limitations and field of use, as specified within the terms of the underlying patent. The applicant shall provide evidence of assignment or consent from all co-patent holders where applicable. Further, any condition imposed relating to certification trade marks used in conjunction with the patented product must be explicitly stated and deemed reasonable under this Act. Failure to adequately define these licence patent terms may result in rejection of registration. An appeal against such a decision lies before the Controller.

The application for registration of copyright, submitted in accordance with the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, shall be examined by the receiving officer to verify compliance with the provisions relating to eligibility under this Act. Provided that any deficiency identified during examination may be brought to the attention of the applicant, who shall have a period of thirty days from the date of notification to rectify such deficiencies or submit further documentation as deemed necessary. The registrar copyrights shall, upon satisfactory completion of the verification process and determination of copyright subsistence, proceed with the registration of the work in the public record. Any objection raised by any person against the proposed registration must be filed within sixty days of publication of the acknowledgement.

Registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been granted in error, and consequently, provided cancelling registration may occur, if it is established that the layout-design was substantially similar to an already registered design under this Act. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the overall impression created by the designs, irrespective of minor variations. An application for cancellation must specify the grounds upon which it is based and identify the prior registered design. The Registrar may require further evidence supporting the claim of substantial similarity before proceeding with a hearing concerning the validity of the design registry registration.

Any person who knowingly makes false statements or submits fraudulent documents relating to an entry appearing in the Entry Register shall be liable to a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred and fifty thousand rupees, and such person shall also be subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may, at any time, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register if it comes to their notice that an entry has been secured through misrepresentation or suppression of material facts. Further, any proprietor whose trade mark is adversely affected by a false entry in the Entry Register shall have the right to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding information contained within the Entry Register document.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be made in the prescribed form and shall include particulars relating to the applicant, the nature of the layout-design, and its intended use. The Registering Officer shall examine such an application and if satisfied that the layout-design is original and not infringing any existing right, including rights arising from a patent invention, he may proceed with registration. Upon acceptance, the layout-design shall be entered in the register as provided herein, specifying the date of entry and the name of the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register or by an erroneous entry in the register sub section (2) may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of such decision.

Where an applicant seeks to claim a priority date under this Act, such claim shall be substantiated by submission of certified copies of the application as originally filed in the country of origin, duly authenticated by that nation’s competent authority. The Controller may require the petitioner to furnish petition particulars detailing the precise nature of the invention disclosed in the foreign application and demonstrating its correspondence with the subject matter of the Indian patent application. Provided that, if the applicant fails to submit these particulars within thirty days from the date of request, or provides information deemed insufficient by the Controller, the claim of priority date shall be rejected without further notice. The burden of proving the validity of the claimed priority date rests solely upon the applicant.

For the purposes of this Act, “regulations deposited section” means a portion of an official record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry containing particulars relating to conditions, limitations, or restrictions imposed upon the registration of a trade mark, and which are expressly recorded as part of the registered instrument. Such regulations shall be deemed to form an integral component of the registered trade mark. An assignment denomination pertaining to a trade mark subject to a regulations deposited section shall clearly indicate the applicability of those specific conditions in any subsequent transfer or licensing agreement. The Registrar may require such indication under this Act.

Any broadcasting organisation that reproduces any copyrighted work in a programme for public transmission without obtaining requisite permission from the owner of copyright shall be liable to pay remuneration determined by the Controller. This liability extends to instances where the reproduction is substantially similar to the original work, irrespective of whether it constitutes an exact copy. Failure to remit such remuneration within ninety days of demand notice served under this Act will attract a penalty equivalent to three times the amount due. The Controller may, upon receiving complaints regarding non-compliance by a broadcasting organisation, issue directions for rectification and impose further penalties as deemed appropriate. Any aggrieved copyright owner may appeal against orders issued by the Controller relating to remuneration or penalties.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process respect patent for the manufacture of a substance and the invention claimed involves one or more steps relating to chemical reactions, the Controller may require the applicant to disclose the best method known to them for carrying out such reaction. Such disclosure shall be made in a prescribed form and shall include details regarding reagents employed, reaction conditions maintained, and yield achieved. Failure to provide this information as directed will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Director responsible for examining applications pertaining to chemical processes may, at his discretion, extend the time limit for compliance with such disclosure requirements by a period not exceeding three months, provided that reasons for extension are recorded in writing. Any subsequent request for further clarification shall be addressed promptly and completely.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act pertaining to a copyrighted work, such license shall be deemed contractual in nature and subject to the terms stipulated therein. The licensor shall not, without express written consent from the exclusive licensee, grant further licenses or assignments that would diminish the scope of exclusivity previously conferred. Provided that, any action taken by the licensor which demonstrably prejudices the commercial exploitation of the work by the exclusive licensee may be challenged before a competent civil court. Furthermore, the exclusive licensee shall maintain detailed records pertaining to distribution and sales of the copyrighted work, accessible for inspection upon reasonable notice from the licensor, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these record-keeping requirements shall render the license subject to review and potential termination.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it appears that the invention claimed in a patent application is anticipated by prior art existing in a 6referred convention country, the Controller may grant the patent only if the applicant demonstrates that the said prior art was not reasonably discoverable by a person skilled in the relevant field within India at the time of the application’s filing. The burden of proving such reasonable non-discoverability shall rest entirely upon the applicant. Failure to satisfy this requirement will result in the rejection of the patent claim or, if already granted, may be grounds for revocation under procedures as provided herein. This provision is without prejudice to any remedies available to aggrieved parties, including the right to appeal decisions before houses parliament. The Controller’s decision on discoverability shall be final subject to judicial review.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a description of the functions performed by the integrated circuit. Where a layout-design has been *entered register disclosed* prior to the date of filing the application, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating the nature and extent of such disclosure. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information or documentation deemed necessary for assessing novelty and originality under this Act. Further, any modification made to the layout-design subsequent to its initial *entered register disclosed* status must be reported to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by a justification for said alterations as provided herein.

An artistic work shall be deemed to include photographs, architectural designs and models used in architecture, irrespective of whether such works are fixed on any medium. Provided that an architectural design or model used in architecture shall not be considered an artistic work if it is solely functional in nature and lacks aesthetic merit discernible by a reasonable person exercising due care. The right of the author to issue copies of the artistic work shall subsist until sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author’s death, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding public display and reproduction for educational purposes as provided herein. Any commercial exploitation exceeding fair use guidelines requires prior authorization and adherence to stipulated royalty structures.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed complete upon receipt by the Registrar of the requisite forms, fees, and representation of the mark as specified under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to register a device comprising words and figurative elements, clarity regarding the distinctiveness of each element is essential; any disclaimers required to ensure such distinctiveness must be clearly stated within the india application. The Registrar may require further clarification or amendment of the proposed representation if it lacks sufficient detail for proper examination. An applicant shall provide evidence of prior use of the mark in India, where claimed under this Act, and failure to do so may prejudice the registration process.

Any proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall, upon application by any interested party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from non-compliance with the conditions of registration, furnish to that party a detailed accounting of all fees collected under this Act relating to the certification process. Failure to provide such an accounting within thirty days shall render the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and subject to further action by the relevant adjudicating authority. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of systematic failure to issue timely registration notices to certified users, initiate proceedings against the proprietor for breach of conditions. Such breaches may result in suspension or revocation of the certification trade mark registration.

Where an application trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be on grounds that the refusal was erroneous in law or fact and that the Registrar failed to consider material evidence submitted by the applicant during examination. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the Registrar, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this provision may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days, subject to satisfaction of the conditions prescribed herein regarding deposit of security.

An appeal from an order passed by the Registrar under this Act shall lie to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members to be appointed by the Central Government, having expertise in intellectual property law or related fields. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an appeal with the Appellate Board in the form specified herein. The appeal shall state the orders against which the appeal is made and the grounds on which it is based.

The Appellate Board may, while hearing appeals, require the production of any documents or evidence as it deems necessary. Any indication that a layout-design infringes another’s rights shall be considered by the board during appellate proceedings. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal to the High Court under such conditions as are provided herein.

An application for registration of a registered layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Office may prescribe, including certified copies of drawings illustrating the salient features of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation deemed necessary for assessing the novelty and originality of the layout-design under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing, which shall be conclusive evidence as to such date subject to any appeal filed within the prescribed time limit. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The layout-design must not contain elements dictated solely by technical function and should demonstrate inventive step beyond what is obvious to a person skilled in the art.

Any person who knowingly makes or deals with any plant material derived from a registered variety, infringing the breeder’s rights under this Act, shall be liable to pay compensation equivalent to three times the total value of such infringing plant material. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized multiplication and sale of propagating material involving protected varieties plants ensuring genetic purity, issue an order directing the cessation of such activities and impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of violation. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender subject to further penalties, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. The Authority is empowered to recover costs incurred in investigations related to these infringements.

Where a patent granted persons jointly holds a patent, the rights accruing thereunder shall be deemed to be held as tenants-in-common, subject to any contractual agreements between them regarding the exploitation and licensing of the invention. Any dispute arising concerning the respective shares or obligations of such patentees may be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, provided that either party may elect to pursue a remedy in a court of law. The Controller shall not entertain any application for rectification of the patent based solely on allegations of improper apportionment of rights unless it is demonstrated that the initial grant was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation. Further, an appeal against such a determination lies to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application patent invention” shall mean a new and non-obvious process or product, relating to an article manufactured or produced in India, for which an application for grant of patent has been filed. An invention shall be deemed not obvious if, having regard to the state of knowledge existing as the date of filing of the patent application, it does not involve any element of surprise and is not simply a combination of known elements. The term "invention" includes improvements relating to the subject matter in respect of which an application patent invention has been granted under this Act, provided that such improvement results in material advancement.

An application for a patent of addition may be filed by any person who is entitled to apply for and obtain a patent under this Act, provided that the subject matter of such addition is connected with the invention claimed in the original patent. The Controller shall consider an application for a validity patent addition if it demonstrates a clear link between the added matter and the originally patented invention; however, the inventive step requirement shall be assessed separately for each claim within the patent of addition. Any challenge to the validity of the patent of addition must specifically address whether the additional subject matter satisfies the criteria for patentability as provided herein, irrespective of the original patent’s status. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this connection during examination.

For the purposes of this Act, a “design register” means a public record maintained by the Controller General, containing particulars of registered layouts and designs, including but not limited to the name and address of the registrant, the date of registration, the class and description of the layout-design, and copies or representations thereof. An application for inclusion in the design register shall be refused if the layout-design incorporates a condition declared unlawful under this Act, namely, that it is substantially similar to an existing registered layout-design or contains elements which are dictated solely by technical function or process, thereby lacking originality as provided herein.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall include particulars identifying the applicant, including their address for service, and a representation in a form specified by the Registrar demonstrating the originality of the design. The application must also state whether the applicant claims right to the layout-design as proprietor or as an authorized person. Where the layout-design incorporates elements indicative of geographical indications relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs originating from a specific region within India, the applicant shall provide documentation substantiating their connection to that region and ensuring fair trade practices are maintained. The Registrar may require further information under this Act to ascertain compliance with these provisions prior to proceeding with examination.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced, distributed, exhibited, or performed any work subject to copyright without authorization from the owner thereof shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Where such infringement involves commercial gain, the court may further impose a fine equivalent to three times the value of the infringed work or ten million rupees, whichever is greater. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding assessment of damages under this Act. It shall be the duty of every law enforcement agency to assist aggrieved copyright owners in securing remedies as provided herein. Parliament believes that robust protection necessitates stringent measures against unauthorized use.

Where an applicant patent claimant, being a juridical person, desires to grant a license or assign the rights pertaining to a pending patent application, such authorization shall be executed by a duly authorized officer possessing express power of attorney ratified by the governing body of said juridical person. The instrument of assignment or licensing agreement must clearly identify the applicant patent claimant and the assignee or licensee respectively, along with a comprehensive description of the intellectual property rights being transferred or permitted. Further, any such license granted under this Act shall specify the field of exploitation and the duration thereof, subject to limitations as may be prescribed by regulations framed hereunder. Provided that, prior consent from the Controller General is required for assignments involving transfer of ownership outside the territory of India, demonstrating compliance with foreign exchange regulations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a layout design relation shall subsist where an individual, hereinafter referred to as the ‘owner,’ has expended substantial resources and demonstrated diligent efforts in developing a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. This determination shall consider whether the owner’s actions reasonably anticipate commercial applications relating to applies goods incorporating the said layout-design. Further, it is provided that any entity claiming rights under this Act must satisfy the Registrar that they possess documented evidence of such expenditure and effort, including but not limited to records of design iterations, material procurement, and personnel allocation. The owner’s entitlement shall be contingent upon their adherence to prescribed standards for data security and confidentiality relating to the layout-design.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, as determined by the Court. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction without compensation. The owner of a registered mark may apply to restrain the use of any mark contrary to the provisions herein relating to mark registration act. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall attract penalties as prescribed by law, including daily fines until compliance is achieved.

A specification patent shall be deemed invalid under this Act if it is established that the subject matter disclosed does not constitute an inventive step over prior art, provided that such determination considers whether the invention inherently possesses technical effect and utility sufficient to warrant protection. Furthermore, where a claim in the specification relates to a method of agricultural or horticultural practice, it shall be assessed with particular regard to its impact on food security and rural livelihoods, subject to demonstrating novelty and non-obviousness as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of a patent may only proceed if the petitioner demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that the invention was not adequately disclosed in the specification, failing which the claim will be dismissed.

Where any registered proprietor or other person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of entries in the Register of Designs believes that such decision was made without due consideration of all relevant evidence presented during the registration inquiry, they may apply to the Design Appellate Board for review. The Board shall conduct a fresh inquiry imposing penalty where it finds that the Registrar’s order resulted from demonstrable bias or procedural unfairness. Such an inquiry shall be deemed a quasi-judicial proceeding and the applicant shall have the right to cross-examine witnesses presented by the Registrar. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity to present their case, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision of the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of a trademark has been granted and the certificate of registration issued, any party claiming ownership rights in a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use of the trade mark. The Registrar shall have the power to issue interim injunctions restraining acts of proceeding infringement pending final determination of the matter before an appropriate judicial forum, provided that such action is demonstrably causing irreparable harm to the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered trademark. Further, any representation or false designation made in connection with goods or services utilizing a similar mark shall be considered actionable under this Act.

An applicant seeking protection through an application patent cooperation procedure shall file particulars including the title of the invention, inventor’s name and address, priority details where applicable, and a concise description of the invention as provided herein. The prescribed form shall include claims defining the scope of protection sought; these claims must be clear, precise, and supported by the disclosure. An international application designating India under the Patent Cooperation Treaty constitutes an application for patent rights in India only if a subsequent national phase application is filed within the time limit specified under this Act. Failure to do so will render the initial international application deemed abandoned.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it conflicts with a mark already registered, or applied for by another person, and the Registrar considers that the conflicting mark has been used to create confusion among the public regarding the origin of goods or services, he may allow the applicant’s application if the applicant demonstrates a clear and demonstrable association between their proposed mark and the marks registered associated. Such demonstration shall include evidence of prior dealings, advertising campaigns, or other activities undertaken by the applicant that explicitly link the two marks in the consumer's perception. The Registrar shall provide reasons for any such allowance, which reasons must be recorded in the register. This power is subject to ensuring no undue prejudice results to the proprietor of the earlier mark.

The Appellate Board shall be presided over by an appellate board chairperson appointed by the Central Government. For the purposes of this Act, the appellate board chairperson is a person who holds office for a term not exceeding three years and may be removed from office under such conditions as are prescribed. The chairperson shall exercise all powers necessary for the proper discharge of functions vested in the Appellate Board, including the power to constitute Benches and direct proceedings. Subject to any rules made by the Central Government, the appellate board chairperson is entitled to remuneration as determined by the government. Provided that a person shall not be eligible for appointment as appellate board chairperson if they have previously been convicted of an offence involving dishonesty.

A design registry is constituted under this Act to facilitate the registration of semiconductor integrated circuit layout designs. An application for entry in the design registry shall contain particulars specified by the Authority, including a representation of the layout design and details of the applicant. The Registrar, acting upon representations received from any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority, may entertain an appeal against such decision. Subject to this Act, the Registrar’s determination regarding the novelty or originality of a layout design shall be final. Provided that, the authority registrar case record relating to registration shall be maintained as per regulations prescribed.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a service mark relating to services rendered exclusively through electronic means, verify that the applicant possesses the requisite legal capacity to effect such transmission of services. Where a proprietor seeks to assign or otherwise transmit ownership of a trademark registered under this Act, the assignment deed or other instrument evidencing the transmission shall be executed in accordance with the principles of law governing contractual obligations and shall specify both the cedent and the assignee clearly. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the legal standing of parties involved in any such transmission, including but not limited to certificates of incorporation and board resolutions. Any alteration or modification to a registered trademark following a transmission requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding maintaining distinctiveness.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an applicant for a patent may grant a license under this Act in respect of the invention disclosed in the application patent specification, either wholly or partially, and either for consideration or without consideration. Such license may be granted to any person, including another entity engaged in research and development related to the field of the invention. The terms of such license shall be recorded in writing and filed with the Controller, along with a declaration by the applicant confirming their authority to grant said license. Further, the right to assign the application patent specification or any interest therein may be exercised freely, provided that all assignments are registered as per prescribed procedures. Any subsequent licensee shall be bound by the terms of the original license agreement and subject to restrictions imposed under this Act regarding compulsory licensing.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar by any association of persons, cooperative society, producer company, or individual authorized by such associations or societies representing the interests of the producers of the goods concerned. The applicant shall furnish particulars demonstrating that the said indication is primarily associated with a definite geographical locality and enjoys reputation due to unique qualities originating from that location. Where an objection is raised against registration on the ground that the proposed geographical indication is descriptive of the goods, the applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence establishing distinctiveness acquired through long usage. The Registrar shall consider such objections and submissions before proceeding with examination. Protection under this Act extends only to registered geographical indications; no protection is afforded to an *unregistered geographical* indication. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein regarding distinctiveness and acceptable matter, indicate whether the application is intended to claim priority from an earlier trade mark application filed in a designated Contracting Party under the Madrid Protocol International system. Such indication must be made at the time of filing the application or within such period as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a separate record of applications claiming priority under the aforementioned protocol, noting the date and reference number of the earlier application. Failure to accurately disclose details concerning the priority claim may render the registration vulnerable to challenge during opposition proceedings, subject to judicial review.

A proprietor of a geographical indication, aggrieved by any infringement of the rights conferred under this Act, may institute civil proceedings in the competent District Court for redress. Such remedies shall include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing activity. The court may also order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government. Further, any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, uses a geographical indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards prescribed for that indication shall be liable to pay compensation to the proprietor. A geographical indication shall not be deemed to infringe upon these provisions if its use is solely descriptive of the origin of the goods and not used in an attempt to falsely represent their quality or characteristics.

Where an application for registration of a utility model is granted and subsequently challenged under this Act, the validity of such registration shall be determined by the Controller based upon evidence presented by both the registrant and the challenger. The determination shall specifically address whether the invention in question was novel and non-obvious at the time of filing the application, taking into consideration any prior publications or use. Further, it shall be considered whether the period claimed for exploitation of the utility model exceeded a reasonable period, as determined by the Controller considering prevailing market conditions and technological advancements. Should the challenger successfully demonstrate that registration was improperly granted or has become untenable due to expiry of a reasonable period, registration shall cease immediately upon order of the Controller.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the copyright in a musical work or dramatic work has been assigned by virtue of a license granting exclusive rights of reproduction and public performance, the assignor shall retain the right to grant non-exclusive licenses for the synchronization of the work with audio-visual media, provided that such synchronization does not constitute an act of infringement under this Act. Any subsequent assignment of copyright in the said musical or dramatic work shall be deemed to include these synchronization rights unless explicitly excluded by written agreement between the parties. Further, where a license has been granted for adaptation of a literary or artistic work, the licensor may grant further licenses relating to similar adaptations without prejudice to the original licensee’s exclusive right to exploit their adaptation as provided herein. The terms and conditions governing such sub-licensing shall be determined by contractual agreement.

Any person who, without authorisation from the owner of copyright in a cinematograph film, reproduces the film in an infringing copy, whether for sale or distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the civil court. The amount of such damages shall reflect the reasonable costs incurred by the copyright owner in discovering and proving the infringement, including expenses related to forensic analysis of digital copies. Further, any person found guilty of commercial exploitation of a cinematograph film without due license is subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine that may extend to ten lakhs rupees, or both, as provided herein. This penalty applies irrespective of the medium through which the infringing copy is disseminated.

An invention shall be deemed non-obvious if, having regard to the state of the art as defined under this Act, it does not involve any element that would have rendered it obvious to a person skilled in the art; provided that the determination of whether an invention is obvious or not shall take into consideration technological advancements occurring after the date of filing of the patent application. Where an applicant seeks protection for an invention based on a convention application from an invention convention country, such application must adhere to all procedural requirements as prescribed herein. Furthermore, any registered design incorporated within the claimed invention shall be subject to independent examination and validation, ensuring it meets the novelty and originality criteria stipulated under the Designs Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “essentially derived variety” means a variety that is not clearly distinguishable from the original variety according to the characteristics indicated in its documentation and which, subject to section 29, has been obtained through any conventional techniques like cross-pollination or genetic engineering. A variety shall be deemed essentially derived if it is visibly, functionally, or genotypically identical to the original variety for all traits that are assessed under this Act; however, minor variations arising from stress conditions or geographical location shall not disqualify a variety as non-essentially derived. The india department agriculture shall maintain records pertaining to varietal characteristics and assessment protocols.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by a Controller under this Act is dissatisfied, that party may prefer an appeal to the *order appellate* board. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to present their cases in writing or orally, subject to just rules of procedure as it deems fit. An appeal lies only on a substantial question of law arising out of the order appealed from; however, the Board may, at its discretion, examine the matters of fact decided by the Controller if necessary for proper disposal of the appeal. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted and may direct further inquiry where deemed essential. Any party failing to appear before the *order appellate* board on a date fixed may have their appeal dismissed.

Where an infringement of a patent has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to seek relief under this Act including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the patented invention. Damages adequate to compensate for the loss caused thereby shall also be recoverable, calculated subject to principles of fairness and equity. The measure of damages may include lost profits attributable to the infringement, a reasonable royalty for the use of the patented invention, or in cases where actual damages are difficult to ascertain, such other sum as the Court deems just and appropriate. Provided that, any counterclaim alleging invalidity of the patent shall be adjudicated concurrently with the primary claim of infringement. The defendant may also seek an order requiring the patentee to account for profits made from the sale of products manufactured under license granted in contravention of this Act.

Where an application for proceed case registration is filed in respect of a distinctive sign used in relation to goods, and any interested person objects on the grounds that the applicant is not entitled produce variety relating to those goods, the Registrar shall give notice of such objection to the applicant. The applicant may then submit counter-statements and evidence rebutting the objections. Failure by the applicant to adequately address the concerns raised regarding entitlement to produce variety will render the proceed case registration application liable for rejection. Any person aggrieved by a decision granting or refusing proceed case registration may appeal under this Act within sixty days of such decision, subject to penalties as provided herein for frivolous or vexatious appeals.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, it is alleged that the patent has been assigned, the party asserting the assignment shall bear the burden of establishing, by documentary evidence or otherwise as provided herein, the validity and extent of such assignment. The Controller may require production of original documents pertaining to the transfer and may consider testimony from relevant parties involved in the purported assignment. Should the Controller find that the alleged assignee has not demonstrated a clear chain of title, or that the terms of the assignment are ambiguous concerning the scope of rights transferred, the revocation proceedings shall continue as if no assignment had occurred. Any decision regarding the validity of an assignment is appealable to the Appellate Board.

An application for a patent may include visual recordings, including but not limited to photographic and videographic representations, demonstrating aspects of the invention’s operation or construction, provided that such recordings are supplementary to the written description and claims. The Controller shall consider these visual aids solely for clarity in understanding the nature of the claimed invention; they do not, however, form part of the patent itself unless explicitly incorporated within the textual description. For purposes of determining novelty under this Act, any publicly accessible visual recording depicting a device or process embodying a clause invention shall be treated as prior art, irrespective of whether it contains accompanying written material. The applicant bears the burden of demonstrating that such recordings do not anticipate the claimed invention.

An application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which it is received by the Controller or his representative. For the purposes of this Act, an application relating to a process for producing a substance shall include an application relating to the use of that substance. An applicant may be required to furnish such particulars concerning the invention as the Controller deems necessary for the purpose of examination under this Act. Where an application is filed jointly by two or more applicants, they shall be deemed to have taken steps jointly for the prosecution of the application india and any communication relating thereto shall be sent to one of them.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act, including orders relating to compulsory licensing or revocation of patents, desires to appeal against such order, he may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds of appeal and copies of all relevant documents. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the appeal inadmissible. The Board may, after giving notice to the Controller and opportunity for him to be heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, disposing of the appeal. Any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal under the provisions of the Tribunals Act. Costs relating to the appeal shall be determined by the Board.

Any individual engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or dissemination of visual recordings depicting goods bearing a registered geographical indication, with the intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin of such goods, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act and may also face penalties as prescribed under the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register documenting all instances of suspected infringement involving visual recording evidence, available for inspection by authorized law enforcement agencies and aggrieved proprietors. Upon receiving a complaint substantiated by documented visual recordings demonstrating misleading use of a geographical indication, the Registrar shall promptly notify the relevant police authorities to initiate investigations. Further, any proprietor seeking recourse against such deceptive practices may submit authenticated copies of the visual recordings as prima facie evidence during proceedings before adjudicating officers.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model shall file a request for extension of the period for completing the formalities relating to the grant of the patent under this Act if, owing to unforeseen circumstances arising after the date on which the application was filed, it has not been possible to comply with those formalities within thirty-six months. Such an applicant may submit evidence demonstrating that india filed months were impacted by events beyond their reasonable control, including but not limited to natural disasters or significant regulatory changes affecting patent prosecution timelines. The Controller General shall consider such evidence and may, subject to conditions as provided herein, grant the requested extension, which shall not exceed twelve additional months. Any further extensions require a fresh application and demonstration of continued extenuating circumstances.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed form” means a form specified in the First Schedule or as may be prescribed by the Central Government and includes any alterations or additions thereto directed by the Controller; the term shall also encompass any digital format approved under regulations framed by the government. The manner issuing certificates relating to layout-design registration, including but not limited to those pertaining to extensions of time for filing documents or rectification of errors, shall be as prescribed in the Second Schedule and subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary by the Controller. Any deviation from the prescribed form or manner issuing is void.

Where any person offers or provides a service relating to telecommunications infrastructure, and uses a sign, whether descriptive or not, which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark used by another person for services identical or akin to their own, that first-mentioned person shall be deemed to have engaged in an act of detrimental imitation. Such acts are actionable under this Act as passing off, irrespective of any prior use or registration relating to the imitated mark. Any proprietor of a registered trademark may apply to the relevant adjudicating authority for relief, including injunctions preventing further infringing conduct and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such infringement. The adjudicating authority shall have power to impose penalties not exceeding ten lakhs rupees for each instance of proven violation.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act may, subject to the provisions herein, grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication for goods conforming to the standards established in the registration certificate. Such licenses shall specify the duration and scope of permitted usage, including but not limited to territorial limitations and restrictions on alterations to packaging or presentation. The proprietor shall retain the right to revoke any license granted if the licensee engages in practices detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with the geographical indication. Assignment of a registered geographical indication, or any rights pertaining thereto, is permissible only with prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing licensees. Further, any transfer of ownership impacting the control and management of production within the defined geographical area shall be reported to Parliament year by year for review.

Any person utilizing a statement geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of financial loss suffered by registered proprietors and bona fide users. Such damages may include lost profits, diminution in value of goods, and costs incurred in rectifying misleading representations to consumers. Further, any entity found guilty of unauthorized use or misrepresentation concerning a protected geographical indication is subject to penalties not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees for the first offence, escalating to one million rupees for subsequent violations. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders compelling immediate cessation of infringing activities and confiscation of goods bearing the false designation, as provided herein.

Where a work has been reproduced without authorization from the copyright holder, and such reproduction substantially replicates the original work’s protected elements, it shall be deemed an infringing copy. Provided that, where the alleged infringing copy incorporates only minor alterations to the original work's arrangement or presentation, and those alterations do not constitute transformative creativity as defined under this Act, a determination of infringement may require consideration of whether such alterations were undertaken in good faith for purposes of adaptation or improvement. Further, if the reproduction was made solely for private use and is not offered for commercial gain, it shall be subject to review regarding potential exemptions as provided herein. Any party claiming an infringing copy must demonstrate proof of copyright ownership and evidence of unauthorized reproduction.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, including but not limited to orders relating to revocation, opposition, or infringement proceedings, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal from the said order to the district court. The appeal shall be filed within ninety days of the date of communication of the order to the appellant, subject to a provision for extension of time not exceeding thirty days where the appellant can demonstrate reasonable cause for delay. Upon hearing the parties and considering the record of proceedings before the relevant authority, the district court may confirm, reverse, or modify the original order. The decision of the district court shall be final, provided that an appeal lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. Costs incidental to the appeal shall be determined by the district court in its discretion.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed invalid if, following its grant, it is demonstrated that the applicant did not possess the requisite rights as required under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a registered layout-design may petition the Registrar for its cancellation, provided that such application specifies grounds alleging improper acquisition or lack of originality in the design. The Registrar shall afford the registrant an opportunity to be heard and present counterarguments; however, failure to adequately respond to the allegations presented within the prescribed timeframe will constitute acquiescence. Cancellation justified registration is permissible where it is established that the layout-design infringes upon a prior, unregistered layout-design already commercially exploited in India.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, and presents prima facie evidence demonstrating such infringement, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may direct the respondent to appear and adduce counter-evidence. Subject to appeal to the High Court, any order made by the Appellate Board concerning the admissibility or relevance of said evidence shall be final until reversed. It is provided that no court shall take cognizance of an offence relating to trade mark infringement based solely on a proprietor’s assertion without supporting documentation filed with the Registrar; this constitutes a cognizance offence basis. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision regarding evidentiary matters may appeal within sixty days as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be deemed to have been refused if the prescribed fee has not been remitted within thirty days from the date of issue of the notice under this Act. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates satisfactory cause for the delay in payment, the Registrar may, at his discretion and after affording an opportunity for hearing, extend the time limit by a period not exceeding fifteen days.
