The layout design registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout designs accessible for public inspection, subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the layout design registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" means the three-dimensional representation of an integrated circuit, reduced to a physical form by any manufacturing technique and includes both the arrangement of elements on the semiconductor material and the interconnections between them. The term “element” shall include active and passive electronic components, semiconductors, interconnects, leads, pads, bonding wires, chips, or other functional units. An application for registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the registrar semiconductor integrated, who may require such particulars as are necessary to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public order or morality. The registrar semiconductor integrated shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations under this Act.

The owner of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of the mark upon such terms as may be agreed between the parties, provided that any such license agreement expressly specifies the geographical territory and the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to utilize the trademark. Where a license granted under this Act includes a provision for assignment, the assignee shall be deemed to have stepped into the shoes of the original licensee and subject to all limitations contained within the initial licensing agreement. Further, any transmission of a registered trademark, whether by way of assignment or otherwise, shall require prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by evidence demonstrating consent from all existing licensees. The Registrar may reject such transmission if it deems it detrimental to consumers or unfairly prejudices the interests of other trade mark proprietors.

The owner of a registered Geographical Indication may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in a written agreement, grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to make, use, offer for sale, expose for sale, sell, or import goods that are identifiable as originating from the territory specified within the registration. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and accompanied by a certified copy of the agreement governing the assignment. The Registrar may, after giving the owner of the Geographical Indication an opportunity for being heard, refuse registration of such assignment if it deems the terms unduly restrictive or contrary to the public interest. Further, any licensee or assignee shall be bound by the quality standards and production methods associated with the registered Geographical Indication as defined under this Act.

Any person who, without due cause or reasonable excuse, knowingly uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, or any mark which is likely to be confused with such registered trade mark, shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved proprietor, issue a notice requiring the offending party to cease such use and submit evidence of compliance within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the offender subject to further penalties including but not limited to fines up to one million rupees and potential injunctions preventing continued infringement. The index names proprietors are deemed vital for enforcement proceedings under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a proprietor of an existing geographical indication, not registered under this Act but otherwise eligible for registration, may grant exclusive licenses relating to specific industrial applications of that indication. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry, detailing the scope of permitted use, including product categories and territorial limitations. Any assignment of such a license requires prior notification to the Registry. Infringement unregistered of a geographical indication, even where no registration exists, is actionable under this Act, provided that the proprietor has granted licenses as described above; subsequent licensees shall be bound by the terms of their respective agreements. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the enforcement of these licenses and may require periodic reporting on compliance with agreed-upon usage parameters.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or an authorized signatory, including a legal practitioner representing the applicant. The Registrar may require further documentation to ascertain the identity and authority of any such legal practitioner, particularly where the applicant is a body corporate or a partnership firm. Provided that, if the application relates to a layout-design generated in the course of employment, the verification shall also state the terms under which the layout-design was created and assign ownership rights as provided herein. Any alteration made to the verified document after its initial submission will invalidate the registration process unless approved by the Registrar following notification from the applicant or their legal practitioner.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a sound recording shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year in which the work is first published. Provided that, where the ownership of the sound recording vests in a person other than the producer thereof, such copyright shall endure for a period not exceeding fifty years from the date of publication, unless a longer term is agreed upon in writing between the producer and the owner. The right to reproduce a sound recording shall be deemed an exclusive right, subject to any license granted under this Act or as provided herein. Any person infringing upon said rights may be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of commercial loss suffered by the copyright holder.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to an application and payment of prescribed fees, unconditionally registrar shall grant a license permitting the use of their trademark by another party where such license specifies the geographical area and range of goods or services covered. This authorization may include provisions for royalty payments to be remitted directly to the proprietor, as determined within the licensing agreement. Provided that any assignment of rights under this license must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by evidence of consent from the original trade mark owner. Further, the Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such licenses and assignments, accessible for inspection upon request. Any alteration to the scope or duration of a granted license requires prior approval from both the proprietor and the licensee, and subsequent notification to the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor trade mark shall be deemed to include any mark used or proposed to be used, whether descriptive or not, that distinguishes goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and is registered under this Act. A proprietor may assign his rights in a proprietor trade mark, including the right to sue for infringement, subject to any conditions specified during registration. The owner of a proprietor trade mark shall be entitled to prevent the use by any person of identical or confusingly similar marks in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the trade mark is registered, as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining priority under this Act, the date application patent is deemed to be the earlier of the date on which the application was first filed in India, or the date on which the corresponding application, if any, was first filed in a convention country. Provided that where an application for patent has been made within twelve months from the date of filing a corresponding application abroad, and the applicant fails to comply with the requirements of sub-section (2) of section 8, the application shall be deemed to have been filed on the later of those two dates. Subject to compliance with regulations regarding provisional applications, an applicant shall furnish such particulars as are prescribed relating to the invention claimed. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating adherence to these stipulations before proceeding with examination.

Any person aggrieved by the registration or non-registration of a geographical indication may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to appeal to the High Court. Where it is demonstrated that the continued use of a geographical indication complained of constitutes an unfair trade practice or misrepresentation likely to deceive or cause confusion, the Board shall order its cessation and impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each instance of infringement. Further penalties may be levied where the violation is repeated, potentially doubling the initial fine. The registration variety of a geographical indication shall not protect trivial or minor deviations from the registered form, provided that such variations do not mislead consumers regarding origin.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a public record of all registered draft regulations submitted pursuant to applications for trademark certification. An applicant seeking registration of a mark relating to geographical indications may submit, along with their application, proposed draft regulations governing the use and quality control of goods bearing that mark. These registered draft regulations shall be binding on all users of the certified trade mark, subject to any modifications approved by the Registrar. Any alteration to a registered draft regulation requires prior notification to the Registry and subsequent approval following public consultation as provided herein. The applicant shall ensure that the proposed draft regulations are consistent with existing laws relating to consumer protection and fair trade practices. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or revocation of registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a layout design relation shall exist where two or more persons collaborate in the creation of an integrated circuit layout-design and one person is designated as the owner for the purposes of registering the said layout-design under this Act. Such designation shall be evidenced by a written agreement executed prior to the filing of the application for registration, specifying the respective contributions of each collaborating party. The owner, as defined herein, may grant licenses or assign rights relating to the registered layout-design subject to adherence to the terms outlined in the aforementioned written agreement. Provided that any subsequent transfer of ownership shall require consent from all parties initially involved in establishing the layout design relation, unless otherwise stipulated within their original agreement.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date when the infringement is reasonably suspected to have taken place, subject to just and equitable considerations as determined by the relevant judicial authority. The remedies available to the patentee include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, damages sustained by the patentee due to the infringement, and delivery up or destruction of the patented article constituting the infringement. It is provided that a finding of non-infringement shall not preclude a subsequent action based on substantially identical facts. The determination of whether an alleged act constitutes an *invention* requires consideration of its novelty and inventive step as defined herein.

Where an application for registration is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of rejection. Such appeal shall only be entertained if the appellant deposits with the Tribunal such fee as may be prescribed. The Tribunal shall give notice to the Registrar and any other interested party, affording them an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal under the relevant provisions concerning appeals from tribunals. It is provided that the established registry shall maintain a record of all appeals filed and their corresponding outcomes, accessible for public inspection as may be directed by the Central Government.

An application for patent registration shall include a complete specification describing the invention and setting forth the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention. For the purposes of this Act, an "amendment specification document" is defined as any written material submitted to the Controller after the initial filing date of the application, which alters or clarifies aspects of the original complete specification. Such amendment specification documents may include drawings, claims, or descriptions relating to the invention. The acceptance of an amendment specification document shall be subject to the condition that it does not alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed and is consistent with the information provided during the application registration process.

Where an invention has been patented under this Act, and the patentee demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the invention is being commercially used within India, a right of action shall accrue to the patentee for infringement. Any person who, without authorisation from the patentee, makes, constructs, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports into India any patented article, or attempts so to do, shall be deemed to have infringed the patent and is liable for damages. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint of infringement, issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, provided that such actions demonstrably impede the use invention by others. Penalties for wilful infringement as determined under this Act will apply.

An application for a patent shall disclose the matter which the invention is said to relate to, and it must state the prior art knowledge relating to the subject matter. Where an applicant seeks protection through offices patent, they must demonstrate that the claimed invention is novel and involves inventive step over existing technology; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The description of the invention shall extend to such particulars as would enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. Any drawings filed with the application shall conform to prescribed standards, provided that deficiencies may be rectified upon written notification from the patent office.

Applications for registration of literary works, including computer programs and databases, shall be submitted to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form, accompanied by two certified copies of the work. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue a receipt and assign it an acknowledgement number. The applicant may subsequently request a status update regarding their application through the online portal maintained by the Copyright Office. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the work is original and eligible for registration under this Act, provisional registration shall be granted. Any party disputing the originality or ownership of a work undergoing registration may file an objection with the High Court within sixty days from the date of publication of notice of the application in the Official Gazette.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and the accused pleads registration, the prosecution shall bear the burden of proving the validity of the said registration. Provided that, if the accused successfully establishes material inconsistencies in the record of opposition or examination proceedings before the Trade Marks Registry, the court may direct the prosecution to produce such records for further scrutiny. Failure to do so shall render the trade mark registration liable to be presumed valid for the purposes of the trial. Any person aggrieved by an order directing production of records may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of such order; and penalties for wilful obstruction of justice in relation to these proceedings shall apply as provided herein.

Where a complaint alleging an infringement of a registered trademark is filed before the relevant intellectual property forum, the complainant shall bear the onus of demonstrating prima facie evidence of use ascribing the alleged offence reason to the respondent. The respondent may then present counter-evidence refuting such use or asserting fair dealing under this Act. Provided that, if the respondent claims prior honest concurrent use, they must demonstrate continuous and contemporaneous usage predating the complainant’s registration, subject to conditions prescribed herein regarding geographical limitations and potential consumer confusion. Any appeal against a finding of infringement shall be limited to arguments pertaining directly to the assessment of evidence concerning the alleged offence reason and its impact on the likelihood of deception among consumers.

Where a patent has been granted to a government undertaking engaged in the manufacture or production of essential goods, the Central Government may, subject to conditions as provided herein, issue a compulsory licence if it is satisfied that the patented invention is not made available to the public at a reasonable price within a period of three years from the date of grant. Any person aggrieved by such action may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s publication. Failure to comply with the conditions stipulated in the compulsory license shall render the licensee liable for penalties, including revocation of the licence and imposition of fines not exceeding five per centum of the turnover derived from the patented invention's exploitation.

An application for registration as an issued breeder shall include a detailed statement specifying the derivation of the plant variety, including parentage and any innovative selection or hybridization techniques employed. The application must further identify the geographical location where the initial experimentation and evaluation were conducted, along with evidence demonstrating the novelty and distinctiveness of the variety relative to existing cultivars. Where the applicant claims rights based on traditional breeding methods, documentation substantiating continuous cultivation and propagation by farmers within a defined community may be required as provided herein. The Authority shall consider any objections raised concerning the veracity of these claims before proceeding with assessment; failure to adequately substantiate derivation may result in rejection of the application.

Where proceedings are instituted under this Act challenging the validity of a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition, the burden shall lie upon the petitioner alleging non-infringement to demonstrate that the claimed invention does not satisfy the requirements for a requires patented article as defined herein. It is provided that such demonstration may be achieved by establishing through expert testimony and comparative analysis that the marketed product contains substantially similar active ingredients and dosages to those disclosed in the patent specification, notwithstanding minor variations in excipients or manufacturing processes. Furthermore, any argument asserting that a trade mark consists of a distinctive packaging configuration shall not preclude consideration of the underlying chemical composition’s novelty and inventive step; such arguments are subject to review by the relevant authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice applicant” is defined as an individual or body corporate who has duly filed a request with the Trade Marks Registry to be informed of the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark. Such notice shall be provided in the prescribed form and manner, as detailed in the First Schedule. A notice applicant may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, receive information regarding any subsequent proceedings relating to that trade mark application. The Registrar shall not be obliged to provide notice where the applicant has elected to waive such notification. Further, a notice applicant retains no rights to use registered trade marks.

An aggrieved party seeking review of a decision rendered concerning rectification proceedings initiated under this Act may file an application for an 112a order appellate with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such application must specify the grounds upon which the original determination is challenged, and shall be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documents pertaining to the initial adjudication. The Tribunal shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity to present arguments and evidence in support of their respective positions. Decisions rendered by the Tribunal under this provision are final subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Trade Marks Registry shall direct that the acceptance be published in the Official Gazette. Any person considering himself aggrieved by such publication or by the acceptance of the trade mark may, within four weeks from the date of such publication, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, setting forth particulars of the grounds on which he bases his objection. The Registrar shall give reasonable opportunity to both the applicant and the opponent to be heard under this Act. It is provided that where the goods or services specified in the application are not clearly defined, the gazette require goods specification may be challenged as unduly broad. The decision of the Registrar shall be final, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Central Government shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the manner issuing certificates of registration relating to layout designs and integrated circuits. Such prescriptions may specify forms for application, declarations required from applicants, and procedures for verification of claims made therein. The chairperson shall ensure that all notifications issued under this Act are consistent with established principles of intellectual property law and international best practices. Provided that, where the Central Government deems it necessary to amend or clarify the manner issuing such certificates, a draft notification shall be published for public feedback prior to finalization. This process is subject to review by an advisory committee constituted as provided herein.

A services trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to a prior registered trade mark if, considering the goods or services for which the marks are used or proposed to be used, and having regard to the nature of those goods or services, a relevant consumer is likely to believe that the services provided under the later mark are connected with the business of the proprietor of the earlier mark. Provided that, such likelihood shall not be presumed, but must be determined based on evidence adduced before the Registrar. Any person alleging that a proposed trade mark is deceptively similar may institute an opposition proceeding as provided herein, submitting documentary proof demonstrating the existence and reputation of their prior registered services trade mark and detailing the grounds for objection to registration. The Registrar shall consider all submitted evidence in determining the merits of such an opposition.

For the purposes of this Act, “use registered trade” with respect to a trademark shall mean the employment of the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, or identical thereto, including but not limited to its appearance on labels, packaging, advertising materials, and directly associated with the offering for sale or distribution thereof. Such use shall be deemed continuous where it occurs repeatedly over a period sufficient to indicate an intention to maintain the mark’s presence in the market. A proprietor seeking to demonstrate continued *use registered trade* may submit an affidavit provided under oath detailing such usage, including dates and geographical scope, subject to verification by the Registrar.

Where any person institutes an action claiming to be the owner copyright case of a copyrighted work and fails to establish such ownership to the satisfaction of the Court, that person shall be liable to pay costs including reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the defendant. Any infringement of copyright under this Act may be subject to damages not less than five per cent nor more than ten per cent of the actual loss or damage proved to have been caused to the owner by the infringing act. Further, where an infringer is found to have acted with knowledge of the copyright existing in the work, enhanced penalties as determined by the Court shall apply. The Court may also issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and order the destruction of infringing copies.

Any individual, firm, company or other body corporate who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, for any purpose whatsoever, a board use layout which is substantially similar to the registered layout-design shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Tribunal. Such damages shall not be less than five per cent of the cost of production of the integrated circuit incorporating the infringing layout or such higher amount as the Tribunal may deem just under this Act, taking into account the extent of the infringement and any loss suffered by the proprietor. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may issue an injunction restraining the infringer from further making or selling integrated circuits utilizing the unauthorized board use layout, provided that the proprietor demonstrates continuing harm.

An effected international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations or restrictions contained therein and shall confer upon the proprietor the same rights and remedies as if it were a registered trade mark under this Act, but only in relation to the territory of India and for the goods or services specified in the international registration. Provided that where an international registration includes designations for more than one country, including India, any subsequent amendment affecting the designation of India shall be treated as an effected international registration from the date of its effectuation under the International Convention. The Registrar may require evidence to satisfy him regarding the status and extent of such effected international registration before accepting it for record purposes. Any opposition proceedings relating to an effected international registration shall be conducted in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

Where a patent has become *patent expired*, as determined by the expiry of the prescribed term under this Act, any person may apply to the Controller for an entry in the safeguards prescribed register pertaining to that invention. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is claimed that the continued protection afforded through registration is necessary to safeguard public interest or national security. The Controller may, after affording due opportunity for hearing to all interested parties and considering representations made, direct the inclusion of such patent within the safeguards register, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India, seeking to benefit from the protections afforded by the Madrid Protocol, shall be permitted to grant a license conferring rights relating to the use and exploitation of that trade mark within designated territories. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, provided that the terms are clearly defined within the licensing agreement and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Further, where an international registration incorporates a designation for India based on an earlier Indian application, any subsequent assignment of rights in the underlying patent addition relating to the trade mark shall be deemed to include assignment of the corresponding trade mark registration itself, subject to notification to the Controller. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in ensuring compliance with applicable laws within each designated territory where the licensed trade mark is utilized.

A permitted register trade mark is defined as a trade mark that has been entered upon the Register under this Act and remains so until removed therefrom or subject to an order for rectification. For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief in proceedings concerning a permitted register trade mark, such registration shall be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India relating to the goods or services specified in the register. A trade mark may be considered for inclusion on the permitted register if it is distinctive in its nature and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a statement specifying whether the applicant claims the layout design as an original work, and if so, detailing the nature of their contribution to its creation. Where multiple entities have participated in the conception and execution of a layout design, the application must clearly identify all such participants and state their respective roles in establishing the layout design relation. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the extent of each participant’s involvement, particularly where disputes arise concerning ownership or authorship. Such information shall be deemed confidential and accessible only to parties directly involved under this Act. Failure to accurately disclose the details pertaining to the layout design relation will render the application liable for rejection.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a valid layout-design registration relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses conferring rights to use or exploit such registered layout design, either wholly or partially, for commercial purposes. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall specify the duration, geographical scope, and field of application of the granted right. Assignment of layout designs, including those subject to existing licenses, is permissible with the written consent of all relevant licensees, provided that such assignment does not prejudice any rights already vested in them under this Act. For civil court purposes, disputes arising from licensing agreements or assignments shall be adjudicated according to principles of equity and fairness, considering the reasonable expectations of both licensors and licensees at the time of contract formation. The Registrar may issue guidelines regarding standard license terms for certain categories of integrated circuits.

For the purposes of this Act, “trade mark identity” shall be determined considering the visual appearance, phonetic representation, descriptive content, and conceptual meaning conveyed by the sign. A sign possessing substantial trade mark identity with an earlier registered trade mark shall preclude registration unless it is demonstrated that the conflicting use will not cause confusion among consumers. The Registrar may consider entries in the design register when assessing trade mark identity, particularly where a design incorporates elements of a proposed trade mark; however, such consideration does not automatically establish or negate trade mark identity as provided herein. Any proprietor seeking to challenge registration based on lack of distinctiveness shall bear the onus of proving absence of trade mark identity.

For the purposes of this Act, "commercial exploitation" with respect to a registered layout-design shall include any act that directly or indirectly utilizes the protected design for commercial advantage. Such acts encompass, but are not limited to, reproduction, imitation, and distribution of the layout-design. The right to commercial exploitation is contingent upon the validity of the registration and subject to any conditions imposed during the grant process. A person claiming entitlement to a layout-design may file a date application patent demonstrating prior rights, provided that such claim is substantiated with documentary evidence as prescribed herein. Any act constituting commercial exploitation without authorization shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

Where any person, acting on behalf of or in connection with a commercial establishment engaged in the reproduction, distribution, or public display of copyrighted works, wilfully contravenes any provision under this Act, or abets such contravention, it shall constitute a commission offence. The court may, upon conviction, impose a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Where the offence is committed by a partnership firm, every partner shall be deemed guilty of the offence and liable to punishment. Further, any officer or employee directly involved in the commission of such an offence within the establishment shall also be subject to prosecution and penalties as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted as an application patent invention, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights pertaining thereto, subject to any licenses previously granted under this Act. Such licenses may be assigned or transferred wholly or in part, provided that prior written consent of the Controller is obtained for assignments affecting the scope of exclusivity originally defined within the license agreement. Further, where a licensee seeks to sublicense the patented technology, they shall notify the registered proprietor and provide details of the proposed sublicensing arrangement. The registered proprietor may, within sixty days from receipt of such notification, raise objections which, if not addressed satisfactorily by the licensee, may be grounds for cancelling registration under this Act. Any assignment or sublicense must be executed in the prescribed manner and duly recorded with the Controller.

Where an application for grant of a patent relates to a process by which a substance or article is manufactured, any person claiming to be adversely affected by the manufacture, use or sale of the patented product may petition the Controller. Such petitions shall detail the grounds upon which the claim is based and provide evidence substantiating the alleged adverse impact on the petitioner’s business interests. The Controller may, after affording the applicant and the producers a reasonable opportunity for being heard, direct that the patent be revoked or modified if it is determined that the patented process has demonstrably prejudiced the established commercial activities of domestic producers. Decisions regarding such petitions shall be referred to a Bench consisting of not less than three members of the Controller’s office, ensuring impartial consideration and adherence to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar General plant relating to the registration, revocation, or amendment of a plant variety protection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and stating specifically the grounds on which the appeal is based. Provided that, where an order has been passed by the Registrar General plant imposing a penalty under this Act, the aggrieved party may also seek remedies available to them under the Customs Act 1962 concerning seizure of goods related to the infringing variety. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be rejected by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the design incorporates an element substantially copied from an existing layout-design. Such rejection shall be accompanied by written reasons detailing the alleged infringement and specifying the prior layout-design in question. The applicant shall then have a period of sixty days from the date of notification of such rejection to submit a reasoned response, including counter-evidence, disputing the Registrar’s findings. Upon receipt of this response, the Registrar may either uphold the initial rejection or, if satisfied that the concerns are unfounded, proceed with registration as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards as prescribed. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may specify territory, time period, and type of goods covered by the authorization. Where an assignment of a registered Geographical Indication is made, the assignee shall forthwith notify the Registrar in writing of such assignment, including details of the assignor and the date of transfer. Failure to do so will render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the validity of any license or assignment granted under this Act. Any person claiming rights through a license or assignment shall be bound by the terms thereof, provided that such claims are made promptly and relating plaintiff forthwith to the registered proprietor.

Where a claim is made alleging infringement of a registered layout design, the aggrieved party shall institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority as provided herein. Such claim may assert that an unauthorized person has reproduced, imitated, or otherwise exploited a layout design connected to the registered work, and further alleges substantial similarity exists between the infringing layout design and the original, thereby creating confusion amongst consumers regarding the source of the goods or services associated with said designs. The respondent shall be afforded full opportunity to present evidence rebutting this assertion; however, the authority may consider expert testimony concerning the overall impression created by each layout design in determining whether infringement has occurred, subject to principles of natural justice and due process.

Where any person has made use of a registered trade mark without authorization from the proprietor, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, the proprietor may institute proceedings for recovery of damages. Such damages shall include loss suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing use, together with any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized exploitation of the trademark. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the person from further using the registered trade mark or any confusingly similar representation. It is provided that in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall consider factors including the extent of the infringement and the goodwill associated with the registered *trade mark used*. Any order for account of profits shall be subject to a deduction for any sums which the infringer duly paid to the proprietor as royalties or license fees.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against any decision relating to the revocation of a registration, the Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions herein, confirm, reverse or modify the order appealed from. It shall be open for the appellant to demonstrate that the registered trade mark has not been used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered during the period of five years preceding the date of the application for revocation; and further, that such non-use was unintentional and without reasonable cause. The Board may require the proprietor of the mark uses registered to provide evidence substantiating continued use, failing which the appeal shall be dismissed. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer a further appeal to the Supreme Court.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act by a notice opposition applicant, the applicant for registration shall have the right to file a counterstatement setting forth reasons why the trade mark should be registered. The Registrar shall consider all submissions made in the notice of opposition and the counterstatement, and may afford both parties an opportunity for oral hearing if deemed necessary. Should either party fail to comply with the timelines prescribed herein, the Registrar may proceed ex parte. Any decision rendered by the Registrar concerning such opposition is subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority. Further, any aggrieved party may institute proceedings in a decree civil court seeking redressal of grievances arising from the Registrar's order, provided that such action does not preclude an appeal under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of copyright shall submit a prescribed form, duly completed and accompanied by certified copies of the work in question or where such is not feasible, a detailed description thereof. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding ownership and authorship as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Any objection to the registration, based on grounds including lack of originality or prior conflicting claims, may be filed within a period specified herein. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall either approve the application and proceed with granting registration copyright or reject it, providing reasons for the rejection.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, the patent office shall examine whether such method or process is novel and involves an inventive step in relation to the cultivation of plants, trees or shrubs. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates compliance with prescribed guidelines regarding bio-safety assessments and environmental impact studies, as determined by the relevant governmental authority, the application may proceed for further consideration. The patent office shall also require disclosure of any genetically modified organisms utilized within the claimed method, along with a detailed explanation of their potential effects on biodiversity. Further, under this Act, an applicant failing to provide such information is deemed to have abandoned the application.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to attend personally, or by an authorized representative, at the hearing appointed under this Act. The Registrar may, however, upon review of the circumstances and subject to satisfaction that good cause exists, permit the applicant’s absence and proceed with the examination of the application. Where a trade mark is opposed, any person interested shall be entitled to file evidence in support of or opposing the registration. Such a ‘person interested’ includes, but is not limited to, proprietors of earlier marks, and those claiming rights through assignment or succession. The Registrar may require such persons to furnish security for costs incurred by other parties involved in the proceedings relating to the registrar application pr oceeding.

Applications for registration of plant varieties may include a statement regarding anticipated propagation methods and their impact on genetic stability, as provided herein. The Controller General shall maintain a register detailing all registered plant varieties, including dates of initial registration and subsequent amendments relating to variety denomination or essential characteristics. Subject to appeal under this Act, the term of patent protection for such registered plant varieties shall extend for twenty-one years from the date of first filing, unless the invention incorporates a novel biotechnological process which significantly enhances the inherent traits of the original species. The register shall be open to public inspection, subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

The owner of an attributable geographical indication relating to plant material, including but not limited to seeds, seedlings, and propagating material, may grant a license for the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted use, duration, and any royalty payments due to the proprietor. The Registrar General Plant may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating substantial investment in production adhering to the geographical indication’s code of conduct, facilitate negotiations for a non-exclusive license from the proprietor. Assignment of rights pertaining to an attributable geographical indication shall require prior approval of the Registrar General Plant and be subject to conditions ensuring continued adherence to established quality standards; failure to comply may render the assignment voidable. Any sub-licensing is permitted only with explicit written consent from the original proprietor, as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of the film sound recording, reproduces such recording in any form, including but not limited to digital formats for distribution or public display, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at a minimum of ten times the cost of procuring or producing such infringing copy, or rupees one lakh, whichever is greater. Where the infringement is committed by an employee acting within the scope of his employment, the employer shall also be deemed guilty and subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, any equipment used in the commission of this offence may be seized by authorized officers. The owner of a film sound recording may apply to the relevant judicial authority for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a registration notice to the applicant and each opponent specifying the particulars of the trade mark and the grounds of opposition. The manner issuing such registration notices shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act; provided that the Registrar may, at his discretion, permit service by electronic means where both parties consent or where such electronic service is otherwise permissible under applicable law. Failure to comply with the prescribed manner does not invalidate the notice itself but may affect the enforceability of any subsequent orders against a party claiming lack of due notice. Any aggrieved party may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if they demonstrate prejudice arising from irregularities in the issuance of the registration notice, subject to just cause shown.

An application for registration of a new variety may be filed with the Authority, accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its lineage, breeding history, and morphological characteristics, as prescribed in the First Schedule. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the claimed new variety possesses distinctiveness when compared to commonly known varieties of the same species, through rigorous field trials conducted under conditions approved by the Authority. Provided that, if the application relates to a variety derived from an extant variety, the documentation must explicitly detail the derivation process and demonstrate substantial genetic differentiation. The Authority may require further testing or analysis at the applicant's expense to verify these claims. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding registration or rejection of a new variety may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision.

An action alleging infringement registered may be commenced only within the jurisdiction specified under this Act. Where an applicant registration has been refused on grounds pertaining to distinctiveness, subsequent use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for mark by another party shall not constitute evidence against the earlier refusal. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person claiming entitlement to relief in respect of infringement registered, direct the alleged infringer to appear before the Registrar and submit its defence within a period as determined by the Registrar. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed an admission of the allegations contained in the complaint. Any order made under this Act is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to any fees prescribed herein.

Any person found guilty of knowingly using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, without due cause and for fraudulent purposes, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to pay a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. Where such use is committed by an individual who demonstrates, upon investigation, that they were acting under the direction or control of another person and had no direct intent to deceive consumers, the court may, subject to prevailing sentencing guidelines, impose imprisonment for a term which shall not exceed one year; this constitutes an innocently punishable imprisonment. Further, any goods bearing the infringing trademark are liable to be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

Where a person, with intent to deceive, falsely represents that goods or services are connected with any registered trade mark, and such representation is of a nature likely to injure the reputation of the owner of the trade mark, that person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into account the extent of the deception caused, the loss suffered by the trade mark proprietor, and any profits made by the offending party as a result of the falsifies trade mark. Further, under this Act, an injunction may be granted restraining the person from continuing such deceptive practices. It shall binding on the defendant to cease all use of the falsely represented trade mark immediately upon service of the order. Any goods bearing the false representation are subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to compulsory licensing or revocation of registration may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority. The appellate authority shall consider such appeals expeditiously, affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity of being heard. An application sub section regarding the filing of appeals shall prescribe a time limit not exceeding ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against. Provided that the appellate authority may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are adduced. Further, any question concerning the subsistence of a plant variety right or the validity of a registration shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of a decree civil court not subordinate to the High Court. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final and binding, subject to appeal under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Where any person claiming right to a patent, or alleging that the invention claimed in a patent does not satisfy the requirements of this Act, appeals against an order passed by the Controller under this Act, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the appellant has demonstrated, with reasonable certainty and supported by documentary evidence, that the invention was previously published or described in a manner which makes it available to the public, thereby rendering the application ineligible for grant. Further, where such appeal concerns a 73 convention application, the Board shall also examine if the claimed invention was disclosed within the prescribed time limit from the date of first filing in the relevant convention country, and whether any subsequent modifications or additions materially alter the original disclosure to the detriment of public interest.

An aggrieved party against an order passed by the Patent Office relating to a patent grant, revocation, or opposition may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The Appellant shall serve a certified copy of the order appealed against along with the memorandum of appeal upon the Controller and such other persons as are parties to the original proceeding. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the aggrieved party to furnish security for costs. Any application or document filed before the Appellate Board shall be in compliance with the rules made under this Act concerning procedure. The Opposition Board’s records pertaining to the original opposition proceedings shall be available for inspection by the parties involved in the section 94 appeal.

Where an objection is taken by the Examiner under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a services trade mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their response within the time specified in the notice of examination. Should the applicant fail to respond or the response received does not adequately address the grounds of objection, the Registrar may proceed with further investigation and may direct the publication of the trademark for opposition. In any proceeding arising from such a direction, the registrar shall appear on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry and present arguments pertaining to the maintainability of the registration. The applicant retains the right to be heard in person or through an authorized representative.

An application for the grant of a patent shall be made to the Controller in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required under this Act. The applicant shall specify whether the application relates to an invention or to the design thereof, and shall state clearly the claims supported by proper description. Where the applicant is not the true and first inventor, he shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the Controller establishing his right to make the application. Upon receipt of such application, the Controller may direct that the application be accompanied by such additional information as he deems necessary for examination. The Controller shall register patents in accordance with the provisions herein, subject to a search being conducted and an examination undertaken to ascertain novelty and inventive step. Any person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An applicant making a basic application shall furnish, along with the application, certified copies of all drawings relating to the invention. The Controller may require the applicant to amend any claim in the basic application if it is unclear or ambiguous. Where an applicant has previously filed a patent application disclosing subject matter identical or substantially similar to that claimed in the basic application, the Controller shall notify the applicant and provide an opportunity for response before proceeding with examination. Further, the applicant must declare whether the invention relates to any process known prior to the date of filing of the basic application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application under this Act.

Where an author assigns their copyright in a musical composition to a publisher, that assignment shall be deemed valid only if it explicitly details the specific performance rights transferred, including but not limited to mechanical, public, and synchronization licenses. Such assignments may include provisions for reversion of rights should specified sales thresholds not be met within a period of five years from the date of assignment. The assignor retains the right to terminate the assignment under this Act upon providing six months’ written notice to the assignee, provided that such termination does not prejudice any existing license agreements executed by the publisher prior to the notice. Failure to clearly specify rights assigned in the initial documentation renders the assignment unenforceable against third parties claiming interest based on the purported transfer.

For the purposes of this Act, “effect registered trade” means the visual representation of a registered trade mark as it appears on the register maintained under this Act, including any alterations or additions made thereto pursuant to lawful authority. The depiction shall accurately reflect the particulars specified in the provisional specification completed at the time of application for registration, and may include details concerning colour, material, or other distinctive features explicitly described therein. Any subsequent modification to the registered trade mark, subject to provisions regarding rectification proceedings, will be recorded as a new “effect registered trade” replacing the prior depiction.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all patents granted under this Act. This registrar index shall include, for each patent, its registration number, the title of the invention, the name and address of the patentee, the date of grant, and a concise abstract summarizing the subject matter claimed. Further, the registrar index shall indicate any subsequent modifications to the patent, such as assignments or licenses, as recorded under this Act. Any person may inspect the registrar index and obtain certified copies thereof, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

An application for registration of a copyright design shall be accompanied by such information as the Controller may require regarding the applicant and the proprietor of any trade mark or other right claimed in relation to the design. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct that certain features of the design be altered or omitted if they are deemed to conflict with existing registered designs or trademarks. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Controller shall consider any such appeal and issue an appropriate order, which is final subject to further appeal to the High Court. Where a design incorporates elements already disclosed in prior publications, the applicant must provide detailed justification demonstrating originality as provided herein.

Applications filed under this Act shall be examined by the Controller, who may, at any time during the examination, require the applicant to supply further information or clarification relating to the invention described in the application. The applicant shall comply with such requirement within a period specified by the Controller; failure to do so may result in the rejection of the application. Where an objection is taken under this Act regarding novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity for argument and submission of evidence. The decision of the Controller concerning any such objection shall be recorded in writing and communicated to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the patent office may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The patent office is empowered to conduct searches as it deems necessary for examination purposes.

Where a patentee elects to utilize a standardized biological sequence as an element within their patented invention, and such sequence is explicitly referenced by its accession number assigned under a recognized international database, the patentee shall be obligated to grant a non-exclusive license for research purposes relating solely to that specific form reference act. This licensing obligation extends to institutions engaged in academic or governmental research, provided that the terms of the license are determined through arbitration as provided herein. The patentee may stipulate reasonable royalties and conditions regarding publication of findings derived from such licensed use. Further, assignment of rights pertaining to this limited license shall be permissible subject to prior notification to the Controller, who may review for compliance with public interest considerations. Any subsequent commercial exploitation based on these research findings remains solely within the purview of the licensee’s own intellectual property protections.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, electronically searchable, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act and those applications currently undergoing examination. This index shall include, for each entry, the trademark itself, the applicant’s name and address as filed, the goods or services specification associated with the mark, and the date of registration or filing, respectively. Any alteration to these particulars following initial submission requires notification to the Registrar, who may update the registrar index accordingly, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally alter the nature of the trademark or its designated scope. The public shall have access to this registrar index during normal office hours, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Registrar to prevent disruption and ensure data security.

For the purposes of this Act, “form references act” means the process by which information pertaining to an invention’s subject matter is conveyed through depictions, schematics, drawings, models, or other representational media included within a patent application. Such representations shall be considered integral components for understanding the scope and construction of the claimed invention as provided herein. Where such form references incorporate elements derived from prior art publications, the applicant shall provide detailed annotations identifying these sources and demonstrating their adaptation to the inventive concept. The Controller may require further clarification regarding any ambiguity arising from a form reference act during examination under this Act.

An appeal against any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design shall lie to the Authority Appellate Board. The appellant shall, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an application for appeal with the Board, accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that sufficient cause existed, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period. The Board may, while hearing appeals, require the appellant and respondent to furnish further information or documents relevant to the determination of the dispute. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Authority Appellate Board may apply to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

An aggrieved party claiming damages arising from the infringement of an allow application patent shall institute a suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The applicant for such patent, upon demonstrating to the satisfaction of the court that the infringing activity has caused demonstrable financial loss, may be awarded compensation commensurate with the extent of said loss, including lost profits and reasonable costs incurred in pursuing remedies under this Act. However, a claim predicated on an application section 35 objection relating to prior use or publication shall not be entertained unless it is established that the applicant had knowledge of such prior use or publication at the time of filing the patent application. The court may grant interim injunctions restraining further acts of infringement pending final determination of the suit, provided that sufficient cause is shown.

Where an objection is raised before the Registrar alleging that a proposed trade mark has become a well-known trade mark in relation to particular goods or services, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and any proprietor claiming rights under the registered trade mark. Such proprietors may appear and be heard against the objection, presenting evidence demonstrating consumer recognition and distinctiveness acquired through extensive use and advertising. The Registrar may require further submissions from both parties before reaching a determination. An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of the order; provided that the Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the Registrar’s decision, subject to any evidence deemed relevant by the Board itself.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar may, at any time during the pendency of the opposition proceedings, require both the applicant and the opponent to submit documentary evidence affirming their respective claims. Such evidence shall be submitted within such period as the Registrar specifies by order, and failure to comply with that order may result in the Registrar’s decision against the defaulting party. The Registrar is empowered to examine any person under oath or affirmation regarding matters arising during opposition proceedings. Further, a proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be deemed to have knowledge of earlier marks relevant to their application, irrespective of whether those marks were previously brought to their attention. Any use of a *mark* by another party without authorization from the registered proprietor constitutes an actionable infringement if it is determined that such *mark uses registered* trademarks in a manner causing confusion amongst consumers.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant an exclusive license or assign the right to a patent in respect of an invention for which he has filed an application may execute a written instrument specifying the terms and conditions thereof. Such instrument shall clearly define the scope of the licensed rights or assigned interest, referencing specifically the amendment claim specification as it exists at the date of execution. The patentee shall file such instrument with the Controller within three months from the date of its execution; failure to do so may render the license or assignment voidable. Further provision is made that any subsequent amendment claim specification filed after the execution of a licensing agreement shall be deemed to modify the scope of the granted rights proportionally, unless otherwise explicitly agreed upon in writing by all parties involved.

An applicant seeking registration of a services trade mark relating to financial advisory services may submit evidence demonstrating exclusive use through a licensing agreement, provided that such agreement clearly defines the scope and territory of permitted usage. The Registrar shall consider whether the licensed entity’s activities genuinely reflect the nature and quality of the services as initially proposed by the applicant. Where the licensed article incorporates patented technology essential for service delivery, the application must include details regarding patent ownership and any associated royalty obligations. Failure to disclose such information may render the registration vulnerable to challenge under this Act. The Registrar retains discretion to refuse registration if satisfied that the mark’s association with a patented article creates undue confusion within the relevant market segment.

An application for patent shall be deemed to be published upon its entry into the Publication Application Section, subject to compliance with regulations as provided herein. The Controller may direct that an application not be entered into the Publication Application Section if it contains matter which is contrary to law or morality; however, such direction shall only be given after due opportunity has been afforded to the applicant for representation and revision of the offending material. Further, publication shall be withheld where the applicant requests confidentiality under this Act and provides a duly executed request form along with requisite fees, provided that such withholding may not exceed thirty-six months from the date of filing. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding entry into or non-entry into the Publication Application Section may appeal to an appellate authority as prescribed.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, distributes, leases, or offers to lease a layout-design infringing upon a registered certify layout-design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the actual loss suffered by the proprietor nor exceeding fifty lakhs of rupees. Where the infringement is found to have been committed knowingly, the Court may enhance such penalty up to one crore rupees. Further, any goods manufactured or distributed in violation of this Act are deemed contraband and subject to seizure under procedures as provided herein. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent india claim” shall be construed as a statement defining the scope of protection sought for an invention, delineating the subject matter for which exclusive rights are requested. Such a claim must be clear, concise and supported by the description in the patent specification; otherwise, it may be deemed invalid under this Act. The interpretation of a patent india claim shall take into account the entire disclosure of the patent document and any prior art considered during examination. Further, acquiring restrict imposed through an improperly drafted or overly broad claim shall not be enforced if such restriction unduly impedes innovation in related fields.

A user party proceeding, as contemplated under this Act, refers to an instance where a person who is neither the proprietor of a trade mark nor an applicant for registration thereof, but who possesses a license or otherwise has permission to use the trade mark, becomes involved in legal proceedings relating to that trade mark. Such involvement shall occur when the interests of the user party are directly affected by matters under consideration within the proceeding, including, but not limited to, claims of infringement or challenges to validity. The Registrar may, at any stage of a proceeding, determine whether a particular individual qualifies as a user party and is entitled to participate, provided that such determination shall be made in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Where an application has been opposed under this Act, and the Hearing Officer has rendered a decision, any party affected by that decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall lie on a question of law or fact arising out of the decision of the Hearing Officer. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Further, the Board may direct the Registrar to undertake such actions as it deems necessary to ensure compliance with this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to an application section 71 may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order.

Where any goods are seized pursuant to a seizure notice issued under the Customs Act, 1962, and such goods bear a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, the adjudicating officer shall provide written intimation to the proprietor of the said trade mark. Such intimation shall detail the particulars of the seized goods, the date and place of seizure, and the reasons for suspicion of infringement as provided herein. The proprietor may, within thirty days from receipt of such intimation, submit a written representation outlining their claim of ownership and detailing any demonstrable consumer confusion arising from the use of the mark on the imported goods. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, the adjudicating officer shall consider this representation before determining whether confiscation proceedings are warranted.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person alleging interference with their rights under this Act, direct an inquiry to be conducted into the matter. Such inquiry shall ascertain whether the use registered trade mark by another party is causing demonstrable damage to the complainant’s business interests or reputation. The Director General of Trade Marks shall appoint an investigating officer who will record evidence and submit a report within ninety days. If the investigation reveals that the continued use registered trade mark constitutes a violation of equitable considerations, including but not limited to unfair competition or passing off, the Registrar may issue directions restricting such use. These directions are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The complainant shall bear the cost of the inquiry unless it is determined that the complaint was frivolous or vexatious.

For the purposes of this Act, "advertised acceptance" means the publication of a notice by the Registrar indicating that an application for registration of a trade mark has been accepted, either absolutely or conditionally. Such advertisement shall include particulars identifying the trade mark and specifying any conditions to which the acceptance is subject. Where an advertised acceptance relates to a proposed trade mark identical or similar to a previously registered trade mark, the notice shall also indicate the earlier trade mark and its proprietor. The Registrar may prescribe the form and manner of such advertisements as provided herein. Any challenge to the acceptance under this Act must be made within the period specified in the advertisement.

Where a person alleges infringement of a registered layout design, such person shall file a complaint before the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act was committed, or where the cause of action arose. The complaint shall specify the particulars of the registered layout design, the nature of the alleged infringement, and the relief sought. Upon receipt of such complaint, the Commercial Court may issue interim injunctions restraining the defendant from further infringing activities pending final determination. Evidence pertaining to establishing ownership as the creator layout design shall be presented before the court, including but not limited to documentation demonstrating conception, reduction to practice, and publication. The court shall consider whether the defendant’s integrated circuit layout-design is substantially similar to the registered layout design, taking into account the overall impression created upon an observer skilled in the art.

Where an infringement of patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical substance has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from further acts of manufacture, use, sale or importation. Such injunction may include terms prohibiting the infringing party from exploiting any data generated through reverse engineering of the patented process, provided that such exploitation would constitute an infringement under this Act. The remedies available to a patentee are without prejudice to claims for damages and compensation for losses suffered as a direct consequence of the infringement. Any person found to have knowingly induced or assisted in the infringement shall also be liable for appropriate relief. Further, where the infringing activity involves a substantial misrepresentation concerning the efficacy or safety of the pharmaceutical substance, additional penalties may be imposed as determined by the Controller.

For the purposes of this Act, an “establishment” shall be deemed a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment if it possesses demonstrable physical infrastructure suitable for conducting business operations, including but not limited to office space, warehousing facilities, or manufacturing plants. Such infrastructure must be actively utilized in the promotion, sale, or distribution of goods or services under the trade mark in question.
