An entity maintaining only a registered address or a postal box shall not be considered to possess an establishment as provided herein. This determination is subject to review by the Registrar who may require further documentation substantiating the operational nature and extent of such activities.

A suit alleging a geographical indication falsified may be instituted in the High Court having jurisdiction over the area within which the goods constituting the geographical indication are produced, subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving that their use of a sign similar to a registered goods geographical indication does not indicate an intention to deceive or cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Further, where the plaintiff claims damages arising from such falsification, they must demonstrate actual financial loss attributable directly to the deceptive practices employed by the defendant. The appellate forum may order costs against either party based on the merits of the appeal.

An applicant seeking registration of a literary work, musical work, dramatic work, cinematograph film or sound recording shall submit with the application prescribed forms containing particulars relating to the ownership of copyright in the work. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as he deems necessary for verifying the claim of ownership and authenticity of the work submitted for registration. Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in the work, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present his case under this Act. Registration confers no right of copyright but serves only as prima facie evidence of ownership, subject to the provisions regarding rectification of entries. Any alteration or correction to particulars entered in the Register may be made as provided herein upon application and verification.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a goods geographical indication, or by any act of contravention of the provisions concerning protection afforded thereto, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order or occurrence. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by the Board, subject to review by the appellate authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order issued under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to pay damages, not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable through civil suit. Further, repeat offenders may face prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, in addition to fines as determined by the court.

For the purposes of this Act, “layout-design” means the three dimensional representation of any integrated circuit embodied in a mask; provided that such representation is defined by the arrangement, however expressed, of active and passive components and interconnections on an integrated circuit, and does not include features solely for mechanical support or interconnection with external connectors. A person shall be deemed to have made an application for design apply registration when such application contains all particulars as may be prescribed; further, a layout-design is considered registered upon the grant of a certificate of registration by the Registrar, subject to any appeals under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to comply with all prescribed requirements relating to the submission of documentary evidence substantiating the claimed user date. Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates reasonable cause for non-compliance, such as unforeseen technical difficulties in procuring requisite records, the Registrar may, at his discretion and after due consideration of representations made by the applicant, reinstate the application. The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain accurate and readily accessible records detailing all instances of use of the mark within India. Failure to do so may render the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of an application registered proprieto must be brought before the relevant intellectual property tribunal within six months of publication in the Trade Marks Journal.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another party’s use of a sign constitutes an action proceeding infringement under this Act, they shall provide written notice to the alleged infringer detailing the specific infringing activities and outlining the basis for such belief. Such notice must specify the elements constituting the claimed infringement, including but not limited to similarity of signs, identity or relatedness of goods or services, and likelihood of confusion amongst relevant consumers. The proprietor may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, seek an injunction restraining the infringing use. Provided that, any such action proceeding infringement must be initiated within three years from the date of the initial notice, failing which the claim shall be deemed time-barred.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (zb) “trade mark” means a sign, including words, symbols, or logos, used to represent an enterprise and distinguish its goods or services. Any person who, without due cause and with fraudulent intent, applies for registration of a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may institute proceedings in the relevant High Court seeking an injunction restraining infringement under this Act, subject to demonstrating actual and substantial damage resulting from such use. Failure to comply with orders issued pursuant to these provisions will attract penalties including fines not exceeding ten lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license or assign the rights pertaining to a patent granted under this Act, such license or assignment shall be in writing and executed by the patentee or their authorized representative. The Patent Office shall maintain a register of all licenses and assignments recorded as provided herein. Any person seeking to acquire an interest in a patent through license or assignment may apply to the Patent Office for registration, furnishing details including consideration paid, territorial extent, and duration. Subject to payment of prescribed fees, the Patent Office shall record such licenses and assignments, providing notice thereof in the Official Gazette. Provided that any license granted prior to the commencement of this provision which is not registered shall be deemed invalid unless it has been subsequently registered within a period of six months from the date of its execution. The patentee shall retain ownership until full registration occurs.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines and spirits, natural remedies, handicrafts, and manufactured goods shall be made in the prescribed form to the Registrar. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the product or good concerned, the area of its production or association with such territory, and particulars of persons claiming to represent the interests of the producers of the goods. Any objection received under this Act shall be served upon the applicant, who may submit their response within the time specified. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness of the geographical indication and its association with houses parliament year. Decisions regarding objections and responses are appealable to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a design is granted, the person to whom the certificate of registration is issued shall be deemed to be the registration proprietor thereof and shall have exclusive right to exploit the registered design in accordance with the provisions herein. The registration proprietor may assign the entire design or any part thereof, along with the benefit of the registration, to another party subject to compliance with prescribed formalities and payment of requisite fees as determined by the government. Any alteration made to the registered design without prior notification and approval from the Controller shall render the registration proprietor liable for penalties under this Act. Furthermore, the registration proprietor is obligated to renew the registration periodically, failing which it shall be deemed lapsed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a producer of a registered integrated circuit layout design may grant licenses granting rights to utilize the said layout design for commercial production. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacturing, importing, and distributing products incorporating the licensed layout design. Assignment of these licensing rights is permissible, provided that such assignment is documented in writing and registered with the Controller General. The Appellate Board sub-committee may be convened to adjudicate disputes arising from alleged breaches of license agreements or unauthorized assignments, considering factors such as reasonable royalty rates and the extent of infringement. Further, any producer seeking to enforce these provisions must demonstrate valid registration under this Act and adherence to prescribed guidelines relating to layout design protection.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a license granted under section 17 relating to a registered layout-design may be assigned by the licensee, either wholly or partially, provided that such assignment is in writing and duly executed. The assignee shall become vested with all rights and obligations of the original licensee as regards the licensed layout-design. Any transfer of interest in a layout-design, including through mortgage or pledge, requires prior notification to the Registrar of Layout-Designs. Furthermore, where an assignment involves a foreign entity, approval from the Appellate Board is mandatory before registration of such assignment with the Registrar. The Chairperson Appellate Board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, grant or refuse such approval based on considerations of national interest and reciprocity.

Where, upon review under this Act, the Controller finds that a patent application claims an invention disclosed in a corresponding application filed in a 6referred convention country, and such disclosure contains matter not present in the original Indian application, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the claims to conform with the originally filed specification. However, any amendment so made shall only be permissible if it does not substantially alter the nature of the invention as claimed initially. The Controller may, after hearing arguments from both the patent holder and any interested party objecting to the amendment, determine whether such alteration has occurred. This determination is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates prejudice resulting from the Controller’s decision.

Where any individual or entity believes that an unregistered trademark is being used in contravention of provisions under this Act, they may notify the Registrar in writing, specifying the infringing mark, the goods or services affected, and details of the alleged infringement. Such notification shall include evidence substantiating the claim, failing which it may be rejected without further consideration. The Registrar shall then issue a direction to the concerned party to cease the infringing activity within thirty days. Failure to comply with this direction will render the individual or entity liable for damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority and subject to penalties prescribed herein. Any appeal against such a decision is permitted, but will not suspend enforcement.

For the purpose of this Act, “Security India Explanation” means a designation applied to trademarks registered under this Act pertaining exclusively to security-related products and services, including but not limited to surveillance equipment, cybersecurity solutions, and personnel protection devices. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a separate register for Security India Explanations, accessible upon request by authorized government agencies. Applications for registration bearing the Security India Explanation must demonstrate compliance with guidelines issued by the Controller under this Act concerning national security considerations. Such applications may be subject to additional scrutiny and verification procedures as provided herein.

The Authority may, subject to conditions specified therein, grant non-exclusive licenses in respect of rights granted under this Act relating to a plant variety, provided that any such license shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities including but not limited to propagation, sale, and export. Assignment of such licenses is permissible with prior approval from the Authority, and the assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to the original licensee. Further, where an assignment or a license involves benefit-sharing obligations as determined under this Act, the assignor or licensor shall remain jointly and severally liable for ensuring compliance until the expiry of the relevant period. The proceeds derived from such licenses and assignments shall constitute fund which will be utilized exclusively for supporting research relating to indigenous plant varieties and promoting farmers’ rights, as provided herein.

Where any dispute arises concerning whether a territory constitutes a Contracting State for the purposes of this Act, such determination shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar’s initial assessment regarding the territorial extent of trademark protection granted under this Act is deemed prima facie correct; however, this presumption may be challenged by any aggrieved party demonstrating demonstrable evidence to the contrary. Further, a challenge predicated on the assertion that a territory's legal framework fundamentally diverges from principles recognized as essential for maintaining reciprocal trade relations shall be entertained. The burden of proof regarding such divergence rests entirely upon the appellant and must be substantiated with documentary evidence admissible under the Evidence Act.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to lack novelty if it discloses subject matter which is not new, and further, that such substance means new with respect to prior publications or use anywhere in the world. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the inventive step involved in the claimed invention, including detailed experimental data and comparative analysis against existing technologies. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation within the prescribed time shall render the application liable for rejection. Where an invention relates to a process by which a substance is produced, the patent shall only be granted if the process itself is new. The applicant shall pay the prescribed registry fee at the time of filing the application and subsequent fees as stipulated under this Act; non-payment will result in abandonment of the application.

Where any person seeks revocation of a trade mark registration under this Act, alleging that the trade marks proprietor has not used the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered during a continuous period of five years immediately preceding the date of application for revocation, the registrar shall consider whether such non-use was involuntary. Provided that, if the applicant for revocation can demonstrate that the non-use occurred as a result of any act or omission by the trade marks proprietor intentionally creating confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services, the registrar may proceed with the assessment of revocation without further inquiry into involuntariness. Further, where such an application is made, the trade marks proprietor shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence rebutting the allegation of non-use and demonstrating continued use, even if limited in scope.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused, and the applicant appeals such refusal under this Act, the appellate authority shall consider whether the grounds presented demonstrate a likelihood of confusion arising amongst consumers. It is provided that if the appellant establishes, to the satisfaction of the appellate authority, that the mark sought to be registered possesses distinctive character acquired through use subsequent to its initial application, notwithstanding any prior conflicting registration, the trademark may be granted new patent protection subject to conditions as deemed appropriate. For purposes of this appeal, "registered" means registered under this Act and shall include trademarks previously considered but ultimately rejected due to similarity with existing marks. The decision of the appellate authority is final, subject to further appeal to the High Court.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license permitting the use of the mark upon specified goods or services, such license may include provisions relating to the assignment of rights arising from instances of used falsifying trade. The licensee shall be deemed to hold assignable rights in respect of any action brought under this Act against a third party for infringement predicated on the licensee’s unauthorized application of the registered trade mark, provided that such application constitutes used falsifying trade and directly results from a breach of the licensing agreement. Further, the registered proprietor may, by written consent, authorize the licensee to assign these rights to another entity, subject to conditions stipulated within the assignment deed. Any such assignment shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry for evidentiary purposes and shall not prejudice the original proprietor’s right to pursue remedies against infringers independent of the license or subsequent assignment.

Any person applying for registration of a plant variety shall propose an initial denomination that is distinct and readily recognizable, and such denomination shall not include descriptive terms relating to the variety’s characteristics or those of its seed. The Authority may reject a proposed denomination if it finds that it conflicts with existing denominations registered under this Act or any other law, or if it is likely to cause confusion amongst farmers. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment denomination will render the registration application liable for rejection and subsequent penalties as provided herein. Furthermore, unauthorized use of a protected denomination by any third party shall constitute an infringement subject to civil remedies and criminal prosecution under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks incorporate or closely resemble emblems denoting government authority, subject to provisions allowing use with explicit permission. Any person aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal order. Further, where an applicant knowingly submits false information regarding prior trade mark usage or ownership during registration proceedings, that constitutes a cognizance offence under this Act and is punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain records detailing all applications, refusals, and appeals concerning government emblems.

An applicant seeking a patent application shall furnish with the request, particulars as to priority if the invention is claimed as an improvement on or modification of an existing technology. The prescribed fee for such a request shall be remitted at the time of filing and may be subject to revision by notification in the Official Gazette. Where the Controller considers that the information provided regarding priority is insufficient or unclear, he may require the applicant to submit further particulars within a specified period. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the patent application liable for rejection under this Act. The Controller may also direct the applicant to amend any claim where it appears ambiguous or does not clearly define the scope of protection sought. Any such direction must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation, and the applicant shall have an opportunity to respond before a final determination is made regarding the validity of the patent application.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed report verifying its distinctness, uniformity, and stability, as determined through rigorous field trials conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Central Government. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional data or conduct further tests if reasonable doubt exists regarding the veracity of the initial findings. Should any objection be raised against the registration by an interested party, the matter shall be referred to the authority for adjudication. The authority registrar case determination shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector, prioritizing information demonstrating adherence to established protocols concerning genetic purity and lineage tracing. Any decision made by the authority is subject to appeal before a designated appellate body.

An application for registration of a utility model may include an amendment specification relating to the matter disclosed in the original application, subject to the provisions herein. Such amendment shall be limited to clarifying or correcting descriptions, drawings, or claims; it shall not substantively alter the inventive concept underlying the utility model as initially presented. The Controller General shall require detailed justification for any proposed amendment, including a statement affirming its consistency with the disclosure in the initial application and demonstrating that the amended specification remains within the scope of what is considered obvious to a person skilled in the art. Any amendment affecting the essential features of the invention must be accompanied by the prescribed fee as determined under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the computer inspection register relating to a registered trade mark may file a written complaint with the Trade Marks Registry within sixty days of such entry’s publication. The complaint shall specify the grounds upon which the aggrieved party challenges the accuracy or propriety of the information recorded, and must be accompanied by supporting documentation as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Registrar shall afford the applicant whose details are subject to challenge an opportunity to submit a written response within thirty days. Failure to respond may be treated as acquiescence. The Registrar shall then issue an order either confirming, modifying, or deleting the entry in question. Any party dissatisfied with this order may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where any proprietor institutes legal proceedings against a person alleging infringement of a geographical indication registered under this Act and fails to substantiate such allegation before the relevant judicial authority, the Court shall have the power to order, as part of its judgment, court directed forfeiture of assets acquired or utilized by the complainant in connection with the aforementioned litigation. Such forfeiture shall be limited to those assets demonstrably employed for pursuing the unsuccessful claim, including but not limited to legal fees and associated expenses. Provided that, where the Court finds evidence of a bonafide belief in the existence of infringement, it may exercise discretion regarding the extent of such forfeiture, subject to ensuring fairness and proportionality between the frivolous nature of the allegation and the potential impact on the complainant’s livelihood.

An applicant seeking to amend a patent specification after the date of publication under this Act shall file a request in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. Such request must clearly identify the specific portions of the original specification intended for alteration and provide a reasoned justification demonstrating how the proposed amendment maintains novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The Controller may allow such amendment only if satisfied that the changes do not substantially alter the scope of protection initially claimed and are consistent with the disclosure present in the prior art considered during examination. Further, any patent amendment specification shall be accompanied by an undertaking from the applicant confirming due diligence has been exercised to ensure compliance with all procedural requirements under this Act.

Where a patent granted persons elects to register a security interest relating to their patent rights under this Act, such registration shall be effected by filing with the Controller a prescribed form detailing the nature and extent of the interest claimed. The application for registration must specify the name and address of the patentee or patentees, as well as the details of the secured party. Subject to regulations framed by the government, fees payable for registration shall be determined based on the value of the patent rights covered by the security interest. Any subsequent transfer or modification of such a registered security interest requires notification to the Controller and may necessitate further registration under this Act, provided that the original patent remains valid and in force.

Where an invention is disclosed as being derived from an earlier application filed in an invention convention country, and it appears to the Controller that the applicant has failed to comply with the requirements regarding the priority claim under this Act, the Controller may issue a notice of objection. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the non-compliance and afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard. If, after such hearing, the Controller is satisfied that the failure constitutes a material deficiency in the application, he may reject the patent application entirely or require amendment to ensure full compliance with the provisions relating to convention applications. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

The Controller of Patents shall entertain an appeal against any decision or order made by the patent office central relating to the grant, revocation, or sealing of a patent. Such appeals may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said decision or order to the appellant, subject to provisions for condoning delay where sufficient cause is demonstrated. The Central Government may, by regulations, prescribe the procedure for such appeals, including limitations on the grounds upon which an appeal may be based and requirements regarding supporting documentation. Provided that any challenge to a finding of fact made by the patent office central shall be supported by substantial evidence presented during the original examination proceedings or subsequent hearings.

Any person who, following provisions act in contravention of this Act or any rules made thereunder, makes, uses, imports, exports, distributes, sells, offers to sell, or knowingly deals with goods or services marked with a false trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Where an offence involves the use of a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, such person shall also be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods or services sold. Repeated offences may attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a registered trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark for the sale or advertising of goods or services shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The owner of a registered trade mark may apply to the relevant authority seeking injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and claiming damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the unauthorized use. This provision shall not preclude civil remedies available under this Act.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of a patent under this Act, they shall institute proceedings before the appropriate forum as provided herein. The claimant must demonstrate prima facie evidence of validity and ownership of the article respect patent being asserted. Failure to do so will result in dismissal of the claim without further hearing. In cases where contributory infringement is alleged, the party claiming such infringement bears the burden of proving knowledge and participation in the infringing act. Further, any entity collecting royalties on behalf of a patent holder shall remit fees collected as copyright society fee directly to the Controller General within three months of each financial year-end; default will attract penalties as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another has engaged in acts constituting passing off, and such allegation involves a comparison between goods or services offered by the defendant and those for which a trade mark is registered under this Act, the defendant may present evidence demonstrating due compliance with any registration notice published pursuant to the provisions herein. Such evidence shall be considered alongside all other submissions during proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. The aggrieved party shall bear the onus of proving that the defendant’s actions create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services in question, subject to the defendant's right to challenge this finding on appeal.

Where an objection is taken against a patent application on the ground that the claims are unduly broad or otherwise define an *invention far claimed*, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the claims, subject to the condition that such amendment does not alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed in the specification. The Controller may allow such amendments if satisfied that they address the specific concerns raised in the objection and maintain compliance with the requirements under this Act regarding clarity and support within the description. Any party aggrieved by a decision permitting or rejecting claim amendments may appeal to the Appellate Board, presenting arguments demonstrating either undue breadth or lack of adequate support for the amended claims. The Board’s determination shall be final, provided that it is not contrary to principles of natural justice.

Any party aggrieved by a published application for registration of a design may, within six months from the date of publication, file a notice of opposition with the Designs Office. Such opposition shall be limited to grounds alleging that the registered design lacks novelty or originality as defined under this Act, or that it does not involve an aesthetic feature. The opponent must specify the particulars of their claim and provide supporting documentation demonstrating prior use or disclosure of a substantially similar design. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the opposition being deemed inadmissible. The Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition, after which proceedings will be conducted as provided herein.

The operation of a copyright society established under this Act shall be subject to rigorous oversight by the designated governmental authority, ensuring equitable distribution of royalties amongst its members and adherence to prescribed guidelines concerning licensing practices. Any member aggrieved by the actions or decisions of such a copyright society relating to royalty allocation, licensing terms, or membership disputes may appeal directly to the appellate forum as provided herein. The appellate forum shall consider evidence presented by both the copyright society and the aggrieved member, with particular regard to whether the society’s conduct demonstrably deviates from principles of fairness and transparency. Decisions of the appellate forum are final, subject only to further judicial review on grounds limited to jurisdictional error or violation of fundamental rights.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a filed registry fee as prescribed under this Act; provided that where an applicant elects to file an application electronically, the applicable filed registry fee shall be adjusted as notified by the Registrar from time to time. The amount of the filed registry fee is subject to revision based on prevailing economic conditions and may vary depending upon the class or classes of goods or services for which registration is sought. Failure to remit the prescribed filed registry fee at the time of application will render the application void ab initio. Any deficiency in payment, discovered subsequent to initial processing, shall necessitate a notice issued by the Registrar requiring immediate remittance within thirty days; failing compliance, the application may be deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence of financial hardship, entertain an appeal for waiver or reduction of the filed registry fee, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a competent authority under this Act may appeal to a Bench constituted for that purpose. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. Failure to comply with this time limit shall ordinarily preclude the appellate Bench from entertaining the appeal, subject to just cause being shown. The appellate Bench may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any decision made by a Bench regarding transmission operation law disputes is final and binding on all parties involved, and enforcement shall be pursued through civil courts as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to fulfilling requirements as provided herein regarding distinctiveness and acceptable matter, provide evidence demonstrating compliance with Article 3(2)(d) of the Madrid Agreement concerning the international Registration of Marks. Such evidence must include a certified copy of the basic application or registered trade mark upon which the international registration is based, translated into English if originally in another language. The Registrar may require further documentation to ascertain the status and validity of said basic application or registration, including details regarding any oppositions or cancellations filed against it under the laws of the designating country. Failure to submit satisfactory evidence shall render the international mark vulnerable to rejection during examination.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a proposed trade mark as a certified trade mark, such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating compliance with prescribed quality standards and adherence to specified production processes. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating these claims, including audit reports from accredited certification bodies. Registration as a certified trade mark is conditional upon continued conformity with the initially declared standards; any material deviation or failure to maintain requisite levels of quality shall render the registration liable for cancellation under this Act. Further, the proprietor of a registered certify trade mark must submit annual declarations confirming ongoing compliance and may be subject to periodic inspections by officers authorized by the Registrar.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, any person desiring to oppose such application may file a Notice of Opposition with the Registrar within the time period as prescribed. The Notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of a Notice of Opposition, the Registrar shall promptly serve a copy thereof on the applicant for registration.

The applicant for registration may, subject to any conditions specified by the Registrar, file a counterstatement in response to the Notice of Opposition within a period determined by regulations. The Registrar may, after giving both parties an opportunity of being heard, determine whether the grounds for opposition are sufficient to warrant the rejection or modification of the application. A notice opposition applicant shall be afforded due process as per rules framed under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the design and confirming that the applicant is either a legal practitioner, or a person registered in the prescribed manner as a layout-design agent, or a person in the sole and regular employment of the principal. The Registrar may require further documentation to establish the applicant’s entitlement under this Act, including proof of prior use or publication, provided that such requirements shall be reasonable and proportionate to the complexity of the design involved. A practitioner person registered as an agent shall adhere to a code of conduct prescribed by the Controller, failure to do so rendering them liable for disciplinary action and potential revocation of registration.

For the purposes of this Act, "associated trade marks" shall mean two or more trade marks owned by different entities but relating to goods or services that are complementary, similar, or closely connected. Such trade marks may be registered jointly as associated trade marks subject to an application being made in that regard and fulfilling conditions prescribed herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the commercial relationship between the owners of such associated trade marks, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the entities are affiliated through common ownership. Registration as associated trade marks does not confer any right upon one owner affecting the rights of another under this Act.

Where any question arises as to who is the true and first inventor of a claimed invention, the Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, determine such question based on evidence presented by all interested parties; provided that in determining priority, the Controller shall consider not only documentary proof establishing the date of invention but also testimony regarding diligent efforts undertaken towards reduction to practice. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller concerning inventorship may further petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review, and failure to comply with a Board order shall render such party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The determination of inventorship is binding on all parties involved in any proceeding under this Act.

The use of a sign for goods or services shall give rise to exclusive rights under this Act, subject to any conditions specified therein. Provided that, where an objection is raised by a third party challenging the validity of such exclusive rights on grounds of prior honest usage, the Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continuous and uninfringing application of the mark throughout the territory in question. Any aggrieved party disputing this determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, the Tribunal shall consider whether the alleged prior usage genuinely predates registration and constitutes a reasonable expectation of continued use by the claimant, failing which the exclusive rights remain valid as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license for use of the mark under this Act, such license shall be deemed an assignment unless explicitly stated otherwise within the licensing agreement. Any subsequent transfer or disposal of the licensed undertaking by the licensee shall require prior written consent from the grantor, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Furthermore, where the proprietor advertises acceptance of a trade mark application to a third party through any medium, including but not limited to publication in a journal or online platform, it shall constitute an irrevocable offer subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. The recipient of such advertised acceptance may accept the offer by fulfilling the prescribed formalities as detailed within the advertisement itself.

A legal practitioner engaged by an integrated circuit design house shall be deemed to hold confidential information pertaining to any layout design work undertaken for that house, subject to compliance with the non-disclosure agreements executed between the practitioner and their client. Such confidentiality obligations remain enforceable notwithstanding the termination of the employment or contractual relationship, provided that such termination does not arise from a breach by the design house itself. The term of patent protection granted under this Act shall not extend beyond twenty years from the date of filing the application; however, any information disclosed by a practitioner in good faith during proceedings related to validity challenges may be admissible as evidence. Further, a practitioner found to have wilfully violated these confidentiality provisions is liable for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein.

Where an act constituting an infringement of copyright is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence. This determination shall not preclude prosecution of the initial actor, who remains liable for their individual participation in the infringing activity. Any aggrieved party may appeal against a finding that a commission offence has occurred, presenting evidence demonstrating lack of direction or control; provided that the appellate authority shall consider whether the alleged directing person possessed the means and opportunity to influence the actions leading to copyright infringement. The burden of proving absence of such direction or control rests upon the appellant.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, where a variety registered under this Act is developed by an institution funded wholly or substantially by public funds, the rights pertaining to such variety shall vest initially with that institution. However, the registering authority may, upon application from said institution, specify rights assigned by the institution to any third party, including but not limited to commercial entities engaged in agricultural research and development. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and Registrants, detailing the scope and duration of the licensee’s privileges concerning production, sale, and distribution of propagating material derived from the registered variety. The institution retains the right to revoke such assignments under conditions of non-compliance with agreed upon terms, as provided herein. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by a third party shall require prior written consent from both the registering institution and the Central Government.

Where an appeal lies under this Act from any order made by a Registrar, the register court shall have power to entertain and determine the said appeal. The register court shall not be bound by any decision previously rendered in relation to the matter appealed from but may take into consideration such decisions as it thinks relevant. Subject to any rules made under section 65, the register court shall observe such procedure as it deems appropriate for the disposal of the appeals brought before it. Provided that the register court may, at its discretion, require parties to submit written arguments or documents in support of their case.

The amount of registry fee required for the examination of an application for registration of a trade mark shall be determined as per the prescribed schedule; however, any applicant disputing the assessment of such fee may, within thirty days from the date of notification of the assessed amount, file an appeal with the Trade Marks Appellate Tribunal. Provided that the appellant shall deposit twenty-five percent of the disputed registry fee pending the adjudication of the appeal, failing which the appeal shall be deemed withdrawn. Further, where the Registrar deems the deposited sum insufficient to cover administrative costs associated with processing the appeal, a supplementary payment may be demanded, and non-compliance therewith will render the appeal inadmissible as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by a Hearing Officer considers such order to be manifestly unjust or without due regard to the evidence presented, that party may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Controller shall, after affording both parties an opportunity for being heard and considering all relevant materials, confirm, vary, or set aside the order appealed against. Any objection regarding the competence of a Hearing Officer, including challenges pertaining to their impartiality or adherence to procedural norms as provided herein, shall be raised during the original inquiry; failure to do so may preclude appeal under this Act. The Controller’s decision on such appeals is final, subject to further review by an adjudicating officer if deemed necessary for clarification.

Where an objection is raised before the Controller regarding the originality of any work claimed to be subject matter for copyright under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the designated Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Controller. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum of grounds specifying the errors apparent on the face of the record and setting out the points of law or fact which the appellant desires the Appellate Board to consider.

The Appellate Board shall give notice to the Controller, who may file its written submissions within thirty days from the date of receipt of such appeal. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, hear oral arguments from both parties. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal to the High Court under provisions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the refusal of registration or revocation of a registered layout-design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. Failure to pay the requisite fee shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a *design registry central* for facilitating efficient processing of applications and maintaining records relating to layout-designs. Registered layout-designs are entitled to *exclusive rights* under this Act, and any infringement shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by a Copyright Society relating to the collection or distribution of royalties, or concerning disputes arising from licensing agreements as provided herein, desires to appeal against such order, he may prefer an application before the appellate board established under this Act. The appellate board shall consider such applications within ninety days and issue reasoned orders which are final subject only to further appeal to the High Court on a point of law. Failure by a Copyright Society to comply with directions issued by the appellate board shall render its officers liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable from them jointly and severally.

An application for registration of a described trade mark shall be refused if the proposed marks are so similar as to likely cause confusion or misrepresentation concerning the identity of the applicant or connect with any goods or services in relation to which the applicant has previously used the mark. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such further particulars, documents and specimens relating to the use of the trade mark as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the application is complete. Where a patent shall be granted for an invention incorporating elements identifiable within a registered described trade mark, the grant does not prejudice existing rights under this Act. The Registrar may extend the time allowed for filing documents provided that the applicant satisfies him that sufficient cause exists for such extension.

For the purposes of this Act, where an integrated circuit layout design is transmitted by way of digital signal or electronic medium, such transmission means transmission irrespective of whether it involves physical movement of storage media. The right holder shall have standing to pursue remedies under this Act if a person copies or does any act restricted under this Act relating to a layout design that was communicated to them through such a transmission. Provided that, the communication must be for a lawful purpose and not in violation of any contractual agreement restricting access. Further, where an unauthorized copy is made following such transmission, the onus shall lie on the recipient to demonstrate due diligence in preventing further dissemination if they were unaware of the infringing activity at the time of initial receipt as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “biotechnological process” includes any technique utilizing living organisms or biological systems for the production or modification of products or processes, and shall be interpreted broadly to encompass advancements within genetic engineering, cell culture methodologies, and enzyme-based reactions. A biotechnological process shall be deemed patentable only if it results in a product or substance means new, exhibiting characteristics not previously known or predictable based on existing biological knowledge. Provided that the novelty of such a product is established through rigorous experimental data demonstrating its unique properties and utility, subject to the provisions regarding obviousness under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘design mark’ is defined as any symbol, letter, numeral, device, trademark or representation of an identifiable characteristic which is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of another and shall be registrable if it is not descriptive of the characteristics or quality of such goods or services. The registry shall place design marks submitted for registration in a register of design marks, subject to verification by the Office under this Act. A party proceeding notwithstanding any opposition filed against a design mark application may submit counter-arguments within the timeframe prescribed as provided herein.

Where a complaint alleging infringement of layout-design rights is received, the Controller shall initiate a procedure investigation to determine prima facie validity. Such investigation may include inspection of premises, seizure of materials and examination of witnesses under oath, subject to due process as provided herein. The Controller shall issue summons requiring production of relevant documents pertaining to the alleged infringing activity or trade mark recognised in connection with the layout-design. Failure to comply with a summons shall render the non-compliant party liable for penalties as prescribed. Any person aggrieved by an order issued during this procedure investigation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days, provided that such appeal does not suspend the operation of the order.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any decision or order made by the Controller relating to the revocation of a registered design, or concerning the validity of a copyright design, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the Controller erred in law or fact. The appellant shall be required to demonstrate that the decision was manifestly unjust or unreasonable, considering all relevant evidence presented during the original proceedings. Furthermore, any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may appeal further to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the grounds for appeal are limited to questions of law arising out of this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor registered trade mark includes any person who is entered on the Register of Trade Marks as the registered owner of the mark and holds exclusive rights therein, subject to any limitation or restriction specified in the register. Where an amendment specification relating to a registered trade mark is filed with the Registrar, it shall be deemed to constitute a request for alteration of the particulars of registration; provided that such amendment does not extend the description of goods or services associated with the proprietor registered trade mark beyond those already covered under this Act. The Registrar may require further information regarding any proposed amendment specification before proceeding with its consideration.

Any breeder who, having obtained a registration issued act for a plant variety, knowingly markets or distributes seeds or other propagating material that does not conform to the characteristics specified in the registration certificate shall be liable to pay a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also face revocation of the registration. Further, any person found to have made false representations during the application process leading to the grant of such an act is subject to a fine extending up to one hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. The Registrar shall issue notices prior to imposing penalties, providing opportunity for explanation as provided herein. Repeated offenses will attract enhanced penalties and potential prohibition from applying for future registrations under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered draft regulations” shall mean a set of rules pertaining to the application, acceptance, or maintenance of a trade mark registration, formally submitted to the Registrar and acknowledged as being under consideration by him. Such registered draft regulations shall not alter existing provisions relating to distinctiveness, but may clarify procedural aspects concerning the examination process. Where these regulations propose modifications impacting the assessment of design elements incorporated within a proposed mark, the Registrar shall provide an opportunity for public comment before final determination. Any such regulation remains provisional until formally adopted and published as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to be made in accordance with this Act if it contains a clear representation of the mark sought to be registered and a list specifying all the goods or services in relation to which the applicant desires that the mark should be registered. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark or the specification of goods or services where such amendment is necessary to conform to the provisions herein. Where a mark contains elements adopted from existing marks already registered under this Act, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating that use of the applied-for mark will not cause confusion amongst consumers. Marks indications serve primarily to identify and distinguish goods or services; therefore, any mark which is likely to be confused with an earlier mark shall be rejected. The Registrar may require further information from the applicant at any stage of the examination process.

Where an applicant for registration of a trademark utilizes a deceptive representation regarding the nature, quality, characteristics, geographical origin, or production process of goods or services, such application shall be deemed invalid under this Act. Any person found to have knowingly made false statements in support of a trademark application, or engaged in practices intended to mislead consumers concerning the source or composition of goods bearing a registered trademark, is liable for an offence. Such offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also subject to penalty thousand rupees, recoverable as a fine.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall include particulars verifying ownership and detailing the date of first commercial exploitation, if any, outside India. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered design under this Act or another jurisdiction, provided that evidence demonstrating independent creation is submitted alongside the application. Any modification to a registered layout-design following registration requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days, detailing the alterations and their impact on the original claim of novelty. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in cancellation of the relating registered design upon review by the relevant authority.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an order adjudicating officer concerning rectification proceedings relating to registered trademarks may, within ninety days of communication of such order, file an application for review before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the order is challenged and must be supported by affidavits verifying the material facts presented. Provided that a delay in filing the application may be condoned by the Tribunal if sufficient cause is demonstrated.

The adjudicating officer shall serve a copy of the order, along with notice of the right to appeal, on all parties involved in the rectification proceedings. Further, any interlocutory orders issued during the course of the proceedings are subject to review under this Act upon application made to the Tribunal. The Tribunal may dismiss frivolous applications or those lacking merit, and shall award costs as it deems appropriate.

Where any party institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, such proceedings shall be commenced within the jurisdiction of the High Court designated to entertain suits relating to intellectual property rights in the State where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose. Notice of institution of these proceedings must be served upon the defendant by registered post with acknowledgment due, and a copy simultaneously furnished to the Registrar. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such commenced infringement actions, including details of parties involved and the trade mark in question. Failure to adhere to prescribed service protocols may render the proceeding vulnerable to challenge under this Act. Provided that, where an interlocutory application is filed concerning discovery or inspection of documents, the High Court may direct any party to produce relevant materials as deemed necessary for a just determination of the matter relating to proceeding infringement.

The Central Government shall establish and maintain a National Gene Fund for the purposes of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing benefit-sharing compensation to traditional farming communities. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from registered plant variety breeders, as determined by regulations framed under this Act, and any grants received from international organizations or philanthropic entities. The Central Government may also direct that a portion of royalties derived from licensed propagating material be credited into the National Gene Fund. An advisory committee shall be constituted to oversee the management and disbursement of funds; it shall prescribed chairperson appointed by the Central Government from amongst eminent scientists and agricultural economists. All accounts pertaining to the Fund shall be audited annually, and reports submitted to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall admit appeals only if the appellant demonstrates, through a duly completed ZM form petition, that they have suffered substantial prejudice due to the error apparent on the face of the record. Subject to this requirement and provided that the appeal relates to a decision concerning the grant or refusal of Plant Variety Registration, the Authority shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the original proceedings to the Appellate Board within thirty days. The Authority’s determination regarding procedural irregularities during initial proceedings act authority is final unless demonstrably impacting fairness as determined by the Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding twenty years from the date of the grant, and may be assignable subject to registration of the assignment with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license is assigned under this Act, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights and privileges which were vested in the licensor immediately prior to the assignment. The Registrar may, upon application by any party claiming interest, investigate whether a license has been granted in contravention of section 36e ixd, particularly where the terms restrict competition unreasonably or impose undue burdens on licensees. Any such investigation shall be conducted as provided herein and findings made are binding.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall remit a filed registry fee as prescribed under this Act at the time of presentation of the application to the Trade Marks Registry, failing which the application shall be deemed not to have been made. Provided that an applicant who has previously filed an identical or confusingly similar trade mark in respect of related goods or services may, subject to conditions determined by the Registrar, apply for a waiver of all or part of the filed registry fee. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding such a waiver may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Trade Marks Registry shall not proceed with examination of an application until evidence of payment of the requisite filed registry fee is received and recorded. Failure to pay this fee constitutes grounds for rejection of the trade mark application.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed marks are descriptive of the goods or services with which they are associated. However, an applicant may overcome this refusal by demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, provided that such use occurred prior to the date of publication under this Act. The registration sub section dictates that any alteration to a registered trade mark shall be subject to similar scrutiny as the initial application, ensuring continued compliance with the provisions regarding deceptive similarity or generic character. Further, an appeal against refusal under this registration sub section lies before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute a suit in the competent court against a defendant geographical indication for relief from acts of manufacture, processing, packaging, sale, hire, exhibition, or use which constitute an infringement of their exclusive right under this Act. Such infringement includes any representation, mark, label, notice, sign, or symbol falsely suggesting association with the registered geographical indication, or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. The court shall grant such remedies as it deems appropriate, including injunctions restraining further infringing acts and an order for the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. Damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered by the proprietor, provided that wilful infringement is established. Costs of litigation shall be determined according to prevailing rules.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a pharmaceutical substance, the Controller may, subject to compliance with regulations prescribed by the Central Government, direct that particulars of such patent be published in the Official Gazette at intervals not exceeding six months from the date of grant. Such publication shall include details pertaining to the claimed therapeutic use and dosage regime as specified within the patent specification. Further, where a compulsory license has been granted under this Act, the period for which said patent remains in force shall be determined by the Controller. Upon expiry of the term stipulated therein, or upon revocation of the compulsory license, the patent shall published expiry notification, disseminated through the Official Gazette and other media as deemed appropriate by the Central Government.

An act constituting a commission offence under this Act occurs when any person, without authorization or lawful excuse, reproduces, distributes, exhibits, performs, or translates any work protected by copyright, knowing or having reason to believe that such action infringes the rights of the owner. Such knowledge shall be presumed where the infringing activity is conducted on a commercial scale or involves the use of specialized equipment designed for reproduction or distribution. The burden of proving lawful excuse rests upon the accused. Where an offence is committed in circumstances involving multiple actors, each person contributing to the infringement may be held accountable as per provisions herein relating to joint liability.

An application for registration of a geographical indication submitted under this Act shall be deemed an *application corrected* where the Registrar, following examination and prior notice served upon the applicant detailing deficiencies or non-compliance with the provisions herein, receives a response from the applicant within the stipulated period. Such response must address all points raised by the Registrar and demonstrate adherence to prescribed standards for distinctiveness and traceability of goods originating from the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation if the submitted correction remains ambiguous or incomplete. Provided that the corrected application satisfies all requirements as provided herein, it shall proceed towards consideration for registration; otherwise, rejection proceedings will be initiated.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks are identical with any existing trade goods services, or contain an indication that is indicative of the nature, quality, or geographical origin of such trade goods services. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application if satisfied that there exists no likelihood of confusion on the part of the public arising from the use of the identical or similar marks in relation to those trade goods services. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard before passing any order. Evidence presented before the Board shall be admissible according to rules framed for that purpose.

A trade mark shall be deemed established where the applicant demonstrates continuous use of the mark in commerce within India for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application, subject to compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act. Provided that, if the trade mark is intended for export purposes only, the aforementioned usage requirement may be satisfied through demonstrable marketing and promotional activities directed towards foreign markets, as certified by an authorized Export Promotion Council. Furthermore, evidence of widespread recognition of the trade marks established shall be presented to the Registrar, including but not limited to consumer surveys and market research data, confirming that a substantial portion of relevant consumers associate the mark with the applicant’s goods or services. The Registrar may require additional documentation as deemed necessary to verify these claims.

Appeals arising under this Act shall be made to the Appellate Board established for the purpose. The Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, being persons having experience in copyright law, intellectual property rights administration, or judicial matters. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to any matter specified under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said order. The Appellate Board shall follow such procedure as the Central Government prescribes, provided that it affords all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding subject to further appeals only to the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.

Where an application for registration of a design is deemed likely to affect national interests, the Designs Registrar shall refer the matter to the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, for assessment. The Secretary may, after consultation with such authorities as they deem appropriate, recommend whether or not a prejudicial security india exists concerning the proposed design. Such recommendation shall be binding on the Designs Registrar in respect of proceeding further with the application. If the Registrar is satisfied that the registration of the design would compromise the operational capabilities or strategic assets of India, the application may be rejected outright. Any party aggrieved by such rejection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed identical to a previously registered mark in respect of identical or similar goods or services, subject to the proviso that demonstrable evidence of consumer recognition and established goodwill associated with the earlier mark must be presented. Furthermore, any entity found to have employed a deceptively similar mark, knowing that such use infringes upon the existing trade mark identity, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the infringing sales achieved during the period of infringement. A specification patent shall be required for any trademark incorporating novel technological elements beyond common design features, and failure to provide this will render registration voidable.

Any assignment of a patent, or any interest therein, including the right to grant licences under this Act, shall be in writing and executed by the assignor or their duly authorized representative. Such assignments may include provisions relating to royalties, territory, duration, and other conditions governing the exploitation of the patented invention as agreed upon between the parties. Where an assignment incorporates a licence agreement, the terms thereof shall be deemed part of the assignment and subject to scrutiny under this Act. A registered practise patent agent may facilitate such assignments and licences on behalf of their clients, acting as agents for both assignor and assignee; however, they must disclose any personal interest held in the transaction. Further, any sub-licence granted pursuant to an initial licence shall require notification to the Controller within thirty days of its execution.

A proceeding appellate under this Act is defined as a formal process initiated by an aggrieved party seeking review of an order passed by the Registrar or any other authority empowered to adjudicate disputes concerning layout-design rights. For the purposes of such a proceeding, “aggrieved party” includes but is not limited to the registered proprietor, a person claiming ownership through assignment or license, and any individual demonstrably prejudiced by the decision under review. The appellate body shall be constituted as provided herein and may entertain appeals only against orders relating to registration refusal, revocation, or infringement determinations. Subject to regulations prescribed, oral arguments may be permitted at the discretion of the appellate authority.

Where a patent is granted in contravention of any provision under this Act, or where information disclosed in the application for patents contains matter which does not meet the requirements of novelty or inventive step as provided herein, the Controller may, subject to due process and affording an opportunity for hearing, declare the patent invalid. Any person who knowingly makes, uses, sells, or imports a patented invention without authorization from the patentee shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence attributable to the act of infringement. Provided that such acts are undertaken with the intent to derive commercial benefit from the unauthorized exploitation of the intellectual property rights vested in the patent holder. The Controller may also issue directions for rectification of the patent, if necessary.

Where a layout design owner desires to grant a license conferring rights to utilize a protected integrated circuit layout design, such license may be assigned or transferred subject to approval by the Controller. Any assignment or transfer of a license shall require notification to the Controller within thirty days of execution and shall include details of the assignor, assignee, and the scope of the licensed rights being conveyed. The Registrar shall register proposed assignments of licenses only upon verification that the terms do not contravene any provisions under this Act relating to fair competition or anti-trust measures. Further, a license granted prior to registration of the layout design itself may be registered as an assignment if the original owner provides satisfactory evidence of their entitlement and the assignee consents in writing. The Controller may require additional documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding potential infringement risks associated with the licensed use.

Where a registered proprietor alleges that any person has contravened section 10 relating to unauthorized reproduction or importation of a protected integrated circuit layout-design, the aggrieved party shall institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Upon receipt of such an allegation and after providing due notice to all parties concerned, the registry shall place the matter for preliminary assessment regarding the prima facie validity of the claim. The Central Government may, subject to guidelines issued by it, direct the registry to undertake further investigation into any aspect of the alleged contravention. Any party dissatisfied with the findings of the registry following such an assessment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within a period specified under this Act. Remedies available upon successful adjudication shall include injunctions and damages as provided herein.

An amendment specification relating to a registered breeder variety shall be submitted to the Authority in Form-D, accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act. The application must detail the proposed alterations to the phenotypic characteristics previously recorded during examination and registration, providing justification for such modification based on observed field performance or subsequent scientific analysis. Where the amendment concerns traits impacting essential derivation or distinctiveness, an expert’s report substantiating the continued compliance with the criteria for a registered breeder variety is mandatory. The Authority may require further trials or data submission to assess the impact of the proposed changes. Any alteration approved under this process shall be recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and publicly notified as per the prescribed procedure.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be accompanied by a registry fee as determined by notification published by the Trade Marks Office from time to time.
