This fee is non-refundable, subject to exceptions provided herein relating to applications rejected under this Act due to formal deficiencies. Any applicant seeking to avail of expedited examination procedures must pay an additional processing fee, calculated according to scales prescribed in the First Schedule. Failure to remit the full registry fee at the time of application will render the application deemed not filed until such payment is made. The Trade Marks Office may require proof of remittance for any application where doubts arise regarding compliance with these provisions concerning fees and surcharge.

For the purposes of this Act, the “relevant entry register” shall mean the official record maintained by the Registrar pertaining to a trade mark application or registered trade mark, including but not limited to details concerning prior usage, opposed applications, and assignments. The relevant entry register is deemed conclusive evidence of particulars entered therein, subject to any order made under appeal. Any party seeking to challenge information contained within the relevant entry register must do so through appropriate rectification proceedings as provided herein. Information pertaining to consumer perception of a mark, while potentially relevant in certain disputes, shall not be considered part of the relevant entry register itself.

The Registrar may, upon application made by any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act, issue a certificate specifying the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is registered and indicating the date of registration. Such application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and shall state the grounds for requesting the issuance of the certificate. The Registrar shall consider the application and may require further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for verification. Upon satisfactory examination, the Registrar shall issue the certificate in the form as provided herein, which certificate shall be prima facie evidence of the proprietor’s rights subject to any rectification proceedings under this Act. Any challenge to the validity of a trade mark registered shall not invalidate the certificate issued by the Registrar unless proven otherwise before an appropriate forum. The certificate remains valid until amended or revoked according to procedures established within this legislation.

Any person found to have made any false statement or suppressed material fact in an application for registration of a plant variety shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, where infringement of farmers’ rights occurs due to unauthorized use of registered varieties, aggrieved parties may institute proceedings in a decree civil court seeking injunctions and damages. The Authority shall provide assistance to such courts upon request regarding technical aspects relating to plant breeding and genetic resources. Any order passed by the decree civil court concerning enforcement of these provisions is final, subject to appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Repeated or willful violations may result in revocation of registration and further penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for patent includes subject matter disclosed in a prior publication, whether in printed or electronic form, the controller shall assess novelty under this Act considering such publication as constituting prior art. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates, through documentary evidence accepted by the controller, that the said publication was made without the consent or knowledge of the applicant and contained information not publicly available before the date of filing of the patent application, the assessment may proceed disregarding the publication. For civil court purposes relating to infringement claims arising from patents granted under these conditions, the burden of proving lack of knowledge on the part of the applicant shall rest upon the claimant. A form reference act is deemed to have occurred when such a prior publication directly informs a claim element.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, a broadcasting organisation engaged primarily in the dissemination of news and current affairs programmes shall be deemed to have obtained sufficient consent for the inclusion of copyrighted works incidental to such broadcasts. Provided that, where such use is contested by the copyright holder, the broadcasting organisation bears the onus of demonstrating reasonable efforts were made to secure appropriate permissions prior to transmission. Any aggrieved party may appeal a determination regarding the sufficiency of these efforts to the relevant High Court, presenting evidence pertaining to the nature and extent of the copyrighted material utilized and the potential prejudice suffered as a consequence of its unauthorized use by the broadcasting organisation.

Where any person knowingly and wilfully uses a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered *provisions act mark* without the consent of the proprietor, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringing use, the profits made by the infringer, and any other relevant factors deemed just and equitable under this Act. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may order the delivery up to the Registrar for destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark, packaging materials, advertising matter, and printing blocks used in connection therewith. Any person found guilty of such infringement shall also be subject to a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as provided herein.

Where a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition is granted, any person who manufactures, uses, offers for sale, or imports the patented invention without authorization from the patentee shall be deemed to have infringed the patent. The patentee shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining such infringing activity and damages commensurate with the loss suffered as a direct result of the infringement. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates prior use of the process for manufacturing the composition in India before the date of application for the patent, the liability for damages shall be reduced proportionally. A share patent shall not preclude enforcement against acts committed after the expiry of the term of the patent, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory infringement.

A notice registered breeder is a person who has applied for registration of a plant variety and whose application has been accepted by the Authority but not yet granted registration. Such a breeder shall be entitled to certain rights as provided herein, including the right to use the designation "notice registered" in conjunction with the name of the variety. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a notice registered breeder may initiate a procedure cancelling registration under this Act, subject to demonstrating that the applicant does not fulfill the requirements for registration or has acted fraudulently. The Authority shall consider such petitions and render a decision as per prescribed guidelines.

An application for grant of a breeder's right shall be filed with the Plant Varieties Registration and Farmers’ Rights Authority in Form A, accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, origin, method of reproduction, and any distinguishing characteristics. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the variety is distinct, uniform, and stable. Where the application relates to a variety derived from another variety, the application must specify the parentage and details of the derivation process.

The Authority may require the submission of additional data or clarification regarding the novelty assessment. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the grant or refusal of a breeder's right may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The applicant shall be liable to pay prescribed fees as determined by the Central Government, subject to exemptions provided for farmers and research institutions.

Applications received for registration of plant varieties shall be examined by a Registration Committee constituted by the Authority, and the composition of this Committee will reflect expertise in relevant fields including botany, agronomy, and intellectual property law. The Authority may establish specialized sub-committees within the Registration Committee to address specific technical aspects of applications concerning genetically modified organisms or varieties exhibiting novel traits. Any person aggrieved by an order of a sub-committee under this Act may appeal to the Registration Committee itself. Committees necessary for evaluating breeder’s rights claims and farmers' participatory plant breeding efforts shall be constituted as per guidelines issued by the Central Government, ensuring representation from relevant stakeholders including seed companies and agricultural universities.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication comprised of Darjeeling tea shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement under this Act. Such infringement includes any use of a sign liable to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods, or where such use constitutes an unfair appropriation of the reputation associated with the registered geographical indication. Remedies available to the proprietor include injunctions restraining further infringing acts and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer. Provided that, in determining damages, due consideration shall be given to any bonafide use prior to registration. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, direct any person found to be using the geographical indication deceptively to cease such use and pay compensation for losses incurred.

An application for rectification of a registered layout-design, or for any other purpose as provided herein, shall be in Form D annexed to these regulations. The petitioner shall furnish with such application detailed particulars contained within a schedule specifying the alleged errors or omissions requiring correction, along with supporting documentation demonstrating their impact on the validity or enforceability of the design registration. Where the rectification sought involves an indication certification trade mark appearing on the layout-design, the applicant must provide evidence of prior use and established reputation associated with that mark. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding the petition particulars contained therein, and shall afford the respondent a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-statement. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person aggrieved by the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, direct the hearing of the matter before an intellectual property officer. Such officer shall record evidence both oral and documentary, and determine whether the grounds for opposition are substantiated to the requisite legal standard. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the intellectual property officer may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of that decision. The safeguards prescribed register shall be maintained accurately reflecting all such decisions and appeals, ensuring transparency in the registration process and providing a clear record for future disputes concerning ownership or use of trade marks as provided herein.

Any person who performs or causes to be performed publicly any *dramatic work* without obtaining license from the owner of copyright therein shall be deemed to have infringed under this Act. Such infringement is actionable at the suit of the copyright owner and may result in damages proportionate to the loss suffered by such owner, but not less than fifty thousand rupees for a first offence. Repeated infringements shall attract penalties escalating up to two hundred thousand rupees per instance. Where an infringing performance includes music or other copyrighted material, liability shall extend to all copyright owners implicated in that portion of the *dramatic work*. The court may also order seizure and destruction of equipment used in facilitating such unauthorized performances, provided that due notice is given to the accused.

Where an application for patent contains deficiencies in the disclosure relating to the matter disclosed, and such deficiency renders the specification not fulfilling the requirements of completeness under this Act, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a further statement or drawing. Failure to comply with such requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable for rejection. Any amendment complete specification submitted pursuant to this process must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying its accuracy and conformity with the original disclosure. Knowingly submitting a false declaration in said affidavit constitutes an offence, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine. The Controller shall record any such conviction.

Any person holding rights pertaining to a plant variety shall, subject to conditions specified by the Registering Authority, be obligated to contribute a percentage of royalties received from the commercialization of propagating material to the National Gene Fund. This contribution shall be deemed a license fee for the utilization of germplasm resources accessed under this Act and may be adjusted based on the extent of indigenous genetic material incorporated into the registered variety. Assignment of plant variety rights, whether partial or complete, shall not absolve the assignee of the obligation to contribute to the Gene Fund as determined by the Central Government. Further, any agreement for transfer of technology relating to a protected variety must explicitly detail provisions regarding ongoing contributions to the National Gene Fund, ensuring equitable benefit sharing with resource providers and promoting conservation efforts.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a trade mark, direct the removal of a reference use mark from any material where it is displayed. Such direction shall be issued only after due consideration of an objection filed by the proprietor of the trade mark to which the reference pertains, and provided that the Registrar finds that the continued display of the reference use mark creates confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of goods or services offered under the reference use mark. An appeal against such direction lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; however, the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if it is shown that the applicant failed to provide adequate notice to the proprietor prior to the initial application.

Application for registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, containing particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, and the area of its origin. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin as provided herein. Where an application for registration includes a collective mark or certification trade mark relating to the geographical indication, the Registrar may require further information concerning the constitution and functioning of the association proposing to use such mark. Registration shall apply only to the applicant who meets all requirements under this Act and submits the necessary fees. Any alteration to the registered particulars must also be submitted for approval.

Where the Controller publishes an application registration notice, indicating acceptance of a patent application subject to any conditions specified therein, such acceptance shall not preclude assignment or licensing of the invention claimed. Any party possessing a relevant ground for opposition under this Act may file a pre-grant opposition with the Opposition Board within the prescribed period following publication of the application registration notice. The assignor of a patent application shall provide written notification to the Controller regarding any subsequent transfer, and such notification shall be recorded as provided herein. Further, licensees granted rights under an invention claimed in a pending patent application may, subject to the terms of their license agreement, participate in opposition proceedings before the Opposition Board relating to that application.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an entry in the design register shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of the registered layout-design and prior right of the registrant therein, provided that any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration or rejection of a layout-design may, within sixty days from the date of such decision, file an appeal as provided herein. The Appellate Tribunal may allow such appeal if it is satisfied that there has been an error apparent on the face of the record; however, this shall not preclude consideration of other grounds where the applicant demonstrates substantial prejudice due to a demonstrable procedural irregularity during the registration process. An application for rectification of entries in the design register may be made by any interested party and will be subject to similar appellate review.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of registration, or concerning any right conferred thereby, seeks redressal, such person shall be entitled to file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Provided that the Tribunal may entertain appeals filed after the said period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal within the stipulated time, and such delay did not substantially prejudice the respondent. Applications under this Act concerning rectification proceedings shall adhere strictly to the manner applications clause prescribed in Schedule II, ensuring all requisite forms and declarations are duly completed. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application.

A performer shall be deemed to have performed exclusively for the purposes of this Act if such performance was rendered during the course of employment under a contract specifying the terms and conditions of service. Provided that, where a contract does not explicitly address ownership of copyright in respect of performances, the default position shall be that the performer retains all rights unless evidence demonstrates otherwise through documented agreement prior to the performance’s rendition. The right of a performer to control the reproduction of their performance is subject to any existing contractual obligations undertaken with producers or broadcasting organizations. Furthermore, where a performer's actions are deemed integral to an audiovisual work, as determined by prevailing industry standards and judicial interpretation, limitations on rights transfer may apply under this Act.

Any proprietor of a design registered under this Act shall be entitled to sue for and recover damages suffered by him as a consequence of an infringement of his design. Such damages shall include loss of profits, reasonable royalties that the proprietor would have received had the infringement not occurred, and in determining such loss, account shall be taken of any benefit accruing to the infringer from the use of the registered design. Provided that where the infringement was knowing, the court may increase the amount of damages up to three times the actual damage established. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity and for the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing design. Further, any person found guilty of contravention of this Act shall be liable to pay such sum as the court deems fit, subject to limitations prescribed herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee under a patent granted by the Patent Office shall be entitled to assign or pledge their license to any other person, either gratuitously or for valuable consideration. Such assignment or pledge may include all or any portion of the licensed rights and territory specified in the original patent grant. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating that the assignee possesses sufficient financial resources or technical expertise to effectively exercise the licensed rights, particularly where the underlying invention relates to pharmaceuticals or agricultural technology. Further, an application for registration of such assignment shall be made within three months from the date of the transfer, and failure to do so shall render the assignment voidable at the option of any aggrieved party. The Patent Office may prescribe a form for such applications as it deems appropriate.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is opposed under this Act, the Authority shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and may direct that the hearing be conducted in person or through video conferencing. The grounds for opposition shall include, but not be limited to, allegations that the variety does not possess any new characteristic resulting from deliberate breeding or selection; or that the description provided by the applicant is inaccurate or incomplete. It shall be conclusively presumed that the specification does disclose all information relevant to assessing novelty and distinctiveness unless proven otherwise by the applicant. The burden of establishing such a deficiency rests entirely upon the opponent, subject to the provisions regarding procedural fairness as provided herein.

Any proprietor who makes use of a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions of this Act, or in any manner which falsely suggests an association with the goods for which the indication is registered, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the High Court. Furthermore, where such misuse has resulted in substantial loss of reputation or goodwill to the registered proprietor, the court may award exemplary damages in addition to compensatory relief. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the aggrieved party under general principles of law. Where a person is found guilty of engaging in deceptive practices relating to a geographical indication, the Court shall order the aforesaid committed forfeiture of all goods bearing the false or misleading indication and any materials used in their production or packaging.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall include particulars demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the specified geographical area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating this claim, including but not limited to affidavits from producers and trade organizations operating within the defined territory. Any opposition filed under this Act against inclusion in the register shall be adjudicated based on whether the impugned indication is primarily indicative of a quality or characteristic linked to that geographical origin. The Registrar shall maintain an included register geographical, accessible for public inspection, detailing registered indications and their respective areas of origin, subject to provisions regarding confidentiality where trade secrets are involved.

Any person seeking to use a certification trade mark relating to goods other than those produced by members of a defined organization shall make an application to the Controller, setting forth the particulars of the organization and its constitution, including details regarding the process for membership assessment and revocation. The application must also specify the standards of quality or characteristics which the certified goods are required to meet, and demonstrate that these standards are objectively verifiable through regular audits conducted by independent bodies approved by the Controller. Such approval shall be granted only after a thorough examination of the audit methodology and reporting procedures. The Registrar may require further information concerning the organization's financial stability and governance structure before proceeding with registration. Any alteration to the defined organization’s membership criteria or certification standards requires prior notification and consent from the Controller, failing which the certification trade mark shall be deemed liable for cancellation.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the registration of copyright, or concerning the refusal to register marks indications customary to a trade or business, may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures for submitting applications and associated documentation shall render the application liable for rejection without further notice. The Registrar Copyrights shall have the power to issue summonses and administer oaths in relation to any inquiry undertaken pursuant to this Act, and wilful disobedience of a summons or false evidence given before the Registrar may attract penalties as determined by the Central Government. Repeated violations concerning the accuracy of information provided during copyright registration proceedings will result in revocation of said registration.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to terms and conditions agreed upon in writing between the parties. Such licenses shall be assignable along with the underlying registered trade mark, provided that notice of assignment is filed with the Trade Marks Registry within three months of the transfer. Any subsequent proprietor acquiring rights under an assignment shall be bound by any existing license agreements pertaining to the registered trade marks. Further, a license granted under this Act may contain provisions restricting the licensed user’s activities, including geographical limitations and quality control standards as determined by the grantor. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these conditions before registering an endorsement of assignment involving licenses for registered trade marks.

Where any person considers that another party has infringed his right to apply patent invention, he may institute proceedings for relief in the manner prescribed herein. Such proceedings shall involve demonstrating prima facie evidence of the patented invention and establishing that the defendant’s actions fall within the scope of claims as defined in the granted patent. The remedies available under this Act include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff, and costs of litigation. Provided that, where the infringing act relates to a drug intended for use as medicine, the Court may also order the destruction of the infringing goods. Further, any party aggrieved may appeal against any decision under this Act to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Any proprietor desiring to grant a license concerning the use of their registered trade mark may execute an assignment agreement transferring such rights, subject to the conditions stipulated therein. A party proceeding shall notify the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of any such licensing arrangement or assignment, providing details of the licensee or assignee and the scope of permitted usage. Further, where a license is granted for a specific territory, the proprietor remains responsible for ensuring that the use by the licensee does not infringe upon existing rights held by others under this Act. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the business undertaking to which the trade mark relates shall be deemed notification to the Trade Marks Registry and will require no further action from the previous proprietor provided that all records are updated accordingly.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work only if it is original and has been fixed in a tangible form, whether written or otherwise recorded. Provided that works produced for certain purposes specified under this Act, namely, those undertaken by government departments or public institutions for official use, may be exempted from the requirement of originality as defined herein. The author of the copyright in such work shall be deemed to be the department or institution concerned. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, or communicate a copyrighted work commercially must obtain prior written permission from the owner of the copyright, demonstrating compliance with prescribed royalty rates and usage guidelines as provided herein. Failure to secure such authorization constitutes an infringement under this Copyright Act.

A creator claiming protection under this Act for their layout designs shall submit detailed technical specifications alongside the application form, demonstrating adherence to established industry standards regarding circuit functionality and component placement. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the submitted design incorporates elements substantially derived from previously registered layout designs or publicly available documentation without demonstrable original contribution. Furthermore, any applicant asserting novelty must provide a sworn affidavit confirming absence of prior publication or commercial use of the claimed creators layout designs anywhere in the world within the preceding twelve months. This requirement shall not apply if such prior activity was undertaken with explicit written consent from the rightful owner of the underlying intellectual property.

A design registry shall maintain a register of geographical indications in respect of goods or services originating from specific territories within India. The register shall contain particulars including the name of the geographical indication, the territory it identifies, the class of goods or services to which it relates, and the proprietor thereof. An application for registration as a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons or producers engaged in producing goods or rendering services with that geographical origin; provided that such an applicant shall demonstrate control over the qualities defining the defendant geographical indication.

For the purposes of this Act, a "geographical indication" means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. A geographical indication may include signs, symbols, shapes, pictures, letters, numerals, words, configurations, sounds or any combination thereof. The distinctive qualities associated with a geographical indication shall be inherent in the product and directly linked to its specified geographical location; provided that such link must be demonstrable through established production practices or historical usage. Any use of a geographical indication which does not conform to these requirements shall be deemed invalid under this Act.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been abandoned if, following an invitation under this Act requiring the applicant to submit specific details regarding the fabrication process, the applicant fails to respond within the prescribed time limit. Furthermore, where a registered layout-design is subsequently found to be substantially similar to a prior unregistrable design, or where it has been determined that the registration was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for cancellation. In such instances, the cancelled registrar layout shall remain accessible for public inspection as provided herein, with appropriate notations indicating its status and the reasons for cancellation. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the cancellation of a registered layout-design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods claiming origin from a registered geographical indication shall be liable for prosecution under this Act if it is established that such enterprise has knowingly utilized a sign identical or confusingly similar to the protected indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an authorized user or any interested party, initiate inquiries into alleged instances where a geographical indication falsifies the reputation of genuine products originating from the designated area. Such inquiries shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, affording the accused enterprise an opportunity to present its defence and counter-evidence. Appeals against decisions made by the Registrar concerning allegations of geographical indication falsification may be filed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights to use the trademark within a defined geographical territory or for specific goods and services, such proprietor shall submit a form petition to the Trade Marks Registry. This petition must detail the scope of the licensed rights, including any limitations on usage and duration of the license. The Registrar shall appear before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if any party objects to the proposed licensing arrangement, citing concerns regarding dilution or unfair competition. Provided that the registered proprietor affirms their continued responsibility for ensuring compliance with trademark law by the licensee, the Trade Marks Registry may approve the assignment or sub-license of these rights subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all approved licenses and assignments on the public register.

Where an international registration designating India is opposed, the Hearing Officer shall afford the proprietor of the trade mark and the opponent both a fair opportunity to be heard, subject to such rules of procedure as may be prescribed. The determination of whether use of a sign in connection with goods or services constitutes permitted use for the purposes of demonstrating genuine use under Article 5 of the Madrid Protocol shall be considered an integral part of the opposition proceedings. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Hearing Officer relating to such international registration, including but not limited to orders concerning the assessment of genuine use, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement, and such proceedings are stayed pending determination of an earlier conflicting application or registration, the proprietor shall remain entitled to pursue remedies against any party proceeding notwithstanding the stay. This right includes, but is not limited to, seeking interim injunctions and damages relating to acts committed during the period of the stay. Provided that, where a subsequent registration is granted following resolution of the conflict, the proprietor’s claim for damages shall be assessed with due consideration to the reasonable costs incurred by the infringing party in reliance on the conflicting application or registration prior to its revocation or amendment. The Tribunal may order compensation against any such party found to have acted in bad faith during this period.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Designs Register, or by a failure to make an entry, may apply to the Controller for rectification of register. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller shall afford the applicant and any other interested party an opportunity of being heard under this Act. Where the rectification sought involves a matter relating to priority established under the Budapest Treaty, the Controller shall consider evidence pertaining to international design applications and registrations. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding service of notice or representation may result in dismissal of the application. The Controller’s order concerning rectification register is final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an individual, through the use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, induces consumer confusion regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services, such actions shall constitute a deemed falsify trade. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party demonstrating reasonable likelihood of deception amongst consumers, initiate inquiries under this Act. Such inquiries will involve notice to the alleged infringer and an opportunity for them to present their defense. If, following due process and consideration of all evidence presented, the Registrar finds that a deemed falsify trade has occurred, they may issue an order directing the cessation of the infringing activity and potentially award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the trademark proprietor. The aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal any such decision before the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled, subject to any conditions specified in the registration, to restrain the application of identical or deceptively similar marks to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered. Where such restraint has been obtained, the proprietor may further seek damages from any person who, prior to the institution of the proceeding, had infringed under this Act and acted in good faith. It shall be a defence for the alleged infringer to demonstrate that their use of the mark did not create confusion among the relevant public concerning the origin of the goods. The remedies available to the proprietor are without prejudice to any other right or remedy available under this Act or otherwise by law relating to passing off or unfair competition involving these goods.

Where an application for registration of a breeder registered variety is refused, the applicant may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Controller shall consider any objections raised by third parties regarding the distinctiveness or uniformity of the claimed variety and may require further evidence as deemed necessary under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an entry in the register references pertaining to a breeder registered variety, including but not limited to claims of infringement or unauthorized use, shall have the right to file a complaint with the Controller within ninety days from the date such entry became public. The Controller shall investigate such complaints and may order rectification of the register if it finds the entry to be erroneous or misleading, subject to due process and opportunity for all parties to present their case.

Any patentee desiring to grant a license, assign ownership, or otherwise transfer rights pertaining to a patented invention shall make an application before the Controller. Such application shall specify the details of the proposed transaction, including the identity and address of all parties involved, the scope of the rights being transferred, and any royalties or other considerations agreed upon. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the terms of the agreement and demonstrating that the transfer is consistent with public interest. An applicant seeking to enforce a license granted under this Act may file a court application alleging infringement by a party failing to adhere to the stipulated conditions. This right shall be subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein, and any dispute arising from such an application will be adjudicated according to established principles of equity and natural justice.

Where an application is made for registration of a translation, the Registrar shall require particulars to be furnished regarding the original work, including its title, author, and country of origin. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating ownership or authorization to create the copies translation ii. Provided that if the original work has been published outside India, the applicant must submit an official certificate confirming such publication and detailing its date. Furthermore, the application shall specify whether the translation is intended for public distribution or private use only. Any subsequent alterations made to the registered translation after registration require notification to the Registrar and may necessitate a fresh assessment of copyright ownership under this Act.

Where a copyright infringement has been committed by a corporate body incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, or any other law for the time being in force relating to companies, the expression "company" shall be construed as including its directors, managers, and officers who were directly involved in the decision-making process leading to the infringing act. For the purposes of determining liability under this Act, a company proved offence shall include acts such as unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of copyrighted works. The responsibility for ensuring compliance with copyright law rests upon those individuals authorized to manage the company’s operations and intellectual property assets.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of layout-design rights under this Act, and seeks injunctive relief, the Registrar may require submission of specific documentation demonstrating reasonable efforts to ascertain the identity of the alleged infringer. This requirement is intended to prevent frivolous claims and ensure due diligence in pursuing remedies. Such documentation shall include, but not be limited to, records of online searches, inquiries with distributors, and any correspondence undertaken to identify the responsible party. The Registrar’s determination regarding whether sufficient effort has been demonstrated shall be final and binding on all parties subject to appeal before a designated appellate tribunal. Failure to comply with the registrar prescribed requirement may result in the rejection of the infringement claim or imposition of costs against the claimant.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through an application filed under the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to hold such registration for the territory of India subject to any modifications made as provided herein. Any alteration to the layout of the goods or services specification appearing on the original Indian registration, following extension under the Madrid Agreement, requires prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry and may necessitate further examination. Failure to provide timely notification regarding alterations in registered proprietor layout shall render the extended registration liable for revocation by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Penalties for such non-compliance will be as prescribed; repeated offences invite substantial monetary fines and potential injunctions preventing continued use of the mark.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to request the Registrar to allow an amendment to their application at any stage of the proceedings, subject to compliance with the provisions herein relating to distinctiveness and acceptable representation of the mark. Such requests may include alterations to the identification of goods or services associated with the trade mark, clarification of the description of the trade mark itself, or adjustments to the claimed geographical extent of protection. The Registrar shall consider such amendment requests in light of whether they are merely clerical corrections or constitute substantive changes impacting the registrability criteria as defined under this Act. An application permit amendment only if it does not prejudice any prior rights or existing registrations.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed; provided that the Board may, in its discretion, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are shown for the delay. The Board shall hear parties and evidence adduced and make such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside or modifying the order of refusal. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Board under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order; marks registered accordance with section 27 shall be subject to review upon application by any interested person.

Where a registered trade mark owner desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark, such license may be granted either exclusively or non-exclusively, subject to the terms stipulated therein relating to quality control and territorial scope of application. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include all rights pertaining to licenses previously granted under this Act, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to the conditions of those existing licenses. Failure to maintain such adherence may constitute infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4. The Registrar may require disclosure of details regarding any sub-licensing arrangements entered into by a licensee and shall have the power to intervene where such arrangements demonstrably prejudice the reputation of the trade mark. Further, a license granted under this Act is deemed assignable alongside the underlying trade mark registration.

The Registrar may, upon receiving objection under this Act from any party claiming an interest in preventing the registration of a proposed trade mark, direct that the trademark application be refused. Such direction shall be accompanied by reasons in writing detailing the grounds for refusal, specifically addressing whether the proposed *name* conflicts with existing rights or is otherwise contrary to the provisions herein. Any applicant aggrieved by such a direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order. The Board shall hear the appeal and consider any counter-arguments presented by the objector, ensuring due process as provided herein. Further appeals from the Board’s decision are permissible under the appellate jurisdiction provisions relating to section 94 appeal.

Where any imported goods are suspected of infringing a registered trade mark, an officer authorized under this Act may, subject to compliance with regulations prescribed by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, detain such goods pending verification of their origin and intended destination. The owner of the registered trade mark shall be notified promptly of such detention, providing details regarding the consignment and the basis for suspicion of infringement. Provided that, if the imported goods are accompanied by a valid certificate of origin issued under the auspices of an international agreement to which India is a party, the officer may require further documentation demonstrating compliance with applicable provisions of the Customs Act 1962 before releasing the goods. Any determination regarding infringement shall be made in accordance with procedures established herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the Office, specifying the name and address of the applicant and containing particulars identifying the layout-design. The layout-design shall be represented graphically by drawings or photographs which are clear and legible; provided that where the layout-design incorporates elements derived from a previously registered layout-design, such derivation must be explicitly declared in the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification deemed necessary for examination under this Act. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application and invite objections within a prescribed period. Any person aggrieved by the proposed registration may file an objection with the Registrar, stating the grounds thereof. The Registrar shall consider all such objections before proceeding with the registration process as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a design register layout shall furnish to the Registrar a detailed specification including all views necessary for understanding the layout-design. The specification must clearly identify any mask works incorporated within the layout-design and their respective owners, provided that such identification does not compromise trade secrets. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may request further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with these requirements. If the applicant fails to provide the requested information within the stipulated time, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. The design register layout, once registered, will be recorded in the Register of Layout-Designs and open for public inspection as provided herein.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application by a registered user party seeking leave to institute proceedings relating to revocation of a trade mark may be entertained only if such application is filed within six months from the date on which the applicant received notice of the institution of the rectification proceeding. The Registrar shall serve a copy of such application upon the proprietor of the trade mark and any other interested parties as identified by the registered user party, providing them with a period of thirty days to file their response. Failure by the Registrar to provide timely notification shall not invalidate subsequent orders made under this Act. A registered user party may also apply for intervention in rectification proceedings initiated by another party, provided that they demonstrate a material interest and potential prejudice resulting from the outcome of those proceedings.

The owner of an internationally registered trade mark designating India may grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark within Indian territory, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Further, where an international registration referred to under this Act has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed to be the proprietor for the purposes of using and enforcing rights relating to the trade mark in India. The Registrar may require production of a certified copy of such assignments or licenses as evidence of title. Any subsequent dealings concerning the licensed use or ownership shall also be subject to notification requirements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment of copyright in respect of performances by a performer shall be deemed to be an exclusive right granted to the assignee for the term specified therein. Such assignments may relate to all or any portion of the performer’s rights under this Act, including but not limited to the right to reproduce, distribute, and communicate the performance to the public. Provided that no assignment shall be valid unless it is in writing and signed by the performer or their duly authorized agent. Where a performer assigns their copyright, they retain the right to receive equitable royalties as determined through negotiation with the assignee, reflecting the commercial value generated from the licensed work. Further, an assignee may sub-license the performance rights subject to conditions agreed upon within the original assignment agreement and in accordance with principles of fair dealing.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, be entitled to grant licenses allowing use of the mark upon goods or services as specified in the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof relating to royalties, duration, and territory shall be governed by contractual arrangement between the proprietor and licensee. Where a registered draft regulations pertaining to trade mark usage are proposed, the Registrar may require submission of a detailed plan outlining intended implementation and impact on existing licensees. Any party adversely affected by such draft regulations may file an opposition within the prescribed time limit, detailing grounds for objection based upon undue restriction or prejudice to their contractual rights under previously granted licenses. The Registrar shall consider all oppositions before finalizing the registered draft regulations.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark as an international registration referred is opposed under this Act, the evidence presented by the applicant shall be considered alongside any counterstatement filed by the opponent. The Appellate Board may, upon review of such evidence and counterstatement, determine whether the grounds for opposition are substantiated to the extent that they affect only the designation of India within the international registration. It is provided that if the proprietor registered layout of the mark incorporates elements previously used in commerce without authorization, this shall be a material consideration in assessing the distinctiveness of the mark as against the opponent’s claim. The Board may order rectification of the register accordingly, subject to principles of natural justice.

Where two or more trademarks are registered as associated trade marks, the proprietor shall ensure that the use of each such trademark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered under those marks. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party and after due consideration of all relevant factors including but not limited to the similarity of the marks and the relatedness of the goods or services, direct that a proprietor cease using one or more of the associated trade marks if such use is deemed likely to cause dilution of another mark within the association. Such direction shall be subject to appeal under this Act. The proprietor must provide evidence demonstrating compliance with any conditions imposed by the Registrar regarding the continued registration of associated trade marks.

An aggrieved party, including any registered proprietor dissatisfied with a decision concerning renewal or alteration of their trade mark registration, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. This right to appeal shall extend to decisions relating to rectification proceedings initiated against a registered trade mark, and also encompasses disputes arising from objections raised during the examination process under this Act. Provided that, if the aggrieved party fails to file the appeal within the specified period, the order or decision in question shall be deemed final and binding. The Board may, subject to just considerations and reasons recorded in writing, entertain an appeal filed after the expiry of the appeal specified period only if adequate cause is demonstrated for the delay.

Where an application for registration of a mark is accepted by the Registrar, either absolutely or subject to conditions, the applicant shall be entitled to proceed with payment of the requisite fees as determined under this Act. Failure to remit such fees within the period specified in the acceptance notice shall render the acceptance liable to revocation. Any party aggrieved by a condition imposed upon an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of notification of the acceptance, and the Board’s decision shall be final. The Registrar may, at any time prior to registration, modify or remove such conditions if satisfied that they are no longer necessary or appropriate, provided that due notice is given to all interested parties. Any person claiming damages resulting from reliance upon an application accepted conditions may pursue remedies under the general law relating to torts and contract.

Where an application for a patent has been granted and subsequently lapses due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may file a request for revival of the lapsed patent subject to conditions prescribed under this Act. Such request shall be accompanied by the necessary fee calculated on the basis of the number of years for which the renewal fees remained unpaid, plus an additional surcharge not exceeding fifty percent of the said unpaid fees. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued novelty and industrial applicability of the invention as at the date of the request. Further, where a patent has been revived under this provision, it shall be subject to all limitations and conditions that would have applied had the renewal fee been paid on time.

Where a layout design owner seeks to grant a license or assign rights in respect of a registered integrated circuit layout design, the application shall specify, with particularity, the scope of such license or assignment. The form petition particulars accompanying the application must clearly delineate the geographical territory covered by the proposed arrangement and any restrictions on use as may be agreed between the owner and licensee or assignee. Further, where an alleged offence arises from a breach of conditions stipulated in a licensed agreement, the Registrar may require submission of supplementary documentation detailing the contractual terms relevant to the dispute. The layout design owner shall provide evidence demonstrating due diligence in monitoring compliance with the license or assignment, subject to regulations prescribed under this Act concerning confidentiality and trade secrets.

An application india filed relating to a process for producing a novel pharmaceutical intermediate shall be deemed invalid if the applicant has previously published or publicly disclosed the invention outside India unless such publication or disclosure was made under conditions preventing exploitation of the patented subject matter. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party regarding prior publication, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the publication did not compromise the novelty and inventive step requirements as provided herein. Further, if the application incorporates subject matter derived from a previously filed application india filed by another person, the applicant must provide written consent from the original applicant confirming the transfer of rights and acknowledging compliance with all relevant provisions concerning divisional applications.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been improperly filed if it contains any information indicating a prior claim or share patent relating to the same design by another party, unless such prior claim is expressly acknowledged and consented to in writing by the claimant holding that right. Upon discovery of such improper filing, the Registering Officer may issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the application within thirty days. Failure to comply with this notice shall result in the committed forfeiture directed by the officer; all fees paid towards registration shall be remitted to Government funds. The layout-design remains subject to challenge under this Act pending final determination of any such forfeiture proceedings.

A person shall be deemed a Member for the purposes of this Act if that person is registered as such under the prescribed manner and holds a valid certificate of registration issued by the Registrar. Any individual aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the eligibility criteria for becoming a Member, or concerning the revocation of their Membership, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. Provided that, where the decision relates to a matter of fact, the Tribunal shall confirm such decision unless it finds that there has been a material error or misapprehension. The Registrar may, notwithstanding anything contained herein, require further documentation from an applicant for Membership if reasonable doubt arises regarding their compliance with this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and where the applicant has filed a counterstatement to the notice of opposition, the Registrar may, upon review of the evidence submitted by both parties, direct that the proceedings be stayed pending resolution of certain disputes concerning ownership or prior use. Such direction shall only be given if the dispute directly impacts the determination of whether the trade mark is distinctive or deceptively similar to an earlier mark. The rights and obligations of a *proposed registered proprietor* in respect of any such stay shall be determined by the Registrar, taking into account the potential prejudice to both the opponent and the applicant, provided that the applicant demonstrates good faith in pursuing registration.

Any person who knowingly reproduces or distributes a work in violation of the provisions sub section relating to copyright infringement shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender is liable for imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both. Further, where such reproduction or distribution has been made for commercial gain, the court may enhance the aforementioned penalty by a multiple of five. The owner of copyright shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings against any person infringing their rights as provided herein, seeking damages and an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. Repeated offences shall attract progressively higher penalties at the discretion of the Court.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act is dissatisfied, such party may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall be in respect of any question of fact or law arising out of the decision or determination made by the Controller. Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are tendered, subject to its discretion. The manner applying appellate proceedings before the Tribunal shall be as provided herein and shall not preclude the Tribunal from directing any party to furnish further information or evidence deemed necessary for a just resolution of the dispute.

The proprietor of a registered mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to their registered mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, provided that such use constitutes an infringement under this Act. Where a person has made use of a mark infringing the rights of the proprietor without reasonable grounds to believe that they were entitled so to do, the court may award damages against them equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement. Further, in cases where the infringing mark is applied in an unauthorized manner to goods or affixed to packaging, the court shall order its destruction or other disposal as it deems fit. The proprietor may also seek injunctions preventing further acts of infringement and account for profits derived from the infringing use of the mark.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by detailed petition particulars, specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and the date of first commercial exploitation, if any. The petition must also include a complete list of all persons who have contributed to the creation of the layout-design, along with their respective roles. Failure to provide accurate or complete petition particulars may result in rejection of the application under this Act. Where the applicant demonstrates compelling circumstances and satisfies the relevant authority, a compulsory licence may be granted permitting use of the registered layout-design for purposes of research and development, subject to conditions as provided herein.

An aggrieved party, including any registered proprietor or authorized user of a geographical indication, may institute legal proceedings in the competent civil court for relief against infringement of that geographical indication. Such infringement includes any use of the indication which is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods. An application registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the proprietorship of the geographical indication unless proven otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence before the court. The remedies available under this Act include an injunction restraining further infringing acts, damages sustained by the aggrieved party, and the disposal of infringing goods as per rules framed by the Central Government. Provided that any action taken by the Registrar or any officer acting under his direction shall not be challengeable in any civil court.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design alleging infringement under this Act, direct the alleged infringer to submit within sixty days a written response detailing their defense. Such response shall include particulars of any circumstances demonstrating that the layout design in question was created independently or derived from publicly available sources. Further, if the Registrar determines that the infringing activity involves the unauthorized transmission operation law relating to a layout design previously registered, they shall issue an interim order restraining such activity pending final determination. The applicant for registration may petition the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal against any decision of the Registrar concerning this matter within thirty days from the date of communication of said decision. Any appeal under this Act shall be made only on grounds of law and not otherwise.

An applicant seeking protection for an invention may file a patent application with a provisional specification detailing the substance of the invention. Such a provisional specification need not comply with all requirements applicable to a complete specification under this Act; however, it must adequately describe the invention and enable a person skilled in the art to understand its nature. The filing date of the provisional specification shall establish an initial priority date for the invention. An application claiming priority from such a provisional specification must be filed within six months following the date of the provisional specification. Failure to file a complete specification within this stipulated period will render the provisional application lapsed, and any subsequent claim based upon it inadmissible.

Where an objection is raised against a proposed mark registration act on the grounds of likelihood of confusion with any existing mark registered under this Act, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier mark with an opportunity for written submissions and oral hearing. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions and hearings, direct that the marks be accepted or refused, or impose limitations on the scope of either registration, provided that such limitations are demonstrably necessary to avoid a likelihood of confusion as assessed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any direction issued by the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “requires patented article” shall be deemed to exist where the functionality or intended use of a product is inextricably linked to the application of a process protected by a valid patent, such that the absence of said patented process renders the product non-viable for its prescribed purpose. This determination shall consider not only the direct manufacturing steps but also any essential ancillary processes. Furthermore, in instances involving specialized machinery incorporating elements derived from a patented invention, the layout registered under this Act as a “registered user layout” may be relevant to establishing such dependency.

Where, subsequent to the grant of registration for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, it is determined that an error occurred during the examination process or the recording of particulars relating to the registered design, the Controller may entertain an application for amendment. Such application shall be accompanied by a duly affirmed affidavit detailing the nature of the error and demonstrating its material impact on the accuracy of the register. The applicant shall further provide such documentary evidence as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate the claim. Notice of the application for error amendment shall be served upon the registered proprietor, who may file objections within sixty days from the date of service. Any objection received shall be considered by the Controller and a reasoned order issued, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement where there has been use of any layout-design which is substantially similar to or used as a substitute for the distinctive elements of the said trade mark. Such use shall constitute an infringement only if it is employed in connection with goods or services identical or closely resembling those for which the trade mark is registered, and without the express written consent of the proprietor. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint alleging such infringement, direct any person found to be using a layout-design in the authorised prescribed manner that they cease such use within a period not exceeding ninety days, provided that the respondent demonstrates reasonable grounds for continued application under this Act.

Where any proprietor fails to comply with a direction issued by the Geographical Indications Registry under this Act regarding the use of a geographical indication in relation to goods for which registration has been granted, or otherwise acts in contravention of the conditions of such registration, the Registrar shall issue notice requiring compliance within a specified period. Failure to rectify the non-compliance within that period may result in an order directing the aforesaid committed forfeiture of the registered geographical indication to the Central Government. An appeal against such an order lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to provisions regarding timelines and grounds for appeal as provided herein. The Board shall consider any evidence presented by the proprietor demonstrating due diligence or mitigating circumstances prior to affirming, modifying, or reversing the Registrar’s decision concerning registration geographical indication.

Where an objection is taken to the grant of a patent for a pharmaceutical substance on the ground that the invention is not novel or does not involve inventive step, the Controller shall issue a notice to the applicant and any other person interested in making representations. Such representations shall be filed within a period specified in the notice, and the Controller shall consider all submissions received before proceeding with examination. The Controller may, after giving an opportunity of being heard to both sides, either allow the patent as applied for or reject the application entirely. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act may appeal to the appellate board. The appellate board shall hear appeals from the orders of the Controller and may confirm, vary, or reverse such orders, subject to the provisions herein.

An owner of a registered geographical indication shall, upon discovery of any use or activity infringing their exclusive rights under this Act, institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such remedies may include an order restraining the alleged infringer from further use of the protected name or mark, as well as compensation for losses suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. The Registrar may, suo moto or upon complaint, investigate allegations of misuse or deceptive practices relating to a registered geographical indication, and issue directions to prevent such actions. Further, particulars relating registration shall be maintained with utmost accuracy reflecting changes in ownership, authorized users, or boundaries defining the geographical origin. Any alteration to these particulars requires prior notification to the Registrar and may only occur subject to their approval.

Any individual who produces, markets, distributes, or exports goods bearing a geographical indication which is demonstrably false, misleading, or constitutes a geographical indication falsified, shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. Such an alleged offence carries a minimum fine of fifty thousand rupees and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees, alongside imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. Where the goods are exported, additional punitive measures including seizure of the consignment and revocation of export licenses shall apply. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify further conditions relating to the assessment of damages and enforcement procedures under this Act.

Any person making an application for registration of a layout-design, or for any matter ancillary thereto, shall pay such fee as may be prescribed. Failure to remit the requisite application fee accompanied by proof of payment within thirty days from the date of presentation of the application shall render the application void ab initio. The Controller may, subject to conditions specified in the regulations, entertain an application where the fee is deficient, provided that a request for rectification and full remittance is received within fifteen days of notification of deficiency. Repeated failure to comply with this provision, or providing false information regarding payment status, constitutes an offence punishable with monetary penalties as determined under this Act. The Controller shall maintain records of all fees paid and may conduct audits to ensure compliance.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively the name or depiction of any drug, unless such use is authorized by or under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the proposed trade mark distinguishes the goods from those of other persons in relation to the said drug. Where a trade mark includes a representation of a medicinal plant, the application shall include a botanical description sufficient for identification purposes as provided herein. Further, any alteration made to a registered trade mark relating to a drug after registration shall be subject to approval by the Registrar and may only occur with demonstrable justification related to packaging or presentation.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a trade mark relating to any specified goods, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity for cross-examination and oral hearing. The grounds for such objection must be clearly stated in writing and supported by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates through documentary proof a period of continuous use of the mark on identical or similar goods prior to the date of the objection, the Registrar may consider this as a relevant factor. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar under this Act relating to the acceptance or rejection of any application for registration of goods may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Any person who infringes copyright in any work or contravenes any provisions of this Act shall be liable for damages comprising a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two lakh rupees. Such damages may be awarded to the owner of the copyright, or otherwise as determined by the competent court.
