Where an infringement has been committed wilfully and for commercial advantage or gain, the court may increase the amount of damages up to five times the actual loss suffered by the copyright owner. Further, a person found guilty of such infringement shall also be liable to pay costs incurred by the copyright owner in legal proceedings under this Act. The remedies available to the copyright owner are without prejudice to any other remedy or right which they may have under this Act or otherwise as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “artistic work” includes any graphic, photographic or artistic creation whatsoever, irrespective of its reproduction method, and shall encompass designs incorporated within such works that are independently copyrightable. Where an artistic work incorporates a registered trade mark as an element thereof, the existence of such registration shall not affect the subsistence of copyright in the artistic work itself; provided that the use of the trade mark remains consistent with the rights afforded to the proprietor under the Trade Marks Act. Any adaptation of an existing artistic work, whether original or derivative, shall be deemed a new artistic work subject to the provisions relating to moral rights and ownership as provided herein.

Where an applicant has failed to comply with a notice issued under this Act requiring him to amend his specification or drawings, or to furnish statements relating thereto, the Patent Office shall give him a further opportunity to do so within a period not exceeding two months, provided that such failure does not relate to a matter of substance affecting the patentability of the invention. If, after the expiry of that extended time, the applicant still fails to comply, the application for patents shall be deemed abandoned and all fees paid by the applicant shall be forfeited to the Government. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Controller’s decision shall be final. The grant of a patent in respect of any invention shall create offices patent conferring upon the patentee certain exclusive rights as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patentee may grant exclusive licences relating to the making, using or selling of the invention claimed in the patent within India. Such licences may be granted freely, and the terms thereof shall not be subject to scrutiny under this Act except where such terms are manifestly unfair to the public interest. Where an exclusive licence is assigned or otherwise transferred, the assignee or transferee shall be deemed to be the substitute for the original patentee with respect to all rights conferred by the patent relating to the licensed territory. Further, a person holding a valid and enforceable license may apply for permission to import the patented product in quantities not exceeding those manufactured under the authority of the licence, even if such importation would otherwise constitute an infringement; this is specifically allowed importation patented goods where the manufacturing occurs within India pursuant to a legally binding agreement.

Where any infringement of design rights under this Act is established, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing conduct, subject to the provisions regarding interim orders as provided herein. Damages recoverable shall be assessed based on the loss suffered by the proprietor of the layout-design, or a reasonable royalty if the infringer proves that they were unaware and had no reason to suspect that their actions constituted an infringement. A design agent person who knowingly participates in infringing activities may also be held liable for damages, jointly and severally with the primary infringer. Furthermore, the Court may order the delivery up or destruction of any articles made in contravention of these rights. The proprietor shall have the burden of proving both the existence of the layout-design right and the infringement thereof.

Any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice from the Trade Marks Registry, continues to use a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable for damages sustained by the trade proprietor registered as a consequence of the infringing use, calculated in such manner as may be prescribed. Further, repeated contravention of this provision may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The Trade Marks Registry shall have power to issue injunctions restraining any person from engaging in activities that constitute infringement under this Act, provided that the trade proprietor registered demonstrates demonstrable consumer confusion.

Where any party aggrieved by the rejection of a business basic application for registration of a trade mark alleges that such rejection was effected without due consideration being given to the distinctiveness arising from the novel design elements incorporated within the mark, the Registrar shall, upon review, consider whether the applicant has demonstrated sufficient acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and marketing efforts. The aggrieved party may submit evidence pertaining to sales figures, advertising expenditure, consumer surveys, and market research data to substantiate their claim. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied that the rejection was manifestly erroneous in failing to appreciate this acquired distinctiveness, the application shall be deemed to have been conditionally approved, subject to a further hearing where both parties may present arguments under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Government undertaking” means any body corporate or other entity owned or controlled by the Central Government or State Governments, either directly or indirectly through holding, management, or control; provided that an entity shall not be deemed a Government undertaking merely by virtue of receiving financial assistance from the government. The expression "control" with reference to a Government undertaking includes the power to appoint the majority of its directors or other governing body members and to direct its policy decisions concerning research and development activities relating to inventions, subject to any specific exemptions as may be notified under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered owner of a variety registered act, produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports or exports such variety shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Authority. The amount of damages shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees nor more than two hundred and fifty thousand rupees for each instance of infringement. Further, any person found guilty of contravention under this Act may also face prosecution before a criminal court, where they may be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, as deemed appropriate by the court. The Authority shall have power to issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement.

Any person who knowingly manufactures, uses, imports, or sells goods made using a process that infringes upon a patent shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing party licensed the patented invention from the patentee. Further, where infringement is proven, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from continuing such acts, subject to considerations of public interest and equitable principles. The patentee shall also be entitled to recover costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies under this Act, provided that the infringement was substantial and deliberate. Any appeal against a finding of infringement may only be made after deposit of twenty-five percent of the awarded damages.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be liable for penalties under this Act if, despite reasonable efforts to prevent it, the use of an identical or deceptively similar sign in relation to identical or similar goods or services creates confusion among the public. This liability shall extend to instances where such use is undertaken by a party lacking consent and demonstrably exploits the reputation associated with the registered trade mark. However, limitations on enforcement may arise if the infringing use falls within the scope of fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, provided that such use is accompanied by an acknowledgement of the source and does not prejudice the distinctive character or repute of the trade mark as provided herein. Any wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties.

Any entity seeking to utilize a registered Geographical Indication for commercial purposes relating to Alphonso mangoes shall obtain a non-exclusive license from the proprietor of the Geographical Indication, provided that such license is granted on terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The proprietor may grant licenses subject to royalty payments reflecting the scale of utilization and geographical scope of distribution. Assignment of rights in a registered Geographical Indication, including the right to grant licenses, requires prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued protection against deceptive use. Further, any product bearing a mark deemed falsify geographical indication of Alphonso mangoes without proper authorization shall be subject to seizure and forfeiture. The proprietor may pursue legal remedies for damages sustained due to unauthorized use or attempted assignment contrary to provisions herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a registered layout is defined as the three-dimensional representation of the original works described in section 4, fixed on or incorporated into a semiconductor integrated circuit; and includes both the circuitry elements and the interconnections between such elements. A registered layout shall be deemed to include any specification amended during the pendency of an application for registration, provided that such amendment does not alter the essential features of the original design as initially presented. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical documentation demonstrating the originality of a claimed registered layout, subject to guidelines issued by the Controller General.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be submitted to the court registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the description of the goods or services for which the geographical indication is sought, and a map accurately depicting the territorial limits of the geographical area. The court registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Upon receipt of an application, the court registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of receipt. Any objections received under this Act concerning the distinctiveness or reputation of the geographical indication must be promptly communicated to both the applicant and the relevant authorities for consideration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in relation registered trade marks may apply to the Registrar for registration as a registered user. Such application shall specify the geographical extent within which the use is made and shall state the reasons why the applicant did not directly use the trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the continued and substantial use of the trade mark by the proprietor, or a licensed user, prior to the date of the application for registration as a registered user. Further, an application under this Act shall be refused if it is established that the proposed use is detrimental to the distinctive character and repute of the original trade mark. The Registrar may grant such registration provided that all conditions precedent are fulfilled.

The Controller shall maintain an entry register for all applications filed under this Act, detailing each stage of processing including examination, hearing, and determination of patentability. Such entries shall be made in the prescribed manner, utilizing forms as notified by the Patents Office from time to time. The entry register shall record the date upon which any communication is dispatched to the applicant or any other person interested in the application, along with a concise summary of the contents thereof. Any modification to an existing entry must also be recorded, clearly indicating the original and revised information. Failure to adhere to the prescribed manner during registration may render such entries voidable at the discretion of the Controller. The register shall be open for public inspection subject to any restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets or confidential commercial information.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant specifying the grounds of refusal and the amount of the prescribed fee. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of service of such notice, elect to pursue the application by paying the specified fee. Failure to pay the fee within the stipulated period shall render the trade mark application deemed abandoned, and the Registrar shall record accordingly in the Register of Trade Marks. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the fee payable notice may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such decision, subject to payment of the prescribed appellate fee. The Board’s order shall be final and binding.

An advertisement application registration shall be deemed invalid if it is found, upon investigation under this Act, that the layout-design was copied from an existing work without due authorization. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the validity of such registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall be entitled to relief only if they demonstrate substantial prejudice arising directly from the erroneous determination. Furthermore, where infringement of layout-design rights is established following an advertisement application registration, the owner shall be empowered to seek injunctive relief and claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory infringement. The Registrar may require production of relevant documentation substantiating originality at any stage during proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment of copyright in a musical composition shall be deemed an exclusive license unless the instrument explicitly states otherwise. Such assignments may cover all or part of the rights specified under this Act, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and public performance. Where a patent addition relating to a copyrighted software program is granted, the assignor’s obligations regarding royalties and attribution shall extend to encompass any derivative works created as a consequence of said patent addition. A copyright case arising from an unauthorized adaptation of such a work will be adjudicated considering both the original copyright assignment and the implications of the related patent addition. Further, sub-licensing rights may be granted by the assignee subject to prior written consent from the assignor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.

For the purposes of this Act, “rectification register court” shall mean the High Court exercising jurisdiction under this Act and designated by notification in the Official Gazette to entertain applications for rectification of entries in the Register of Patents. The term “patent office” refers specifically to the governmental body established under this Act responsible for receiving, processing, and examining patent applications; it includes all divisions, branches, and officers thereof authorized to perform functions related to patents. Applications relating to matters concerning the register shall be made to the rectification register court subject to any procedural requirements as provided herein. The patent office is empowered to issue notices and conduct hearings pertaining to objections under this Act.

A breeder seeking to commercialize a new variety shall demonstrate, through documented field trials conducted over at least three crop cycles, that the proposed *breeder variety registered* exhibits stability and uniformity consistent with established agricultural practices for that species. The application for registration must include detailed morphological data, including but not limited to plant height, flowering time, disease resistance scores as determined by standardized protocols, and seed germination rates under varying environmental conditions. Further, any indication of genetic modification shall be explicitly declared within the application, subject to verification by the Authority appointed under this Act. The Registrar may reject an application if the submitted data fails to adequately establish these characteristics or if the proposed variety poses a demonstrable risk to existing agricultural biodiversity as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be finally determined by the Board, and its decision shall be binding on all parties concerned. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration containing a representation of a mark that includes three-dimensional characteristics, require the applicant to furnish a specimen demonstrating such characteristics in relation to the goods or services with which the mark is associated. Marks registered accordance with the provisions herein are entitled to protection against use by any person without due cause and consent from the proprietor. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all marks registered in accordance with this Act, available for public inspection.

An applicant seeking registration of an invention shall furnish with the application a complete specification detailing the subject matter claimed. The complete specification must include a clear and concise description of the invention sufficient to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use it, along with drawings where necessary for understanding the invention. Claims defining the scope of protection sought shall be annexed to the complete specification and presented in a manner that is distinct from the descriptive matter. The Registrar may require amendments to claims if they are ambiguous or do not clearly define the subject matter of the invention as disclosed within the claim complete specification. Any alteration to the complete specification after its initial filing shall be permissible only with the consent of the Controller, provided that such alterations do not broaden the scope of protection initially sought.

An application for patent shall be deemed to include an inventive step if it involves more than the mere arrangement or combination of known elements and possesses novelty as provided herein. Where an applicant seeks protection based on a convention application, the date of priority shall be determined from the first filing date in the invention convention country. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the claimed invention, including details concerning its experimental results and technical specifications, if deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any request for information issued by the Controller must specify a reasonable timeframe for compliance; failure to respond within that period shall be considered as abandonment of the application. The determination of obviousness will consider existing knowledge accessible to a person skilled in the art at the time of the invention’s disclosure, irrespective of whether such knowledge was formally published or otherwise disseminated.

A cessation patent arises where a patent holder fails to satisfy obligations as provided herein, resulting in the automatic termination of rights granted under this Act. Such failure includes, but is not limited to, non-payment of prescribed renewal fees within the stipulated time frame and inability to demonstrate continued commercial working of the patented invention in India for a period exceeding three years from the date of grant. The Controller may issue notice regarding impending cessation patent, affording the patent holder an opportunity to rectify the deficiency; however, failure to do so shall result in the patent ceasing to have effect on the specified date.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed botanical description conforming to internationally recognized taxonomic standards and specifying the genera species specified in Schedule D. Such description must accurately reflect the essential characteristics distinguishing the variety from other known varieties within its kind, including data relating to morphological traits, disease resistance, and yield potential. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation, including propagation protocols and genetic purity assessments, if deemed necessary for evaluation. Provided that any applicant demonstrating adherence to established customary practices in relation to traditional knowledge concerning the plant variety shall be afforded due consideration during examination.

The proprietor of a registered trademark relating to offices may grant a license conferring the right to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to terms and conditions agreed upon in writing. Such licenses shall be assignable alongside the underlying trademark ownership, provided that notice of assignment is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days. Where a force cessation patent pertaining to a process integral to the manufacture of goods bearing the licensed trademark occurs, the licensee may negotiate with the proprietor for adjustments to royalty payments reflecting such disruption, as determined by an independent valuation. The proprietor shall retain ultimate control over quality standards associated with the use of their offices trade marks under any license agreement. Any sub-licensing activity requires prior written consent from the original proprietor and must adhere to conditions mirroring those stipulated in the primary license.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall declare that they are the rightful owner of the layout-design, or are duly authorized to make the application on behalf of the owner. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the registration common regulations regarding clarity and completeness of information. If the Registrar finds any deficiency in the particulars provided, they shall issue a notice requiring rectification within sixty days. Failure to rectify the deficiencies as directed will result in rejection of the produced registrar application. The applicant may appeal against such rejection under procedures prescribed herein.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, applies for or uses a trademark that is identical or confusingly similar to a previously registered trademark relating to the same or closely related trade goods services shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, and the trademark application shall be deemed invalid ab initio. Further, any proprietor of a registered trademark aggrieved by such infringement may apply to the relevant authority seeking an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark, as provided herein. The authority may also order the destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark.

An application for a certificate registration relating to a plant variety shall include particulars specifying the denomination, field reference number, geographical location where the variety is being cultivated and details regarding its distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation pertaining to lineage tracing and genetic purity as deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Provided that an applicant demonstrating prior traditional use or cultivation of a plant variety shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence substantiating such usage. Upon satisfactory evaluation and verification of the submitted information, the Authority shall proceed with the examination process; rejection may occur if the application fails to meet prescribed criteria concerning novelty or poses a threat to existing farmers' rights as provided herein.

An application for patent protection may include one or more claims defining the scope of the invention; however, subject to this Act, any claim specification amendment sought after the initial filing date shall only be permissible if it does not alter the inventive concept disclosed in the original complete specification. Such amendments are allowable solely to clarify language or correct minor errors that do not broaden the protection initially sought. A request for a claim specification amendment must explicitly state the basis for its necessity and demonstrate how it remains consistent with the disclosure contained within the originally filed documents, as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, notify any persons by way of publication in the Trade Marks Journal who claim to have rights in relation to that trade mark. Such notification shall specify the grounds on which such right is claimed and provide a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such notification within which the claimant may file written opposition under this Act. The Registrar shall, prior to publishing any notice, verify the accuracy of the information contained therein with the applicant. Provided that, where the trade mark contains a geographical indication as defined herein, additional notifications may be issued to relevant producers’ associations or authorities concerned with protecting such indications.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any collective management organisation seeking to operate as a copyright society shall submit to the Copyright Societies Registrar a comprehensive schedule detailing all works proposed for administration and the terms governing their exploitation. This schedule must specify the percentage share allocated to right holders and users under each licensing scheme. Assignment of rights to a copyright society, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, requires formal registration with the Registrar, accompanied by irrevocable consent from the assignor. The Copyright Societies Registrar may, after due notice and opportunity for hearing, reject any proposed assignment deemed detrimental to the public interest or inconsistent with principles of fair dealing as provided herein. Further, any modification to existing licensing terms must be pre-approved by the Registrar before implementation, ensuring transparency and equitable distribution of royalties among stakeholders.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the register disclosed under this Act may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file a rectification application before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such application shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and state the grounds upon which such rectification is claimed. Failure to comply with prescribed forms or payment of requisite fees shall render the application void. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, direct amendment, deletion, or addition to the register. Any order made by the Board under this provision is final and binding, subject to appeal before a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the registered trade mark has its principal place of business; penalties for non-compliance shall apply as provided herein.

Where a registered layout design is infringed, the owner shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. The appropriate remedy shall include an injunction restraining the infringer from further infringing acts, and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner, subject to a minimum amount determined by the Intellectual Property Tribunal. Further, any articles manufactured or imported in violation of this Act may be seized and destroyed at the owner’s expense. An appeal against an order made by the Intellectual Property Tribunal concerning the assessment of damages or the manner applying appellate jurisdiction shall lie to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. The aggrieved party may also seek interim relief pending determination of the matter, provided that security is furnished as deemed fit by the court.

Where a patent is jointly owned by multiple applicants, each owner shall hold an equal share patent in the invention, subject to any contractual agreements executed prior to the grant. Such agreements may specify varying percentages of ownership and define rights pertaining to exploitation of the patented invention. The Controller may, upon application from one or more joint owners, facilitate the transfer or assignment of a share patent to another party, provided that all other co-owners consent in writing or demonstrate an inability to participate in the commercialization efforts. Any license granted by one joint owner shall be deemed to bind all other joint owners unless explicitly excluded within the original agreement establishing the share patent arrangement. Further, any action taken concerning the patent’s enforcement requires the collective authorization of the holders of a majority share patent interest.

An appeal under this Act is deemed a proceeding appellate and shall be instituted within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged. For the purposes of such an appeal, the aggrieved party may submit written arguments and supporting documentation as prescribed by regulations framed hereunder. The manner applying appellate jurisdiction shall require that all appeals are first heard by a single member of the relevant tribunal, unless otherwise directed by the Chairperson. Decisions on interlocutory matters during the proceeding appellate shall be subject to review by the same tribunal. Further appeals from such decisions may only be entertained with leave granted by the tribunal.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a design registered layout, the Appellate Board shall admit such appeal if it appears that the Registrar has acted without due consideration of the evidence presented and that substantial questions of law relating to novelty or original authorship are involved. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the Registrar’s interpretation of the criteria for originality was flawed, subject to the proviso that the Respondent may present counter-arguments regarding the layout's similarity to prior art. Any order made by the Appellate Board concerning a design registered layout shall be final, provided that any party aggrieved by such an order may petition the Supreme Court within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” in relation to a trade mark includes not only the application of the mark upon goods but also any act whereby the sign is reproduced, including its appearance on packaging, labels, or associated documents. The term "trade mark uses" shall extend to acts undertaken for the purpose of advertising, promoting, or otherwise bringing goods or services to the attention of the public. Use may occur directly by the trade mark proprietor or indirectly through authorized users, subject to any conditions stipulated in a licensing agreement. A use is deemed deceptive if it creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of the goods or services.

For the purposes of this Act, "used falsifying trade" with respect to a registered trademark shall mean the application to any goods or services of a sign that is identical or confusingly similar to the said mark, and which creates a false or misleading impression as to the nature, quality, origin, or characteristics of those goods or services. Such use shall be deemed deceptive if it is likely to cause confusion among the public regarding the trade source of the goods or services. Nothing in this definition shall prevent the use of a sign that describes the applicant's goods or services, provided that such use does not constitute used falsifying trade as defined herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "integrated circuit” shall mean any microchip whether or not containing discrete components and includes any set of connected wires, transistors, and other circuitry elements intended to perform a specific function; “layout-design" means the three dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, layers and all other relevant information necessary for the fabrication of an integrated circuit. The term "mask” refers to a template used in the manufacture of semiconductor devices. An application for registration shall be filed with the registrar semiconductor, who may require such particulars as are necessary for identification of the layout-design and verification of its originality, provided that any confidential information disclosed during examination remains protected under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision to register patents thereof may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant of patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice must specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or existence of identical inventions. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the opposition invalid and without merit. The Controller may, after providing an opportunity for hearing to both the patentee and the opposition applicant registration, dismiss the opposition or refer the matter to a specialized forum for further adjudication. Any party found to have filed a frivolous or vexatious opposition is liable to pay costs and penalties as determined by the Controller.

Where an objection is raised by any person, other than the applicant, against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall decide such objection within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt thereof. The decision of the Registrar shall be based solely on the evidence submitted and arguments presented by both the applicant and the objector, provided that any evidence pertaining to prior use or reputation of a sign shall be carefully scrutinized. Further, should the Registrar find that the transmission operation of data relating to the objection has been compromised, rendering the integrity of the record uncertain, he may direct a fresh hearing. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal under this Act.

Where a patented process involves the use of one or more biological materials, including but not limited to microorganisms, plant cells, or animal tissues, such process shall be deemed to be subject to review under this Act if it results in the production of an article intended for use as food, feed, drug, or cosmetic. Provided that, where the biological material is rendered incapable of reproduction at the time of its use in the patented process, a determination regarding patentability shall consider whether the inventive step contributes significantly to the advancement of technology and is not merely the application of known techniques. Further, any modification to the patented process which alters the intended outcome or functionality of the final product must be disclosed accurately in supporting documentation submitted under this Act.

An appeal lies to the Authority Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to revocation of registration or rectification of layout-design registrations. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order appealed against, and the appellant may file such appeals in the prescribed form along with a copy of the order sought to be appealed. The Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Subject to this, the Board shall hear parties and evidence adduced before it, and may pass such orders as it deems just and equitable. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Authority Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall record its reasons for decision in writing, provided that any confidential information disclosed during proceedings shall be treated accordingly.

The Registering Authority, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, shall forward the same to the Standing Committee constituted under subsection (3) of section 14. The Committee shall examine the application and any objections received in accordance with the provisions herein relating to public notice and opposition proceedings. Following such examination, the Committee shall submit its findings and recommendations, including observations on distinctiveness and reputation as may be relevant, to the Registrar within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt of the application by the Standing Committee. The Registrar shall consider the report of the Standing Committee and any further submissions made by the applicant or objector. A comprehensive parliament year report detailing the number of applications received, registrations granted, oppositions filed, and decisions rendered under this Act will be laid before both Houses of Parliament annually.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the subsistence of copyright, or to any question of fact arising under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Tribunal shall follow such procedure as the Central Government may prescribe in this behalf and shall have the same powers as it possesses in relation to appeals under other provisions of this Act. Any order passed by the Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The determination of ownership in a copyright case shall be governed by principles of natural justice and fair hearing, ensuring all parties are afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging an infringement of his registered trademark, and it is established before the relevant adjudicating authority that the defendant has knowingly used a mark identical or deceptively similar to the plaintiff’s registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which said registration subsists, then such defendant shall be liable for damages as provided herein. Further, where the infringement constitutes a commercial fraud, or involves wilful deception intended to gain unfair advantage, or causes grievous harm to the reputation of the proprietor's trademark, the court may impose punishable imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall be determined at the discretion of the court. Any employee acting under the direction of such defendant remains subject to similar penalties.

Where an invention far claimed extends to a process for producing a substance intended for use or employed in the manufacture of a pharmaceutical product, and such product is subsequently marketed without due regard to established clinical trial protocols as prescribed under this Act, the patentee shall be liable for damages. Such damages may include compensation for losses suffered by consumers demonstrably harmed by the unauthorized marketing practices, and further encompass punitive measures proportionate to the scale of the deceptive conduct. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party or acting suo moto, order inspection of manufacturing facilities and clinical trial data relevant to the patented process. Failure to comply with such orders shall constitute contempt under this Act and render the patentee subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person claiming an infringed copyright shall furnish to the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority a sworn affidavit detailing the nature of the infringement, including but not limited to unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of the copyrighted work. Failure to provide this affidavit within thirty days of discovering the alleged infringement will preclude such claimant from seeking injunctive relief under this Act. The authority may, after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, issue an order restraining further acts of copyright violation and directing the destruction of infringing materials. Any party failing to comply with a lawful order issued by the Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. It is incumbent upon applicants to diligently register copyrights as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The appellant shall serve a copy of the memorandum of appeal on the Registrar not less than thirty days before the date appointed for hearing the appeal. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed from. If the Intellectual Property Appellate Board allows an appeal, it shall direct that the trade mark be registered as originally applied for, or with such modifications as determined by the Board. The proprietor proposed registered may also file a counter-statement to any appeal.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a person has engaged in activities contravening provisions relating to farmers’ rights concerning saved seed, it may issue an order directing such person to cease and desist from the offending conduct. Subject to compliance with due process as provided herein, any aggrieved party may apply to a competent court for an injunction restraining the enforcement of said order. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the Plant Variety Protection Authority’s determination. The court may grant a temporary or permanent injunction, or such other relief as it deems just and equitable, provided that the applicant demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of success on the merits. An order injunction sub judice shall not prevent the authority from undertaking further investigations.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed on the ground that its use would be contrary to morality or public order, or would otherwise constitute a condition declared unlawful under this Act, the Appellate Board shall hear and determine such opposition. The Board may, after affording the applicant and the opponent a reasonable opportunity of being heard, dismiss the opposition if it finds that the alleged unlawfulness is unsubstantiated; however, should the Board find merit in the objection raised by the geographical indication plaintiff, registration shall be refused or, where already granted, revoked. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods" shall include commodities, articles, and any product manufactured, processed, or altered for sale or distribution, whether tangible or having intangible characteristics. Goods may be classified under distinct categories as determined by the Registrar, considering their nature, use, and intended consumer base. The term “goods” extends to packaged products, containers used in the packaging of goods, and labels affixed thereto, provided such labels clearly identify the goods contained within. xii shall exempt certain agricultural produce from being considered "goods" for the purposes of infringement proceedings under this Act, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending, and prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark has been established by another party, the Registrar may, upon review of documentary evidence demonstrating such prior use, entertain objections notwithstanding that the earlier use predates the filing date of the applicant’s trade mark. This power shall be exercised cautiously, balancing the interests of both parties and considering any demonstrable goodwill accrued by the later applicant through honest commercial dealing. However, where it is demonstrated to the Registrar's satisfaction that the prior user had knowledge of the pending application and continued use despite such knowledge, an amendment antedating registration may be refused in order to prevent unjust enrichment.

Where an invention application is deemed, upon examination, to lack clarity as provided herein, the Controller shall issue a communication specifying the deficiencies and affording the applicant an opportunity for amendment. Such amendment shall be permissible only where the originally filed specification could reasonably have been construed to encompass the altered matter; otherwise, the application shall stand rejected. An appeal against this determination may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of such communication. The Board’s decision on any question arising from the interpretation of “reasonable construal” shall be final and binding, subject to a further petition for special leave to the Supreme Court arguing manifest error of law.

Where an application is filed by a person claiming to be a farmer for registration of a plant variety, and such claim is disputed on the grounds that the applicant does not fulfill the definition of “farmer” as provided herein, the Authority shall give notice thereof to all interested parties. Any party aggrieved by this determination may appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted regarding the applicant’s farming activities and landholding records, subject to verification through a designated officer appointed for that purpose. An India application shall be deemed invalid if the farmer's claim is ultimately found unsubstantiated by the Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall not be accepted if it is deemed identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark relating to identical goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use, provided that such use has occurred prior to the date of the aforementioned application and satisfies conditions as provided herein regarding duration and geographical extent. Further, a registered trade mark shall cease to be protected if the proprietor fails to file renewal forms within the prescribed time limit or pays the requisite fees. Any alteration to a registered trade marks representation requires consent from the Registrar, subject to compliance with regulations concerning clarity and accuracy of depiction.

Where an application for a patent has been granted and subsequently assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignee or licensee may, with the consent of the assignor or licensor respectively, file a request to amend the said application. Such amendment shall be permissible only if it does not substantially alter the scope of protection initially sought in respect of the invention as described in the original specification and claims. The Controller shall consider any such request for an application amend taking into account the impact on existing licensees or assignees, ensuring that no undue prejudice arises from the alteration. Further, where a license agreement contains provisions regarding further patent applications based on the licensed technology, the amendment process shall be conducted in accordance with those contractual obligations, subject to compliance with all other requirements under this Act.

Where an applicant patent claimant seeks to amend the description of the invention disclosed in a patent application subsequent to its publication under this Act, such amendment shall be permissible only if it clarifies matters relating to the claimed invention. The Controller may require the applicant to submit a declaration affirming that the amended description remains consistent with the original disclosure and does not introduce any new matter. Further, an examiner assessing the patentability of the invention following such amendment shall consider whether the clarification unduly broadens the scope of protection sought or prejudices the interests of third parties who have relied upon the originally published specification. The applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to respond to any objections raised by the examiner concerning the amended description. Any decision regarding the permissibility of an amendment is subject to appeal under this Act, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “trade description” means an affirmation, statement, or indication, whether in words, figures, symbols, marks, labels, designs, illustrations, or any other form whatsoever, which is used to describe the nature, quality, characteristics, quantity, origin, ingredients, properties, capabilities, style, grade, condition, or suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services. A trade description shall be deemed to include representations relating to the geographical origin of goods; and where a trade description denotes that goods are manufactured in a specific region, such designation must accurately reflect the place of manufacture as provided herein.

Applications for patents relating to inventions made in respect of processes involving microorganisms shall be accompanied by a deposit certificate, issued by an authorized body as specified under this Act. Such certificate must confirm the accession number assigned to the deposited microorganism and details regarding its preservation conditions. Where an applicant elects to utilize the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Microorganisms for the purposes of disclosure, the Controller may require submission of a certified copy of the relevant treaty provisions alongside the deposit certificate. The requirements concerning the form and content of such certificates shall be as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Failure to provide these documents or discrepancies therein may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before an appellate authority.

An international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein and shall confer upon the proprietor the rights which accrue under this Act as if the trade mark were registered in India with that date of application for registration. For the purposes of determining entitlement to remedies for infringement, a resulting international registration shall be deemed to be a registered trade mark within the meaning of this Act. Where an international registration includes denominations relating to agricultural produce or other products, denomination variety shall be considered as part of the indication and afforded protection accordingly, provided that such use does not create confusion among consumers.

For the purposes of this Act, “transmissible use layout” means a layout-design in respect of which the right to make, sell, import or offer for sale integrated circuits incorporating that layout-design has been transferred by contract or otherwise, and where such transfer includes the right to grant further licences or assignments relating to the layout-design. A transmissible use layout shall be deemed to include any modification made to the original layout-design with the consent of the initial owner, provided that such modification does not alter the essential character thereof as defined under this Act. The scope of a transmissible use layout is subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the transfer agreement.

Where an application for registration of a utility model is granted under this Act, the Controller may specify conditions regarding the manufacture, use, or exploitation of the registered utility model, provided that such conditions are reasonable and do not unduly restrain competition. Any condition declared unlawful by order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be deemed null and void from the date of such order; however, registration remains valid subject to any modifications directed by the Board. The applicant for registration shall furnish an affidavit verifying compliance with all specified conditions at the time of renewal application. Failure to adhere to a lawful condition may result in suspension or revocation of the utility model’s registration as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark shall diligently maintain its distinctiveness and reputation following grant; failure to do so constitutes grounds for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint from any interested party demonstrating material damage resulting from use contrary to accepted regulations concerning registration common regulations, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register. Such complaints must be substantiated with documentary evidence establishing ongoing misrepresentation or dilution of brand identity. Any person found guilty of knowingly employing a deceptively similar mark shall face penalties including fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment extending to three years; repeat offences will attract enhanced sanctions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the rectification of a registered trademark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The proprietor of an application registered proprieto shall be deemed guilty of an offence if, without reasonable justification, they fail to comply with any direction issued under this Act regarding the quality control or standards for goods or services associated with the mark. Such failure constitutes a violation and renders the proprietor liable to prosecution before a criminal court. Further, where a trademark is used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial property, the aggrieved party may apply to restrain such use through an injunction granted by a competent civil court. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which may be available to the aggrieved person under any other law for the time being in force.

The Registering Authority may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, direct the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the quality and characteristics of the goods or products for which the indication is sought, provided that such direction shall be accompanied by reasons in writing. Any person claiming proprietary rights in relation to the geographical indication may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Registering Authority. The Registering Authority shall consider any opposition received and provide an opportunity for both the applicant and the opponent to be heard. Unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication by any person other than an authorized user is prohibited, subject to exceptions as provided herein relating to prior uses. The definition of *geographical indication use* includes employing the indication in a manner that falsely suggests the origin of the goods or services.

An applicant seeking to amend a patent specification after the publication of the application under this Act shall file with the Controller a request in writing setting forth the proposed amendments. Such request must clearly identify each alteration sought and provide justification for its necessity, demonstrating how it clarifies or supports the originally claimed invention. The Controller may require the applicant to submit a declaration affirming that the amended specification continues to disclose the subject matter of the original application as understood by a person skilled in the art at the priority date. Further, any patent amendment specification shall not introduce new matter which extends beyond the scope of the initial disclosure; such additions will be deemed invalid and may render the granted patent susceptible to revocation proceedings. The Controller’s decision regarding acceptance or rejection of an amendment is final, subject to appeal under procedures as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce the layout design in any form, including but not limited to manufacturing integrated circuits. Any person who without authorization from the registered proprietor makes, imports, or offers for sale an integrated circuit incorporating the proprietor layout design shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the relevant court, taking into account factors such as the extent of infringement and lost profits. An application for registration, constituting an india application, must disclose full details regarding the applicant’s claim to being the first inventor of the layout design. Provided that rectification proceedings may be initiated under this Act if it is demonstrated that a proprietor layout design has been registered in error or through misrepresentation.

An application for a patent may claim as an invention an addition to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter already existing, provided that such addition results in a new and useful article or process. Where a patent has been granted based on a claim for an addition validity patent, the Controller shall not entertain any challenge questioning the novelty or inventive step solely on the basis that the underlying invention was previously known. Any party aggrieved by the grant of such a patent may institute proceedings under this Act seeking revocation; however, it shall be presumed that the addition confers a substantial and commercially exploitable advantage unless proven otherwise through expert testimony and demonstrable evidence of diminished utility. Failure to provide such evidence will result in dismissal of the challenge and imposition of costs as determined by the Controller.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication may be refused if the Registrar, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, is satisfied that the proposed indication does not primarily identify goods as originating from a specific region in India, based on factors such as natural conditions and traditional practices. Any party aggrieved by such a refusal order shall have the right to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The Board may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision. Further appeals from orders of the Appellate Board are permissible to the High Court on grounds specified herein.

A complete specification, when amended subsequent to the initial filing date but prior to the sealing of the patent, shall be treated as a substitute for the original specification for all purposes under this Act. The amendment itself must clearly indicate the changes made to the originally filed description, claims, and drawings. Such amendments are permissible only if they do not alter the inventive concept disclosed in the complete specification as initially presented. Any addition or alteration that introduces new matter is prohibited. A patent examiner may require further clarification regarding the scope and effect of a complete specification amended in this manner, provided that such requirement does not unduly delay the processing of the application.

Where a trade mark registration subsists in India and an application for the same or a similar trade mark is filed in a Contracting State, the Registrar shall, upon receiving notification from the Trade Marks Office of that Contracting State, conduct such inquiry as he deems necessary to ascertain whether the use of the foreign trade mark has created confusion amongst consumers within the territory of India. This determination shall be made irrespective of any distinct denomination variety employed by the applicant in either jurisdiction. Provided that, if the notified application relates to goods or services identical with those for which registration is already granted in India, the Registrar may require the Indian proprietor to submit evidence demonstrating continued and substantial use of the trade mark within India.

Any person found guilty of contravening the provisions relating to benefit sharing under this Act, including unauthorized commercialization of plant varieties registered hereunder, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for the first offence. Subsequent offences may attract penalties up to ten lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Authority established as provided herein may issue cease and desist orders directing any infringing party to immediately halt activities violating farmers’ rights or intellectual property protections. Further, damages equivalent to thrice the value of profits derived from such unauthorized use shall be recoverable. This applies particularly where infringement occurs in direct disregard of stipulations outlined under section 41 clause (b), concerning geographical indications.

Any person found, upon investigation under this Act, to have engaged in the unauthorized reproduction or importation for commercial purposes of a layout-design, where such act involves the means transmission operation of digital data relating to the said layout-design, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the cost of establishing the layout-design. Further, any party seeking to challenge the validity of an infringement claim may submit an affidavit provided registrar, detailing evidence demonstrating fair use or lack of substantial similarity. Failure to comply with procedural requirements outlined herein regarding submission of such affidavits will render them inadmissible during subsequent proceedings. Repeated violations shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer and subject to judicial review.

Where any applicant, being a business india applicant, files an application for the registration of a trade mark that includes a geographical indication associated with agricultural products exclusively originating from India, the Registrar may require such applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive use and control over the quality characteristics defining said geographical indication. Failure to provide satisfactory proof within the time stipulated under this Act shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any person employing a registered trade mark in a manner that falsely suggests association with or approval by the business india applicant shall be guilty of an offence, punishable with imprisonment and a fine as provided herein.

Any individual engaging in the design, manufacture, import, or distribution of semiconductor integrated circuits layouts shall be deemed a practitioner person under this Act. Any act of unauthorized copying, reproduction, or adaptation of a registered layout-design by such a practitioner person constitutes an infringement actionable at law. Where a registered user shall discover evidence of such infringement, they may initiate civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. Failure to comply with prescribed security measures relating to confidential layout-design information will attract penalties as provided herein. Furthermore, any practitioner person found guilty of wilful inducement of infringement faces enhanced financial sanctions and potential criminal prosecution subject to judicial discretion.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar trade marks relating to the acceptance, refusal, or advertisement of a trademark application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellant shall serve notice on the respondent, namely, the Registrar, along with a copy of the grounds of appeal. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. Where the appeal concerns a matter of fact, the Tribunal may require the appellant to produce evidence supporting their claim. Under this Act, the registrar trade marks is obligated to provide reasons in writing for any decision that adversely affects the interests of an applicant or registered proprietor. The tribunal’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions governing judicial review.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act, and it is subsequently determined by the relevant judicial authority that such proceedings were manifestly frivolous or vexatious, or undertaken with the primary intent to harass or obstruct another party’s lawful activities, then the court may order the proprietor to pay damages to the aggrieved party. Furthermore, any individual found guilty of knowingly making false representations concerning the ownership of a trade mark, intending to deceive or mislead the public, shall be punishable with sentence imprisonment term which may extend to five years and with a fine not exceeding one million rupees. Such conviction may also result in disqualification from registering marks under this Act for a period as determined by the court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person aggrieved by an act patent may institute a suit for damages or seek injunctive relief against any party infringing upon the rights conferred thereby. Such infringement shall include, but not be limited to, unauthorized making, use, sale, offer for sale, or importation of the patented invention. The registered proprietor person shall be liable to pay compensation for all losses sustained by the aggrieved party as a consequence of the infringement. Failure to comply with an order restraining such acts may result in penalties including fines and imprisonment, as determined by the court. Further, wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties under this Act.

Where a patentee, by assignment or otherwise, has transferred rights pertaining to a registered invention, and the assignee subsequently desires to grant a license for exploitation of such patented invention, notice rectification shall be initiated if the register fails accurately to reflect the details of said licensing agreement. The Controller may, upon receiving an application supported by requisite documentation demonstrating the terms and scope of the license granted, direct that the register be amended to include particulars of the licensee’s name and the extent of their rights under this Act. Provided that any existing patent holder or other interested party may submit objections to such rectification within a period as prescribed herein. The Controller shall consider all submissions before issuing an order regarding notice rectification. Such orders are subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein.

Any person who, having knowledge of registered marks under this Act, makes use of an identical mark or a mark which is deceptively similar to a registered mark in connection with goods or services for which the registration has been made, shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be assessed by the Commercial Court and may include compensation for loss of profits, dilution of goodwill, and any other consequential losses suffered by the proprietor of the trade marks. Further, where an infringement is established, the court may order the infringer to account for all profits derived from the infringing use, subject to a statutory cap as determined by the Central Government. The Registrar shall also be empowered to issue injunctions against continued deceptive practices relating to the Marks Act 1999.

Application for registration of a literary work shall be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by copies of the work as may be required under this Act. The Registrar shall register such work upon being satisfied that the applicant is the author or rightful assignee thereof and that the work fulfills all requirements for originality as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a work may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The provisions sub section (1) shall not apply where the work has been previously registered in another country under an agreement to which India is a party. Further, registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership for the purposes of civil proceedings.

Where a trade mark is registered in relation to goods or services of one class, and subsequently applied for registration in relation to goods or services of another class, the Registrar may grant such subsequent registration subject to proof that the earlier registration does not create an unreasonable likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation as to the identity of the source of the respective goods or services. Any proprietor aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to the refusal or acceptance of a mark separately registered may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Further, any person who, without consent, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a mark separately registered shall be liable for damages sustained by the proprietor of the mark.

Where a proprietor institutes a suit for infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4, the court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including an injunction restraining the defendant from any further acts of infringement or passing off. Damages shall be assessed according to principles of fairness and proportionality, taking into consideration the extent of the plaintiff’s loss and the defendant's gain derived from the infringing activity. The court may also order the defendant to provide a full account of profits made as a result of the infringing conduct, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates reasonable efforts to ascertain such profits. Further, subject to any terms specified by the court, the proprietor is entitled to an order for the delivery up or destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark or get-up. The defendant shall be responsible for all costs associated with compliance with this order.

Any person who, without due cause or consent from the proprietor of a registered trademark, uses any mark which is identical or deceptively similar to such proprietor’s trademark, shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages recoverable shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringing use and the profits made by the infringer. Further, where an infringement has occurred, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark or packaging thereof. It is provided that any registered proprietor trade marks shall be afforded protection against dilution even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services associated with those marks.

An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, at any time during the pendency of the application and prior to the publication thereof under this Act, submit to the Registrar an error amendment notice detailing any inadvertent errors or omissions contained within the submitted documentation pertaining to the layout-design. Such notice shall be accompanied by a duly affirmed affidavit verifying the accuracy of the corrections proposed therein. The Registrar shall consider each error amendment notice received and may, subject to satisfaction that the proposed correction does not substantially alter the original claimed design or prejudice the rights of any other party, grant permission for the amendment. Any decision regarding an error amendment notice shall be communicated in writing to the applicant within sixty days from the date of receipt. Failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein may render the error amendment notice invalid and without effect.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark seeks to alter the representation of that trade mark, such alteration shall not be permissible without prior approval obtained under this Act. The application for such approval must specify the nature and extent of the proposed modification, accompanied by representations demonstrating its continued distinctiveness following the change. Provided that an alteration does not affect the essential characteristics or connotations associated with the registered trade mark, it may be approved. Furthermore, any proprietor seeking to amend their trade mark shall provide evidence confirming that consumers are likely to recognise the altered representation as denoting the same goods or services previously indicated under this Act. The provisions act shall govern all applications for alteration and subsequent registration thereof.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark proceeds to final hearing, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the applied-for mark within India. Such evidence must pertain to the period commencing from the date of first use as claimed in the application and continuing up to the date of the hearing. The Registrar shall consider any submissions made by interested parties regarding the extent or nature of such use, provided these are supported by documentary proof or affidavits verified according to prescribed procedures. Failure to adequately demonstrate a *trade mark used* will constitute grounds for refusal of registration. Further, where an objection is raised concerning non-use, the applicant may be called upon to rebut this challenge with satisfactory evidence of ongoing commercial exploitation under this Act.

Applications for registration of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works shall be made to the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. Every application so filed shall contain a statement of ownership by the applicant and particulars of the work, including its title, author, nationality, and first publication details, if any. The Registrar may require such further information from the applicant as he deems necessary for verification under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar is empowered to conduct searches and inquiries as deemed appropriate for ensuring compliance with the provisions herein.

An application for trade mark registration shall be deemed to be refused if, upon examination, the Trade Mark Registrar finds that the proposed mark lacks distinctiveness by virtue of its composition consisting exclusively of non-figurative elements commonly used in relation to the goods or services. Provided that, such refusal may be withdrawn if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application, supported by evidence of substantial market penetration and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall consider documentary proof submitted by the applicant, including advertising expenditure, sales figures, and consumer surveys, in assessing whether acquired distinctiveness exists. Further, an appeal against a refusal under this Act lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Authority shall establish a Grievance Redressal Sub-Committee for each agricultural zone within three months of its constitution under this Act. The composition of such Sub-Committees shall be determined by notification issued by the Authority and may include representatives from registered breeders, farmer organizations, and relevant government departments. Any aggrieved party seeking redress relating to decisions made by a Plant Variety Protection Committee shall first file a written representation with the Grievance Redressal Sub-Committee concerned. The chairperson shall oversee the functioning of all such Sub-Committees, ensuring adherence to procedural guidelines as provided herein. Decisions of the Sub-Committee shall be binding on the Authority subject to an appeal process detailed in Schedule B. The Authority may issue further directives regarding timelines and processes for filing appeals.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any patentee or person duly authorized by the patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under conditions specified therein.
