Such licenses shall be assignable, whether in whole or in part, and may include rights relating to manufacture, sale, and importation. Where a license is granted through a collective management organization functioning as a copyright society fee collector for related technological applications, the terms of such grant shall be subject to review by the relevant governmental authority to ensure equitable distribution amongst licensees. The patentee shall provide notice of any assignment or license to the Controller within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope and duration of rights transferred. Failure to comply with this provision may render the assignment or license voidable as provided herein. Any subsequent protection invention convention relating to the patented subject matter requires prior consent from the original assignee.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of licences granted under this Act for works comprising cinematograph films. An application for registration of a licence may be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by certified copies of the agreement creating such licence and details of the assignor and assignee. The applicant shall declare whether the licence is exclusive or non-exclusive and specify the territory within which it operates. Upon satisfactory verification of the particulars furnished and subject to payment of the requisite fee, the Registrar may register the licence and enter its particulars in the aforementioned register. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a licence may appeal to the Controller. The registered licences shall be open to public inspection as provided herein.

Any individual, firm, company, or other body corporate who, without authorization from the registered owner, engages in the manufacture, reproduction, importation, sale, offer for sale, or distribution of any integrated circuit layout-design incorporating a transmissible use layout shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act. Such infringement carries a penalty not exceeding three years imprisonment and a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees, or both. Where the infringing activity is continued after conviction, a further fine not less than fifty thousand rupees for every day during which such continuation occurs, as provided herein, shall be imposed. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding assessment of damages incurred due to infringement.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to include an assertion of plaintiff right geographical over the goods specified therein. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an application, issue a public notice inviting objections from any interested party, provided that any objection must specify the grounds on which it is based and demonstrate a substantial interest in maintaining the distinctiveness of similar goods. Where an objection is received, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to file a reply addressing the concerns raised. The relationship proposed registered between the geographical indication and the goods shall be scrutinized by the Registrar for conformity with the standards prescribed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board relating to the infringement of plant variety rights under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate court shall have the same jurisdiction as it would have in respect of original suits under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Claims purposes section concerning revocation of a granted Plant Variety Protection shall be subject to judicial review on grounds of procedural irregularity or demonstrable error of law. Further, remedies for infringement, including injunctions and damages, are available as provided herein; however, wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties determined at the discretion of the court. The burden of proving prior use lies upon the claimant seeking revocation.

The Register of Patentees shall maintain a record for each patentee registered under this Act, detailing particulars including but not limited to their principal place of business, designated representatives where applicable, and any changes occurring therein. An application for registration as a patentee may be submitted electronically through the prescribed portal, accompanied by supporting documentation verifying identity and address as per rules framed hereunder. The Controller shall provide an acknowledgement receipt upon successful submission; however, this does not constitute acceptance of the application. Any alteration to information previously provided must be notified to the Register within thirty days, failing which penalties as provided herein may apply. Further, a patentee is obliged to update their contact details annually or face suspension of certain rights under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to cosmetic products shall include a detailed specification outlining the composition, manufacturing process, and intended use of such cosmetics. This specification is deemed part of the trade mark’s description under this Act and will be subject to scrutiny by the Registry to ensure clarity and accuracy. The applicant must provide sufficient information enabling assessment as to whether the proposed trade mark conflicts with existing registrations or prior usage, particularly concerning similar goods covered under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Any alteration to the application patent specification after its initial filing may be permitted only with the Registrar’s approval, provided that such changes do not substantively alter the nature of the cosmetic product being represented by the trade mark.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of a design relating to articles intended for use in connection with defence or national security, the Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard and may require the applicant to submit such evidence as he deems necessary to demonstrate that the design does not compromise necessary security india. The Controller’s decision on whether a design poses a threat to national security is final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. An appeal under this Act shall lie only if it can be demonstrated that the Controller acted without due consideration of relevant material or exercised his discretion in an arbitrary manner, and such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that the proposed mark lacks distinctive character, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice of the opposition to the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier trade mark or right relied upon in the notice. The applicant may then file a counter-statement rebutting the grounds of opposition. Upon consideration of the counter-statement and any further submissions made by either party, the Registrar shall determine whether the proposed mark possesses sufficient distinctiveness acquired through use as demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Registry. It is provided that where the application relates to a mark incorporating an element which demonstrates an inventive step in relation to goods or services, the applicant may adduce evidence establishing such inventive character. The trade mark proprietor shall be afforded opportunity for cross-examination during proceedings under this Act.

A certification trade mark shall be registrable if application demonstrates that it conforms to an approved standard relating to the characteristics, quality, origin, production methods, or other relevant attributes of the goods or services. The applicant must specify the institution responsible for administering such standard and ensuring compliance by those using certified goods or services. Registration is conditional upon ongoing adherence to the prescribed procedures for certification and periodic audits conducted by the Registrar. Any alteration to the approved standard requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, failing which registration may be revoked. Further, a trade mark shall not be registered as a certification trade mark if it conflicts with any well-known trade mark already established in India, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to exploit commercially the layout-design and to prevent others from doing any act prohibited under this Act. Such exploitation includes, but is not limited to, reproduction, modification, sale, hire or import of integrated circuits incorporating the proprietor layout design. Provided that, where an integrated circuit containing a proprietor layout design is manufactured for export out of India, the registered proprietor shall be deemed not to have contravened any provision relating to unauthorized exploitation. The right conferred under this Act shall be enforceable against any person who, without authorization, does anything which constitutes infringement as provided herein.

Where an appeal lies against a determination made under this Act regarding the originality of a creators layout designs, the Appellate Authority shall consider whether the alleged copying constitutes substantial similarity, taking into account both the overall impression and any distinctive features. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the finding of the original determining authority was erroneous; however, the respondent may present evidence to rebut such claims. It is provided that a determination regarding infringement shall not be invalidated solely on grounds of minor procedural irregularities. Further, the Appellate Authority may order discovery of relevant documents if it deems necessary for just resolution of the dispute and subject to reasonable restrictions as prescribed by regulations.

A trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be entitled to exclusive rights over the representation of the trademark for which registration is granted, encompassing all forms and variations thereof that create an identical or confusingly similar impression. Such entitlement extends to preventing the use of any sign by others in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade proprietor’s mark is registered, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding descriptive use. The Registrar may, upon application by a trade proprietor, record particulars relating to assignment or transmission of rights under this Act, including details of the assignor and assignee. Further, any alteration to the registered trademark shall require prior approval from the Registrar and be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its botanical name, origin, method of reproduction, and any distinctive features readily discernible by experts. Upon receipt of an application, the Plant Varieties Registry shall publish a notification inviting objections from interested parties within a period specified under this Act. Where no valid objection is received, or where such objections are withdrawn or dismissed, patents shall entered in the Register of Plant Varieties. The Registrar may require applicants to submit additional data relating to the stability and uniformity of the variety. Patents shall entered subject to the provisions regarding compulsory licensing as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model may, prior to the grant of the certificate, submit a request for amendment of the specification detailing the functional characteristics and intended use of the invention. Such requests shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement justifying the proposed alterations and demonstrating their consistency with the original disclosure. The Controller General, after affording an opportunity for objection from any interested party, may allow or reject the requested amendment subject to the condition that it does not substantially alter the claimed novelty or inventive step as initially presented in the application. Any specification amendment introduced post-publication shall be deemed a material variation and require fresh examination under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication authorised under this Act shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement. Infringement occurs when any person, without due cause or consent, makes use of, or devises any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication, in relation to goods with which the indication is primarily associated. Such actions may include the sale, offering for sale, importation, or exposure for sale of goods bearing the infringing mark. The remedies available to the proprietor shall include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to considerations of equitable principles. Further, any goods found to be infringing the geographical indication are liable to be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and any other goods or services, provided that such user does not constitute a permitted use under this Act. Any person who, without due cause or consent of the proprietor, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be liable for damages, including loss of profits and royalties. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party, investigate allegations of such infringement and issue injunctions restraining further use of the infringing mark. Determining trade mark distinctiveness shall consider all relevant factors, including acquired reputation and consumer perception. Further, an owner seeking to enforce their rights under this Act must demonstrate that the alleged infringer had knowledge of the registered trade mark.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute an action in the High Court alleging that another party has engaged in deceptive practices undermining the distinctiveness and reputation associated with their protected designation. Such an action arises when it is demonstrated, through clear and convincing evidence, that goods or services offered by the respondent are presented as originating from the geographically defined area, thereby falsifies genuine geographical indications recognized under this Act. The respondent shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present counter-evidence establishing either lack of deceptive intent or demonstrating that their products possess characteristics substantially similar to those traditionally produced within the indicated region. Decisions regarding similarity and consumer confusion remain subject to judicial review on appeal.

A good faith use of a name indicating the origin of goods does not constitute a falsification under this Act if such use is in accordance with equitable principles and established trade practices. For the purposes of this legislation, "falsifies genuine geographical indication" means any act which misrepresents or creates an erroneous impression regarding the true geographical origin of goods. This includes, but is not limited to, the application of a sign liable to be confused with a registered geographical indication, or the use of a mark that suggests such origin where it does not exist. Such acts shall prejudice the interests of the producers of the genuine product and mislead consumers as provided herein.

Any person employing a registered certify trade mark in relation to goods or services shall be liable to prosecution under this Act if such employment constitutes an unfair representation likely to deceive or cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services. Where a false or misleading statement is made concerning the nature, quantity, or production method of goods bearing a registered certify trade mark, the offender shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The proprietor of the certified trade mark shall have standing to bring an action for damages arising from such infringement as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, or refusing or revoking registration, may appeal from such order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall allow such appeal only if it is satisfied that the original decision was erroneous in law or fact. In determining whether there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, regard shall be had to the similarity between the marks, taking into account not merely the appearance thereof but also their phonetic and conceptual components. The assessment of trade mark similarity shall consider all relevant surrounding circumstances, including the nature of the goods or services and the state of mind of the average consumer purchasing those goods or services. Any proprietor demonstrating such confusion has arisen may seek an injunction under this Act.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional crafts, including those concerning uniquely designed and constructed placed houses parliament, shall be filed with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the goods or services for which it seeks to be distinctive, and the area comprising the territory from which the goods originate. Evidence demonstrating the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the indicated products attributable to their origin shall accompany the application. The Registrar may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions herein. Objections to an application may be filed by any interested party within a period specified under this Act. Such objections must state the grounds upon which they are based and supported by relevant documentation, subject to review by the Geographical Indications Registry.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “patent controller” shall mean the officer appointed by the Central Government and designated as such, who is responsible for exercising powers and performing duties relating to the examination of patent applications, determining whether an invention meets the criteria for patentability under this Act, and granting or refusing patents in accordance with prescribed procedures. The patent controller may delegate any of their functions to other officers working under their direction, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. Decisions made by the patent controller are appealable as provided herein, and such decisions shall be binding until modified or reversed by an appellate authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where any photographic work is created by an artist acting as agent for another person, such other person shall owner copyright therein; provided that if the terms of engagement between the artist and the principal specify that the copyright belongs to the artist, then the artist shall be deemed the first owner. Further, it shall be the duty of any person claiming ownership under this Act to display a notice indicating such claim on all copies of the work available for sale or distribution. Failure to provide such registration notice shall not invalidate the copyright but may affect remedies available against infringement. Any wilful and knowing reproduction or communication to the public of a copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages, including actual loss and profits derived from the infringing activities, as provided herein.

Any person acting as an agent for the purposes of procuring, protecting, or enforcing patents shall be deemed a registered patent agent subject to fulfilling requirements prescribed under this Act. Failure to maintain adequate professional indemnity insurance, as specified in the regulations, will render such registration liable for immediate revocation. Any individual falsely representing themselves as a registered patent agent and engaging in activities related to patent filings or litigation shall face penalties including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Controller is empowered to initiate suo moto proceedings against any person suspected of violating these provisions, without prejudice to civil remedies available to aggrieved parties.

Where any trade mark is found to be identical to a prior registered trade mark in respect of identical or similar goods or services, such registration shall be deemed invalid upon application by an aggrieved party. Any person claiming damage as a result of the registration of a trade mark identical to their own existing right may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, including loss of profits and costs incurred in challenging the infringing registration. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, order rectification of the register removing such offending entry. Failure to comply with an order under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue, without prejudice to any other remedy available under this Act.

An applicant intending to seek international registration of a trade mark shall file a request for recording the certified copy of the Indian trade mark register with the Registrar, provided that such request is accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, upon verification of the authenticity of the certificate and compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act, record the said request in a separate Register maintained for the purpose of international registrations. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered trade mark shall be notified to the International Bureau within thirty days from the date on which such alteration is recorded in the Indian register. Failure to notify the International Bureau as provided herein may render the applicant liable to penalties, subject to appeal before an appellate authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a “distinguishable registered layout” means a layout-design which, when presented to a person reasonably informed in the matter, does not present an overall impression substantially similar to any other registered layout. This determination shall take into account the shape, configuration, arrangement and appearance of the integrated circuit as a whole. A layout-design is deemed not to be distinguishable if it incorporates elements that are commonplace or standard within the semiconductor industry. Further, a layout-design may be considered indistinguishable where its features are dictated solely by technical function, subject to the provisions regarding originality under this Act.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears to be erroneous by reason of a clerical error, inadvertence, or misapprehension of fact, any person aggrieved may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application shall specify the particulars of the alleged error and state the relief sought. The Controller shall give notice to all interested parties as provided herein, affording them an opportunity to be heard in opposition to the proposed rectification. Upon consideration of the evidence presented, and subject to compliance with principles of natural justice, the Controller may direct that the register shall be rectified accordingly. Rectifying register shall not extend to matters involving questions of patentability or validity unless specifically raised during the initial examination process.

Publication in the Official Gazette shall constitute conclusive evidence for all purposes under this Act regarding the existence and validity of a registered design. Where an application for registration of a design is deemed to be incomplete or contains deficiencies, the Designs Office may require the applicant to submit further particulars or amendments within a period specified therein; failure to comply with such requirement shall render the application void. Any notification issued by the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding any other matter as provided herein, shall be published in the Official Gazette. Furthermore, where a design is amended after initial registration, the date of amendment shall priority date for determining rights under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act in respect of any use of an identical or confusingly similar mark which is produced limits india. Where such infringement involves the passing off of goods as those of the registered proprietor, the remedies available include damages sustained by the proprietor, and further account of profits made by the infringing party. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing to use the infringing trade mark or any confusingly similar representation in relation to the impugned goods or services. Provided that, a finding of infringement shall not preclude a claim for passing off where the elements of deception and misrepresentation are independently established. Any order made under this Act may be enforced as if it were a decree of the Court.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others and whether it conflicts with any existing rights under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the nature of the goods or services in relation to which registration is sought, provided that such request is made within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of receipt of the application. If the Registrar finds that the proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark registered under this Act, or if it contains any matter which is likely to be deemed offensive, he shall issue a notice of objection to the applicant, specifying the grounds for such objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to file a reply addressing the objections raised by the Registrar. Following consideration of the applicant’s response, the Registrar shall proceed with further examination as provided herein.

The proceeding appellate board established under this Act shall consist of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, not being less than three in number, possessing expertise in intellectual property law, semiconductor technology, or related fields. The Board shall exercise jurisdiction to hear and dispose of appeals arising from orders passed by the Controller under this Act relating to layout-design registration, infringement proceedings, and civil remedies. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final subject to appeal to the High Court within a period specified herein, provided that such appeal is limited to questions of law only.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent under this Act based on a prior application made in a convention country, a convention application shall be filed within twelve months from the date of the earlier application. Such convention application must contain particulars identifying the basic invention as claimed in the first-mentioned application and shall include a statement indicating the convention country and the date upon which that initial application was lodged. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish certified copies of the said prior application, including any amendments or modifications thereto, if deemed necessary for examination purposes. Further, provided that the translation of such documents is submitted in English unless otherwise permitted by the Controller. Any deficiency in compliance with these requirements shall be brought to the attention of the applicant, who shall have an opportunity to rectify the same within a prescribed period as provided herein.

Where the controller is satisfied that any patented invention is necessary to prevent further undue exploitation of an earlier invention, or where such patented invention relates to a process for producing a substance already commercially available, the controller may permit another party to apply patent for the said invention subject to conditions as he deems fit. Such conditions shall include provisions regarding royalty payments and other financial considerations payable to the original patent holder. The agreement governing this permission to apply patent must be registered with the Controller within three months of its execution, detailing the scope of permitted use and duration. Failure to register such an agreement may render it unenforceable under this Act. Further, any assignment or license granted in relation to a permitted invention shall also require registration as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication relating to Alphonso mangoes may, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, grant non-exclusive licenses in respect of the use of the said indication. Such license shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the geographical indication and the goods or services to which such utilization pertains. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication, including assignments arising from the transfer of ownership of a licensed right, requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all terms and conditions previously stipulated in any existing license agreement. Further, where an infringement of the geographical indication occurs through unauthorized use, the registered proprietor may pursue remedies available under this Act and also initiate proceedings under the Indian Penal Code for offences involving fraud or forgery related to the false representation of origin.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of their mark upon third parties. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may specify geographical limitations or restrictions on the goods or services in relation to which the license is granted. Assignment of a trade mark, or any interest therein, including such licenses, shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person acquiring an assignment under this Act shall be deemed the new proprietor for all purposes. Where a license agreement includes provisions concerning quality control measures relating to goods bearing the marks indications serve to identify their origin or characteristics, these provisions shall be binding on both licensor and licensee. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with such quality control standards.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registrable under the law of the designated country, subject to any limitations specified by that country’s legislation concerning the scope of protection afforded. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with all applicable regulatory requirements in each designated territory prior to recording an international registration basic to a trade mark registered in India. Such evidence shall include, but is not limited to, declarations from authorized representatives confirming registrability and any necessary translations of the mark or application. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as provided herein may result in refusal to record the international registration basic.

Any applicant found to have wilfully misrepresented any fact relating to the invention during the examination process before the patent office shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Such misrepresentation includes, but is not limited to, false statements regarding prior art or the inventive step of the claimed subject matter. Further, an application rejected due to wilful misstatement may not be refiled under this Act for a period of three years from the date of rejection. The Controller shall issue notice to the applicant detailing the specific allegations and providing opportunity for response before imposing any penalty. Failure to comply with directions issued by the patent office concerning rectification of errors or submission of clarifications will also attract penalties, as provided herein.

Any applicant seeking to alter an existing claim specification within a patent application shall file a formal request with the Controller, detailing the proposed modifications and providing justification demonstrating their consistency with the original disclosure. Such requests are subject to rigorous examination; any amendment deemed to introduce new matter or substantially broaden the scope of protection beyond that originally described may be rejected outright. Failure to adequately substantiate an amendment claim specification can result in imposition of a monetary penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Controller shall provide written reasons for any rejection, and appeal against such decision lies with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Repeated frivolous attempts at amendment will attract progressively higher penalties, potentially leading to application abandonment.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against any decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, the Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions herein, confirm, vary, or reverse such decision. The appellant shall be required to demonstrate before the Appellate Board that the grounds for rectification are substantiated by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising from the use of another sign in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court, but only on a question of law. The determination of whether a trade mark relation exists shall be final and binding unless overturned by the High Court.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the Registrar’s decision. The appellant shall state the grounds of appeal and serve a copy thereof on the applicant. Provided that if the objection relates solely to the absolute ground under section 9 concerning deceptiveness, the applicant may, within thirty days of service of the copy of the grounds of appeal, file its written response. It is established that ‘carry business india’ constitutes a descriptive phrase used by the respondent, and any claim to exclusive right therein shall be subject to challenge based on demonstrable lack of acquired distinctiveness.

Where a person, by representing any goods or services as being used with the approval of another, or as being in relation to such goods or services, without his consent, applies for registration of a trade mark under this Act, the Board may, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, refuse the application if it finds that such representation is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public. Provided that where the owner of the goodwill has subsequently given consent, or otherwise acquiesced in the use of his name or mark by the applicant, registration shall be permissible as provided herein. The Board may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion before proceeding with consideration of the application.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, relating to the determination of infringement or validity of a registered layout-design, desires to appeal, such party shall, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an application for leave to appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal may, after hearing all parties involved and subject to satisfaction that the order in question is erroneous in law or on the facts, grant leave to appeal. Provided that if the aggrieved party fails to apply for leave within the stipulated period, such omission shall be considered a waiver of the right to appeal, and no further proceedings relating to the matter shall be entertained unless the Tribunal deems it fit to condone the delay on sufficient cause shown. The procedure for appeals before the Tribunal shall be as provided herein.

Where any person without due authorization makes use of copyright in a work, constituting an act of infringement copyright work, such person shall be liable to action by the owner of the copyright. The aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings seeking equitable relief, including but not limited to permanent injunctions restraining further acts of reproduction or distribution. Provided that where the alleged infringing activity involves fair dealing for research or private study, the defendant may adduce evidence demonstrating such use was undertaken in good faith and without any commercial advantage accruing thereby. The court shall consider whether the extent and nature of the copying were reasonable under the circumstances; a finding against this consideration shall be subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining patent validity under this Act, an invention shall be considered obvious if, prior to the date of filing of the patent application, a person skilled in the art could have derived the claimed invention from existing knowledge using only straightforward and predictable combinations. This determination shall take into account the totality of the circumstances, including the nature of the problem addressed and the level of ingenuity involved in arriving at the solution. The assessment of whether such derivation was obvious requires consideration of the time elapsed between the publication of relevant prior art and the filing date; a reasonable period shall be deemed to vary according to technological field.

Application for registration of a biological entity shall be accompanied by a detailed report specifying the method of isolation and cultivation, including all relevant data pertaining to stability and genetic purity. The Controller may require submission of further documentation demonstrating reproducibility of results and absence of prior public disclosure concerning said entity. Upon satisfactory review, the grant patent act will proceed with examination as per established procedures. Any challenge to the validity of a registered biological entity must be filed within six months from the date of publication of acceptance. Further, the applicant shall provide an undertaking guaranteeing adherence to bio-safety protocols during commercial exploitation and ensuring equitable access to derived technologies, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations issued under this Act.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license to use the mark, whether exclusively or otherwise, subject to conditions as provided herein, such license may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the registered proprietor, unless the license agreement expressly prohibits assignment; provided that any such assignment shall not operate to discharge the licensee from any obligations undertaken under the original licensing agreement. Further, where a dispute arises concerning the validity or scope of an injunction interlocutory restraining the use of a trade mark pursuant to a licensing arrangement, the court may consider the terms and conditions of the license in determining whether the restraint is reasonable and equitable. The registered proprietor shall be deemed to retain ownership of the trade mark notwithstanding any such assignment of a license.

An appeal lies to the Authority Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to the registration of a layout-design or concerning rectification proceedings initiated against a proprietor registered trade mark incorporated within a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order appealed against, and the Board may, if it considers expedient so to do, entertain appeals received after the expiry of that period if satisfactory reasons are shown for the delay. The Authority Appellate Board may call for such records or evidence as it deems necessary for the purpose of hearing an appeal, and shall have the same powers as a civil court trying cases under code of civil procedure, 1908.

Where an application for a patent contains particulars relating to more than one invention, the Controller may require the applicant to restrict the claim to one or more inventions so as to comply with the provisions of this Act. Such requirement shall be served on the applicant within six months from the date of filing of the application or where a request for examination has been made, within six months from the date of such request. The applicant may, subject to any directions given by the Controller, amend the claims to restrict them accordingly and shall comply with this obligation within three months from the date of service of the requirement. Failure to do so shall render the application liable to be refused. For the purposes of determining entitlement to a patent, an *applicant patent person* shall be deemed to be the true inventor unless the applicant proves otherwise. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating such proof as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act is dissatisfied, such party shall have the right to appeal from that order to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of service of the order appealed against and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. Upon receipt of an appeal, the Appellate Board may entertain the same only if it is satisfied that the appellant has worked out sufficient remedies available under this Act prior to seeking appellate relief. The Board shall have power to affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against and may grant such further relief as it deems just and equitable in the circumstances of the case. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that order; these proceedings act as the final recourse available under this Act.

Where a patent is granted in contravention of or prejudice to any right subsisting under this Act, the central government may, subject to such inquiry as it deems fit, direct that the patent be declared invalid, wholly or in part. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The High Court shall admit the appeal only if it is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for interfering with the decision of the central government. Costs of the appeal shall be determined by the High Court. Further, where a patent has been declared invalid under this provision, any person who was prevented from exploiting the invention by the existence of the patent may apply to the central government for relief, including compensation proportionate to the loss suffered.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a map of the area from which the goods originate and such map shall clearly delineate the boundaries of the geographical territory. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the history, characteristics, and qualities associated with the goods in question, demonstrating their unique connection to the specified geographical origin. Provided that an application for a geographical indication relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs shall include details concerning traditional production methods employed within the defined area. Any prior registration of a trademark under the Trade Marks Act shall not preclude consideration of an application for a goods geographical indication as provided herein, subject to assessment of potential conflict and consumer confusion.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall commercially exploit a registered layout design without the prior written consent of the registered proprietor. Such consent may be granted upon such terms and conditions as the proprietor deems fit, including but not limited to limitations on geographical area, field of use, or duration of exploitation. Where consent is given for the use layout design, the licensee shall ensure that any integrated circuit manufactured pursuant to such license adheres strictly to the registered layout design specifications as filed with the Controller General. Any alteration to the registered layout design during manufacturing, without express written permission from the proprietor, constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the manufacturer liable for damages. The right to use layout design is deemed infringed if it involves reproduction or adaptation that substantially replicates the original design’s features.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of the rejection order. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an appeal and after affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard, either confirm or reverse the decision of the initial examining officer. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this process may further petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review. It is provided that any representation made to the *Registrar person act* during these proceedings shall be considered without prejudice to the rights and remedies available to other parties concerned, including those claiming prior use or similar rights in respect of the trademark.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting a geographical indication authorised to a collective body or consortium may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds that the registration was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or that the collective body or consortium does not meet the requirements for eligibility under this Act. The Board may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Further, where a geographical indication authorised infringes upon existing breeder's rights relating to plant varieties, remedies available under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act shall apply concurrently with those provided herein. Any infringement of a registered geographical indication shall be actionable as a civil wrong, entitling the proprietor to seek injunction and damages.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if, upon examination, it appears that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition prior to the date of the application. Evidence presented in support of this demonstration shall include market research data, sales figures, and advertising expenditure relating directly to the trade mark's usage. Any person aggrieved by a refusal order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. The Board’s decision is final subject to further appeal under this Act. Consideration shall be given to whether the use has created an appreciable association in the minds of consumers.

Where a proprietor institutes a case proceeding against an alleged infringer under this Act, and demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe that the infringing activity involves the unauthorized use of their trade mark for proprietor certification purposes, the Court shall grant such relief as is equitable and just. This includes, but is not limited to, injunctions restraining further infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and costs incurred in bringing the case proceeding. Provided that, if the alleged infringer demonstrates good faith reliance on an honest belief that their use of the trade mark did not constitute infringement, the Court may reduce or deny the award of damages as it deems appropriate. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such proceedings and make them available for public inspection subject to confidentiality restrictions imposed by the Court.

For the purposes of this Act, every owner of copyright in an artistic work or musical work shall be entitled to control the incorporation and communication of Right Management Information. Such information may include, but is not limited to, the name of the author, the title of the work, the copyright owner’s identification, and terms and conditions for use. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register of declared Right Management Information, upon application by the copyright owner accompanied by prescribed fees and supporting documentation establishing ownership. Any person who knowingly alters or removes such information without authorization is liable to prosecution under this Act. Provided that, registration of Right Management Information does not confer any additional rights beyond those already vested in the copyright holder as provided herein.

Applications for the registration of varieties registered shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Authority deems necessary for assessing novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The application must include a detailed description of the variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, method of reproduction, and any relevant phenotypic characteristics observable under standard conditions. An applicant may submit data generated through field trials conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Authority to demonstrate these qualities. Any person claiming an objection to the registration of a variety shall file such claim within three months from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The Authority shall provide the applicant and objector opportunities for hearings, subject to procedural rules as provided herein. Decisions regarding claims of novelty or distinctiveness are final, barring appeals to the Appellate Board.

Where an application for patent includes drawings depicting functional elements through schematic representations, such representations shall be considered as constituting form references acts under this Act. Such depictions must clearly delineate the operational relationship between components without disclosing inventive steps beyond those explicitly claimed within the specification. The Controller may require applicants demonstrating reliance on form references acts to submit supplementary documentation detailing the underlying principles of operation if clarity is deemed insufficient. Provided that, such requirement shall not impede the grant of a patent where the functional elements are readily ascertainable by persons skilled in the art and do not obscure the essential features of the invention as described herein.

Any individual who knowingly provides false or misleading information to an investigating officer during any inquiry under this Act relating to infringement of a registered trademark shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Such penalties may be recovered as if they were debts due to the Government. Where it is established that such false information was provided with the intent to obstruct investigation or prejudice the rights of the trademark proprietor, further enforcement action including criminal prosecution under the Indian Penal Code shall be initiated. It is a material factor in determining culpability that the prosecutor gave information which directly influenced the direction of the inquiry and subsequently proved inaccurate, impacting investigations concerning citizens India.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a proposed trade mark, or the rectification of the Register, the Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the Registrar to hear the matter again. The Board shall allow all parties concerned the opportunity to present arguments and evidence afresh before the Registrar. It is provided that if the appeal concerns a claim that a trade mark is deceptively similar to a previously registered trade mark, the Appellate Board may require expert testimony on matters of consumer perception. For the purposes of this Act, “registered” means registered in the Trade Marks Register maintained under this Act and shall include any variation or amendment duly recorded therein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “denomination variety sub” shall mean a denomination assigned to a plant variety that has been registered as per the provisions herein and which is further subdivided into distinct lines or varieties exhibiting specific characteristics not readily apparent in the original registration. Such subdivision shall be documented with the Authority, detailing the phenotypic differences and genetic stability of each sub-variety relative to the parent variety. The Authority may require demonstration of continued uniformity within a denomination variety sub through established testing protocols. Any alteration affecting essential characteristics of a registered denomination variety sub requires notification and approval under this Act, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registered in India under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, and the Board may order rectification of the register or grant damages as it deems just. Where an international registration includes goods or services for which the mark is registered in India prior to the date of designation, any subsequent infringement shall be actionable under this Act irrespective of whether the earlier Indian registration was obtained before or after the initial filing date of the international application. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the infringer liable to a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs rupees.

Where a trade mark is registered internationally under the Madrid Protocol and such international registration incorporates a designation of India, the proprietor shall maintain the validity of that registration for so long as the underlying Indian registration remains in force. However, where an article patented incorporating the trade mark is subsequently withdrawn from sale within India or ceases to be manufactured therein, the proprietor may apply to the Registrar for a modification of the international registration’s scope relating to those specific goods. Failure to do so within six months of such cessation shall constitute grounds for revocation under this Act. The period of protection afforded by an international registration remains subject to the same renewal requirements as would apply to a domestic Indian trade mark, and any lapse in renewal will impact years international registration status accordingly.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed under this Act, the registrar shall register the trademark if he is satisfied that it is distinctive in its own right and not confusingly similar to any prior marks. Provided that, where the applicant seeks protection based on use, evidence of such use satisfactory to the Registrar must be submitted within the prescribed timeframe; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, an international registration designating India under the Madrid Protocol shall be examined in accordance with these provisions and may be refused if it contravenes any provision as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar relating to registration or refusal thereof may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, "well known trade mark" with respect to particular goods or services means a trademark which has attained considerable recognition amongst the relevant section of the public, irrespective of whether that recognition is direct or indirect. A mark shall be deemed to be well known if, through association and use over time, it signifies a specific source or quality of those goods or services. The determination of whether a trade mark is well known shall take into account factors including duration of usage, geographical extent of the trade, reputation and get-up of the mark, and advertising expenditure incurred in relation to the mark as provided herein.

Where an applicant has made a request for amendment to a patent application under this Act and such request incorporates subject matter not disclosed in the original complete specification, the Patent Office may require the applicant to submit a declaration stating whether the amended application is based on any prior published document. If the applicant fails to provide such a declaration within the time specified by the Controller, or if it is determined that the amendment introduces new inventive concept beyond what was originally sought, the application shall be deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by an order abandoning a filed application india may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review under law.

Where an individual, acting as an agent or representative of a patent applicant or patentee, knowingly makes a false statement or conceals material information relating to the invention described in a patent application or during post-grant opposition proceedings, such act shall constitute a commission offence attributable to both the individual and the applicant or patentee. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of such an offence, issue a notice requiring the accused to appear before a designated officer for examination. Failure to attend as directed without reasonable cause, or providing evasive responses, shall be deemed conclusive proof of guilt regarding the false statement or concealment. Further, any person assisting in the commission of this offence may also be held liable under this Act. The penalty for such offences shall be determined based on the severity and impact of the misleading information provided.

Any person employing a service mark in relation to services specified alphabetically within Class 35, relating to business administration, office functions, and management consultancy, shall be liable for damages if such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the services offered. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation or unfair competition arising from such employment, issue an injunction restraining further use. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment and a fine as determined by the adjudicating officer. This provision applies irrespective of whether registration of the mark has been secured under this Act; however, remedies available to registered proprietors are not prejudiced.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee may grant a licence patent conferring on the licensee specified rights to make, use, exercise, sell, or import the protected invention. Such licences shall be granted in writing and may specify the field of exploitation, duration, and any royalties payable. An application for compulsory revocation of a licence patent under this Act may be made by any interested person demonstrating that the terms and conditions of the licence have been violated by the licensee, or that the licensee has otherwise acted contrary to the provisions of the agreement. The Controller shall give notice to both the patentee and the licensee before proceeding with any inquiry relating to such an application. Further, the Controller may require the parties to submit evidence and arguments pertaining to the alleged breach.

The right to authorize or prohibit the creation of printed copies through translation shall vest solely with the copyright holder. Any person desiring to undertake a printed copies translation of an original work, be it literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic, must first obtain written consent from the owner of copyright in that work. Such consent may be granted subject to terms and conditions regarding royalties, duration of exclusivity, and territorial limitations as agreed upon between the parties. Provided that, where a printed copies translation is licensed under this Act, the original copyright holder shall retain the right to assign or transfer their underlying copyright without prejudice to the licensee’s rights concerning the translated work. Further, any assignment of such translation rights must be registered with the designated Copyright Office and shall be deemed invalid unless so recorded within three months of its execution.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered prior to the commencement of this section may enter into an assignment agreement for the benefit of another party, provided that such agreement explicitly acknowledges the continued validity of the original registration. The Registrar shall maintain a public register detailing all assignments and licenses granted concerning trademarks under this Act, accessible upon application and payment of the prescribed fee. Further, where a provisional specification claim is made regarding a mark’s distinctiveness during an assignment process, the registrar accordance with established procedures will require submission of supporting documentation demonstrating acquired reputation within the relevant territory. Any subsequent transfer or sub-license shall be subject to similar disclosure requirements, ensuring transparency and facilitating orderly trade practices relating to registered trademarks.

Where a person alleging infringement of a registered layout design demonstrates, subject to verification by the Controller, that another has reproduced the said layout design for commercial purposes without due authorisation, and it is established that such reproduction creates a substantial similarity with the original layout design, then the infringing party shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner. Such damages may include not only lost profits but also reasonable royalties which the owner would have received had the license been granted. Further, any person found guilty of contravention under this Act relating to a layout design relation is subject to penalties as provided herein and may be ordered to deliver up for destruction all infringing articles.

For the purposes of this Act, a "Government undertaking" shall mean any body established by or under any law passed by the Parliament or a State Legislature and owned or controlled by the Central Government or such State Government. An application for registration of an invention made by a Government undertaking may include a proposed application registration mark relating to the invention, subject to the provisions regarding distinctiveness and non-infringement as provided herein. Such mark shall be deemed part of the patent documentation and its use regulated accordingly. The Central Government may, in consultation with relevant sectoral ministries, issue guidelines concerning the scope of activities undertaken by a Government undertaking for purposes of this definition.

Where an authorized user applies for registration as a collective bargain or a guarantee mark indicating a particular good conforming to a specification, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish detailed documentation substantiating the traditional knowledge associated with that geographical indication. Such documentation shall include verifiable records of agricultural practices, processing methods, and quality control measures employed by producers within the defined geographical area. Upon finding evidence of misuse or unfair competition affecting the reputation of the registered geographical indication, the Registrar shall issue a cease-and-desist order to the infringing party. Further, where such infringement continues despite the issuance of said order, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all activities constituting the violation and may be subject to penalties as provided herein. A specification patent addition relating to novel processing techniques can be included in subsequent amendments.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of a layout design register, or any other decision made under this Act concerning the validity or enforceability of registered rights, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony where necessary, and shall pass a reasoned order affirming, reversing, or modifying the original decision. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements for filing an appeal may result in its rejection. Remedies available under this Act for infringement of registered layout designs include injunctions, damages, and account of profits derived from the infringing activity, as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act for goods including those comprised in the class "cosmetics" as defined by the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, an appeal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance of the mark. Such appeal may be brought on any ground showing that the registration was wrongly granted, including but not limited to allegations of deceptive similarity to a prior trade mark used in relation to similar goods or services. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, affirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from; provided that the Board shall not substitute its own findings for those of the Registrar unless it is satisfied that such findings were based on an erroneous interpretation of the law or evidence.

Any person who is registered as a Member under this Act shall be subject to penalties for acts constituting infringement. Such penalties may include imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, which may be extended to two hundred thousand rupees, where the infringement is proven to have been committed with the intent to deceive or cause loss to the registered owner. Further, any Member found guilty of repeated violations shall face enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Compensation for damages suffered by the registered owner is recoverable from the defaulting Member under procedures outlined herein.

Where any person infringes a registered layout design, such person shall be liable to pay damages to the proprietor registered layout equivalent to a reasonable royalty that could have been granted by way of license had the infringement not occurred, subject to adjustments as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the infringer to account for profits made from the infringing activity, provided that such profits are demonstrably attributable to the unauthorized use of the layout-design. Further, any person found guilty of wilful infringement shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees; however, in cases where the infringement is committed by a company, its officers who were responsible for the conduct of business at the time of the offence shall be deemed guilty.

The term "entitled produce variety" shall mean a plant variety which has been formally registered under this Act and whose rights are vested in a breeder or other eligible person, subject to any conditions stipulated during registration. Any person claiming entitlement to an entitled produce variety may institute proceedings before the Appellate Board alleging infringement of their rights by another party cultivating, selling, or distributing propagating material derived from that variety without authorization. Provided that such claim must be substantiated with documentary evidence demonstrating prior registration and continued adherence to the terms outlined therein. The Board shall consider any counter-claims presented by the alleged infringer asserting bona fide use or customary cultivation practices predating the registration of the entitled produce variety, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an integrated circuit shall be defined as a set of circuits manufactured on a semiconductor material and includes three-dimensional arrangements of such circuits. An integrated circuit may incorporate active and passive elements, including but not limited to transistors, diodes, resistors, capacitors, and inductors. Subject to any modifications notified under this Act, the term "integrated circuit" shall also encompass layouts depicting structures intended for use in manufacturing an integrated circuit, provided that these layouts are capable of being reproduced or used directly in the manufacture of such a circuit. The definition excludes circuits solely designed for military applications as determined by the Central Government.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish with their registrar application a representation of the mark sufficient for reproduction thereof under this Act. The Registrar may require such further particulars as he deems necessary for proper adjudication of the application, including details regarding colour claims and disclaimers of particular elements within the mark. Provided that where the mark consists exclusively of a word or words, a representation is not required unless the applicant specifically requests it to facilitate clarity during examination. Any alteration made to the trade mark after the initial registrar application is filed shall be subject to approval by the Registrar, who may require payment of an additional fee for such amendments. The Registrar’s decision on any amendment request is final, subject to appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “Technical Member” means a person who possesses specialized knowledge or experience in matters relating to technology, engineering, science, or any other relevant technical field and shall be appointed by the Central Government under such conditions as may be prescribed. A Technical Member is deemed to possess such expertise if he holds a degree in an appropriate branch of engineering or natural sciences from a recognized institution or possesses equivalent professional qualifications as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The decision of a Technical Member, when dealing with technical aspects of a case, shall carry significant weight and may be binding on other members of the tribunal, subject to reasoned dissent.

An applicant seeking to obtain protection for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall file an application with the Controller in such form and containing such information as may be prescribed. The application must include a copy of the layout-design, a statement of the priority claimed, if any, and details regarding the applicant’s entitlement to seek protection under this Act. Where the applicant is not the original creator of the layout-design, the application shall specify the basis for such claim, subject to verification by the Controller. Any alteration or addition to the particulars contained in a filed application is permissible only with the written permission of the Controller and upon payment of the prescribed fee. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further documentation or clarification deemed necessary for assessment of the filing application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder registered variety” shall mean a variety that has been formally protected under this Act and for which a certificate of protection has been granted to a person fulfilling the conditions as provided herein. Such registration confers upon the breeder exclusive rights in relation to the production, sale, distribution, and importation of propagating material of the breeder registered variety. Further, nothing in this Act shall prevent a breeder from simultaneously seeking an international application patent for their variety under applicable international treaties, subject to compliance with all relevant regulations pertaining to such applications. The Registrar may specify conditions relating to benefit-sharing arrangements concerning any breeder registered variety.

Where a registered layout-design is exploited without authorization through a process involving the unauthorized transmission operation of data relating thereto, the owner may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such proceedings are subject to the condition that the claimant demonstrates reasonable efforts were undertaken to prevent the initial dissemination of the infringing information. It shall be presumed, absent contrary evidence presented by the alleged infringer, that any commercial use of a layout-design incorporating elements substantially similar to those protected under this Act, occurring within five years of its registration, constitutes unauthorized exploitation unless it can be shown that such use was independently developed or derived from publicly available sources. The burden of proving independent development rests entirely upon the defendant.

Any person found to have manufactured, imported, distributed, sold, or offered for sale any pharmaceutical substance infringing upon a patent granted under this Act shall be liable to pay an indemnity of not less than ten times the value of goods produced or imported or dealt with. Such infringement includes acts that directly or indirectly exploit the patented invention without authorization from the patent holder. The Controller may, after giving notice and opportunity for hearing to the accused party, issue an injunction restraining further infringing activities. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the offender subject to a daily penalty of fifty thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. Further, any property used or acquired in connection with the infringement shall be liable for seizure by enforcement officers as provided herein.

The owner of copyright in any cinematograph film or sound recording shall be entitled to grant a license authorizing reproduction and distribution of the work in another country, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the copyright holder, and the consideration for such grants shall be agreed upon between the parties involved. Where an assignment of copyright has been made, the assignee shall possess all rights pertaining to licensing under this Act, including the power to sub-license the work within the territory specified in the assignment agreement. Provided that any license granted prior to an assignment shall remain valid and enforceable unless expressly revoked by the assignor, subject to applicable principles of equity. The terms of a license relating to copyright are deemed contractual obligations binding on all parties involved.

Any application filed by an eligible breeder seeking registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, as determined by notification issued by the Registrar. The amount of such fee shall vary depending on the applicant’s status, with reduced fees applicable to small and marginal farmers, tribal communities, and research institutions engaged in public interest activities. Failure to remit the requisite fee at the time of filing shall render the application void ab initio. Further, any appeal against a decision of the Registrar regarding registration or revocation may be pursued by any party aggrieved, but such appeals shall necessitate payment of an appellate fee, as specified under this Act. Fees in any proceeding are subject to periodic review and adjustment by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, "petition particulars contained" shall mean the specific details relating to a registered layout-design, as delineated in Schedule B annexed hereto. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the date of first fixation, the geographic location where the layout-design was initially made available, and a comprehensive description of the circuit elements comprising the integrated circuit.
