Failure to accurately reflect these petition particulars contained during registration proceedings may render subsequent claims of infringement registered less defensible under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all such particulars as provided herein.

An international application form submitted pursuant to this Act shall be deemed a record of assignment only if it explicitly identifies the assignor and assignee, along with a clear description of the rights being transferred relating to the underlying trademark. Such assignments are subject to registration under this Act to be considered valid against third parties; failure to register an assignment documented within the international application form will render the transfer unenforceable. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the validity of any such assignment, including but not limited to corporate resolutions or power-of-attorney documents. Any licensee granting sublicences based on rights detailed in an international application form must provide a written notification to both the assignor and assignee within thirty days of the sublicense agreement’s execution. This provision applies irrespective of whether the trademark is already registered under this Act.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a farmer has suffered demonstrable economic loss due to the failure of a protected plant variety to perform as represented, and where such failure is attributable to the actions or omissions of the registered breeder, the Authority may order the breeder to contribute to a compensation deposited gene pool. This contribution shall be equivalent to a sum determined by the Authority, taking into account the extent of the farmer’s loss and the breeder's annual turnover as provided herein. Any dispute arising from such determination or the calculation of the contribution may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further judicial review under this Act on grounds limited to jurisdiction only.

Any party seeking to oppose an application for trade mark registration under this Act shall file a Notice of Opposition with the Registry within the prescribed time limit as determined by regulations framed hereunder. Such Notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or registration of a similar sign in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. The Registrar may require the party filing the opposition to furnish further particulars and evidence supporting their claim, subject to payment of additional fees as prescribed. Failure to comply with such requirements within the stipulated period shall render the Notice vulnerable to dismissal. An applicant facing an opposition registration may submit a counter-statement addressing the grounds raised by the opponent, also within a timeframe determined by the Registrar. The Registrar shall then proceed according to established procedures for resolving oppositions.

Where a plant variety is deemed to possess essentially derived characteristics from an existing variety, and a claim of *breeder breeder complied* status is asserted by the claimant seeking protection, the Examining Authority shall issue a notice to both the original breeder and the alleged essentially derived variety applicant. Such notice shall detail the grounds for assessment concerning whether the subsequent variety satisfies the conditions as provided herein regarding novelty and distinctiveness, taking into consideration any technical data submitted demonstrating derivation. The original breeder may submit objections within sixty days of receipt of the notice, outlining reasons why the claimed status is not justified. Further, the Authority may request additional information or conduct hearings to ascertain the veracity of claims relating to the breeding process and contribution of each party. Decisions regarding *breeder breeder complied* determinations shall be recorded in writing and made publicly available on the designated online portal.

No trade mark shall be registered if, in the opinion of the Registrar, it consists exclusively of a *name* which is indicative of the kind, quality, or characteristic of goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that such a *name*, though descriptive, has acquired distinctiveness through use to warrant registration; failing sufficient demonstration, registration shall be refused. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Where a registered trade mark infringes upon an earlier right in a *name*, the proprietor of the earlier right may apply for rectification and seek its removal from the Register, subject to penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “accused offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of section 27, section 29, section 30, or section 51, as provided herein. Where such an accused offence is alleged to have been committed by a corporate entity, the responsibility for the said offence shall be deemed to lie upon the directors, managers, and other officers of the corporation who were directly involved in the decision-making process leading to the infringement. Nothing in this definition shall preclude the imposition of liability on any individual or entity beyond those specifically identified as being part of that decision-making process, subject to demonstrating their direct participation in the accused offence.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act seeking rectification of a registration for layout-design, the Registrar shall, upon receiving notice thereof from such proprietor, issue a direction to the respondent requiring them to appear and answer the claim. Failure by the respondent to file a written response within the time specified in the direction may be taken as an admission of the facts alleged in the complaint, subject to the right of the respondent to subsequently challenge any order made based on such deemed admission. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act concerning layout-design registration or rectification proceedings may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registrar person shall ensure that all notices are served as per the prescribed manner, and a copy is also displayed prominently at the registered office of the respondent.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall register the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application only after considering all evidence submitted by both the applicant and the opponent. The Registrar may, at any time during the opposition proceedings, require either party to furnish further information or submit additional documents relevant to the dispute. Any order passed by the Registrar determining the merits of an opposition is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice due to any delay in processing the application, the appellate board may condone the delay and entertain the appeal.

An application for registration of an integrated circuits layout design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or photolithographic masks representing the layout. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the creation of the integrated circuits layout, including details regarding the date of first manufacture and the place where such manufacture occurred. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to provide all requested information, an affidavit explaining the reasons for omission may be submitted under this Act. Any person claiming rights in a registered integrated circuits layout design shall notify the Registrar of any change in ownership or control affecting those rights, within thirty days of such alteration as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board relating to the revocation of protection, or the imposition of conditions on the grant of protection, may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate court shall have the same jurisdiction as it would have in respect of original suits under this Act and may entertain appeals against orders concerning claims purposes, including but not limited to disputes regarding essential derivation or farmer’s rights. Provided that, where an appeal is preferred, the Board's order shall remain suspended unless the High Court directs otherwise. The appellant shall be liable to compensate any respondent for costs incurred in defending the appeal if the appeal is found to be frivolous or vexatious. Further, a party may apply to the appellate court for interim relief pending disposal of the appeal, subject to such terms and conditions as the court deems fit.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming invention arising from agricultural processes shall be deemed to be a producer for the purposes of applying for patent protection. Applications filed by producers relating to such inventions must include a detailed statement outlining the intended scale and method of commercialization within three years of grant, as provided herein. Failure to submit this statement or demonstrate reasonable progress towards implementation may result in compulsory licensing under this Act. The Controller General shall have power to issue notices requiring clarification regarding these commercialization plans and may conduct inquiries with relevant stakeholders. Any challenge to the validity of a patent granted under these provisions based on non-working or inadequate working shall be adjudicated by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, following established procedures. Producers are obligated to maintain accurate records pertaining to production quantities and sales data for inspection upon request.

Subject to the provisions herein, registration of works under this Act shall confer upon the applicant a presumption of ownership of india rights in respect of the work claimed. An application for registration may be made by the author or any person claiming through him, and shall include particulars as prescribed regarding the nature of the work, date of its creation, and details of first publication, if any. Where an application is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Controller within a period specified; such appeal shall be finally determined by the Controller after affording the applicant an opportunity for being heard. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify claims made in the application concerning ownership or prior assignment of india rights.

For the purposes of this Act, an “applicant patent person” is defined as any individual or legal entity who files for a grant of exclusive rights relating to an invention. An applicant patent person shall be deemed to include not only the original filer but also any subsequent assignee or representative authorized under this Act to act on their behalf in proceedings related to the patent application. Where multiple individuals are jointly seeking protection, each such individual shall constitute an applicant patent person with equal standing. The rights and obligations of an applicant patent person are subject to the provisions relating to inventorship as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "means transmission operation" includes the electronic or optical transfer of data representing a layout design from one storage medium to another, whether temporary or permanent, and such transmission shall be deemed an act of reproduction only if it results in a perceptible change to the original layout design. Any person engaged in the commercial provision of services facilitating such means transmission operation shall register with the Controller under procedures as provided herein. The Controller may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe standards for registration and ongoing compliance relating to data security and integrity during transmission. Subject to any contractual agreements between parties, no civil action shall lie against a service provider solely on the basis of an incidental means transmission operation occurring within the normal course of their business. Provided that, such services must adhere to guidelines issued by the Controller regarding measures taken to prevent unauthorized copying or distribution.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed containing a representation that the trade mark is used internationally, the applicant shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within thirty days of the request made by the Registrar, documentary evidence demonstrating such international use. Such evidence must clearly indicate the territories where the trade mark is being employed in commerce and the dates upon which such use commenced. The Registrar may require further clarification or additional documentation if the initial submission is deemed insufficient to satisfy the requirements as provided herein. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the application liable for rejection, subject to an opportunity granted to the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a stipulated period. Informing international usage does not, however, constitute a right of exclusive ownership in any jurisdiction.

Where any person institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief for infringement of a registered trade mark, and such person has previously paid an act fee relating to the application for registration of the said trade mark, they shall be entitled to claim from the infringing party compensation proportionate to the expenses reasonably incurred in bringing those proceedings. Such expenses shall include, but not be limited to, legal fees, expert witness charges, and costs associated with gathering evidence demonstrating infringement. Provided that, a claimant seeking such compensation must demonstrate a direct causal link between the act fee paid and the subsequent need for litigation. Further, the amount of compensation awarded shall be subject to review by the relevant adjudicating authority to ensure fairness and proportionality, considering the nature and extent of the infringing activity.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the civil court registrar designated by the State Government for that purpose. The applicant shall provide detailed particulars regarding the history and characteristics of the goods or products associated with the proposed indication, including maps delineating the geographical area of origin. Any interested party may file an objection to the application within three months from the date of publication under this Act; such objections will be adjudicated by the civil court registrar after providing due opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the objector. The registrar shall record his findings and reasons for decision, which shall be final subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

A practitioner person registered under this Act may grant a non-exclusive license to utilize a registered integrated circuit layout design for the purpose of manufacturing semiconductor devices, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the written agreement executed between the licensor and licensee. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to geographical territory and field of application. Assignment of rights under this Act relating to a registered layout-design is permissible with prior notification to the Controller, who may require submission of documentation verifying due diligence regarding any existing licenses granted. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses the design, they shall ensure that the original licensor receives equitable consideration as provided herein and documented in the sub-licensing agreement. Any alteration made to the layout-design by the licensee requires prior consent from the registered owner.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Registrar shall direct that notice of such acceptance be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal and in such other publications as the Registrar deems appropriate. Any person may, within sixty days from the date of first publication of the advertisement, file with the Registrar a written objection to the proposed registration, stating clearly the grounds upon which such objection is founded; provided that any such objection shall not be entertained if it relates to matters which could have been raised in an earlier proceeding under this Act. The Registrar may, after giving all parties interested an opportunity of being heard, either dismiss the objection or direct further inquiry into the matter. Registration shall advertised notwithstanding any pending objection unless otherwise directed by the Registrar.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable geographical to the goods and which originate from the asserted geographical origin. The Registrar shall consider such statement in determining whether the applicant has established, to a reasonable degree of certainty, that the alleged connection between the goods and the geographical origin is inherent and not solely due to temporary factors. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the genuineness of the claimed geographical origin, the applicant shall be required to furnish documentary evidence substantiating the claim. The Registrar may, after affording the objector an opportunity of being heard, dismiss the application if satisfied that the asserted connection lacks a demonstrable basis. Any interested party may appeal against such a decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety shall be permitted to grant licenses for the commercial use of propagating material derived from that variety. Such license agreements may include stipulations regarding geographical limitations, specific end-uses, or restrictions on sub-licensing, as mutually agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. Further, assignment of such rights, including licenses, requires registration with the Plant Varieties Registry, detailing all relevant terms and conditions pertaining to royalty payments and benefit sharing arrangements. Any sums received by the assignee through exploitation of the assigned variety shall be subject to contribution into the National Gene Fund, proportionate to the commercial gains derived, as determined by the Authority. This provision applies equally whether the assignment arises from section 21 Indian or any other legal basis for transfer.

The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall be liable for damages in respect of any loss or damage suffered by any person as a result of a false or misleading representation that goods or services have been certified in accordance with the regulations governing the use of the mark. Such liability shall extend to instances where the proprietor, through negligence or willful misconduct, permits the certification trade mark to be used on goods or services not conforming to the prescribed standards. Any person aggrieved by such a false representation may institute proceedings against the proprietor seeking an injunction restraining further use of the mark in that manner and claiming compensation for losses incurred. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate allegations of misuse and issue directions to rectify the situation; failure to comply with these directions shall render the proprietor liable to penalties as provided herein.

An aggrieved party, having received notice of an adverse determination regarding copyright infringement made by the Trade Mark Registrar acting in his capacity under this Act, may appeal such determination to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice and must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including demonstrable errors of law or fact. Provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to just cause shown, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of said period. The Trade Mark Registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the original determination to the Appellate Board within thirty days of receiving a request for them. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for an appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall be considered only if it discloses the method of manufacture or production in sufficient detail as to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use the invention without undue experimentation. The applicant must demonstrate that the claimed process yields a product meeting established pharmacopoeial standards, unless such deviation is explicitly justified and supported by data demonstrating equivalent efficacy and safety. Furthermore, where the application incorporates information derived from prior publications, the applicant shall provide an exhaustive list of all such references, confirming their accuracy and relevance to the invention as claimed. Any alteration to the disclosed process post-application filing requires notification and may necessitate re-examination under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “placed houses parliament” means any structure erected within the designated geographical area of Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, traditionally constructed using techniques passed down through generations of artisan families and intended for residential occupancy; such structures shall be deemed to possess unique characteristics attributable to their location and method of construction. The term includes dwellings modified or expanded while retaining the original architectural style and craftsmanship. Any alteration which fundamentally deviates from these established practices will disqualify a structure from being considered “placed houses parliament.” Further, the Registrar may require documentation substantiating adherence to traditional building methods.

Where a proprietor demonstrates that representations have been made in the course of trade likely to deceive the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, and that such misrepresentation has caused, or is likely to cause, damage to the goodwill associated with those goods or services, an action for passing off may be initiated under this Act. The proprietor shall provide evidence establishing a substantial connection between the misrepresented goods or services and those for which the claimant possesses reputation. Provided that, if the defendant proves that the public associates the sign used in the misrepresentation with the defendant’s goods or services rather than those of the claimant, relief may be refused. Such relief is subject to considerations of fair use and honest practices in industrial competition as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a design relates to a pattern which is primarily dictated by technical function or process, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that such pattern constitutes an aesthetic choice distinct from the functional requirements. For the purpose of determining novelty under this Act, any published description or illustration relating to the design shall be deemed to constitute prior publication. Where a design incorporates elements derived from existing works, a form reference act shall apply; namely, the applicant must provide detailed documentation identifying each source element and demonstrating substantial modification sufficient to establish originality as provided herein. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application.

The proprietor of any trade marks registered under this Act may grant licenses conferring the right to use such trade marks, subject to conditions specified therein and filed with the Registrar. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that notice of assignment is given to the Registrar within three months of the date of transfer. Where a license includes a restriction on territory, goods, or services for which the mark may be used, subsequent assignments of the trade marks registered shall remain subject to those limitations unless expressly modified by written consent from the original proprietor and notification filed with the Registrar. Any person acquiring rights in a trade mark through assignment or sub-license shall be bound by all conditions applicable to the use of the trade marks registered prior to such acquisition. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding the validity of any license granted.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must clearly describe the goods or services for which the geographical indication is sought, along with details establishing its connection to the territory from which it originates. Any person claiming an interest in opposition to the registration may file a notice of opposition under this Act within the time specified. The Registry shall serve a copy of such notice on the applicant and provide them an opportunity to submit their response as provided herein. Upon receipt of the response, the Registry may proceed with an inquiry into the matter, affording all interested parties a chance to be heard. Decisions made by the Geographical Indications Registry are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

A Mark Certification Trade, as provided herein, signifies a mark used to guarantee that goods or services conform to a specified standard, quality, characteristic, or production method. Such standards must be defined with precision in the regulations submitted alongside the application for registration. The applicant seeking certification trade mark registration shall demonstrate control over the conformity assessment process and possess the requisite authority to use the proposed mark. Further, the Registrar may require evidence of ongoing compliance with the prescribed standards throughout the duration of the registration. Any alteration to these standards requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar.

Any person who knowingly makes a false statement material to the inclusion of a variety in the entry register variety shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of such misstatement. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information regarding fraudulent entries or deliberate concealment of relevant data pertaining to a candidate variety’s distinctiveness or stability, initiate suo moto proceedings to review and potentially expunge said entry from the entry register variety. Failure to comply with directions issued by the Registrar during such review proceedings shall attract further penalties up to ten thousand rupees per day until compliance is achieved. Repeated offenses may result in disqualification of the applicant from applying for registration under this Act, as provided herein.

Where any patent shall be assigned, the instrument effecting such assignment shall be executed by all assignors and the assignee, or their duly authorized representatives, and shall contain a declaration verifying the truth of the statements made therein relating to the ownership of the invention and the consideration, if any, given for the assignment. Such assignment may relate to the entire patent or to the right to use the patented invention for specific purposes or in designated territories. The Controller General may require such assignments to be registered, subject to payment of prescribed fees. A patent shall assigned only upon terms that do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition under this Act. Any subsequent dealing with the assigned patent, including sub-licensing and further assignment, shall also adhere to these principles of fair practice and transparency as provided herein.

Where an infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to damages shall accrue to the proprietor of the article and extend to cover all losses directly attributable to the infringing activity. Such damages may include, but are not limited to, lost profits reasonably foreseeable, diminution in value of the patented article, and costs incurred in mitigating the effects of the infringement. The Controller may, upon application by the aggrieved party, issue an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, provided that it is demonstrated that irreparable harm would result without such relief. Any person found guilty of contributory infringement shall be liable to penalties as determined under this Act. Furthermore, a proprietor seeking remedies for breach of their article respect patent must demonstrate clear evidence of unauthorized use or exploitation of the invention.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an objection may be raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark by any person claiming an interest in a similar trade mark already registered under this Act. Such objection shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and must demonstrate likelihood of confusion or deception arising from the proposed permitted register trade. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to file a counter-statement addressing the objections raised, and both parties may submit evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. A decision by the Registrar following such consideration may be challenged before the Tribunal within three months of its communication, asserting errors of law or fact.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier right, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file its written submissions and evidence in response to such objection. The Registrar may, after considering the said submissions and evidence, direct the party holding the earlier right to present their counter-submissions within a prescribed period. Failure by either party to comply with these directions may result in the Registrar’s decision being rendered ex parte. Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the Registrar's order under this Act relating to conflicting rights may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such an appeal is filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the order and subject to regulations governing appeals. The trade mark proprietor bears the onus of proving non-infringement in any proceeding.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the defined geographical area consisting of specified hillsides and valleys within the Darjeeling district of West Bengal, as notified by the Register; such production being subject to adherence to traditional processing methods including orthodox or green leaf processing. The term “defined geographical area” shall include any subsequent modifications thereto as provided herein. Any use of the word "Darjeeling" in connection with tea not meeting these provisions shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, and may result in penalties as determined by the relevant authorities. This definition is without prejudice to other provisions relating to quality standards for registered geographical indications.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a comprehensive alphabetical index classification of goods and services for the purposes of examination under this Act. This index, accessible to all applicants and stakeholders, will facilitate efficient assessment of trademark applications against existing registered marks and pending applications within similar classes. The Registrar may, from time to time, revise and update the alphabetical index classification to reflect evolving commercial practices and technological advancements, provided that such revisions are published for public comment prior to implementation. Any party aggrieved by a classification assigned under this Act may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the procedural requirements as provided herein. The Registrar’s determination regarding the appropriate class of goods or services shall be binding pending any appellate review and is deemed quasi-judicial in nature.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a specification of goods or services, that specification shall be deemed to define the scope of protection afforded by the registered trade mark. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Mark Registrar regarding the accuracy or appropriateness of such description may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days. Failure to comply with this provision renders the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and rejection of the application. The Registrar shall have power to issue directions requiring amendment of a goods services description if it is found to be misleading or unduly broad in scope, subject to affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, reproduction by means of reprography shall be permissible only where such reproduction is undertaken for private and non-commercial use. Provided that, where the work reproduced comprises literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, a reasonable number of copies may be made for educational purposes within institutions recognized by the Central Government, provided further that prior written permission from the copyright holder is not required in such instances. However, any commercial distribution or public display of materials obtained through reprography shall constitute an infringement under this Act and render the distributor liable to prosecution. The right to control reprography extends to all forms of works fixed in a tangible medium, as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the grant of a patent, and such objection challenges the status of the applicant as a true india patentee, the Controller shall provide both the objector and the applicant with an opportunity to present evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. The determination of whether an individual or entity qualifies as a india patentee is subject to judicial review, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from any error apparent on the face of the record. Further, if the invention relates to technology originating outside India, the Controller may request clarification and supporting documentation from the International Bureau regarding prior art disclosures relevant to assessing novelty and inventive step.

An application to apply patent shall include particulars of the invention, specifying the technical field to which it relates and stating the prior art knowledge known to the applicant as of the date of filing. The term "invention" for the purposes of this Act means a new technical solution to a problem in any field, subject to exclusions provided herein relating to discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, schemes or methods for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business, and programs for computers. A patent shall not be granted for an invention that is contrary to public morality and order, human life or animal life, or inventions the use or commercialization of which are prohibited under any law.

Any individual acting as a patent agent without possessing a valid certificate of registration, obtained through examination conducted by the Controller, shall be deemed to have engaged in unauthorized practice and will be liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each instance of such activity. Furthermore, any person employing an unregistered individual as a patent agent shall face a similar penalty, recoverable from both parties jointly and severally. The Controller may, upon receiving credible information regarding violations under this Act, issue notices requiring production of registration certificates; failure to comply will result in summary suspension of the alleged agent’s activities pending investigation. Repeated or willful contravention may lead to prosecution for offenses punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be the proprietor of a mark shall file an application for registration in the prescribed form with the Registrar. The application shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the mark proposes to be registered and shall include a representation of the mark. Where the mark incorporates a geographical indication, the applicant shall furnish a declaration confirming that they are entitled to use the indication under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the application, including evidence of prior usage if the mark has been used before the date of filing. An adverse report from any person objecting to the registration of the mark shall be considered by the Registrar during examination and may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

A consumer shall have recourse under this Act where it is established that another has engaged in conduct constituting a trade mark falsified. Such falsification occurs when an individual reproduces, adapts, or imitates a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services, creating likelihood of confusion amongst purchasers and prejudicing the reputation associated with the original mark. The proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification, as well as damages commensurate with the financial loss suffered due to the deceptive use. Provided that, where the infringing conduct is demonstrably unintentional or undertaken in good faith without knowledge of the registered trade mark, a court may exercise discretion in mitigating remedies. The proprietor must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the actions constitute a trade mark falsified and have caused demonstrable harm.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file a counter-statement rebutting such grounds. The Registrar may, after giving notice to both parties and affording them a reasonable hearing, determine whether the alleged conflict is sufficient to preclude registration. Provided that, if either party disputes the Registrar’s decision, appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such appeal shall be on grounds relating to legality or other error apparent on the record and concerning the proper interpretation of this Act in relation to trade goods services.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may only be pursued if the grounds for refusal are demonstrably based on a conflict with existing rights relating to similar goods or services. The appellant must provide evidence satisfying the tribunal that their proposed trade mark does not create confusion amongst consumers, and that any similarity is incidental or negligible. Further, the applicant shall demonstrate diligent efforts were undertaken to distinguish the mark from prior uses, as provided herein. A successful appeal requires compliance with prescribed timelines for filing documentation and payment of applicable fees; failure to adhere to these conditions will render the appeal invalidating the trade mark relation.

Where an application for registration is rejected, the Registrar shall provide a reasoned order specifying the grounds for rejection. Any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The manner issuing notices pertaining to appeals under this Act shall be as prescribed in the First Schedule; however, any deviation from these prescriptions must be demonstrably justified due to circumstances specific to the appellant’s location or disability. Provided that, if the Registrar considers the rejection manifestly without merit, he may issue a corrigendum and proceed with registration, but such action is subject to challenge by any interested party within thirty days thereafter.

Where an invention relates to a method or process, and such method or process is capable of being applied to the manufacture of a substance by a chemical or biochemical process, the Controller may grant a patent of addition for the substance so manufactured, provided that the application for the patent of addition is filed within thirty-six months from the date of first filing of the related application. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing a patent of addition may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding one thousand rupees for each day of default, subject to a maximum limit of ten thousand rupees.

For the purposes of this Act, a cinematograph film shall be deemed as an artistic work and copyright therein shall vest in the producer who owns the rights necessary for the creation of the film. Where such producer is not the author of the cinematograph film, the right to claim ownership shall be subject to demonstration before the Controller that all requisite permissions and assignments relating to underlying works incorporated within the film have been duly obtained and recorded. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, exhibit or trade in a cinematograph film contrary to the provisions herein shall first apply for permission from the Controller, furnishing details of the intended use and providing evidence of compliance with applicable regulations. The Controller may grant such permission upon payment of prescribed fees and subject to conditions as deemed appropriate, provided that no permission shall be granted which would infringe on any existing copyright.

The Central Government may, upon receiving a written representation from any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, direct that the case be referred to a High Court Judge for inquiry and report. Such reference shall specify the grounds of appeal and the new evidence, if any, which the appellant desires to submit. The High Court Judge so appointed shall afford all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, and shall record his findings on matters of fact and law. A copy of the report submitted by the High Court Judge shall be furnished to the Central Government, who shall consider the same before making a final determination. Any person dissatisfied with the decision of the Central Government following such a reference may approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The expenses incurred in connection with any inquiry made pursuant to this provision shall be borne by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication in connection with goods for which it is registered. Such license shall specify the territory within which and the time during which the licensee is authorized to use the geographical indication, and the conditions under which such use is permitted. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to receive royalties or other consideration from the licensee as agreed upon between them, provided that any assignment of a geographical indication or of rights granted by license requires prior approval of the Registrar. Further, where the Government intends to utilize a protected geographical indication for public purposes, it shall obtain a binding government license from the registered proprietor, compensating them fairly and in advance for such use, as determined through an arbitration process established under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the grant of a patent, or any condition imposed therein, may within sixty days from the date of such decision file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and must include particulars of the invention as claimed in the patent, along with supporting documentation demonstrating invalidity under this Act. Where an objection relates to the non-patentable subject matter, or lack of novelty, the aggrieved party shall bear the burden of proving such deficiency. The Opposition Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, dismiss the opposition or refer the matter back to the Controller for further inquiry. Costs associated with the proceedings before the Opposition Board shall be determined as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “authorised user” means any person who has been granted a license or otherwise permitted by the registered proprietor of a geographical indication to use such indication in connection with goods belonging to the class specified in the registration; provided that an authorised user shall not be deemed to infringe under this Act if the use is consistent with the terms and conditions of the authorisation, and subject to compliance with all applicable laws. Any act involving the application or use of a registered geographical indication in a manner prejudicial to the public interest, or constituting an offence under the Indian Penal Code, shall be actionable as per provisions herein. Registration respect for authorised users is paramount.

For the purposes of this Act, “layout design” means the three dimensional representation of an integrated circuit upon a semiconductor chip resulting from the arrangement or combination of active and passive components and interconnections; provided that such representation is defined by reference to a pattern. The term "integrated circuit" has the meaning assigned to it under the Patents Act. An application for registration shall be deemed to include a claim extending to layout designs that are substantially similar to the design claimed, as determined by the Layout Design Registrar considering the overall impression created upon an informed user. The Layout Design Registrar may require further clarification of any aspect of a layout design during examination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered breeder shall be entitled to perform acts including multiplication, sale, distribution and import of propagating material of the plant variety for commercial purposes. Such entitlement is conditional upon adherence to the prescribed quality standards as determined by the Central Government from time to time; failure to comply with these standards may result in suspension or revocation of registration. The registered breeder shall also be obligated to provide relevant documentation pertaining to lineage, genetic purity and field performance data upon request from the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Further, any modification to the plant variety subsequent to its registration, undertaken without prior written consent from the Plant Variety Protection Authority, will render the registered breeder liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence against another person under this Act, such proceedings shall be deemed to be civil suits for the purposes of limitation. The remedy available to the proprietor shall include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the alleged offence, and may encompass injunctive relief preventing further acts infringing upon registered trade marks. Provided that, in determining the quantum of damages, the Tribunal shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating reasonable belief on the part of the defendant that their actions did not constitute an infringement. Further, a proprietor seeking remedies under this Act must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the alleged offence; otherwise, claims for exemplary or punitive damages shall be disallowed. The defendant may offer proof mitigating the severity of the alleged offence, subject to scrutiny by the Tribunal as provided herein.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date the patent ceased to have effect and shall state the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to pay was unintentional or attributable to circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating these claimed circumstances, including but not limited to documentation relating to financial hardship or administrative error. Restoration of a patent under this provision shall revive the patent as if it had not lapsed, subject to any applicable fees and penalties determined by the Controller.

The Controller shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a design, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the design is capable of being registered under this Act. Where it appears to the Controller that the registration of a design would be prejudicial to the interest of the security of India, or likely to affect public order, he may direct the Registrar to refuse the registration and shall provide reasons for such refusal in writing to the applicant. Any party aggrieved by an order refusing registration under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding the assessment of potential threats to national security arising from registered designs. Information submitted during examination shall be treated as confidential and not disclosed unless required for proceedings before the Appellate Board.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act alleging that another person has, without due cause, infringed his right in the said trade mark, the Court may grant such remedy as it deems just and equitable. This includes an injunction restraining the defendant from using any *name* or mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration subsists. Further, the Court shall order the delivery up of all infringing materials, including labels, packaging, advertising matter, and any other articles bearing the unauthorized *name*. Provided that where the defendant proves prior honest concurrent use of the impugned *name*, the injunction may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Court considers appropriate to safeguard the interests of both parties. The proprietor shall also be entitled to damages sustained by reason of the infringement, or an account of profits made by the infringing party.

Where a person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act relating to the registration, revocation or amendment concerning a breeder registered variety, or by any condition attached thereto, may within sixty days from the date of publication of such decision in the Official Gazette, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider appeals upon statements of objections and replies submitted by all parties concerned, and may affirm, reverse or modify the order appealed from, subject to just considerations and natural justice. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the order, provided that the grounds for such appeal are limited to questions of law arising out of this Act.

Any person employing a sign identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark without due cause shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such liability extends to instances where the use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services. The proprietor of the registered trade mark may apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining such infringing activity, provided that evidence demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof is presented. Further, any party found in violation shall be subject to a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and repeat offenders may face enhanced penalties as determined by the court. The principle of trade mark accordance dictates that all users must respect existing registrations.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising out of orders relating to infringement and rectification proceedings. An appeal shall only be admitted if the appellant deposits with the Appellate Board such sum as may be determined by the Board, representing costs incurred by the respondent. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two members, one of whom shall be a cial Member or a Technical Member of the Appellate Board and possess expertise in semiconductor technology. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeals under the relevant provisions concerning judicial review.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that it is contrary to declared public policy or morality. The Registrar may, prior to refusal, afford the applicant an opportunity for their representation regarding such considerations and shall record the reasons for any decision made under this Act. Where a proposed trade mark contains a geographical indication which is protected under another enactment, the Registrar shall require evidence from the applicant demonstrating due cause for use of said indication in connection with the goods or services specified in the application. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of that order, as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been rejected by the Controller under this Act, and the applicant desires to challenge said rejection, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall give notice to the Controller requiring him to submit his reasons for such rejection within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of service of the notice. Upon hearing the appellant and the Controller, and considering all relevant evidence presented, the Board may allow the appeal and direct that the patent be granted as originally applied for, or may modify the application and direct that a patent be granted according to such modification, or may dismiss the appeal. The court permits patent grant only after due consideration of the Board’s findings, subject to any legal challenge brought before it under established procedures as provided herein.

Where an applicant files a provisional specification disclosing the invention for which patent protection is sought, such specification may include a provisional specification claim relating to a particular aspect or feature of the invention. The acceptance of a provisional specification shall not be construed as an indication that the claimed subject matter is novel or non-obvious under this Act. Upon filing a complete specification within the prescribed time limit following the provisional application, the applicant shall clearly indicate the relationship between the claims in the complete specification and the disclosures made in the earlier provisional specification claim. Failure to do so may result in objections being raised during examination of the patent application. The Controller may require the applicant to amend or clarify any such indication if it is deemed insufficient for establishing a clear link as provided herein.

Where an application for patent is filed relating to a process by which a substance is produced, the invention disclosed shall be taken to include the composition of matter obtained directly from that process. Provided that, if such a process involves a form reference act wherein the claimed invention relates solely to the method of producing said substance and does not encompass the substance itself, the controller may require the applicant to demonstrate with reasonable certainty that the resulting substance possesses properties substantially different from those previously known or described in prior art. Furthermore, subject to compliance with regulations pertaining to industrial scale production, such a requirement shall be waived if the process is novel and involves an inventive step beyond mere manipulation of existing chemical reactions.

An applicant seeking a patent shall furnish an international application form in accordance with the Patents Rules, detailing the priority claim and specifying the countries where protection is sought; provided that such form must be accompanied by a certified true copy of the original priority document. The determination of the term of patent shall commence from the date the initial application was filed, irrespective of subsequent amendments or additions to the claims. Where an international application claiming priority arises, the expiry date for the patent will remain consistent with the twenty-year period as provided herein, calculated from the earliest priority date claimed in the original Indian application. Any discrepancies found during examination may necessitate further clarification under this Act.

Where a license is granted for the use of a registered trademark, including any y description which is made available to potential users and prominently displayed on product packaging or promotional materials, such license shall be assignable subject to the terms stipulated therein. The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor, record an assignment of such license, provided that notice thereof is given to all licensees prior to registration. Any subsequent use of the trademark following a valid assignment shall be deemed to be authorized by the assignee. Further, where a trade mark owner seeks to sub-license rights pertaining to a particular y description, consent from the original proprietor must be obtained in writing and filed with the Registrar. This requirement does not apply if the initial license explicitly permits such sub-licensing without further authorization.

The Controller may, at any time, require the patentee to furnish such further particulars relating to an invention as he deems necessary for maintaining the accuracy and completeness of the register. Such particulars shall include, but are not limited to, details regarding manufacturing processes, commercial exploitation, and any modifications made to the originally claimed subject matter. The Controller shall provide a reasonable opportunity to the patentee to comply with such requirement, affording them at least thirty days from the date of notification. Failure to furnish the required particulars within the stipulated period may result in the imposition of a monetary penalty as determined by the Controller. All information submitted under this provision shall be treated as confidential and accessible only to authorized personnel subject to provisions regarding data protection. The particulars comprising register are considered public documents, available for inspection upon application and payment of prescribed fees.

An application for registration of copyright shall be made in the prescribed form and shall contain a statement of ownership, specifying whether the applicant is the author or an authorized assignee. The application must identify the work in sufficient detail to allow for its unambiguous identification; this includes providing particulars regarding title, authorship, date of first publication where applicable, and language of the work. Every such application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Where the work is a musical composition, the application shall also include details pertaining to lyrics or associated text. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. An incomplete application may be rejected, and notice of rejection shall be served upon the applicant, providing an opportunity for amendment within a stipulated period.

Where infringement of a patent granted under this Act has occurred, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the patented invention. The plaintiff shall be entitled to claim damages commensurate with the loss suffered by reason of such infringement, calculated on the basis of reasonable royalty or actual profits made by the infringer, whichever is higher. Provided that, in determining such damages, the Controller may take into account any measures taken by the patentee to prevent infringement and the extent to which the infringing activity was due to a lack of knowledge regarding the existence of the patent. The right to seek rectification of entries relating to respect patent granted shall not preclude remedies available under this Act for acts of infringement.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark under this Act may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark. Such licenses shall be registrable as assignments if they include provisions for royalty payments and duration, and explicitly state the geographical territory covered by the permitted usage. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all registered licenses alongside the primary trademark registration. Any subsequent assignment of the trademark, whether partial or complete, must disclose any existing license agreements to the Registrar at the time of application. Failure to do so may render the assignee jointly liable for obligations under those pre-existing license arrangements. The Registrar’s decision regarding the validity of a registrar application pr esented concerning an assignment is final and binding.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include representations regarding the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of goods associated with that indication; provided that such representations are demonstrably accurate and verifiable through established scientific or traditional practices. Where an applicant seeks to register a geographical indication relating to handloom fabrics originating from a specific region, they shall submit detailed documentation outlining the unique weaving techniques employed and the historical significance of those methods. Any use of a registered geographical indication which is deemed to be an indication falsified, by employing misleading packaging or promotional materials that suggest a different origin than the officially recognised area, constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the user liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an Adjudicating Officer concerning infringement proceedings relating to registered trademarks or designs may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal must be lodged within ninety days from the date of communication of the order; failure to adhere to this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. Further, the appellant is obligated to deposit a sum determined by the Central Government, which may vary based on the nature and value of the dispute. An Adjudicating Officer period for considering counter-claims or objections raised during proceedings shall not exceed six months, extendable only with reasoned justification recorded in writing.

Subject to compliance with all applicable regulations under this Act, any person seeking registration of a plant variety shall submit detailed documentation pertaining to its lineage and morphological characteristics. The application for a variety registered act must include evidence demonstrating that the proposed variety possesses distinctiveness from existing varieties, as determined by established testing procedures. Furthermore, the applicant shall provide an undertaking guaranteeing adherence to bio-containment protocols if genetically modified techniques were employed in the development of the plant variety. Any alteration to the documented characteristics following registration requires prior approval from the Authority and may necessitate a reevaluation of the variety's distinctiveness. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, revoke a certificate of registration if it finds that the applicant acted fraudulently or misrepresented information during the application process.

A geographical indication relates to goods specified in the application and produced exclusively within a defined geographical area, subject to compliance with established production methods detailed in the technical file submitted during registration. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party demonstrating that the use of the geographical indication is causing or likely to cause damage to the reputation of similar goods originating from another region, initiate proceedings for amendment or revocation. Registration shall cease if it is determined, following due process and opportunity for hearing, that the conditions stipulated in the technical file are no longer met, or where production has demonstrably ceased within the defined geographical area for a period exceeding three years, provided that this does not prejudice any existing contractual obligations.

Where an application for renewal of a patent has been rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is challenged. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the Controller and affording him an opportunity of being heard, confirm or vary the order appealed against, or remit the matter for reconsideration. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Appellate Board under this provision may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days, subject to such conditions as are provided herein regarding costs. The continued validity of the patent remains in abeyance pending final determination of the appeal.

Any proprietor seeking to maintain registration of a geographical indication may apply for renewal under this Act, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent as provided herein. Failure to submit the prescribed application and accompanying documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall render the geographical indication liable for removal from the Register of Geographical Indications. In instances where an application for renewal is filed after the expiry date but prior to the lapse of six months thereafter, a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the original registration fee shall be payable. This fees surcharge prescribed under this Act aims to discourage undue delay in renewal processes and ensure timely maintenance of registered geographical indications. Any person aggrieved by an order removing a geographical indication from the Register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such order.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of their registered trademark under this Act and such allegation is contested by the defendant, the court shall afford both parties full opportunity to present evidence pertaining to the similarity between the impugned mark and the plaintiff’s registered mark, considering inter alia the phonetic, visual, and conceptual aspects thereof. Should the court find that the defendant knowingly and wilfully employed a mark deceptively similar to the registered trademark with intent to mislead consumers, such conduct shall be deemed an offence. Upon conviction, the offender shall be subject to punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to pay a fine, notwithstanding any appeal filed against the judgment.

Where an invention infringes a patent granted under this Act, the patentee shall be entitled to seek remedies including, but not limited to, permanent injunctions restraining the infringing party from further exploitation of the patented technology. The determination of infringement shall hinge upon whether the accused product or process falls within the scope of any one or more of the claims in the specification claim. Provided that, a finding of literal infringement is not required; equitable estoppel may be invoked where the alleged infringer has knowingly adopted practices substantially similar to those disclosed in the patent’s description. Subject to demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing the patent invalid, a party may challenge the validity of a patent by way of revocation proceedings before the Controller. The patentee shall bear the burden of proving that the specification claim clearly defines the scope of protection granted.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any registered breeder of indigenous plant varieties may apply to the appellate board for review of a decision concerning infringement of copyright in respect of their propagated material. Such an application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be reviewed and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods under this Act. The appellate board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, vary or reverse any such decision. Further, an appeal lies to a High Court from any order passed by the appellate board, provided that the appellant deposits with the court the amount specified as costs.

Any proprietor issuing certificates bearing a proprietor certification trade mark shall maintain accurate records detailing the standards for conformity and processes followed in assessing adherence thereto. Failure to do so constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the proprietor liable to penalties as prescribed herein, including but not limited to fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and suspension of certificate issuance privileges. Any person knowingly using goods or services certified under a proprietor certification trade mark that fail to meet the declared standards shall be deemed guilty of an offence and subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or both. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such non-compliance, initiate investigations and impose corrective measures as provided herein.

Where a person considers himself aggrieved by an act or omission relating to the grant, revocation, or validity of a patent, or by infringement claim patent asserted against him, such person may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The court shall have jurisdiction to determine all questions concerning the construction of this Act and the interpretation of any patent granted under it. Any party found to have wilfully infringed a patent shall be liable to pay damages amounting to three times the actual loss or harm suffered by the patentee, whichever is higher. Further, the court may issue an injunction restraining the infringing activity, subject to considerations of public interest as provided herein. Costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined at the discretion of the court.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design and has entered into a relationship proposed as a registered license with another party, the application for registration shall disclose fully the terms of that relationship. The Registrar may require further particulars concerning such a relationship proposed registered if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application based on the existence of a relationship proposed registered may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be the duty of the applicant to ensure that the terms of the relationship proposed registered do not contravene any provisions under this Act, particularly those concerning fair competition and public interest. Failure to disclose such a relationship or providing false information relating thereto shall render the application liable for rejection.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license for use of a registered geographical indication relating to “placed houses parliament” shall, in the application for such license, clearly state the scope and duration of the permitted use, including any restrictions on territory or product characteristics. Such licenses may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively, as determined by the proprietor; however, any exclusive license shall be recorded with the Registrar within three months of its execution. Assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication, including those arising from licensed usage, requires prior written consent of the registered proprietors and must be notified to the Registrar for public recordation. Further, sub-licensing is permissible only if expressly stipulated in the original license agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding royalty payments and quality control measures to protect the reputation of “placed houses parliament”.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Contracting Party” shall mean any person who enters into a written agreement with the Registrar for the provision of services relating to trade mark registration, renewal, or opposition proceedings. Such an agreement shall clearly define the scope of services undertaken and the remuneration payable under this Act. A Contracting Party may be an individual, partnership, company, or other legal entity duly registered as per applicable law. Provided that a Contracting Party shall not include any person acting solely as an employee or agent of another party unless such employee or agent is expressly named in the agreement with the Registrar and consents to being designated as a Contracting Party.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is filed after the expiry of the prescribed time limit under this Act, or where any documentation submitted with such application is found to be incomplete or deficient, the Registrar may, subject to conditions as provided herein, accept the application upon payment of a surcharge. This surcharge shall be equivalent to fifty percent of the registration fee initially stipulated and payable at the time of filing. Further, if the applicant fails to rectify deficiencies within thirty days from the date of notification by the Registrar, the application shall stand rejected. Any appeal against an order rejecting an application due to non-compliance with these provisions is subject to a further fees surcharge prescribed by the Central Government.

Any person who, without authorization from the patentee or their duly appointed agent, utilizes a patented process for the manufacture, use, or sale of any substance or article shall be deemed to have infringed upon the rights conferred under this Act. Such infringement will attract penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods produced in contravention of the patented process are subject to seizure and forfeiture. The patentee is entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such unauthorized exploitation of the article patented process.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person owning a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the use is permitted, and the geographical area covered by the license. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding the remaining period of protection of the trade mark, provided that the terms of the license are clearly defined within a written agreement executed between the licensor and licensee. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include an explicit declaration regarding any existing licenses attached to the recognition trade mark, detailing their scope and duration. The assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights and obligations under such licenses. Any alteration or modification to these licensed terms requires prior written consent from both the original licensor and the licensee, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein.
