Failure to comply with a cease and desist order issued pursuant to an infringement action constitutes a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, at the discretion of the Court. The determination of validity of a patent india claim shall be conclusive against all parties to the proceedings; provided that any party demonstrating fraud in obtaining the patent may pursue remedies as provided under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "photograph" means a fixation of an image on light-sensitive material produced through a process involving optics and chemical or electronic means. A photograph shall be deemed to include any positive or negative representation derived therefrom, whether such derivation involves alteration or manipulation of the original image. The term “photograph” does not extend to representations that are primarily artistic in nature, even if created using photographic techniques; however, where a photograph incorporates substantial elements of originality beyond mere mechanical reproduction, it may be considered an artistic work subject to protection under this Act. As provided herein, ownership of copyright in a photograph shall vest initially in the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the photograph’s creation have been undertaken.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, examine whether the proposed marks are distinctive and not descriptive of the goods or services with which they are associated. Rules carry provisions regarding the form of applications, including requirements for representation of the mark and specification of goods or services. An applicant seeking to utilize a previously registered trade mark under license shall file an application for registration as an authorised use mark, providing evidence of consent from the proprietor of the original trade mark. Such authorisation must clearly define the scope of permitted usage and geographical territory. The Registrar may reject any application if it appears that the proposed mark is confusingly similar to an existing mark, subject to consideration of the goods or services involved.

Any proprietor who discovers that any person has contravened section 51 of this Act shall be entitled to institute appropriate proceedings for damages and seek an injunction restraining further infringement. Where a person is found, upon investigation by the Registrar or through civil suit, to have used a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark without due cause, they shall be liable to pay compensation reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringing use, as determined by the Court. Further, such an accused offence section will trigger a mandatory review of all related registrations held by the infringer and may result in their cancellation if found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation. The Registrar may also impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees for each day the infringing activity continues.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an order adjudicating officer relating to the registration of a layout plan or building map submitted for approval under this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such order, file an application for review before the designated appellate authority. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the applicant challenges the order and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents supporting the claim. Provided that the appellate authority may, after hearing the concerned parties, confirm, vary or set aside the order of the adjudicating officer. Further, where an order is varied or set aside, the appellate authority may issue an order injunction directing the restoration of the layout plan to its original form, as deemed necessary for compliance with regulations.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of their registered design, such allegation shall be substantiated by evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the impugned article and the design as recorded in the register. The proprietor bears the onus of proving that the alleged infringing article creates confusion amongst purchasers regarding its origin or association with the proprietor’s enterprise. However, where the defendant demonstrates prior use of a similar aesthetic feature, subject to reasonable limitations on such use as may be prescribed by regulations, the Court may consider this factor in determining whether infringement has occurred. The proprietor shall have recourse to appeal any decision finding against them, provided that the appellate authority deems the original determination to be manifestly erroneous.

A trademark shall be eligible for registration under this Act if it is used in relation to the specified goods or services. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating such use prior to acceptance of the application, particularly where the mark has not been previously registered. Where a proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the character or quality of the *mark registered goods*, registration shall be refused unless the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use over a significant period. This requirement applies irrespective of any prior publication or advertising undertaken by the applicant. Further, an application may be opposed by interested parties claiming rights in earlier marks, provided that such opposition is filed within the prescribed timeframe as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to section 51, any copyright subsisting in a recorded performance shall be assignable by way of license or otherwise. Such assignment may relate to the entire term of copyright or for such period as the assigning party deems fit, and shall be valid only if executed in writing and duly attested. Where a performer has granted an exclusive license concerning their performance, subsequent assignments relating to the same rights are void unless consented to by the original licensee. Further, any cessation patent related to the underlying musical composition performed shall not affect the assignability of the performance copyright itself; however, such cessation will be noted in all assignment documentation. The assigning party retains the right to terminate an assignment under this Act if material breach occurs, as provided herein.

Applications for registration shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain whether the mark is distinctive and not deceptive. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark or any other relevant matter. Where an application relates to a composite mark consisting of words, devices, or three-dimensional features, the representation of each element shall be clearly delineated in the application. Matters included register are subject to periodic review by the Registrar and may be amended or removed if they no longer comply with the provisions of this Act or any rules made thereunder. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to matters included register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A trade mark shall not be registrable if it exclusively consists of the shape of goods, provided that such shape is wholly determined by factors such as the nature of the goods themselves, their intended function, or requirements for handling or preservation. For the avoidance of doubt, shapes dictated solely by manufacturing processes or packaging considerations are excluded from protection under this Act. The determination of whether a shape possesses distinctive character shall be assessed considering consumer perception and recognition in relation to the relevant goods or services. A shape which is primarily functional and offers no non-functional advantage shall not qualify as a trade marks shape for registration purposes, subject to any demonstrable acquired distinctiveness.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Designs Register, or by a refusal to enter a design, may apply to the Controller for rectification of register. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller shall give notice of the application to the concerned party and afford them an opportunity of being heard, subject to just cause shown. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act concerning rectification proceedings constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment or fine, or both. Any order made by the Controller regarding rectification register is final, provided that an appeal lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where a patent relating to any invention is jointly owned by multiple patentees, they shall hold such ownership as share patents, subject to a written agreement specifying the respective rights and obligations of each co-owner. Disputes concerning the interpretation or enforcement of such agreements may be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, provided that either party furnishes evidence demonstrating good faith efforts toward amicable resolution prior to initiating legal proceedings. The Controller shall entertain applications for revocation challenging the validity of a share patent only if it is demonstrated that the agreement governing the co-ownership was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, and that such deception materially impacted the inventive step claimed in the patent.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite license under this Act or without leaving due acknowledgement in the work from which the extract is taken, reproduces any substantial portion of a copyrighted work infringes the copyright in that work. Such infringement shall render the offender liable to prosecution and subject to penalties as provided herein. The remedies available to the owner of copyright include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, damages reflecting lost profits or reasonable royalties, and delivery up or destruction of infringing copies. Provided that fair dealing for research, private study, criticism, or review does not constitute infringement, subject to conditions regarding acknowledgement and limitation of use. Where the infringement is committed by a corporate body, its officers in default shall also be deemed liable.

Where a practitioner person registered under this Act alleges infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, they shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of reproduction, adaptation, or commercial exploitation without authorization. Such injunction may include orders prohibiting the import, sale, or distribution of infringing products subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success in establishing infringement. The right to damages shall accrue to the registered owner, calculated as the greater of the actual loss suffered by them or a royalty determined based on prevailing industry rates for similar layout-designs. An application registration may be challenged within ninety days from its publication if it is shown that the design was substantially similar to an earlier unregistered layout-design. Provided that any such challenge fails, subsequent actions for infringement will not be barred.

An appeal against any order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of a layout-design or concerning any matter arising under this Act shall be made to the Appellate Tribunal. The application for appeal shall be in the prescribed form and shall specify the order appealed from, the grounds on which it is sought to be set aside, and the relief claimed. Such an application must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. The Registrar may, before entertaining any such appeal, require the applicant to satisfy himself as to the maintainability of the appeal and may direct him to file additional documents or information as deemed necessary. The manner applying appellate jurisdiction is governed by regulations framed under this Act. Further, a registrar application prescribed for submission of evidence shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying its authenticity.

Where a registered layout design owner desires to grant a license conferring any right or rights therein, such license agreement shall be recorded with the established registry. The application for recording shall include particulars of the licensor, licensee, and the scope of the licensed rights, clearly defining whether the license is exclusive or non-exclusive, and the duration thereof. Subject to compliance with regulations prescribed by the Central Government, any assignment of a registered layout design, or any interest therein, may also be recorded in like manner. Provided that no such recording shall prejudice any prior existing right or claim against the layout design owner. The established registry shall maintain a record of all licenses and assignments so recorded, accessible for public inspection as provided herein, upon payment of prescribed fees.

Where a complaint is filed alleging non-compliance with breeder complied provisions relating to farmers’ rights concerning access to propagating material, the Biodiversity Board shall initiate an inquiry. The complainant shall bear the burden of demonstrating, through documentary evidence and witness testimony, that the registered plant variety has been reproduced or distributed in violation of conditions stipulated under this Act regarding benefit sharing with local communities. Should the Board find merit in the complaint, it may direct the breeder to provide compensation as determined by a Disputes Resolution Panel constituted for this purpose. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Authority within sixty days, presenting arguments demonstrating substantial compliance or procedural irregularity.

The right to use a denomination variety shall vest initially with the breeder or registrant as recorded in the Register. Provided that, subject to an agreement in writing, such breeder or registrant may grant licenses allowing others to propagate and market plants of the registered denomination variety for commercial purposes. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to a denomination variety must be executed by a notary public and filed with the Plant Varieties Authority within thirty days of execution; failure to do so shall render the assignment void. Further, where a license is granted incorporating design elements integral to plant presentation or packaging, the licensor retains ownership of those designs and may separately enforce their intellectual property rights therein. The licensee shall not be permitted to sub-license such rights without prior written consent from the original breeder or registrant as provided herein.

Where an application for patent protection is published under this Act, any person possessing knowledge or reason to believe that the invention claimed therein does not fulfill the criteria for patentability as provided herein may, subject to fulfilling procedural requirements, file a notice of opposition with the Controller within the prescribed period following publication. Such notice shall clearly specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and provide supporting documentation. The applicant shall then be afforded an opportunity to respond to the opposition in writing. Following consideration of both submissions, the Controller may direct a hearing where parties may present oral arguments. Any party aggrieved by the Controller's decision on an application notice opposition may appeal to the relevant appellate authority within the time stipulated under this Act.

Where an infringement of layout-design rights has been established under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including, but not limited to, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. The Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of infringing integrated circuits, layouts, or any materials used in their manufacture. In cases where the infringer has knowingly and willfully engaged in persistent and widespread unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a registered layout-design, the Court may direct forfeiture directed of all assets derived from such infringement, including profits realized and equipment utilized in the unlawful activity. This power of forfeiture is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act or at law, provided that due process considerations are observed throughout proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use, or assign, the benefit of the invention claimed in a complete specification relating to such patent. Such license or assignment shall be deemed to include the right to make, use and sell the patented invention within India, unless the license agreement expressly restricts these rights. Where a complete specification contains multiple inventions, a licensee may elect to receive rights pertaining to only a subset of claims defining one or more of those inventions, provided that such election is clearly stated in the written instrument effecting the assignment or license. The patentee shall provide a certified copy of the claim complete specification to the assignee or licensee upon request and payment of the prescribed fee. Any subsequent modification to the invention as claimed shall require prior consent from the licensee, unless otherwise stipulated within the agreement.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a registered user layout shall cease to confer rights under this Act upon the expiry of the term for which it was initially registered, or upon revocation thereof. Any person aggrieved by an order revoking a registered user layout may within sixty days from the date of such order prefer an appeal to the Tribunal. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. It is provided that the determination of whether a person qualifies as a registered user layout shall be subject to judicial review only on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record.

Any licensee granted rights under a registered layout-design pursuant to a contractual agreement may, subject to the terms of such agreement, assign or pledge said license to any third party with their prior written consent from the owner of the layout-design. Provided that, where an assignment or pledge is made, the assignee or pledgee shall be bound by all covenants and restrictions contained within the original licensing agreement. Further, if the licensee defaults in performance of obligations as stipulated under this Act concerning security measures protecting the layout-design, the registered owner may initiate proceedings for committed forfeiture directed towards any licenses granted to such defaulting party. Such forfeited licenses shall revert entirely to the ownership of the layout-design proprietor and become available for re-licensing according to prevailing terms.

The registered layout design shall remain the exclusive property of the registrant, subject to any license granted as provided herein. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered layout design must be executed in writing and attested by at least one witness competent to testify under this Act; such assignment shall include a detailed description identifying the specific layout-design being transferred and the scope of rights conveyed. The Registrar may require submission of documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding any proposed sublicensee, particularly where the sublicense involves commercial exploitation outside territorial jurisdiction. Further, an owner of a registered layout design may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting reproduction or adaptation, provided that such licenses do not conflict with existing contractual obligations and are duly recorded with the Registrar to maintain transparency amongst interested parties.

Any person who, having made an application for registration of a trade mark and having paid the requisite act fee, subsequently fails to comply with any direction issued by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act relating to the submission of documentary evidence or other information, shall be deemed to have abandoned the application. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory proof that such non-compliance was unintentional and due to circumstances beyond the applicant’s reasonable control, grant a reprieve, but only after levying a penalty not exceeding twice the original act fee paid. Producers who deliberately obstruct investigations into suspected trade mark infringement, or fail to provide requested information regarding their production processes, are liable for fines as provided herein.

Where a patent granted persons seeks to assign their rights under this Act, such assignment shall be made by instrument in writing and executed jointly by all patentees. The application for registration of any such assignment shall be filed with the Controller, specifying the full name and address of both the assignor and assignee. Subject to verification of identity and due diligence checks as provided herein, the Controller may register the assignment upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any patent granted under this Act relating to an invention territory India shall remain valid for a term of fourteen years from the date of application for patents, or five years from the date of grant, whichever is shorter. Provided that, any subsequent modification to the patented invention requires prior approval from the Controller.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and any relevant distinguishing characteristics as determined through established testing procedures. The Authority may require submission of additional data or clarification regarding the applicant’s claim that the variety is new and possesses stability in its expression. Prior to acceptance for examination, the application shall be subject to a preliminary assessment to ascertain compliance with the requirements under this Act concerning essential derivation. Publication of the application will occur within three months of receipt by the Authority, unless the applicant requests deferral due to commercial considerations, provided that such deferral cannot exceed six months and requires written justification. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all published applications for denomination varieties.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the copyright in a photograph shall vest initially in the photographer. Any agreement for the creation of a photograph may stipulate that the right to assign the copyright subsists with another party, provided that such assignment is executed in writing and duly registered under procedures prescribed by the Central Government. Where a photograph is commissioned by an individual or entity other than the photographer, the contract of commission shall expressly define the ownership of copyright therein; absent such clarity, copyright shall remain with the photographer. Further, where a photograph incorporates elements subject to pre-existing copyright, such as architectural designs or artistic works visible within the frame, the assignment of copyright in the photograph does not extend to those underlying rights unless explicitly agreed upon by all relevant right holders. The transfer of copyright relating to a photograph is deemed complete upon registration.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the indication upon third parties. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to production, processing, packaging, distribution, sale, and export of goods identified by the geographical indication. Any assignment of a registered geographical indication, or any license granted thereunder, requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such approval shall not be unreasonably withheld. The Registrar may impose conditions on assignments and licenses to safeguard the integrity and reputation associated with the register geographical indications. Further, the proprietor is obliged to ensure licensees adhere strictly to quality standards as defined under this Act.

Where a layout-design owner grants a license conferring rights to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating their protected design, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to prior written consent from the licensor, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all terms and conditions of the original license agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or scope of an assignment under this Act shall be referred to the proceeding appellate board for determination. The board’s decision on such matters relating to assignments is final, subject to appeal only on grounds of legal error demonstrable in the record of proceedings before it. Further, a layout-design owner may assign their entire design rights, including all pending license agreements, with notification provided to all existing licensees as stipulated under this Act.

Where a claim is made that a particular compilation constitutes a literary work, and such claim is contested on the grounds that the selection, arrangement, and presentation of the material within the compilation are not original, the burden shall lie upon the claimant to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, the exercise of intellectual labour sufficient to warrant copyright protection. Provided that, in determining originality, regard shall be had to whether the choices made in compiling the work reflect a distinctive creative approach or merely represent a mechanical or predictable process. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the originality of a literary work may appeal to the relevant High Court, subject to such conditions as are prescribed under this Act concerning timelines and costs.

Where a party seeks redressal against an order passed by the Controller relating to the validity of a registered layout-design, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellant is required to file with the Appellate Board a detailed statement setting forth the grounds of appeal and demonstrating how the original decision was manifestly unjust or beyond the scope of the Controller's jurisdiction under this Act. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the dismissal of the appeal. Furthermore, the petition particulars filed by the appellant must precisely identify the specific findings challenged and provide supporting documentation as evidence. The Board may require further clarification regarding the petition particulars if deemed necessary for a just determination.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark, or by the Trade Marks Registry, against the acceptance of an application for registration, the Registrar shall consider the grounds of such objection and afford the applicant an opportunity to submit their response. The Registrar may require both the objector and the applicant to furnish further information or documents relevant to the determination of the objection. Subject to this, the decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of the objection shall be final, provided that any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The applicant’s right to registration shall not arise until all objections have been resolved and the trade mark is formally registered as provided herein.

Where, in determining whether a trade mark is distinctive, reference is made to the context otherwise requires,— (h) “international application” means an application for registration of a trade mark filed with the Office under the Madrid Protocol and designating India as a designated Contracting Party. An appeal against a refusal to register based on a prior conflicting international application shall be maintainable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates diligent examination of the design registry pertaining to the earlier mark. The Board may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter if it finds that the Registrar failed to adequately consider evidence submitted regarding acquired distinctiveness or use in commerce predating the filing date of the international application.

Where any proprietor institutes legal proceedings alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, the Court shall determine whether the defendant maintains a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment utilizing the impugned sign. It shall be presumed, subject to rebuttal by evidence adduced by the defendant, that use in advertising materials alone does not constitute such an establishment under this Act. Further, where the proprietor demonstrates demonstrable goodwill and reputation associated with the trade mark within India, the Court may grant interim relief pending final determination of the matter, provided that a bond is furnished as deemed appropriate by the Court to compensate any party found to have acted without sufficient cause. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving the absence of such an establishment if the proprietor establishes a prima facie case of infringement.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, a "visual recording" shall be deemed to include any representation captured through electronic or digital means, irrespective of whether such representation is fixed in a tangible medium. The right of the producer of a cinematograph film incorporating such a visual recording shall extend to preventing the reproduction, adaptation, and public display of that portion of the work where the visual recording is prominently featured, subject to judicial review if any party claims fair use or incidental inclusion. Any aggrieved person disputing this restriction may appeal to the relevant High Court, demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the producer’s exclusive right; provided that such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of the contested action.

Where any interested party opposes the registration of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall serve notice upon both the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. The Registrar may require the submission of further documentation from either party to clarify the nature of the claim or objection. Following such service, the registrar shall hearing be convened within ninety days, unless circumstances demonstrably preclude adherence to this timeline; a reasoned order detailing any deviation must then be recorded. During the hearing, both parties shall present arguments and evidence relevant to the opposition. The Registrar’s decision, provided that it is in writing and accompanied by reasons, shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use registered layout design. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover all or part of the rights conferred by registration, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation. Any assignment of ownership of a registered layout-design shall include any existing licenses granted under this Act relating thereto, unless otherwise expressly agreed in writing between the assignor and assignee. The terms and conditions of any license agreement shall be governed by contract law as provided herein; however, nothing in this provision shall preclude the Registrar from intervening where such agreements demonstrably impede access to essential technologies or unfairly restrict competition within the semiconductor industry.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act believes that the order was manifestly unjust or based on an erroneous interpretation of the law, such person may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of grounds specifying the errors apparent on the face of the record and demonstrating prejudice suffered as a direct consequence thereof. Failure to provide this comprehensive justification within the prescribed time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. Regarding the *form petition particulars* required for such appeals, these must strictly adhere to Schedule B annexed hereto; any deviation may be deemed a procedural deficiency warranting dismissal. The Tribunal may, at its discretion, require further clarification or supplementary documentation from the appellant.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark for edible oils discovers that another person is manufacturing, selling, or distributing food products containing adulterated substances, such proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such activities. The application may include evidence demonstrating the misrepresentation caused by the use of a deceptive label or packaging resembling the registered trade mark, and establishing that the adulteration constitutes a violation of the Food Adulteration Act. Damages recoverable under this provision shall encompass not only lost profits directly attributable to the infringement but also compensation for harm to the reputation and goodwill associated with the trade mark. Provided that any order granted by the Court shall be subject to review on appeal within ninety days, as provided herein.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is filed alleging that the registered proprietor has failed to use the trade mark in accordance with conditions specified under this Act, the Registrar shall serve notice on the registered proprietor requiring him to show cause why the trade mark should not be expunged from the Register. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the application for rectification is based and provide a period of sixty days within which the registered proprietor may submit his response. Failure by the registered proprietor, or any person acting as the registered proprietor proposed, to adequately demonstrate continued use or adherence to stipulated conditions will render him liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt.

Where the copyright in a literary work has been assigned under this Act, the assignor shall be prescribed to grant a license to the original author of that work for non-commercial research purposes. Such license shall permit reproduction and distribution of reasonable excerpts solely for academic study or critical analysis, provided that such use is accompanied by due acknowledgement of the copyright holder’s ownership. The scope of this prescribed license may be further defined in the assignment agreement itself, subject to the limitations imposed herein regarding fair dealing. Any subsequent assignee of the copyright shall be bound by the terms of the initial assignment and any licenses therein stipulated. This provision applies irrespective of whether the author was a party to the original assignment transaction. The right to enforce this prescribed license remains with the author until such time as they relinquish it in writing, registered with the designated authority.

Where an aggrieved party believes that an order relating to the validity or enforceability of a registered layout-design has been passed erroneously, they may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for its review. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the original order. The tribunal may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard and considering evidence submitted, confirm, vary, or set aside the order in question. Notably, any *order cancellation* passed by a tribunal under this Act is subject to judicial review by the High Court. Provided that the tribunal shall not entertain any application if the aggrieved party failed to exercise due diligence in pursuing remedies available under this Act prior to seeking recourse through the tribunal.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark” means a mark capable of being represented graphically and shall include a device, brand name, heading, label, sign, word, letter, numeral, shape, configuration, air mark, colour or combination thereof adopted to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of others under this Act. A trade mark may incorporate three-dimensional shapes, provided that such shapes have acquired distinctiveness through the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services and are capable of distinguishing them. The registration of a india trade mark confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark for the goods or services specified in the register.

Any person found to be engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of copyrighted works originating within India shall be deemed guilty of an offense under this Act. Such infringement, particularly where it involves commercial exploitation without due license or authorization, carries a penalty not exceeding three years imprisonment and a fine commensurate with the extent of damages caused to the copyright owner. Repeated acts of infringing upon intellectual property rights may result in enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The right to seek injunctive relief against further acts of india infringing is explicitly vested in the copyright holder. Compensation for loss of revenue and damage to reputation shall be recoverable through civil proceedings, subject to limitations prescribed herein.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention relating to a process for producing a substance controlled under this Act, the Controller may, subject to due process and after affording the patentee an opportunity of being heard, issue directions restricting the manufacture, sale, or importation of that substance by any person other than the patentee or persons authorized by the patentee. Such directions shall specify the conditions governing such restricted activities, including but not limited to limitations on quantity, duration, and intended use. The Controller shall consider representations made by interested parties concerning the impact of acquiring restrict upon public health, safety, or national security during proceedings under this provision. Any person aggrieved by an order issued under these provisions may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order.

A registered user seeking to exploit their right to make use of a trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting the use of the trademarked goods or services under conditions specified therein. Such licenses may include restrictions on territory, duration, and scope of permitted activities relating to the trade mark. The owner of the trademark shall be notified in writing of any such licensing arrangement prior to its implementation, affording them an opportunity to object based solely on grounds that the licensed use is detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered trade mark. Assignment of a registered user’s rights under this Act relating to their registered user trade may occur with the consent of the trademark proprietor and subject to such terms as they deem fit. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by all prior obligations undertaken by the original registered user.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the evidence submitted by the applicant fails adequately to demonstrate acquired distinctiveness in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, the Registrar shall register the mark only if satisfied that use consistent with honest practices has been undertaken prior to the date of publication of the application. Provided that any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration on grounds of lack of acquired distinctiveness may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The applicant shall be liable for costs incurred by the appellant if the appeal is unsuccessful, as determined by the Board. Furthermore, failure to comply with procedural requirements during opposition proceedings may render an application ineligible for registration.

Where a Board constituted under this Act has made an order relating to revocation of a patent, or concerning rectification of the register, any person aggrieved by such order may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate court shall have power to confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against, and may also direct that the matter be remitted to the Board for further consideration. An appeal shall lie notwithstanding any error apparent on the face of the record in the order sought to be challenged. Provided that an appeal does not suspend the operation of the order unless the High Court otherwise directs. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the procedure for filing and dealing with appeals under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be refused under this Act if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout-design incorporates any protected design already registered, or for which an application has been filed, provided that such incorporation does not constitute independent creation. Any applicant aggrieved by an order of refusal made by the Registrar shall have the right to appeal to the proceeding appellate board. The Board shall hear appeals from the orders of the Registrar and may confirm, vary, or reverse any such order as it deems fit. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject only to judicial review under law.

For the purposes of this Act, a valid registered proprietor shall be deemed to possess such title to the trademark as is evidenced by the certificate of registration issued under this Act, subject to any rectification proceedings pending before the relevant intellectual property forum. Where an application for registration has been accepted and published in accordance with the prescribed procedures, the shall established registry shall maintain a record thereof, accessible to the public upon payment of the requisite fee. Any person claiming rights as a registered proprietor must demonstrate that such claim is not vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation during the examination process.

For the purposes of determining novelty under this Act, “substance means new” shall be interpreted strictly and applied with due regard to the principles of inventive step. An invention shall not be considered novel if it is disclosed, or demonstrated as publicly available, in a manner that would have rendered it obvious to a person skilled in the art at the date of filing the patent application. However, this determination shall be subject to consideration of any conflicting evidence presented by the applicant demonstrating unforeseen results or unexpected advantages arising from the combination of prior art elements. The Controller may, upon review and after affording an opportunity for argument, determine whether the claimed invention possesses a degree of ingenuity sufficient to overcome the presumption of lack of novelty as provided herein.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act, any patent applicant or proprietor is found to be deceased or otherwise unable to appear personally, the Controller shall proceed with due diligence to ascertain whether such deceased or incapacitated individual has appointed a legal representative. The determination of who constitutes the appropriate legal representative for the purposes of challenging an objection regarding the validity of a patent, particularly concerning allegations of improper use certification trade practices employed by the proprietor, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. It is provided that any party aggrieved by the Controller’s decision identifying a legal representative may petition the Appellate Board within sixty days of such determination, demonstrating clear prejudice resulting from the appointment.

Where any person makes, uses or imports an article, or offers to make, use or import an article, which embodies or contains the invention claimed in a patent granted under this Act without the authorization of the patentee, such person shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent granted. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party alleging infringement, issue notices to both the complainant and the alleged infringer requiring them to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified in the notice. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller shall determine whether or not an act of infringement has occurred. Where it is established that falsifying trade marks was employed as part of the infringing activity, the Controller may consider such conduct when assessing remedies and penalties. The patentee shall be entitled to seek relief including injunctions and damages as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, including particulars of ownership and goods or services associated with each mark. Any party aggrieved by an entry, or omission thereof, in the registrar index may, within sixty days from the date such index is made publicly available, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appellate tribunal shall consider any evidence submitted by the appellant demonstrating material error or demonstrable prejudice arising from the inaccuracy of the registrar index. Provided that, a decision regarding the accuracy of entries in the registrar clause section relating to geographical indications shall be subject to further review under provisions concerning specialized designations as provided herein.

Where the owner of copyright in an artistic work desires to grant a license or assign their rights therein, they shall submit a formal application to the designated Copyright Office, detailing the scope and duration of the proposed arrangement. Such application must specify the territory covered by the license or assignment and identify all parties involved, including the licensor, licensee, or assignee. The owner may reserve certain exclusive rights under this Act, provided that such reservation is clearly stated within the application and does not unduly restrict the reasonable use of the work. Any subsequent modification to a granted license requires another application, subject to approval by the Copyright Office. An assignment shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the office, and failure to register will render the assignee unable to enforce their rights under this Act against third parties.

Where any patent is granted and subsequently the patentee fails to comply with a notice issued by the Controller requiring him to furnish proof of working or production relating to the patented invention, the Controller may, after giving opportunity for hearing to the patentee, issue an order declaring the patent to be withdrawn. Such declaration shall not prejudice the right of the patentee to challenge the correctness of the order under appeal before the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the order. The Controller shall consider any representations made by the patentee in response to such an appeal and may, if satisfied that there were sufficient grounds for non-compliance, set aside or modify the order declaring the section withdrawn.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an international application filed under the Madrid Protocol, designating India as a designated Contracting Party, any opposition proceedings initiated prior to the date of effectuation of such designation shall be deemed to continue with full force and effect. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification from the International Bureau regarding the extension of protection, entertain objections based solely on grounds available under this Act at the time of original registration, notwithstanding any subsequent changes in law or practice relating to international registrations. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning an internationally registered trade mark’s effectuation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the order appealed against.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall include a detailed schematic representation conforming to the standards prescribed by the registrar and accompanied by a technical specification outlining the functionality and intended use of the design. Such applications must also demonstrate compliance with all relevant safety regulations as may be notified from time to time under this Act. The registrar, in assessing an application, may require submission of additional data pertaining to manufacturing processes or security protocols employed. Failure to satisfy a registrar prescribed requirement regarding these submissions will render the application liable for rejection. Further, any subsequent grant of registration based on incomplete information could potentially impact claims arising from patent consequences related to similar inventions.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent for non-obviousness, evidence is presented demonstrating a substantial similarity between the claimed invention and prior art publications originating outside India, the burden shall lie upon the patentee to demonstrate that such foreign publications did not reasonably inform any person skilled in the relevant art at the time of the patent’s grant. Provided that, if the Controller finds that the said publications were disseminated through official gazettes or other publicly accessible channels within India, the presumption shall be against the patentee unless rebutted by affirmative evidence. For the purposes of this section, “treaty means Budapest” and any reference to a publication's dissemination includes its availability via electronic databases as may be prescribed. Any appeal arising from such determination is subject to review based on demonstrable error of law.

Any patentee desiring to grant a license conferring rights to exploit an invention for which he has claimed a priority date shall execute a written assignment or licensing agreement specifying the scope of such rights. This agreement must clearly delineate the field of exploitation permitted, including geographical limitations and product categories. The patentee may assign this right to any person, firm, or company, subject to the condition that the assignee adheres to the terms initially stipulated in the original license or assignment. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses the patented invention, they shall provide the patentee with details of such sub-licensing arrangements within thirty days. Failure to do so may result in revocation of the initial license under this Act. The priority date claim remains vested solely with the patent holder unless explicitly transferred through documented legal means as provided herein.

Any copyright accruing by virtue of this Act in respect of any work published or otherwise made available to the public prior to the commencement of this section shall be assignable by the owner thereof, subject to any existing contractual obligations. Such assignment may be absolute or for a specific term, and shall include the right to grant exclusive licenses relating to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public performance of the work. Where an assignment is made, particulars thereof shall be registered in the prescribed manner and published in the Official Gazette for information of all parties concerned. Failure to register such assignments within three months from their execution shall render them voidable at the option of the assignor. The assignee may enforce the copyright as if originally vested in him or her, provided that any subsequent assignment requires similar registration and publication.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to a patent granted or applied for under this Act may assign, license, or otherwise transfer their rights in respect thereof, either wholly or partially, to another person. Such assignment or license shall require execution in writing and registration with the office patent office within thirty days of its creation; failure to register shall render the assignment voidable at the option of any subsequent assignee or licensee. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating prejudice resulting from a non-registered transfer, direct the registration of such transfer or refuse it entirely. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the field of exploitation and duration thereof, as provided herein. Further, the Central Government may issue guidelines regarding royalty rates for compulsory licenses relating to patents assigned after the commencement of these regulations.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to “Kashmir Apples” shall include detailed particulars regarding the agricultural practices employed in cultivation, harvesting, and processing unique to the specified geographical area. The Registrar may require submission of maps delineating the boundaries of the region, along with affidavits from growers’ cooperatives attesting to adherence to traditional methods. Any use of the indication "Kashmir Apples" or any confusingly similar designation on products not originating within that defined territory shall be deemed a *geographical indication falsifies* the registered right. Provided that, this restriction does not apply where such use is incidental and does not suggest an origin in Kashmir. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaints, initiate inquiries into alleged instances of geographical indication falsification.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Trade Marks Registry shall direct that the acceptance be published in the Official Gazette. Such publication shall include particulars of the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark has been accepted and any disclaimer contained in the application. Any person considering himself aggrieved by such acceptance may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file a representation with the Registrar against the registration of the trade mark as published in the gazette require goods. The Registrar shall consider all representations received and may direct that the trade marks deemed to be registered be amended or refused accordingly. Notice of any such direction shall also be published in the Official Gazette for public information. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An international registration sub shall be deemed to be infringed if there exists a use of an identical mark in relation to identical goods or services, or related goods or services, within the territory of India without the authorization of the proprietor of the international registration. The owner of the registered trade mark may institute suit for relief against any person infringing such sub, and shall be entitled to all remedies available under this Act as if the international registration had been applied for directly in India. Provided that, where an opposition is filed against an application for registration arising from an international registration sub, the Registrar may require the proprietor of the mark to furnish evidence establishing reputation and distinctiveness of the mark in relation to the goods or services concerned within the Indian territory.

For the purposes of this Act, a *registered layout* means a layout-design that has been registered under this Act in accordance with the provisions herein relating to registration. A registered layout shall include not only the three-dimensional representation of the integrated circuit but also any design or arrangement of elements incorporated therein which are original and possess aesthetic merit. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to fulfilling all prescribed conditions, grant a certificate of registration for a *registered layout*, conferring exclusive rights against infringement as provided herein. An unregistered layout shall not be afforded protection under this Act.

Applications for registration of a Plant Variety shall include a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed by the Register, encompassing morphological characteristics, physiological traits, and data pertaining to its expression across diverse agro-climatic zones. The application must specify the duration of vegetative propagation, if applicable, and provide evidence demonstrating genetic uniformity within the variety. Any prior disclosure of the Plant Variety, whether through publication or commercialization, shall be disclosed in the application; failure to do so may render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Assessments by Examining Authorities will incorporate principles of crop sciences indian methodology, including but not limited to field trials conducted according to established protocols and statistical analysis of relevant data. The Register may require supplementary information as deemed necessary to ascertain distinctiveness and stability.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design incorporates elements derived from a protected film sound recording, and such incorporation constitutes a substantial reproduction without due authorization, the owner of the copyright in the film sound recording shall have the right to demand assignment of the relevant layout-design rights. This assignment shall be executed within ninety days of written notification served upon the assignee, detailing the infringing elements and their provenance. Failure to comply with this demand will render the assignor liable for forfeiture directed of the integrated circuit layout-design, which may then be licensed by the copyright holder under terms deemed equitable by a designated adjudicating officer. Any sub-licensees deriving rights through such assignment are bound by the original licensing conditions as stipulated in the forfeited layout-design documentation and shall remain subject to this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication or the revocation thereof, or any other matter provided herein, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during application for registration shall render the application liable for rejection and subsequent penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. The Central Government may, subject to due process, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees upon any individual or entity found guilty of using a registered geographical indication without authorization, or engaging in deceptive practices intended to mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods. Such penalties shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

Applications for registration of copyright shall be made to the Copyrights Appellate Board in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish with the application a certified true copy of the work or, where the work is not capable of being copied, a still or other visual representation of the work. Upon receipt of an application, the Board shall issue an acknowledgement containing the date of its receipt. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar of Copyrights relating to the registration of copyright may appeal to the Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Board may entertain appeals filed after the said period only if the appellant satisfies it that there was a sufficient reason for the delay.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent relating to a process for producing a novel pharmaceutical compound shall be required to disclose, in the prescribed form, details regarding all individuals who have provided scientific advice during the development and refinement of said process. Such disclosure must include the name, qualifications, and nature of services rendered by each such individual. Where an independent scientific adviser has been engaged to evaluate aspects of the invention’s novelty or non-obviousness, a declaration from that adviser confirming their impartiality and absence of any vested interest in the applicant's enterprise shall be submitted alongside the patent application. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements may render the patent registration liable for revocation under this Act.

The assignment of copyright in any musical work registered under this Act, or subsequently registered following an alteration to such work, shall require prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignor, assignee, and the precise scope of rights transferred. Such notification must be accompanied by a sworn affidavit verifying the authenticity of the agreement and confirming that the assignor possesses full proprietary interest in the copyright being assigned. The Registrar may, after providing reasonable opportunity for objection from any interested party, record the assignment and issue a certificate thereof, which shall be prima facie evidence of the transfer. Any subsequent licensing of performing rights within the assigned work requires consent of the assignee, unless explicitly permitted under the recorded assignment agreement. Failure to notify the Registrar prior to assignment will render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks contain a false trade description relating to the nature, quality, characteristics, geographical origin, production method, or other qualities of the goods or services in connection with which it is used. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence establishing the genuineness of any claim made within the application that might constitute a false trade description; failure to provide such satisfactory evidence shall result in rejection. Where the use of a trademark incorporates information susceptible to interpretation as a false trade description, the proprietor shall be obligated to rectify or withdraw such misleading representation under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an action taken concerning a false trade description may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons, cooperative society, producer company, or other organization engaged in production, processing, and marketing of goods originating from that territory, or by an individual authorized by such producers. The Registrar shall refuse registration if the proposed geographical indication is deemed to be descriptive of characteristics of the goods, qualities, reputation, or other attributes associated with them, or if it comprises surnames or pseudonyms without authorization. Further, registration shall not be granted for any *unregistered geographical* indication which would be likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The applicant must demonstrate exclusive rights over the use of the proposed indication within the defined geographical area as provided herein.

Where any question arises as to whether a layout design infringes a registered layout design, the Tribunal shall determine such question based upon an examination of the substantial similarity between the two designs, considering both their overall appearance and the interplay of their constituent elements. It shall be presumed that a registered layout design is infringed if the alleged infringing layout design copies or has been derived from the registered layout design, subject to proof by the registered proprietor demonstrating lack of such copying or derivation. The respondent may adduce evidence establishing independent creation of the allegedly infringing work, provided that such evidence demonstrates a clear absence of access to the registered layout design prior to its creation. Any appeal against an order made under this Act shall lie to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order.

An application for registration of a patent shall include particulars specifying the invention, its claims, and details relating to priority, if any. The applicant shall furnish a declaration stating that they are the true and first inventor of the claimed subject matter. Where an assignment of rights in the invention has occurred prior to the filing of the patent application, documentation substantiating such assignment must be submitted alongside the registration request. Failure to provide complete and accurate information regarding the invention or its ownership may result in rejection under this Act. The Controller General shall maintain a register of all patents granted, accessible for public inspection as provided herein.

The provisions act shall extend to claims made concerning deceptive similarity between registered trade marks, even where such similarity arises solely through alterations in colouration or font style. An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board against any order determining that a mark is deceptively similar, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the registration of the impugned mark. Further, registration shall apply equally to marks used in connection with services and goods, notwithstanding variations in presentation across different media. The burden of proving deceptive similarity rests upon the complainant; however, where the allegedly infringing mark incorporates a dominant element of the registered trade mark, such presumption may be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence demonstrating lack of consumer confusion.

An application to register said geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or producer group being owners of the said geographical indication, or authorised users thereof. The application shall contain a statement of such particulars concerning the geographical indication as are required to be furnished under this Act, including but not limited to its name and origin. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue a notification for public inspection, specifying the geographical indication sought to be registered and inviting objections from any person or organisation claiming interest in the matter. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit their response within the time prescribed. The Registrar shall consider all submissions before determining whether to accept or reject the application, provided that the Registrar may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary.

For the purposes of this Act, “India-produced goods” shall mean any goods manufactured, processed, assembled or otherwise produced wholly or partly within the territory of India. Where such goods are subsequently exported and re-imported into India, they shall continue to be considered as India-produced goods unless substantial transformation has occurred outside India, determined according to regulations framed under this Act. Goods initially imported into India and then subjected to minimal processing or alteration within India shall not, by virtue of that processing alone, qualify as India-produced goods; the determination of “substantial transformation” shall consider factors including labour content and value addition. The Registrar may issue guidelines clarifying application of these principles concerning "imported india produced" articles.

Where a person, through false representation, uses a *trade description applied* to goods offered for sale or provided as services, intending to deceive the public regarding their nature, quality, quantity, origin, or other characteristics, such person shall be guilty of an offence. This offense is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods in respect of which the false representation was made are liable to seizure and forfeiture. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify authorities empowered to investigate offenses under this Act and exercise powers relating to search and arrest as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Designs Register, or by a failure to enter particulars relating to a design, may apply to the Controller for rectification of register. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as prescribed under this Act. The Controller may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, order rectification as claimed or otherwise dispose of the matter in conformity with principles of natural justice. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Controller concerning rectification register proceedings constitutes a punishable offence, attracting penalties as determined under this Act. The layout design government may intervene in such matters where public interest is concerned.

Where, in proceedings under this Act relating to a registered trade mark, the defendant fails to appear or contest the allegations made against them, the plaintiff shall be entitled to apply to the court for an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing activities. Such application may be granted if the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that infringement has occurred and that damages would not provide adequate relief. Provided that, before granting any such ex parte injunction, the court shall direct that notice of the proceedings and the proposed order be served upon the defendant within a specified period, allowing them an opportunity to challenge the application should they choose to do so. The plaintiff must demonstrate due diligence in attempting service; failure to do so may render the injunction vulnerable to appeal.

An applicant seeking examination of a patent shall file a form filed patent accompanied by the prescribed fee and particulars relating to priority, if any, claimed in respect thereof. The statement of inventiveness required under this Act shall clearly delineate the novelty and non-obviousness of the invention over prior art. Where an application incorporates by reference designs or layouts, the applicant must provide evidence demonstrating ownership or a valid license pertaining to those incorporated elements. Layout design vested rights are not affected by the filing of a patent incorporating such designs unless expressly authorized in writing by the registered proprietor of the layout design. The Controller may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the form filed patent and shall afford the applicant an opportunity to respond within the timeframe prescribed. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure the proprietor of a registered trade mark, uses an identical or deceptively similar mark relating to goods or services for which the said registered trade mark is registered shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where such use also infringes patent rights relating to the manufacturing process of those goods or services, the aggregate penalty shall be doubled. The proprietor may further seek injunctions preventing future infringing acts as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the revocation or infringement of a patent concerning a pharmaceutical composition alleges that such order was manifestly unjust or made without due regard to the evidence presented, they shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board may, after affording all parties concerned a fair hearing and opportunity to submit written arguments, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. In determining whether an order is manifestly unjust, the Appellate Board shall consider not only the findings of fact but also any errors of law apparent on the record. Further, under this Act, the Controller may designate one or more officers to act as adjudicating officer for specific types of appeals and disputes relating to patent validity and enforcement.

An applicant seeking patent protection may file an application including a provisional specification in lieu of a complete specification, provided that such provisional specification contains sufficient particulars relating to the invention to enable a person skilled in the art to put the same into practice. The Controller General shall have the power to require, by notification in the Official Gazette, the furnishing of further information or documents concerning any matter mentioned in the provisional specification if deemed necessary for clarity and completeness. Failure to furnish such requested information within the time specified may result in rejection of the application under this Act. A complete specification must be filed within a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of filing the application accompanied by the provisional specification, and shall comply with all requirements prescribed herein regarding form and content.

A trademark shall be considered deceptively similar to another if, in the course and circumstances of use, it is likely to create confusion or cause mistake among the public as to the identity of the origin of the goods or services. This assessment shall take into account the visual appearance, phonetic composition, ideational content, and overall impression of the marks involved. Where an application for registration includes a manner of application clause specifying particular goods or services, the comparison for deceptiveness shall be limited to those specified categories only. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates a substantial reputation in respect of goods or services not explicitly covered by the manner applications clause, the assessment may extend to consider potential dilution effects on such reputation.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming through assignment or succession against a registered design, alleging that the design lacks novelty or originality as defined under this Act, such objection shall be deemed to constitute grounds for appeal. The Appellate Board may, upon hearing both the proprietor of the design and the objector, determine whether the design in question satisfies the requirements for registration. Provided that, if the objector demonstrates that identical or substantially similar designs were imported into India prior to the date of application for registration, and such importation occurred in violation of the Customs Act 1962, this shall be considered a material factor in assessing novelty. The Board’s decision on appeals relating to design sub section matters shall be final.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee or prospective patentee may grant a license to use and exploit a patented invention or an invention for which a patent application is pending, specifying the field of use, territory, and duration of such license. Such licenses shall be assignable under this Act in like manner as the patent itself. Where a license has been granted prior to the publication of the patent application, the term "india filed months" from the date of filing shall constitute the period during which the licensee’s rights are deemed vested, provided that the patentee provides evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating the terms and conditions under which the license was initially executed. The Controller may require a declaration detailing royalty payments and other considerations associated with such licenses, ensuring transparency and preventing exploitation. Further assignments of sub-licenses shall be subject to similar disclosure requirements as primary assignments.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, nothing shall prevent the registration of a trade mark if it is used as honestly intended to describe the quality or other characteristics of any goods or services. Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark has granted consent for another person’s use of the mark, that subsequent user shall be deemed a registered user with rights equivalent to those held by the original proprietor. The proprietor may revoke such consent at any time, provided that reasonable notice is given to the affected party. Upon revocation, the permitted use shall cease immediately and all advertising materials bearing the mark must be withdrawn from circulation within thirty days. Any person continuing such use after this period shall be liable for damages to the registered proprietor. Further, remedies under this Act are available against any act of passing off arising from the continued unauthorized use following consent revocation.
