For the purposes of this Act, an “application register proprietor” means a person whose name is entered upon the Register of Trade Marks as the proprietor of a trade mark solely by virtue of being the applicant for registration thereof, prior to the grant of such registration. Such entry shall not confer any right or title to the trade mark other than that which arises from the subsequent grant of registration under this Act. An application register proprietor may, subject to prescribed conditions and as provided herein, assign or transmit their interest in the pending application. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and transmissions affecting an application register proprietor’s rights.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive if, in determining trade mark registrability, it possesses inherent distinctiveness or has acquired distinctiveness through use, subject to the provisions of this Act. For the purposes of this determination, ‘inherent distinctiveness’ means that the sign is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, irrespective of any period of use. A mark consisting exclusively of a word or words having no trade significance shall not be considered inherently distinctive unless it has acquired such distinctiveness through reputation and continuous use as provided herein.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, it shall be incumbent upon the defendant to demonstrate that the alleged infringing use constitutes fair dealing. Such demonstration requires proof that the *mark use* was solely for the purpose of criticism or review and that no undue advantage was taken of the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. The proprietor may seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, as well as damages to compensate for losses suffered directly attributable to the defendant’s actions. Provided that the court finds the infringing use has caused dilution of distinctiveness, it may award additional compensation reflecting such harm. Further, any party found guilty of intentional and substantial infringement shall be liable to pay enhanced damages, subject to considerations of proportionality and public interest.

The Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of a mark registered respect of goods or services, and after due notice to all interested parties as provided herein, direct the removal of any false or misleading statement appearing on any goods or their packaging. Such direction shall be binding if the statement creates a likelihood of confusion with another trade mark registered under this Act, or otherwise misrepresents the nature, quality, or origin of those goods. The proprietor seeking such direction must demonstrate that the infringing representation is being made without consent and causes demonstrable harm to the distinctiveness of their registered mark. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant exclusive licences under the patent and such licence shall be irrevocable unless expressly stated otherwise in the terms thereof. Where a patent has been assigned or an exclusive licence granted, the right to exercise any prerogative vested in the patentee shall vest concurrently in the assignee or licensee, as applicable. An assignment or exclusive licence relating to a patent may be made by way of instrument in writing and executed by or on behalf of the assignor or licensor, and such instrument shall be admissible as evidence under this Act. The International Bureau, acting under the Budapest Treaty means budapest, shall maintain records of assignments and licences for public inspection, subject to any confidentiality agreements entered into pursuant to regulations framed thereunder. Further, a licensee may sub-license rights granted under an exclusive licence, provided that such sub-licence does not contradict the terms of the original agreement.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed manner and form. The application must contain a clear representation of the trade mark and a list specifying all goods or services for which registration is sought, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements of this Act. If any defects are found, the Registrar may intimate them to the applicant for rectification. The Registrar may also require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning the trade mark or its intended use. A registrar application presented under this Act is subject to scrutiny regarding distinctiveness and potential conflicts with existing registered marks.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and such documentary evidence as the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated deems necessary to establish ownership and validity. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design or its claimed originality, and failure to comply within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Upon receipt of a request from an interested party, the Registrar shall publish notice of the pending application in the Official Gazette, inviting objections under this Act. Any objection received shall be promptly communicated to the applicant, who may submit a written response. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall determine whether to proceed with registration or reject the application. The registered layout-design remains valid for a period as provided herein, subject to published expiry notifications issued by the Registrar periodically.

Any person who, having obtained a certificate registration produced under this Act, knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses material facts in relation to the layout-design during the application process shall be deemed to have committed an offence. Such act constitutes a violation of the integrity of the register and undermines the rights afforded to legitimate registered proprietors. Further, any individual found guilty of such deceptive practice shall liable penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the cancellation of the certificate registration and prohibit further commercial exploitation of the layout-design.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication may be made to the Registrar by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the quality and characteristics which are unique to that territory. Such an application shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication, the class of goods to which it relates, the area of the originating locality, and a map of the geographical area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application. Where the registered geographical indication pertains to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or wine, a specification patent shall be included detailing production methods and quality control measures ensuring authenticity. Any interested party may inspect the application and file an opposition under this Act within the prescribed period. The Registrar shall consider all objections received before proceeding with registration.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication relating to Darjeeling tea, desiring to grant a license conferring the right to use said indication on any other person for commercial purposes, shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form. Such application shall detail the scope and duration of the proposed license, including specific restrictions on product quality and packaging as deemed necessary to maintain the distinctiveness of Darjeeling tea. The Registrar may approve or reject such application after affording the applicant and any interested party a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Upon registration, the license shall be recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications. Further, assignment of rights under a registered geographical indication requires prior consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent will not be unreasonably withheld. Registration shall confer upon the assignee all rights previously held by the assignor relating to the licensed use.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall provide written notice thereof to the applicant, detailing the grounds for such objection and affording the applicant an opportunity to file a reply within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice. The applicant’s reply, or lack thereof, shall be considered by the Registrar in determining whether to proceed with registration. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within three months of such decision; provided that the Appellant shall deposit before the Board a sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the prescribed fee for appeals. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the relevant provisions of the law relating to civil procedure.

An application for registration of an application registration mark shall be deemed to disclose the nature of the goods or services associated with said mark. Where the Controller is satisfied, upon examination, that the mark as applied for is not registrable under this Act, but that the invention disclosed within the supporting documentation relating to its use constitutes a new invention, the applicant may be directed to amend the application to reflect only the inventive aspects of the process or product. Such amendment shall not prejudice any prior rights held by third parties. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the technical details underpinning the claimed novelty and industrial applicability, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay processing.

Where the author of an invention, having previously assigned their rights therein, subsequently seeks to rectify the register relating to a patent granted to another party, such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating both the original assignment and the grounds for rectification. The Controller may, upon receiving such an application, issue notice to the registered patentee, affording them an opportunity to submit objections under this Act. Should the Controller find merit in the author’s claim, they may order the variation of the register to reflect the true ownership or interest in the invention, provided that any such alteration does not prejudice existing licensees or assignees acting in good faith and without notice rectify register of the original assignment. The Controller shall ensure due consideration is given to the impact on third parties who have relied upon the published patent information.

Where a registered trade mark is involved in a case proceeding concerning infringement, and where such proceedings are settled through an agreement between the parties involving the assignment of rights relating to the mark, the assignor shall provide a formal notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the settlement. This notification must detail the scope of the assigned rights, including any geographical limitations or product categories covered by the assignment. The assignee shall be deemed substituted for the assignor in respect of those specific rights as provided herein. Further, where a license is granted during such a case proceeding to utilize the registered trade mark, the terms and conditions of that license are subject to review under this Act upon request from either licensor or licensee. Any subsequent assignment of the entire undertaking shall automatically transfer all associated licenses and assignments.

The registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to be vulnerable to cancellation proceedings where it is established, through evidence presented before the Controller, that the applicant knowingly misrepresented facts pertaining to prior publication or availability of the design. Such misrepresentation must be material to the assessment of novelty and originality as required under this Act. Furthermore, registration may be cancelled if it becomes apparent that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from an unregistered work, and the applicant failed to acknowledge such derivation in the application. The Controller shall issue a notice to the registered proprietor prior to any order for cancelling registration registered, affording them an opportunity to submit their response and counter evidence.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “pharmaceutical composition” shall be deemed to include any novel combination of active pharmaceutical ingredients intended for therapeutic or prophylactic use, provided that such combination results in a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual properties of the constituents. The Controller General may require applicants seeking registration of a pharmaceutical composition to submit detailed data demonstrating said synergistic effect and its clinical relevance. Further, an application relating to a process for producing a pharmaceutical substance shall include particulars regarding all critical parameters affecting product quality and stability. Any alteration in these parameters without prior notification to the Controller General may render the registration liable to revocation.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act and a proceed case registration is sought by the applicant, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to all interested parties. Any party aggrieved by the granting of a proceed case registration may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts as provided herein, seeking a declaration that the registration is invalid or unenforceable. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing such proceedings shall be deemed conclusive evidence against the claimant’s right to challenge the validity of the proceeding. The Court may impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees upon any party found to have acted in bad faith during proceed case registration, obstructing due process and prejudicing the interests of other parties involved.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trademark incorporating a geographical indication as per this Act, they shall submit to the Registrar, along with the application, detailed regulations deposited section outlining procedures for ensuring continued authenticity and exclusivity of that geographical indication. These regulations must specify mechanisms for monitoring production standards, preventing adulteration, and maintaining consumer confidence in goods bearing the mark. The Registrar may, after consultation with relevant stakeholders including producers' associations representing the geographical indication, approve or reject the proposed regulations based on their adequacy to safeguard the distinctiveness of the trademark and protect the interests of those engaged in producing goods under that indication. Any alteration to these deposited regulations shall require prior approval from the Registrar and notification through public advertisement.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, broadcasts that work by means of a *broadcast work stating* the source of the work and ownership details shall be deemed to have committed an infringement. Such infringement is subject to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Where the infringement is committed for commercial gain, the court may enhance such penalty up to double the amount specified above. The owner of copyright shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining further acts of broadcasting, provided that they demonstrate reasonable efforts were made to ascertain ownership details.

Where a trade mark is registered subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar, and those conditions are subsequently formalized as registered draft regulations concerning permissible usage or quality standards, any person aggrieved by such registered draft regulations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of publication of the registered draft regulations in the Trade Marks Journal. Such an appeal may be based on grounds that the conditions are unreasonable, discriminatory, or impose a burden disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon the trade mark proprietor. Failure to comply with any provision contained within the registered draft regulations shall constitute a violation under this Act and render the infringing party liable for damages as determined by the Tribunal. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, investigate alleged violations of these registered draft regulations.

An application for registration of a Geographical Indication relating to “Kanthaloor Pepper” shall be considered complete upon submission of documentation demonstrating exclusive use by authorized producers within the defined geographical area, as detailed in Schedule A. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating this exclusivity and adherence to established production standards, including but not limited to traditional farming practices and quality control measures. Should a challenge arise from an interested party alleging improper or misleading association with the Geographical Indication, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity for rebuttal. However, if the Registrar finds that the use of the mark is detrimental to the reputation of “Kanthaloor Pepper” or creates confusion amongst consumers, the plaintiff forthwith ceased any activities contributing to such detriment and the registration may be refused or revoked.

For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to a cinematographic work shall mean the individual or corporate body which has arranged for the making of the film and bears ultimate responsibility for its production. The producer shall be deemed the owner of all copyrights therein, subject to any agreements made with authors, composers, lyricists, photographers, or other individuals contributing to the creation of the work. Provided that where a work is produced jointly by two or more producers, they shall be deemed joint owners of copyright and shall hold such rights as tenants in common. The term "producer" does not include those engaged solely for technical assistance under contract.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a geographical indication, or revoking its registration. Such an appeal may be made by any person aggrieved by the order, including but not limited to unsuccessful applicants and registered proprietors. The Tribunal shall hear such appeals expeditiously, affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Where the grounds of appeal relate to a determination concerning the distinctiveness of the goods or services associated with a registered geographical indication, or challenge the validity of a proprietor layout design incorporated within its branding, the Tribunal may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to judicial review.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any copyright subsisting in a performance shall be assignable by the performer either wholly or partially and either for the duration of copyright or for any period thereof. Such assignment may be made by way of present disposition or as a security interest, provided that the terms of such assignment are clearly documented and registered with the designated authority. Where a performance is undertaken in collaboration between two or more performers, the assignment provisions herein shall apply jointly to all participating individuals unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. Any subsequent transfer of rights under an assignment requires prior written consent from the original assigning party, as stipulated within the initial agreement. The right to receive royalties attributable to such performance remains with the performer unless explicitly relinquished through a documented and registered assignment.

Where an interested party alleges that another person has infringed a patent, they may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court, subject to the provisions regarding jurisdiction as provided herein. The court shall have power to grant such remedies, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and orders for the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods, as it deems just and equitable. Compensation for loss suffered by the patent holder due to the infringement shall be determined by the Court, taking into account factors such as the extent of the damage, the profits made by the infringer, and any measures taken to mitigate the harm. The court may also award costs to the prevailing party in the action. Any challenge to the validity of a patent may similarly be brought before the High Court, seeking a declaration that the patent is invalid or unenforceable. It is imperative that all parties respect patent rights diligently.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, registration of a trade mark encompassing or comprising a representation of genetic material, including but not limited to sequences catalogued within a national gene fund sub-registry, shall be subject to limitations where such representation demonstrably describes a naturally occurring biological process. An appeal against refusal of registration based on this provision may be made to the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal, and the burden of proving that the representation lacks inventive character or is purely descriptive of said natural process shall lie upon the applicant. The tribunal shall consider evidence presented by both the Registrar and any interested party demonstrating potential confusion arising from such registration, provided that a claim of prior use may be asserted under this Act.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and sold without authorization from the owner of copyright, such owner shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by him as a consequence thereof. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the infringement, the flagrancy of the defendant’s conduct, and any profits earned by the infringer attributable to the infringing copy. Provided that, in cases where the infringing copy was made for private or domestic use without any commercial gain, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded, subject to considerations of fairness and equity. Further, the owner shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the defendant from further making, selling, importing, or distributing such infringing copies, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a design register layout may be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout-design does not involve a degree of skill and ingenuity sufficient to constitute an original work. Provided that, such refusal shall only be made after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard under this Act. The Registrar shall require the applicant to furnish detailed specifications including all layers comprising the integrated circuit layout-design, along with a technical explanation demonstrating the novelty and inventive step involved. Further, any modification or alteration to a registered design register layout subsequent to registration requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements as provided herein. The applicant shall also declare whether the layout-design incorporates elements derived from previously published works.

Where the patentee of an invention has filed an international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, and subsequently seeks to assign or license rights pertaining to the subject matter disclosed therein, such assignment or license shall be deemed valid only if it explicitly references the corresponding international application number. The assignee or licensee may exercise rights granted as provided herein relating to the patent, or patents derived from the aforementioned international application, but shall remain bound by any obligations undertaken by the original patentee concerning disclosure requirements and freedom-to-operate searches conducted prior to grant. Any transfer of ownership or licensing agreement must be registered with the Controller within three months of execution; failure to register shall render the assignment voidable at the option of a third party possessing superior rights.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may, by instrument in writing and subject to such terms and conditions as they deem fit, grant a license to use the trade mark for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The provisions act relating to sub-licensing are governed by regulations framed under this Act and published in the Official Gazette; these will detail requirements regarding territorial limitations and duration. A manufactured notification specifying the precise scope of permitted use shall accompany every license agreement, and copies thereof must be filed with the Registrar within fourteen days of the grant. Any alteration to a licensed trade mark requires prior written consent from the proprietor and subsequent registration as a variation under this Act.

An international registration designating India shall be treated as an application for registration under this Act; provided that the applicant shall furnish to the Registrar a certified copy of the international application form and any subsequent amendments or designations. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide such further information relating to the goods or services for which registration is sought as are necessary for the proper examination of the application. Where an objection is raised against an international registration, the procedure applicable shall be that prescribed for opposition proceedings under this Act, with the International Bureau being notified accordingly. The Registrar shall afford any interested party a reasonable opportunity to file evidence in support of or opposing the designation of India within the international registration case. Decisions rendered by the Registrar concerning such designations are appealable as provided herein.

Where any person has contravened clause (a) of section 13 relating to unauthorized reproduction of an integrated circuit layout-design, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining such acts and further damages as provided herein. The measure of damages recoverable shall take into account the loss of profits suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement, as well as any unreasonable profit made by the infringer as a consequence thereof. Subject to an application being made within three years from the date of first proven infringement, the Court may grant a register effect order compelling the infringing party to deliver up or destroy all copies of the integrated circuit layout-design in their possession or control. Provided that such delivery or destruction is carried out under the supervision of a designated officer appointed by the Court.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, distributes, or displays for sale any product containing a layout design commercially exploited in violation of this Act, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringer obtained a license from the proprietor. Further, such infringing acts are deemed civil offenses and may attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer shall also order the seizure and destruction of goods embodying the infringing layout design. Repeated contravention of these provisions will subject the offender to enhanced monetary penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant sections pertaining to fraud and misrepresentation.

An application for grant of a patent shall be deemed to be finally rejected if, after affording due opportunity for hearing, the Controller finds that the invention does not satisfy the conditions specified under this Act. The applicant may, subject to prescribed timelines and fees, file an appeal against such rejection before the Appellate Board. Further, where a request for pre-grant opposition is filed, the patent office shall give notice thereof to the applicant and provide him with a reasonable opportunity to respond in writing. Any communication received from the Controller regarding objections or rejections must be acknowledged within thirty days of receipt. The patent office may require the submission of additional documentation to clarify aspects of the invention’s novelty or non-obviousness, as deemed necessary for assessment.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars relating to its denomination, geographical area where it is cultivated, and details concerning its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information or documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall initiate proceedings for examination, including verification of claimed characteristics and evaluation against established criteria. A key component of registration is varieties compulsory cataloguing; all registered varieties must be included in the National Plant Variety Catalogue maintained by the Authority. This catalogue will serve as a public record accessible to breeders, researchers, and farmers, facilitating transparency and promoting informed decision-making regarding plant variety selection.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against any decision rendered by the Registrar, and the appellant dies pending the determination of such appeal, the appeal shall abate. Provided that, where a trade mark application has been opposed, and the opposition proceeding remains unresolved at the time of the applicant’s death, the estate of the deceased applicant may continue the opposition as if the applicant were living, subject to furnishing satisfactory evidence of representation. Further, in cases involving a counterclaim or cross-examination relating to deceptively similar marks, the appeal shall not abate but will proceed with the substituted party, representing the interests of the deceased appellant. This provision regarding *dies pending proceeding* applies equally where the respondent in an appeal meets their demise before final adjudication.

Any action brought before a judicial forum alleging violation of exclusive rights granted under this Act concerning literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, or any adaptation thereof, shall be subject to the provisions regarding territorial limits. It is provided that where the place of origin of the alleged infringement is uncertain, or spans multiple jurisdictions, the aggrieved party may initiate proceedings in a court having jurisdiction over any location where the infringing act occurred or was reasonably likely to have taken effect. The defendant shall not be precluded from challenging this assertion of jurisdiction by demonstrating, on clear and convincing evidence, that such forum selection is manifestly inconvenient and lacks substantial connection to the cause of action, subject to judicial discretion. Appeals against orders concerning jurisdiction may be made as provided herein.
